Summary

When Lena meets Kara, a soldier home on leave as she waits for her next deployment, at a local coffee shop one afternoon, her life is completely tipped upside down in an instant. As they start talking, Lena feels drawn to Kara; there's something about her warmth and openness that fills the gap left by Lena's troubled childhood.

Growing closer over the next few months, falling fast for each other, the two of them find themselves unable to stay away, but Kara's next deployment is inevitable, and with promises that she'll come home, Lena waits for her.

    Chapter 1

                The café was bustling with activity in Downtown National City, wedged between a used bookstore and a bakery on a little side street that was shaded by the soaring skyscrapers that blotted out the sky. Lena had stumbled upon it by accident, stretching her legs as she tried to shrug off some of the restless energy that had made it hard for her to focus from behind her desk. 

     

                Usually, she would’ve eaten lunch at the office, hardly taking a break from her work to shovel down whatever her assistant brought to her, but the day was unseasonably warm for early January, although not quite warm enough, and the sky was a cloudless pale blue overhead as it reflected off a thousand windows, almost painful to look at. Eager to escape the slight chill, as wrapped up in her layers as she was, Lena had walked past the little café and backtracked before slipping inside.

     

                Ordering a black coffee and an everything bagel, she’d managed to find a small table by the window, the pale sunlight slanting through the blinds and warming her hands as she unpacked her laptop and her Moleskine notebook, a manila folder of neat documents following suit, and she worked quietly, blocking out the noise of the café around her. Voices babbled on and the HVAC stuttered out bursts of warm air and Lena drank her coffee and paid the screeching children no mind, trying to balance the chair with uneven legs as her work consumed her.

     

                Content to stay for longer than she ordinarily would’ve, her attention solely on her work, Lena finished her bagel and shuffled through the documents, looking for a particular one to cross-reference with the figures displayed on her screen, when a light tap on her shoulder broke her concentration. Forehead puckering with a frown as she glanced up, Lena blinked in surprise at the sight of a blonde woman standing beside her table and raised her eyebrows.

     

                With a sheepish smile, nervously fidgeting with her fingers, she spoke above the sound of the café to make herself heard, stooping down slightly. “Sorry, I don’t mean to interrupt you, but would you mind if I sit here? If the seat isn’t taken, I mean.”

     

                The blonde woman rested a hand on the back of the empty chair across from Lena and raised her eyebrows expectantly, biting her lip as her blue eyes filled with hope. Her voice was surprisingly sweet, despite the evident anxiousness to her words, and Lena stared at her as she continued talking.

     

                “Only, well, there aren’t any other free tables.”

     

                Looking around the room, Lena found her words to be true, every table occupied by someone else; friends chatting, college students studying, mothers with their children and businessmen in suits taking a coffee break. Realising that the woman was still waiting for an answer, Lena’s eyes drifted back towards her and she straightened up in her seat, scrambling for her paperwork strewn across the table as she neatly stacked it.

     

                “Oh, yeah, sure. It’s not taken.”

     

                Not the most approachable person in the world, Lena was mildly surprised to have been asked but didn’t want to be rude to the woman. She’d be on her way soon anyway, needed at the office for meetings and phone calls and even more paperwork.

     

                “Thank you,” the woman said with a bright smile, her eyes crinkling at the corners behind her glasses.

     

                Nodding, Lena shifted her laptop closer to her and rapidly typed out notes as the woman sat down, the chair scraping along the floor as she shifted it closer to the table. Pretending she was fixated on her laptop, Lena surreptitiously eyed the woman over the top of the screen, watching as she pulled out a book and flipped it open to a dog-eared corner, slouching slightly in her seat as she silently started to read.

     

                Satisfied that she wouldn’t be disturbed, Lena picked up her pen and made a note in her book before glancing at the woman again. They must’ve been around the same age, her blonde hair was pulled into a braid, strands breaking free and curling slightly around her temples, and a crease formed between her eyebrows in a look of deep concentration. Lena found herself thinking it was endearing, a realisation that shocked her.

     

                When the barista brought the woman’s coffee over, she looked up, an easy smile lighting up her face as she straightened and thanked the young man. Her eyes met Lena’s as she plucked three sachets of sugar from the pot and emptied them into her latte before taking a sip. Pretending that she hadn’t been staring, Lena’s eyes darted to her screen and she shifted in her seat.

     

                “I like your necklace,” the woman said, gesturing towards the locket around Lena’s neck.

     

                Eyes widening a fraction with surprise, Lena cleared her throat as she looked up and met the other woman’s eyes, taking in the crooked smile that softened her face. Her freckled nose wrinkled slightly and Lena quickly looked back down, typing away at her keyboard.

     

                “Thank you,” she murmured.

     

                “Where did you get it?”

     

                Biting back an exasperated sigh at being disturbed from her work, Lena looked up and felt her irritation abate at the warmth on the stranger’s face. Her stomach clenched in an unfamiliar manner and Lena opened and closed her mouth as her fingertips grazed the locket, masking a flicker of pain.

     

                “It was a gift from my brother. For my sixteenth birthday.”

     

                Her shoulders stiffened as she replied, her mood souring as thoughts of her brother crowded in. She didn’t expect this woman to know her by appearance, but Lena was still wary at the direction the conversation had taken and found herself itching to leave before it went further. Despite her reservations, she stayed seated, pretending to work.

     

                “It’s really pretty.”

     

                Eyes flickering up, she caught sight of a smile on the woman’s face and felt an answering one spread across her own face, unbidden, the corner of her mouth curling up slightly. Nodding in acknowledgement, Lena picked up her pen and fiddled with it as she averted her gaze to the street beyond the window.

     

                “Sorry, I’m distracting you, aren’t I?” the woman sheepishly said a moment later, an apologetic wince of a smile crumpling her face as she closed her book over one finger to keep her space.

     

                With a quiet laugh, Lena shook her head as she exhaled heavily, “it’s fine. It’s just … work.”

     

                It had never been just work to Lena, who threw herself into it with reckless abandon, swallowed up by every aspect of the business. But, for once, she didn’t mind the brief reprieve from paperwork and closed her laptop. It wasn’t a good day and her concentration was evasive.

     

                “Oh, no- don’t stop on my account. I’ll be quiet. I just- I talk too much. Never really been comfortable with silence, you know?”

     

                “It’s fine,” Lena assured her, running a hand through her hair as she leant back, before stretching her arms and shoulders. “I’ve been staring at numbers all day anyway.”

     

                With another sigh, Lena picked up her pen and made a few corrections on a piece of paper before jotting down a note in her Moleskine and snapping it shut. Setting the pen down, she looked back up and found the woman studying her with open interest. It would’ve bothered Lena, under normal circumstances, that sort of scrutiny, but there was only kind curiosity in those blue eyes, and it didn’t make her feel uncomfortable to be pinned by her stare.

     

                “My name’s Kara,” the woman eventually said, holding a hand across the crowded surface of the scarred tabletop.

     

                Taking her hand in her cold grasp, Lena found it warm and surprisingly rough with callouses and gave it a gentle squeeze. “Lena.”

     

                Setting her book down, Kara hunched forward and propped her chin up in her hand as she arched an eyebrow, “what’re you working on?”

     

                “I run a … family business,” Lena dismissively replied, purposely skirting around the details.

     

                Her new rebranding and relocation of L-Corp had been splashed across the news recently, a big deal for the tech industry in National City, and she was willing to bet that if she mentioned the name, Kara would’ve known it. It was better to avoid the explanations; and what business did a stranger have knowing Lena’s affairs anyway?

     

                “And you?” Lena softly asked, jerking her chin towards Kara as she delicately arched an eyebrow, “what do you do?”

     

                Her observations of Kara so far led her to believe she was someone kind. Her washed-out yellow sweatshirt with the white collar of a shirt peeking out was gentle, soothing. She would have pegged her for a primary school teacher, or perhaps a librarian with her books and glasses. 

     

                With a grim smile, Kara sighed, “military. Public Affairs Officer, which is code for journalist.”

     

                Eyebrows shooting up in surprise, Lena gave her a sceptical look that made Kara’s cheeks redden. Shrugging half-heartedly, Kara took a sip of her coffee and lowered it.

     

                “Yeah, I know. I don’t look like the soldier type.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena eyed her clothes and bit back a smile. “No, you don’t. It’s … an interesting choice. Controversial, perhaps.”

     

                Sighing heavily, Kara winced slightly, “they paid for college, so …”

     

                “Mm, there’s always that catch, isn’t there? So, you’re home on leave then?” Lena surmised.

     

                She didn’t know why she was asking, never being the type to be interested in other people’s personal lives, but Kara was an enigma sitting before her. An open one, to be sure, but Lena found herself not knowing what was going to surprise her next, and was shockingly eager to find out.

     

                “Mhm. Just got back from the frontlines in Afghanistan a week ago. I’m staying with my sister,” Kara said with an uneven smile.

     

                “It must be a big adjustment, being home.

     

                “Well, they definitely don’t do lattes this good in the army,” Kara joked, holding up her empty cup as she smiled.

     

                Lena let out a quiet snort of laughter and shook her head. She picked up her own empty cup and stared into the dregs of it before scooting her chair back and climbing to her feet. Picking up her cup and Kara’s, Lena gave her a small smile.

     

                “Do you mind watching my things for a minute?”

     

                Gesturing at the table, Kara nodded, her eyebrows rising slightly as she pushed her glasses further up her nose. “Sure. No problem.”

     

                Nodding, Lena wove through the bustling café and joined the end of the queue, glancing back over her shoulder to watch Kara, limned in gold by the sun seeping through the slats of the blinds. She had her book out again, slouched in her seat with her legs stretched out beneath the table, perfectly at ease. Lena supposed you would have to make yourself comfortable anywhere, being in the army.

     

                Setting the empty cups down on the counter and placing an order for another black coffee and a latte, Lena tapped her credit card and pointed out their table before returning to her seat. Shifting her chair in close, she propped her elbow up on the table and rested her cheek in her palm as she watched Kara carefully fold the corner of her book and close it.

     

                “What’re you reading?”

     

                Flushing red, Kara rubbed at the back of her neck as she showed Lena the cover of a very tattered copy of Pride & Prejudice. With a weak smile, Kara shrugged and set it down on the worn table, tapping her finger on the cover.

     

                “I know it’s cliché, but …”

     

                “It’s a classic,” Lena said, her eyes softening just a touch.

     

                “It makes me feel happy to know that two people, so different and flawed, can overcome it all. It’s nice, don’t you think?”

     

                Finding herself subconsciously leaning in closer, Lena smiled faintly, “it is nice. Whether that’s how real life is, is another matter altogether.”

     

                “Oh,” Kara laughed, “a cynic? Somehow, I’m not surprised.”

     

                “What’s that supposed to mean?”

     

                “I bet you’re all business, aren’t you? You’ve read all the classics, but not for enjoyment. You’re scientifically minded and you- you think romance is silly.”

     

                Eyebrows climbing higher with every guess of her character, Lena couldn’t stop the slow smile that spread across her face, her shoulders silently shaking with laughter as her eyes shone. “You have me pegged so well. Have we met before?”

     

                Pressing a hand to her mouth, Kara trailed off, her cheeks pink as she narrowed her eyes in a guilty look, “sorry, am I attacking you? Because it’s not a bad thing to not-”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Lena gave her an amused look, “don’t worry, I’m not offended. You weren’t quite right though. I did enjoy Les Misérables, and I don’t think romance is … silly , I just- I have a string of failed ones so I don’t think it’s quite worth my time.”

     

                “How do you know it’s worth your time unless you give it a shot?”

     

                “That,” Lena murmured, “is a good question.”

     

                “Black coffee?”

     

                Jumping slightly, Lena’s head jerked up to stare at the barista standing at their table. Blinking, she abruptly leant back in her seat, realising just how close her and Kara had been, face to face, and she cleared her throat as she shook her head slightly. Eyes half closing, Lena realised he was waiting for a response.

     

                “I- yes, that’s mine, thank you,” she said, giving him a distracted smile as he set the cup down.

     

                She shifted her pile of work, making more room as she slipped her laptop into her satchel and wedged the folder and Moleskine in beside it. The barista was setting the latte down before Kara, whose face flashed with a look of panic as she opened her mouth.

     

                “Sorry, I didn’t order-”

     

                The barista cast her a quick look, his face crumpling with confusion and Lena reached out to cut Kara off, her fingertips brushing the back of her hand in a fleeting touch. “It was my treat.”

     

                “Oh,” Kara mumbled, her expression clouding with bewilderment, “you didn’t have to do that. Thank you.”

     

                “It’s nothing,” Lena waved away Kara’s gratitude, “you should make the most of good coffee while you’re home, right?”

     

                Nodding, Kara rummaged through her bag and pulled out an old polaroid camera. Giving Lena a shy smile she wrinkled her nose as she explained, “I like to take pictures. Guess it was part of the reason I wanted to become a journalist; they all tell a story. And, being in the army, you never really appreciate the small things until you don’t have them every day, so it’s nice to have a reminder.”

     

                She snapped a quick photo of her coffee and waited for the instant film to print out. Hiding it in between the pages of her book, she waited for the image to appear and gave Lena another shy smile. There was a faint scar in the middle of her forehead and Lena cocked her head to the side as she looked at Kara, trying to make sense of her. Her lunch break had taken an interesting turn, and she slyly messaged Jess to make the appropriate cancellations and rescheduling of her afternoon meetings as she sipped her coffee and listened to Kara talk.

     

                It seemed like she had a never-ending stream of topics to talk about, barely seeming to take a breath as she talked over herself, justifying, explaining, tripping over her words as her cheeks periodically reddened. Lena didn’t know what to make of the fact that she enjoyed watching the faint pink enter Kara’s cheeks as she grew flustered. She would’ve been content to sit there all day and listen to her.

     

                As it was, they talked for hours, the shadows growing long outside and the café slowly emptying, until the last rays of sunlight were reflecting off the windows across from them and pooling on their table in wan grey stripes. Kara trailed off mid-sentence as she looked at Lena, staring at her blankly for a moment before a slow, cautious smile crept across her face and she hunched her shoulders self-consciously.

     

                “Do you- do you mind if I take your photo? The lighting is perfect right now.”

     

                Turning to glance out the window, Lena shaded her eyes against the vivid yellow blinding her and quickly turned away, blinking back dark spots. “Um, sure, if you want to.”

     

                Relief flashed across Kara’s face and she pulled her camera out again, staring at Lena for a moment before she slowly reached out. Her fingertips brushed against Lena’s cheekbones as Kara fixed a wayward strand, and Lena couldn’t stop her eyelids from fluttering closed, her lips parting at the feeling of her touch. Pressing her lips together and swallowing thickly, Lena fixed Kara with a piercing stare and watched her draw back.

     

                “Perfect,” Kara murmured, almost as if to herself, as if Lena wasn’t supposed to hear her, and then she held the camera up to her eye and snapped the photo.

     

                They stared at each other for a long moment as the photo printed, and Kara wedged it between another page in her book. Neither of them spoke as they waited for it to develop, the air oddly charged between them, and Lena couldn’t bring herself to move.

     

                It wasn’t until Kara pulled the photo from the pages and a smile spread across her face that Lena leaned forward, craning her neck to see. Holding it out for her, Kara’s fingers brushed Lena’s as she took it from her, cradling it gently so she didn’t bend the edges as she looked down at her face.

     

                The sun filtered in, bathing one half of her in silver light that brought out strands of red in her dark hair, while the other was left in the shadowed dimness of the café lighting. Lena’s face was all sharp lines, something elegant in the hardness of her face, and while she wasn’t smiling in the photo, there was the faint upturning at the corner of her mouth and a softness to her gaze.

     

                Taking it back, Kara gently put it back between the pages of her book and then safely stowed that in her bag, along with the camera. Sighing, her eyes slid towards the window and the waning sunlight as it slipped behind the skyscrapers, ready to give way to dusk. There was a regretful look on Kara’s face as she looked at Lena and gave her a grim smile.

                

                “Well, I should probably go. I’m supposed to be meeting my sister and her girlfriend for dinner,” Kara said, checking her leather wristwatch for the time.

     

                Nodding, Lena silently started shuffling things around in her satchel before closing the clasp, realising she’d stayed far too long and needed to make up for the lost time. She was no stranger to long nights at the office, and tonight would be no different - if she could concentrate on her work.

     

                They left together, pushing their chairs in and making for the door, Kara calling out a cheerful farewell to the staff before holding the door open for Lena. The aroma of coffee was replaced with the searing taste of warm concrete and car fumes and Lena’s skin prickled at the sudden chill of the day as cars drove past and pedestrians clogged the sidewalk.

     

                Neither of them moved, prolonging the moment as Kara shifted her backpack on her shoulders and Lena smoothed the cuff of her coat. And then Kara looked up with a hesitant look of uncertain hope on her face, chewing on her lip. Cocking her head to the side, Lena’s brow puckered faintly.

     

                “What’s wrong?”

     

                “I was thinking,” Kara blurted out, giving her a quick smile, “maybe, if you’re not too busy, we could- we could maybe see each other again?”

     

                Her voice hitched up at the end, turning it into a question as her eyebrows rose, and she waited expectantly for Lena’s answer. Warmth spread through Lena and she fought to keep her composure, feeling flushed as she held her hand out.

     

                “Let me put my number in your phone.”

     

                She added herself to Kara’s contacts and handed the phone back, fighting back a smile, and gave Kara an equally as shy smile as she spoke, “call me when you’re free.”

     

                Taking her phone, Kara nodded and then lingered a moment longer before saying goodbye, retreating backwards for a few steps, until she bumped into someone and tripped, apologising profusely as she righted her balance. Lena watched on with amusement, covering her mouth as she tried not to laugh. Gesturing helplessly, Kara laughed and then gave her a small wave before turning around and disappearing into the flow of foot traffic.

     

                Lingering for a moment longer with a bewildered expression on her face, Lena eventually broke herself out of her reverie and forced herself into motion, a faint smile playing on her lips as she slowly walked back to the office. There was something about Kara, although she couldn’t quite pin it down. Something about her that was unlike the usual company Lena kept - which wasn’t much, seeing as she had no time for most people - but she found that she liked her. 

     

                For a few hours, she’d forgotten herself completely, shirked all responsibilities and her usual brusque impatience, and for a little while, Lena hadn’t been wracked with guilt or sadness or grief. As she walked back towards the office, her heart was light, and Lena liked the feeling.

    Chapter 2

                It wasn’t until a few days later that Lena received a phone call from Kara. The sun was just setting, the sky the colour of a bruise beyond the skyline as a thousand pricks of yellow lights lit up the dark, the city never sleeping, not even in the cold of mid-winter, when the nights were bitter and there was a palpable feel of laziness in the streets.

     

                Not for Lena though, who holed up in her air-conditioned office for at least twelve hours a day, snapping on the phone and arguing with board members while she redrafted the same plans over and over, until they were perfect. A warm breeze cut through the chill of her office, sweeping in through a vent as she cranked up the heating, and she was busy at her desk, illuminated by fluorescent lights as she read the numbers for the last quarter, left on her desk by Sam, her CFO.

     

                She’d already sent Jess home for the evening, thinking it pointless to make her assistant suffer unbearably long hours to be at her beck and call, and Lena was free to spend all night there, finishing up the latest figures and working on a proposal. No one but the janitors and security occupied the building past five, unless there was a department deadline, and Lena liked the quiet of the office. 

     

                Until her cell phone started vibrating on her desk, an unknown number lighting up the screen. It was Lena’s private number, given out to important employees, clients and acquaintances, and Lena was irritable as she picked up the phone and answered it. 

     

                “Hello?” she bluntly answered, her tone betraying her curt impatience at being disturbed.

     

                There was a moment of silence on the other end before a voice hesitantly spoke her name. “Lena?”

     

                Feeling as if she’d been doused in cold water, Lena immediately straightened in her chair as familiarity shot through her. Opening and closing her mouth as she fumbled, Lena softly cleared her throat and raked a hand through her hair, silently cursing herself.

     

                “Kara?” Lena cautiously replied, her tone much warmer as a shy smile curled the corners of her mouth.

     

                “Hi! Look, I know it’s a bit last minute, but I was thinking of catching a movie and wondered if you wanted to come? If you’re busy, I can call back another time-”

     

                Lena’s stomach lurched and she opened her mouth to butt in, but Kara was still babbling nervously and she had to wait for her to trail off. Her palms felt clammy and her heart was beating rapidly and Lena felt utterly foolish as she bit back a smile, listening to the sound of Kara’s voice.

     

                “I’d love to, I’m actually just on my way out of the office,” Lena lied, closing her laptop and climbing to her feet.

     

                She was doing no such thing, until that very moment, quickly snatching up the piles of paperwork and dumping them in the top drawer of her desk. Removing her bag from one of the cupboards seamlessly built into the walls, she shoved her laptop inside and made sure she had everything, Kara still on the other line as she gave her directions.

     

                “Great. I’ll meet you outside the cinema on Thirty-Third Street.”

     

                They hung up and Lena made sure everything important was locked away, excitement making her breaths shallow, and with slight concern, she wondered what was wrong with herself. Here she was, leaving work early for perhaps the first time in a long while, for a woman she didn’t even know. Just a short phone call had been enough for Kara to coax Lena away from the office, and it was as alarming as it was thrilling.

     

                Saving Kara’s number in her phone, Lena phoned down to security to have her car brought around for her to save time as she stepped out of her office and into the elevator. The Tesla was waiting outside the lobby doors as she called goodnight to the security guards patrolling the lobby and stepped out into the wall of cold. Palm trees lined the wide street L-Corp was situated on, and she could hear a hundred voices mingling above the sound of passing cars.

     

                Climbing into the driver’s seat, Lena buckled up and entered the address into her GPS, most of National City still unfamiliar to her. It was relatively easy to find though, and she parked a few spots down from the cinema, spotting Kara leaning against the brick wall with her hands jammed into the pockets of her corduroy jacket. 

     

                Locking the car, Lena’s heels clicked on the sidewalk, and she worried that she was overdressed in her pressed grey slacks and starched white blouse, but as soon as Kara looked up at the sound of her footsteps, a bright smile lit up her face and Lena forgot about her concerns. Pushing off the wall, Kara pulled her hands out of her pockets.

     

                “You made it!”

     

                She spread her arms and Lena realised a bit belatedly that Kara was leaning in to wrap her in a hug, her affection given freely, not earned. It startled Lena, who stiffened for a moment, causing Kara to quickly pull back, before Lena returned the hug, pulling her close before she could back away.

     

                “Oh, sorry,” Kara murmured, wincing as she pulled back, “I probably should’ve asked if I could-”

     

                Squeezing her arm, Lena gave her a small smile, “it’s fine, it was just unexpected, is all.”

     

                Under normal circumstances, Lena would’ve hated the thought of someone touching her, being so casually familiar with her. Her unapproachable demeanour usually did all the work for her, keeping greasy businessmen at bay as they settled for firm handshakes and lewd looks. This was different, her tall walls not quite as thick or insurmountable in Kara's presence, and Lena realised that that was what friends did - and while she didn’t know Kara enough to consider her as such, they were friendly .

     

                As it was, Lena didn’t realise how much she had craved the warmth of someone else’s touch until Kara had wrapped her in her arms. It had been a good year at least since someone had ever held Lena in such a manner, perhaps more intimately than a friendly hug off Kara, but it still made her crave more. It had caught her off guard, and Lena wished she hadn’t tensed up, but she was so unused to it that she hadn’t seen it coming.

     

                “So what movie did you want to see?” Lena asked, trying to dispel the awkwardness of the situation. 

     

                Kara’s expression brightened up immediately. “It’s an independent cinema so they only play movies that are at least a decade old. One of the ones they regularly show here is Pride and Prejudice. The 2005 one.”

     

                “I’ve never seen it,” Lena said, one side of her mouth curling up into a smile, “sounds great.”

     

                “You’ve never seen it?”

     

                Shrugging as they made for the door, Kara pushing it open and holding it, Lena thanked her and hunched her shoulders in a rueful manner. “I don’t really watch movies.”

     

                “Who doesn’t watch movies?” Kara asked, giving her a puzzled look.

     

                “Not much time for it, I’m afraid.”

     

                With a bewildered smile, Kara stepped up to the counter, the lobby empty of any other customers, and she asked for two tickets to the next showing, starting in fifteen minutes. Ordering a large popcorn with extra butter, Kara deliberated over which drink to pick before settling on a watermelon slurpee. Waiting patiently for her to finish, Lena ordered a bottle of water for herself and slid the cashier her credit card.

     

                Kara protested but Lena assured her it was fine, not wanting to cause a fuss, and with their snacks and drinks, they moved over to the corner, standing near retro movie posters, and waited until they could enter the theatre.

     

                Filling the silence, Kara asked about her day, gave Lena a rundown of what she’d been doing for the last three days, and managed to ask half a dozen questions before Lena even had the chance to answer them. The whole time, she talked animatedly, a smile lighting up her face, her cheeks near-constantly dimpled. Lena was surprised her face didn’t hurt, but it was like Kara couldn’t help herself. Lena had never seen someone smile so much in her entire life; she didn’t even think she’d smiled that much in the past year.

                

                She said as much to Kara as they were allowed to make their way past the usher checking tickets, Lena’s fingers gently pressed against Kara’s lower back as she guided her along, an action that felt like the most natural thing in the world. Making their way to the correct theatre, they stepped into the dark room and found seats in the back row, sitting centre to the wide screen.

     

                Making themselves comfortable, they spoke in whispers, leaning in close as a few more people trickled in, and then the lights dimmed to black and the screen lit up, a bright white that made Lena feel exposed. Pulling away from Kara, she cleared her throat and uncapped her water bottle, taking a sip to steady herself.

     

                To her left, Kara took a large sip of her own drink and froze, her face screwing up as she wrinkled her nose and squeezed her eyes shut. Eyeing her with a dubious look on her face, Lena smiled slightly and watched as Kara slowly opened her eyes and gave her a faintly embarrassed smile.

     

                “Brain freeze,” she whispered, and Lena shook with silent laughter as advertisements for cars and health insurance played on the screen.

     

                Finding it hard to concentrate on the movie with Kara so near, their elbows touching on the shared arm, sharing popcorn as Kara whispered trivial facts and kept up a running commentary, something that endlessly amused Lena as she stared at the screen. She could see the appeal of the adaptation, the romance and tension on the screen playing out for them, and even though she barely paid it any attention, Lena enjoyed herself. 

     

                She couldn’t remember the last time she’d done something normal. This was what friends did, what normal people did; they went to the movies and wasted time. Not that Lena had that much experience with friends, or even dating for that matter - certainly not dates that had entailed movies - but sitting beside Kara, she could see the attraction of having someone to spend time with.

     

                The movie ended and they dumped their rubbish in the trash on their way out, the sky black and the streetlights spaced along the sidewalk, casting a wan, orange glow over the street. The sound of chatter and music spilled out of restaurants and bars, neon lights of arcades and bodegas, minimarts and takeout joints making the city seem vibrant and alive as they walked to Lena’s car in the cool air.

     

                “Hey,” Kara said as they neared the Tesla, a pucker between her brows, “are you hungry?”

     

                The light from a laundrette illuminated the hopeful expression on Kara’s face and Lena’s face softened in turn. She hadn’t eaten dinner yet, used to scrounging up something in the early hours of the morning from whatever was still open, and she wasn’t ready for the night to be over yet.

     

                “Sure, I could eat.”

     

                The wide smile that spread across Kara’s face made her stomach lurch slightly and Lena’s own smile hitched with uncertainty at the unfamiliar feeling. Holding a hand out to Lena, Kara raised her eyebrows suggestively, and Lena shoved her card back into her bag.

     

                “I know the best place for hotdogs in the whole city,” Kara goadingly suggested, raising her eyebrows as she wiggled her fingers.

     

                Letting out a burst of laughter, Lena’s expression crumpled with bewildered amusement as she shook her head and laced her fingers through Kara’s, a warm feeling in her stomach as Kara gave her hand a gentle squeeze. She’d expected Kara to drop her hand soon after, but was only mildly surprised when she didn’t, weaving them in and out of the crowd of city dwellers going about their business.

     

                It was only a few blocks away from the cinema and the walk was peaceful, a slight breeze ruffling Lena’s hair as she eyed the dark shop windows of boutiques and name brands, barbershops and record stores, florists and fresh produce markets.

     

                They came to a stop in front of the little food truck parked on the corner of a street, buskers playing music across the road and some man on an overturned milk crate preaching to passersby. Kara ordered them a hotdog each, insisting on paying this time, and Lena let her, as a matter of pride, while she watched the man pull the pink sausages out of a vat of water and squeeze sauce on them. Kara took a moment to snap a photo on her camera while Lena wondered if that was the best hotdog in the city, she didn’t want to see the worst , and dubiously eyed hers as they started back the way they’d come.

     

                Lena hadn’t spent much time wandering the city and she found a sense of peace in it, the unfamiliar shopfronts busy with strangers she’d never meet, and as she ate her hotdog, she wondered if that was how life was supposed to feel? She felt so small, lost amidst the soaring buildings, illuminated giants dwarfing her as rowdy crowds smoked outside a club and they passed an all-night diner that lingered with the odour of bitter coffee and grease. It was different to the polished part of the city Lena was used to, the five star restaurants and high-end designer stores, the opulent hotels and apartment complexes and the swept streets with neatly tended hedgerows and magnolia trees. There were no alleyways overflowing with trash near her house.

     

                “So, what do you think?” Kara asked, intruding on Lena’s thoughts.

     

                Her head was tilted to the side, eyebrows raised expectantly as she held her hotdog. Turning to look slightly up at her, Lena raised her eyebrows in a reflection of Kara’s expectancy and Kara smiled, giving her hotdog a little wave.

     

                “Best hotdog you’ve ever had or … because if it’s not , you have to take me there.”

     

                With a quiet scoff of laughter, Lena ducked her head and shook it before she looked up and nodded indifferently. “Mhm, definitely the best,” she agreed, before wrinkling her nose as she smiled. “Actually, to be honest, it’s the only hotdog I’ve ever had.”

     

                Surprise flashed across Kara’s face as she gave Lena an incredulous look tinged with scepticism. “What? Actually, or are you joking? How can you not have tried a hotdog before? It’s like … the quintessential American food!”

     

                Shrugging, Lena looked at her with a bewildered look of amusement, her lips pressed together, curling at the corners, while her brow furrowed. “I don’t know, we didn’t eat food like that growing up. It’s good though; what’s in it? Actually, no, don’t tell me. That’ll just put me off.”

     

                Chuckling, Kara gently bumped her with her shoulder, “a wise decision, but … seriously, you’ve never tried a hotdog? What about at baseball games? I mean, that would be the last place to try your first hotdog, so I guess that’s a good thing, but still.”

     

                “I’ve never been to a baseball game either.”

     

                “What? Do you just have a- a blatant disregard for American culture?”

     

                “Oh, is that what American culture is? I’ve been trying to figure it out,” Lena wryly ruminated as her cheeks dimpled, before she turned serious. “I was actually born in Ireland, just so you know. Didn’t spend much time there, clearly, but I think that gives me a pass.”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Kara shook her head in mock despair, “well, in that case, I’m getting us tickets to the next game.”

     

                “I look forward to it,” Lena said, gently nudging her back.

     

                She wasn’t usually so light-hearted but she couldn’t help herself, the easiness of Kara’s company putting her at ease. It felt like she’d known her a long time with the untroubled way Kara seemed to encounter things, taking it all in stride, effortlessly, and it made Lena feel comfortable . It was a startling realisation, for it to feel like the most natural thing in the world to be getting hotdogs with a woman she’d only met once before, laughing and talking, the casual brushes of contact. She was the complete opposite of Lena but there was something so alluring about her.

     

                Kara had already moved on to the excitement of baseball, how a game about numbers and statistics wasn’t as boring as it sounded, much to Lena’s amusement as someone who spent all day staring at numbers and statistics. When Kara gestured a bit to overzealously, a blob of ketchup fell onto her white t-shirt and she came to a stop, groaning as she plucked at the stained cotton.

     

                “Oh, man, I’m such a clutz.”

     

                Letting out a quiet laugh, Lena took her unused napkin and stepped in front of Kara. “Here.”

     

                In the saturated light of an internet café, Lena carefully wiped the sauce off Kara’s shirt, head ducked down, biting her lip in concentration as she gently dabbed at the stain. Peeking up, she smiled faintly at Kara, whose cheeks were pink, her nose wrinkling as she gave Lena a helpless smile in return. Her eyes were so blue in the harsh lighting that Lena’s hand slowed before she remembered herself, scrunching the napkin up in her hand and stepping back.

     

                “Thank you,” Kara exasperatedly replied.

     

                Dropping the napkin into an overflowing trash can, Lena fell back into step beside her as they carried on their way, “no problem.”

     

                They walked all the way back to Lena’s parked car far too quickly for her liking, but it was late, and she didn’t want to keep Kara. If it had been up to her, she would’ve seen the night through to the sunrise, walking the streets, talking about everything as they passed dark shops and pulsing bars and boarded up apartments.

     

                “Did you drive here?” Lena asked their footsteps dwindling to a standstill.

     

                “Oh, uh, no,” Kara said, giving her a wide smile, “my sister drove to work so I caught the bus.”

     

                “Oh, well … do you want a ride home?”

     

                “No, no, it’s fine. It’ll be out of your way.”

     

                Fighting back a smile, Lena jerked her head towards the car and walked backwards, “come on, let me give you a ride.”

     

                Narrowing her eyes as she bared her teeth in a torn grimace, Kara deliberated for a moment before relenting, shrugging as she grinned. “Okay.”

     

                Rounding the front of the car, Lena tapped the card against the circle and unlocked it, climbing inside. Opening the passenger side, Kara slipped into the car and let out a low whistle audible before she slammed the door shut. Raising her eyebrows in amusement, Lena looked at her.

                

                “Nice car,” Kara said, her eyes widening a fraction as she looked at the minimalist interior.

     

                Lips curving into a smile as she swiped her card against the sensor and put the car into drive, the engine inaudible, and Lena shrugged nonchalantly, “it’s better for the environment.”

     

                “Huh,” Kara slowly hummed, narrowing her eyes, “I didn’t take you for an environmentalist.”

     

                Pulling out into traffic, Lena shook her head as she smiled, “you don’t know me very well.”

     

                “Yet.”

     

                That only made her smile wider and she peeked sideways at Kara, who was squinting at the tablet as she tried to figure out how to work it. Reaching over, Lena pressed the music icon and tuned it into the radio with a few brief taps.

     

                “That’s cool,” Kara murmured as music poured out of the speakers.

     

                The city rushed around them as Lena drove, eyes focused intently on the road as she followed Kara’s instructions, changing lanes and turning at the lights, further away from the district Lena lived in, until she was told to stop outside a nondescript apartment building. It was relatively modern, a blocky grey with a security guard in the lobby and a bank of elevators visible through the windows, and Lena put the car into park.

     

                “So, I’ll let you know about the baseball?” Kara asked, as if she doubted Lena’s interest.

     

                “Sure. Just text me.”

     

                “Great,” Kara smiled widely, “well, thanks for tonight. I had fun.”

     

                “Me too,” Lena shyly murmured, her cheeks pink in the dimness of the car.

     

                Reaching out to gently squeeze Lena’s arm, Kara smiled and then opened the door, a flood of warm air rushing in. Pulling her backpack from between her feet, Kara hesitated and then looked at her again.

     

                “Get home safe.”

     

                With a crooked smile, Lena nodded. “Goodnight.”

     

                “‘Night!”

     

                Kara slammed the door shut behind her, waving over her shoulder before she rummaged through her bag, pulling out a set of keys. Lena waited until she was safely inside, watching Kara chat away with the security guard as a warm feeling spread through her chest.

     

                Finally, with a sigh, Lena put the car into drive and pulled out into traffic, muttering to herself as she put her address in on the tablet’s GPS. “Text me. So stupid.”

     

                The ride home was quiet, Lena preoccupied with her thoughts of Kara, unsure of what to make of it all as the radio crooned in the background. She parked the grey Tesla in her designated spot outside the four-storey brownstone and walked up the steps of the stoop, unlocking the pretentiously worn wooden doors that had just been installed and letting herself into the dark house.

     

                The parquet floors creaked under her feet as she kicked off her heels in the foyer and switched on the light sensor, flooding the house with light, and stepped onto the faded grey antique rug. Her house was her pride and joy of moving to National City, sinking a small fortune into the renovations, only recently finished. A gilt mirror hung on the wall above a suede bench, and Lena hung up her coat on the hook inside the door, her handbag on the narrow side table with the car card, and with her heels dangling from her fingers, she jogged up the scarred staircase, sanded back to its original colour.

     

                Her bedroom was on the third floor, a cavernous room with a restored fireplace and a monstrous headboard for the king bed, a set of antique double doors from the front doors repurposed for it, the old green paint partially removed in places. The bed was a mound of linen sheets and blankets, pillows neatly arranged by her housekeeper and the pile of books she’d haphazardly been flipping through the night before straightened up.

     

                Sitting on the bench at the end of the bed, Lena rubbed a hand over her face, feeling worn out, even though she was wide awake and knew sleep would elude her for hours yet, the adrenaline of the night lingering with her. Staring into the empty grate of the fireplace, she slowly smiled to herself as she thought of Kara. 

     

                After a moment, she climbed to her feet and walked into the adjoining wardrobe, just as luxurious as the rest of her house, filled with foreign labels and designer brands. Each item was neatly organised, pressed and waiting on cedar hangers, the sweet smell of the wood lingering in the air as Lena walked over to a row of drawers and fished out loungewear. She cast her reflection a cursory glance in the floor to ceiling mirror, the metal scrollwork too intricate to be wasted in a closet, and then turned and made for the bathroom.

     

                The slate flooring was cool beneath her feet as light flooded the spacious room with a brassy glow. Her clothes went into the laundry basket to be whisked away to the dry cleaners by her housekeeper, and Lena pushed buttons on a wall panel, a sheet of water falling from the massive showerhead set into the ceiling. It had been custom made when she’d moved in, from the imported stone for the floor, to the ceramic tiles and the wide, freestanding tub. Much like every room in her house, plants flourished, and Lena breathed in the sweetness of the living wall behind the bath, mingling with the clean scent of soap.

     

                Soft and pink, she stepped out of the shower feeling marginally more relaxed and changed into the heather grey loose-fitting pants and ribbed sweater made from Mongolian cashmere, so gentle against her skin as she spent ten minutes slowly going through her skin routine, prodding at the faint shadows beneath her eyes.

     

                Refreshed and comfortable, Lena made her way down to the kitchen, the old bones of the house complementing the mid-century modern design that the interior designers had styled the house after. With the parquet flooring and the baroque white walls, it felt ancient, crumbling before she’d swooped in and repaired the leaky pipes and eroding external facade. Now, the house was understatedly opulent, the muted sage green tones of the kitchen cabinets soothing as Lena made her way to the pantry, filled with ingredients she hadn’t touched. 

     

                Bypassing the food, she snagged a bottle of white wine and shut the door behind her, fetching a glass from a cupboard and opening the bottle. She poured herself a glass as she stared through the double doors leading out onto an enclosed patio. The row of houses were built on a sloped hill, and even on the ground floor of the house, the patio overlooked a strip of greenery, tall trees shading the balcony and the variety of potted plants that had taken up residence amidst the garden furniture.

     

                Taking a thoughtful sip, Lena looked out at the darkness, the faint yellow glow of her neighbours across the overgrown alley visible, before she put the bottle away and wearily plodded up three flights of stairs to her office.

     

                The top floor of the house was definitely her favourite, the walls knocked through to turn it into one, sprawling home office. The two shorter walls at either end were exposed brick, each with a large fireplace - the house boasted six in total, and Lena had been loath to remove the original features. Bookshelves lined the other two walls, crammed full of classics and autobiographies, history books and business and finance, physics and fantasy fiction and everything in between. Lena thought it was important to keep her horizons broad, even if she didn’t particularly enjoy the denser topics.

     

                A low sofa faced two armchairs, a coffee table in between with a Go board set up beside her weekly issues of various business and politics magazines she was subscribed to that she was making her way through. A drafting table dominated one corner of the room, nestled in near the fireplace with a tall, industrial style lamp for light, a large wooden table ringed with stools nearby for a workbench when Lena’s work took on a more physical aspect than shuffling paperwork all day, and at the opposite end of the floor, a wide mid-century style desk with two Mac monitors and a neat collection of fountain pens and journals. Behind it, tucked in on either side of the other fireplace were rows of filing cabinets.

     

                It was comfortable despite the office feeling of it, the walls hung with minimalistic pieces, plants dispersed along the shelves with other knick-knacks that were purely for show. Two Jacquard rugs in complementary colours of artfully faded beige and mint green took up most of the floor space and Lena’s bare feet padded across one as she set her glass down on the coffee table and moved over to her bookshelves. They were arranged by genre and then alphabetical by author, and it didn’t take her long to lay her hands on a particularly worn edition of Pride & Prejudice.

     

                Turning it over in her hands, her lips twitched with a smile and she clasped it to her chest before crossing over to an armchair. Sprawling in it, she opened the book to the first page and reached for her wine, taking a sip as she settled into the story. At least, she tried to, but thoughts of Kara preoccupied her mind far too much for her to concentrate. Lena was known for being surly and silent, quietly feared around the office for her quiet intensity, and it wasn’t out of any desire to be perceived as cold and aloof, she just didn’t have much to say and her brusque impatience left little room for warmth and kindness. 

     

                She had a business to run, a lifeline in the midst of the tragedy her life had been, and it didn’t leave Lena with much time for friends, for laughing and socialising like a woman of her age should’ve been doing. Not many people had the capacity to keep a billion-dollar-company churning out the quarterly numbers she did at twenty-four, and Lena prided herself on her brilliance, her knack for business that could only have come from growing up in the family she had. There might not have been much love and praise, but there had been money and the tools to make of herself what she wanted. Now, what she had made herself was the only thing that gave her any purpose.

     

                But she had laughed and smiled all night, and as she sipped her wine, Lena couldn’t help but think about how unusual it had felt. Yet it had come naturally in Kara’s presence, a little stiff, as out of practice as she was with allowing herself to relax and enjoy herself, but it had taken no effort at all on Lena’s part to feel so comfortable . And it troubled her that someone could put her at such ease, when she had struggled for so long to connect with anyone. A string of failed dates and brief flings could attest to that, but this time it felt different.

     

                When it became apparent that she wasn’t going to get much reading done, her eyes skimming over the same line three times, Lena drained the rest of her glass and set it down on the coffee table, snapping the book shut and leaving it beside the glass. Climbing to her feet, she stretched her limbs and made for the stairs, walking down a flight and stepping into her room. The automatic lights bathed the room in a warm glow, and Lena brushed her teeth before climbing into bed, tossing pillows to the floor as she burrowed beneath the soft chambray linens.

     

                The mattress was soft and the room cold, just how she liked it, and even though it was well past midnight and she’d been up with the sunrise, Lena felt wide awake. No matter how hard she tried to relax her mind, let go of the thoughts that consumed her mind, fresh ones always lingered on the edges, waiting to swoop in with little reminders of the exact shade of blue Kara’s eyes had looked in the light, the warmth in her laughter, the way her hands had pressed into Lena’s back as she’d hugged her as if she’d known her her entire life. Sleep was hard to come by, but Lena had never felt so content in her life as she dwelled.

    Chapter 3

                The weekend rolled around and after her sunrise workout in the home gym in her converted basement, Lena was up in her office, sitting at her desk with a pitcher of kombucha, the windows open to the cool day as a gentle breeze flowed inside. The tartness of the kombucha made her grimace for a moment as she took a sip, straightening up in her chair as she scrolled through the emails that had filtered all the way to the top of the chain, replying to the important ones and flagging the rest for later.

     

                Calling Jess, Lena climbed to her feet with her AirPods in ear and glass in hand, rattling off a list of instructions to her assistant as she stretched her legs and made the trip down three flights of stairs to fetch a mid-morning snack. Taking a paring knife, Lena quickly cut a pear into even slices, and stepped out onto the back patio, sunshine filtering down on her as she took a seat on a chair and basked in the sound of birdsong, her plants and the trees rustling in the wind.

     

                “Make sure that dinner is booked for Monday night,” Lena said, taking a sip of her drink, “I want that deal closed by the end of next week at the latest . Two hours should be long enough for three courses and a few drinks to talk it over.”

     

                “Of course, Miss Luthor.”

     

                “And we need- hang on, someone’s calling.”

     

                Pulling her phone out of her pocket, Lena’s stomach dropped at the sight of Kara’s name on the screen, subconsciously sitting up a little straighter, shifting nervously in her seat.

     

                “I’ll call you back, I need to take this.”

     

                “Of course, ma’am.”

     

                Lena barely waited for her reply before she pushed the button to accept Kara’s call, cutting Jess off as her heart fluttered in her chest. She didn’t have time to prepare herself before Kara’s voice came through on the other end.

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “Hi, Kara,” Lena said, smiling as she set her glass down on the circular iron table.

     

                “Are you busy?”

     

                “No. No, I’m not busy.”

     

                With a quiet laugh, the sound making Lena’s skin prickle as she imagined the exact expression on her face, Kara slowly replied. “Well … how about later? Are you free then too?”

     

                “Later?” Lena echoed, her eyebrows rising. “I- yeah, I’m free later. Why?”

     

                “Have you ever been to the carnival down by the bay?”

     

                Choking on a laugh at the thought of going somewhere so time-consuming, Lena pressed her lips together as she tried to bite back a smile. Picking up one of her pear slices, she took a bite, eyes creasing at the corners with amusement.

     

                “Actually, no, I haven’t. I didn’t even know there was a carnival down by the bay.”

     

                “Oh, yeah, it’s been there for decades. It looks a bit dodgy but it’s … fun. Do you- do you want to go? With me? Tonight?”

     

                “Tonight?”

     

                “Yeah. I mean, I got tickets to the baseball game next Saturday so I was going to check if you’re free then too, but then I was thinking and I didn’t really want to spend a whole week not seeing you, you know?” She paused and then let out an embarrassed laugh. “That didn’t sound that silly in my head.”

     

                Softening, Lena couldn’t hide her smile this time, her eyes bright with eagerness as sunlight dappled her face through the leaves of the overhanging trees. “I’d love to go.”

     

                “Really?”

     

                “Mhm. Shall I pick you up at … shall we say five o’clock? Is that too early?”

     

                “No, five is great! You don’t have to go out of your way though.”

     

                “I could always ask my driver to come and get you.”

     

                “You have a- nevermind. I can get a cab.”

     

                Smiling at her stubbornness, Lena grinned to herself and chewed thoughtfully for a moment. “I insist. You can have me or my driver, and I don’t think he’s nearly as good company as I am, but-”

     

                “I want you,” Kara blurted out, letting out a breathless laugh a moment later. “I mean … no need to make someone else come and pick me up if we’re going to the same place.”

     

                “Then I’ll see you at five.”

     

                “Do you remember where I live?”

     

                “Of course,” Lena murmured, sounding mildly surprised at the question, as if Kara believed she hadn’t cared enough to pay attention.

     

                “Okay. Okay, great. Well … I’ll see you at five.”

     

                “Bye.”

     

                As the line went dead, Lena picked up her kombucha and took a long sip as she narrowed her eyes, a thoughtful look clouding her face. What was she supposed to wear to a carnival?

     

                Her focus was gone after that, the day lost to irrational stress about what she should wear and how she should do her hair. Lena’s wardrobe consisted mostly of pressed Italian wool pants, starched shirts and demure dresses and an array of designer shoes. Some things were more casual for her days spent around the house, or from various business trips where she’d had a few days to herself to visit historic sights. In the end, she settled on a long, moss green flared skirt and a white shirt with capped sleeves. 

     

                She made herself a salad for lunch, chopping the vegetables that were stocked in her fridge, seeming to magically appear when she arrived home from work in the early hours of the morning. Lena had only met her housekeeper a handful of times, leaving her to her own devices on the three days she came over, and deposited a generous paycheck into the woman’s bank account every Monday, but she appreciated the subtle signs of someone caring for her nonetheless. 

     

                Lena’s favourite snack foods were always there in abundance, the particular brands of things she liked and a rotation of fruits and vegetables that she never got around to cooking. The thing was, Lena wasn’t very good at cooking, her childhood spent being served by their personal chef and her college years on takeout and whatever could be bought at the nearest convenience store. But she made do with sandwiches and salads, and anything else that didn’t require an oven or stove. Sometimes, she came home to something waiting for her on the counter or in the fridge with instructions to heat up, her housekeeper noticing the fact that her fridge remained relatively untouched, Lena too busy to feed herself sometimes.

     

                Eating her salad at the kitchen counter, sitting on a stool as she flicked through her text messages, ignoring most of them. On her personal phone, she rarely got any calls or messages about business, but she wasn’t sociable enough to reply to the ones off men and women she’d previously ghosted either, and the others … well, they were off her mother and were ignored with a sense of satisfaction. She hadn’t seen her mother face to face in months now, had only briefly spoken to her twice over the phone, but Lena suspected she’d be there at the next quarterly board meeting.

     

                Finishing her lunch, she loaded the dishwasher and made her way back upstairs to her office, sitting behind her desk and half-heartedly tried to work as she bided her time. The afternoon seemed to drag by and Lena barely made it through a single spreadsheet the entire time before it was finally late enough for her to start getting ready.

     

                Showering again, she blow dried her hair and fixed her makeup, sitting at the vanity in her bathroom in her soft, cashmere robe, and then got dressed. Spraying a cloud of sweet perfume around herself, she eyed herself in the mirror, critical and unimpressed as she shrugged her shoulders, trying to make the shirt sit comfortably. 

     

                After a few minutes of primping, she resigned herself to the fact that it was as good as it was going to get before blotting her red lipstick and walking out of the bathroom. Fetching a small purse and a pair of cat-eye sunglasses, she donned the latter and glanced at the clock - she would be early, but the clock was ticking closer to five - and swept out of the bedroom.

     

                Snatching her car card and house keys from the narrow table beside the door, Lena stepped out into the afternoon and locked up behind her. The magnolias spread out as far as Lena could see in either direction, lining the street with their waxy white blossoms, strung like pearls in their branches. Fingers of wan sunlight broke through their branches with significant effort as Lena quickly descended the steps, eager with excitement.

     

                Unlocking the car she tapped her card and buckled up and was on her way, joining in the flow of backed up traffic as people clocked out early or were on their way to night shifts. The sun was starting to sink beyond the buildings, everything bathed a faint golden as the light reflected off every window within sight, and Lena soaked it up, feeling happy as she sat bumper to bumper with everyone else, impatient, yes, but content. With the windows down and music on the radio, on her way to see Kara, she found herself more relaxed than she’d been in weeks, maybe even months. 

     

                She pulled up outside Kara’s building ten minutes early and was pleased to find her already waiting outside, leaning against the wall with the sole of her sneakers planted against it, a jacket folded over her arms as she seemed perfectly at ease in her t-shirt and cropped jeans. Pushing off with a grin, Kara rushed over to the car and pulled open the door, slipping inside. Wisps of hair were escaping from her braid and her glasses caught the last rays of sunlight, her polaroid hanging from a strap around her neck.

     

                “Hi! Thanks for the ride,” Kara said, settling in as she buckled up and stretched her long legs out before her. “How’re you?”

     

                “Hi,” Lena shyly smiled, “I’m good, actually. And yourself?”

     

                “Great! Are you excited for the rides? You look nice, by the way.”

     

                Taken by surprise, Lena glanced down at herself as her stomach tied itself into knots, her hands clammy on the steering wheel and she failed to fight back a smile. “Oh. Thank you. So do you.”

     

                The t-shirt Kara was wearing looked washed-soft up close, the jeans worn in the knees, and Kara looked so perfectly at ease in her own skin that Lena couldn’t help but think she looked beautiful. As casual as she looked, the sunlight limned her in gold light and her skin was tan and freckled and Lena jolted at the direction her thoughts took a moment later, turning her attention back to the road as she cleared her throat.

     

                “Thank you,” Kara said with a wide smile, “so, tell me about your day.”

     

                There wasn’t much to share and Lena skirted around the details of work as she followed the directions on the tablet, courtesy of Kara’s input, taking them across the bridge, the water calm as boats churned up white wakes as they passed by below them. They made small talk the whole way to the bay, the carnival rides lighting up the encroaching twilight long before they arrived. 

     

                Parking the car on a cracked stretch of empty plots of land, overgrown with weeds pushing up between cracks and garbage littering the asphalt, they climbed out of the car as a cool breeze swept in from the bay. As they walked towards the muted sounds of screams and machinery being operated, their shadows elongated on the paved sidewalk and the sky took on an indigo tinge, the dusk kindling excitement in Lena’s chest as she glanced sideways at Kara.

     

                At the entrance to the carnival grounds, they joined the short queue and Lena eyed the gaudy, colourful sign, now rusted and peeling, while Kara people-watched. The smell of greasy food wafted out from beyond the turnstile and Lena craned her neck to look up at the ferris wheel, her stomach plummeting with fear at the thought of being so high.

     

                Once it was their turn, she paid for a roll of tickets each, enough to see them through rides for the whole night, and Kara was ushered through the turnstile before she could protest at Lena slapping down her credit card on the machine before she could get her cash out. Rolling her eyes playfully, Kara thanked her and then turned to face the scene of madness before them, leaning in close to Lena.

     

                “So, what do you want to go on first?”

     

                Her grin was infectious, a childlike sense of excitement to her features, and Lena’s mouth curled into an answering smile as she shrugged, shouting over the noise, “which one is your favourite?”

     

                Biting her lip, Kara eyed the rides spread out before them and then pointed towards a large marquee illuminated within by neon lights as people rode around in karts. “Bumper cars!”

     

                Looping her arm through Lena’s, Kara dragged her along to it, and Lena didn’t mind, leaning into her warmth as it occurred to her that she’d let Kara do whatever she wanted to. But as they stopped outside it, at the start of the empty queue, Lena felt doubt stir within her as she dubiously eyed the collection of karts as they rattled past, the smell of exhaust fumes and rubber thick in the air. She watched as a man rammed the front of her kart into another’s and her eyes widened a fraction.

     

                “Is it safe?”

     

                Laughing, Kara nodded as they waited patiently. “Mhm. It’s fun! I promise.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena sceptically replied.

     

                Once the round was over and the customers filed out through a small gate, they handed over tickets to the guy at the booth and entered the arena. Picking out their own cars, they settled onto the cracked vinyl seats and Lena strapped herself in, a wary tautness to her shoulders as she gingerly grasped the steering wheel. Her feet found the pedals and she tested them out but found herself stationary.

     

                As soon as enough people had trickled in, the switch was flipped and Lena’s kart jolted forward. Gritting her teeth with uneasiness, she pressed her foot down and the kart chugged forward at a snail’s pace, not quite the racecar she’d imagined while standing outside. 

     

                Finding Kara amidst the moving karts, she couldn’t help but smile, steering towards her before a teenage boy rammed his own kart into Lena’s and she startled, the kart pausing for a moment as she was thrown off-course. She caught sight of Kara laughing and shook her head in exasperation, soon getting the hang of things as she cautiously bumped into other people and tried not to feel too irritated by each jolting impact of someone ramming into her.

     

                Once their turn came to an end, she followed Kara out through the gate and watched as she turned around, spreading her hands in an expectant gesture as she raised her eyebrows. “So? Fun? Yes? No?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena truthfully replied, chuckling quietly, “what’s up next?”

     

                “Teacups?” Kara suggested, “they’re always a good time.”

     

                “Lead the way.”

     

                Kara pressed her hand against Lena’s back as she guided her along to the circular enclosure filled with painted teacups, a large teapot in the middle, all of the cups spinning wildly around and around. As they stepped into a blue and white striped cup, the bar locked into place over their laps, Lena was glad that she hadn’t eaten dinner yet, the dizzying circles stealing the air from her lungs as she squeezed her eyes shut and laughed, her grip tight on the bars. 

     

                It was exhilarating nonetheless, and Lena found that she was enjoying herself, and not solely because of Kara’s company. Feeling unsteady as they exited the ride, Kara took her elbow and led her out of the path of people walking the ground, eyes bright as she glanced around for the next thing. She let out a gasp at something and Lena turned to follow her line of sight to what had snagged her attention, finding a long metal shelter harbouring a row of arcade games, from skee ball to pellet guns with rows of rusted ducks.

     

                Letting Kara tow her over to it, her arm looped through Lena’s as she leant in close and smiled, she brought them to a stop before a machine. It was a love tester, two metal rods sticking out of the machine, and Lena let out a scoff of laughter as Kara fished out a quarter and thumbed it into the slot.

     

                “Hold on to the handle,” Kara told her, gripping the other one tightly.

     

                Following her instructions, Lena watched with thinly veiled amusement as the lights lit up the machine, flashing sporadically for a moment before it went dark and a row of lights shot upwards, right to the top of the machine as it let out a chiming noise.

     

                “True love!” Kara crowed, laughing as she pulled her hand back and gave Lena a wry smile.

     

                Feeling her stomach lurch slightly, Lena opened and closed her mouth before blurting out the only thing that came to mind. “You know they- they measure the temperature of your hands to come up with the answer.”

     

                “Or it’s meant to be,” Kara teased her.

     

                Smiling, her eyes crinkling at the corners, Kara placed a hand to Lena’s back to lead her to the next ride, oblivious to Lena’s preoccupied mind. Lena couldn’t stop thinking about how optimistic Kara was, finding enjoyment in the smallest of things, the silliest of things, no matter how inconsequential, and found it a bit startling that someone could be so happy all the time. And then she thought of her in the army, stationed in the middle of nowhere with nothing but her optimism to keep her going, and it all made sense. And it saddened Lena to think of Kara compensating for the things she’d seen out there, and it made her irrationally angry too, that she was there to begin with. But it all made sense and she couldn’t help but wonder what Kara was trying to cope with.

     

                They went on every ride there, including the ferris wheel. Lena hadn’t mentioned her fear of heights and spent most of the ride with her eyes squeezed shut, wedged in alongside Kara’s solid warmth as the wheel rotated with agonising slowness. Each time she opened her eyes to peek, she felt faint with fear, her stomach lurching as a cold sweat covered her.

     

                She came stumbling off it once it was over, pale and shaky, and Kara eyed her with alarm, her eyes wide as she reached out as if to catch her if Lena collapsed. “Are you okay?”

     

                “I- I don’t like heights,” Lena breathlessly gasped, drawing in a deep breath.

     

                “Oh God, why didn’t you say so? We didn’t have to go on it?”

     

                “It’s fine,” Lena weakly laughed, pressing a hand to her chest and feeling the galloping of her heart. “I thought the whole thing was going to collapse . Is it supposed to squeak so much?”

     

                A conflicted look of amusement and concern twisted Kara’s face as she winced slightly and laughed, “I mean … I wouldn’t say supposed to, but it’s safe. I think. I mean, they do check the machinery so … there’s that.”

     

                Closing her eyes and clenching her clammy palms, Lena inhaled deeply and then opened her eyes to find Kara watching her with worry.

     

                “Are you sure you’re okay? Let’s get you some food; you probably need sugar.”

     

                There was a strip of food trucks lining the main path through the carnival grounds and they queued in half a dozen as Lena bought whatever Kara had exclaimed about while in line. They ended up with corndogs and nachos, giant sodas and a bag of churros, toffee popcorn and a few other things that Lena pointed out, swiping her card at each truck as she bickered quietly with Kara.

     

                Arms laden with their purchases, they walked towards the opposite end to the entrance, where the carnival games gave way to a long pier stretching out over the bay. It was lit by strings of colourful lights and a few people had escaped from the noise to sit on the benches spaced evenly along the length. Breathing in the smell of their food as the cool breeze washed over them, Lena felt marginally better away from the stifling crowd and dizzying heights.

     

                “You’re spoiling me,” Kara reprovingly said after a moment.

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, surprise flashing across her face, she turned to look at Kara with wide eyes, taken aback by the fact. “I’ve never had anyone to spoil before.”

     

                “Well, next time it’s my turn,” Kara warned her, taking a sip of her soda as their footsteps thumped along the worn boards of the pier. 

     

                Smiling to herself at the thought of it, Lena was silent as they walked to the end of the pier and took a seat on the bench facing the bay. The quiet sound of the water ebbing and flowing, lapping against the posts, was soothing and they could see the city across the bridge, a thousand specks of light. Gulls cried out as they fought for scraps back at the shore and the muffled sound of a boat’s horn echoed across the water. Only a wan lamppost gave them any light and Lena felt the peacefulness of the evening settled over her like a blanket.

     

                “So, last time you said you were Irish,” Kara said as they spread their food out between them on the bench, “how long have you been in America.”

     

                “Since I was four.”

     

                “Oh, yeah? That’s a long time.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “Do you remember much?”

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena looked away and clenched her jaw as her throat constricted. She closed her eyes for a moment, composing herself before she looked at Kara and gave her a strained smile.

     

                “Not much.”

                

                “Do you ever get to go back?”

     

                “I- no. I’ve been back … once. A few years ago. That’s all. I just- I came to America because … my mom died, so … there’s never been a reason to go back.”

     

                Surprise flashed across Kara’s face, which quickly melted into a look of agonised empathy, and she reached out to touch the back of Lena’s hand. Looking down at their hands, Lena let out a slow breath, feeling a lump in her throat.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Lena shook her head, lips twitching with a rueful smile, she picked up her soda and took a sip. “Don’t be. It was a freak accident.”

     

                “Mine too,” Kara murmured, a sorrowful look in her eyes as Lena tensed and looked at her. “Both of them at the same time. I, uh, I got adopted. I was thirteen at the time so … it was hard. I got a sister out of it though, so it wasn’t all bad.”

     

                The air rushed out of Lena as her shoulders deflated and she gave Kara an agonised look, “I’m sorry.”

     

                Shrugging half-heartedly, Kara gave her a small smile, her eyes glassy as she spoke. “It was … a house fire. My dad managed to get me out and went back in for my mom and …”

     

                She winced at the memory and Lena surprised herself by grasping her hand in a tight grip, giving Kara’s fingers a reassuring squeeze. Lena wasn’t good at comforting people and she felt out of her depth, sitting there sharing her grief with someone she barely knew, but who understood better than most the pain she’d suffered as a child.

     

                “It’s … hard, isn’t it?” Kara said after a long moment.

     

                “I don’t remember much of her,” Lena murmured, “I think it’s better that way, but … sometimes I dream about her. It makes me miss her.”

     

                “What about your dad? What’s he like?”
