                Closing her eyes, Lena exhaled, listening to the sound of her heartbeat echoing in her own ears, her pulse jumping slightly at the thought of explaining to someone just how twisted it all was. She hadn’t understood it as a child, of course, but as she’d grown older, it had filled her with so much anger that Lena was still processing it years later.

     

                “He … he’s dead too. When I was sixteen. But … he wasn’t a good father, so …”

     

                “Oh, I-”

     

                “He was actually married,” Lena blurted out before Kara could apologise again. “He was married with- with a son - my older brother - when I was born. So, um, he took me back to live with them here and … well, I was officially adopted and all of that, but my mom - not the dead one - … she’s still around. I just- I don’t really see much of her. She was never good at the whole ...parenting thing either.”

     

                Slowly, Kara pulled her hand from Lena’s grasp and put it around her shoulders, taking a bite of her corndog. Sitting side by side, they were silent as they brooded over their food and their shared misery, and it wasn’t an uncomfortable silence. It was preferable even, Kara’s warmth a steady presence beside her, both of them sharing something that didn’t need to be spoken aloud to be understood completely.

     

                While they ate and occasionally broke the fragile silence, Kara took a few photos of the bay, safely tucking them in the pocket of her jacket, where the rest lay, and Lena felt as if she could’ve stayed there, sitting on that bench on the edge of the pier and stared out at the water for the rest of the night. There was something about the expanse of darkness before her, pierced by the distant city lights across the sound that made her feel safe, invisible to everything else. Except Kara beside her.

     

                Once they were finished, they gathered up their trash and dumped it in a garbage can, burying their hands in their pockets, even though Lena was possessed with the urge to take Kara’s. She wasn’t brave enough to do it though, and she silently berated herself for even thinking it, acting too much like a teenager with her first crush when Kara was just looking for a friend. In fact, Lena hadn’t even behaved like that when she was a teenager with her first crush, and the thought made her uneasy as they left the carnival behind.

     

                She was reluctant to go home yet though, the night still so young, and when Kara asked if she wanted to walk awhile, Lena was relieved. They wandered aimlessly through the city, the buildings more industrial and rundown on this side of the bridge, with autoshops and tattoo parlours, cigar shops and bodegas and thrift stores.

     

                They ended up in a cheap diner with good coffee after some time, sitting opposite each other on the cracked booth seats, talking over their cups, which never seemed to be empty. It wasn’t until after midnight that Kara threw down a couple of dollars on the table and followed Lena out, walking back to the car.

     

                Lena drove her home, the city still so alive with noise and people, and she felt nervous as she idled in the car outside Kara’s apartment building, not knowing what to say. It had been a strange night, fun and exposing, and Lena didn’t know what she felt, only that her chest felt tight and her breathing was shallow as she looked at Kara, weariness softening her face as pale bruises shadowed beneath her eyes. Giving her a tired smile, Kara sat slumped in her seat for a moment as they looked at each other.

     

                “I had fun tonight.”

     

                “Me too,” Lena murmured.

     

                Saying goodnight, she waited until she was sure Kara was safely inside her building before she drove back across the city and parked outside. Climbing the steps of the brownstone, she unlocked the front door and slowly closed the door behind her, locking it with a pensive look on her face.

     

                Slowly walking upstairs, she thought about the night and everything that had happened and couldn’t explain the feeling in her chest. It felt achingly tender but warm, a gentle fluttering inside that made her feel almost out of breath as she shed her clothes and changed into silk pyjamas and climbed into bed. It was too early for Lena’s usual bedtime but whether from excitement or the relief of an early night for once, she drifted off to sleep.

    Chapter 4

                It was Tuesday the next time Lena heard from Kara, short-tempered from her morning of difficult meetings with clients and investors, all who looked at Lena with condescension, all of them old enough to be her father. It never failed to put her in a bad mood and Lena was brooding in the quiet solitude of her office as she picked at her salad. The sound of her cell phone ringing was grating in the silence of the room but her annoyance quickly abated as she read Kara’s name and quickly snatched it up.

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “Hi! Is now a bad time? I thought it might be easier to call but-”

     

                “Not at all. If anything, it’s a welcome distraction.”

     

                “Rough morning?”

     

                With a scoff of laughter, Lena relaxed in her chair, turning it to face the windows as harsh sunlight blinded her. She could feel the tension bleeding out of her at the sound of Kara’s voice and it made her smile slightly.

     

                “Annoying morning,” Lena sighed, “but how are you?”

     

                “Good! I was just running errands and thought about getting lunch. And then I wondered if maybe you’d already eaten …”

     

                Swiveling her chair back around to eye her salad, Lena smiled faintly, “no, I haven’t.”

     

                “So … how do you feel about Chinese food?”

     

                “Let me just wrap up a couple of things and I’ll meet you there?” Lena suggested.

     

                “I can come meet you at work if you want,” Kara offered, “it might be a nightmare to park your car.”

     

                Pausing, wariness creeping over her at the thought of Kara at L-Corp, Lena opened and closed her mouth before she relented. It would be more convenient, and she’d get to spend more time with Kara as she stretched her legs.

     

                “Sure. Um, I’m at 1200 West Cordova Street.”

     

                “Perfect. I’ll see you soon.”

     

                Hanging up, Lena trashed her salad and pushed the button on the desk phone for Jess' desk right outside the door, trapping the receiver between her shoulder and ear as her fingers flashed across the keyboard. Jess picked up after a second.

     

                “Miss Luthor.”

     

                “I’ll be out of office for a while. Reschedule the workshop; I want to make sure I’m there for it.”

     

                “Yes, ma’am. Anything else?”

     

                Pressing her lips together, Lena thought for a moment as she pulled up her schedule, blocks of colour taking up most of her day. “No. I’ll keep you posted if anything needs to be cancelled. If you hear from Spheerical Industries, patch Jack through to me. I won’t want to miss that.”

     

                “Of course.”

     

                “Thanks, Jess. You can probably take a longer lunch today; I don’t think there’s anything important that needs to be done.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Putting the receiver down, Lena locked her computer and shuffled her papers on her desk, arranging the folders in order and filing them into the cabinets before she grabbed her things and stalked out of the office. Giving Jess a small smile as she passed by the young woman’s desk, she stepped into one of the elevators and pressed the button for the lobby.

     

                It was lunchtime, which meant that the elevator stopped at multiple floors, her employees' faces going slack with shock before they composed themselves enough to climb in. It was rare for Lena to leave her office and despite the fact that she was the youngest person at the office - aside from the summer interns - the array of scientists, business, mechanical engineering and computer science majors all seemed to sober up at the sight of her. They all offered her quiet greetings or nods, but none were brave enough to venture small talk, and Lena lingered at the back of the packed elevator as she glanced down at her watch.

     

                Reaching the lobby, there was some shuffling around as a path cut through the occupants of the elevator to allow her to step off first. Squeezing past them, she stepped out into the sunlit lobby, the wide windows giving her a view of the street outside, and walking past the row of receptionists and security guards, Lena stepped out of the cool interior and into the warmth of the day.

     

                Kara wasn’t there yet and Lena was grateful for it as she lingered outside, her employees trickling out as they gave her furtive glances, the pairs or trios whispering amongst themselves as they gossiped about her, no doubt. Smoothing a hand over the pressed grey slacks she wore, Lena tightened her sleek ponytail and then glanced around again.

     

                Her eyes found Kara immediately, the sun turning her hair to spun gold, the sleeves of her navy plaid shirt rolled up to reveal her lean forearms, a faded NASA t-shirt on underneath it, the picture of ease in her Birkenstocks and paint splattered jeans. Lena wondered if it was from repainting her sister’s apartment or if Kara had a penchant for art, curious to know which it was as she took pleasure in unravelling who she was.

     

                At the sight of her, Kara perked up, a bright smile on her face that Lena couldn’t help but respond to, and she opened her arms as she neared her. This time Lena was ready for the embrace, the tightness of Kara’s grip as she held her close for a moment, breathing in the smell of her apple blossom shampoo. 

     

                “Hi! How’re you?” Kara asked.

     

                “Hi, it’s good to see you.”

     

                Pulling back smiling, Lena caught sight of an employee staring at her with an open mouth and quickly turned around as her face flushed red. Putting an arm around Kara’s back, Lena quickly shepherded her away from the doors of the building, her skin crawling with the feeling of being watched.

     

                “Let’s go,” Lena brusquely replied, and Kara frowned at her pink cheeks before she made eye contact with a guy in a suit and then looked at Lena with confusion.

     

                “Is everything okay?”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena whispered, “we just- I don’t want to start any gossiping at the office.”

     

                “What?”

     

                Kara glanced at the building, her eyes landing on the name above the door, the logo beside it, and then craned her neck to stare at the large letters on the side of the building with an even bigger logo.

     

                “You work here? I thought you said you ran a family business.”

     

                Flushing, Lena towed her away faster, her shoulders hunched as she winced sheepishly, “technically it is a family business. It’s owned by a family, right?”

     

                “So, what do you do there? Statistics? Marketing?”

     

                “This and that,” Lena hedged, feeling Kara’s eyes on her face.

     

                “We’re going in the wrong direction, you know,” Kara said after a long moment.

     

                Exhaling, Lena closed her eyes as they came to a stop on the sidewalk. Opening her eyes, her shoulders went slack at the patient look of expectation on Kara’s face that let her know she’d wait as long as Lena needed her to for her to explain what was making her so tense and curt, but did expect an explanation.

     

                Biting back a quiet groan, Lena pressed a hand to her forehead as she looked away, a ripple of pain crossing her face. “My family are … the owners and majority shareholders of L-Corp.”

     

                “You’re joking , right?” Kara slowly asked, letting out a nervous laugh as she gave Lena a wary look, waiting for the punchline.

     

                Opening and closing her mouth, Lena pressed her lips together and watched the traffic flash past as she fiddled with her fingers. “So, I don’t know if you heard about Alexander Luthor when you were over there-”

     

                “I heard.”

     

                “That’s- that’s my brother - he was my brother - and now … well, I’m the- the sole heiress to the majority shareholdings of the company now. Lena Luthor. I, uh, I was made CEO after he … you know, and I moved the headquarters out here so …”

     

                Making a choked sound, Kara gave her an incredulous look, lips parted and eyes wide, speechless for a few moments. Looking away, she let out a slightly hysterical laugh.

                

                “So, you’re … rich.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “No, but like … rich rich.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena folded her arms over her chest, baring her teeth in a grimace as she rocked slightly in her heels, hating that she was eye-to-eye with Kara in them as it left her pinned by her shocked stare.

                

                “Yes! I’m … disgustingly wealthy.”

     

                “And just how old are you again?”

     

                “Twenty-four.”

     

                “Oh God,” Kara managed to choke out, cupping the back of her neck as she stared at Lena with unabashed disbelief. “That’s- you- why are you wasting your time with me?”

     

                Flinching back with shock, Lena’s expression crumpled as she looked at Kara with puzzlement, blinking at her for a moment before she managed to reply. “I- what?”

     

                “I mean … you could … be friends with anyone . Don’t you have other- other billionaires to hang out with? Shouldn’t you be in … I don’t know, Mauritius on vacation?”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena shook her head with bewildered amusement. “Kara … I don’t have any friends. I don’t … take vacations, or- or really do anything besides work. Every day you ask me how my day was and it’s embarrassing that nothing’s happened except for pushing paperwork around my desk and making a million phone calls and meetings.”

     

                “You- you don’t have … any friends?” Kara quietly echoed, as if she’d heard Lena incorrectly, confusion and pity shining in her blue eyes.

     

                Throwing her hands up, Lena sighed and laughed defeatedly, “honestly, when would I have the time?”

     

                “Right.”

     

                “But this is good,” Lena firmly said as she stared at her, gesturing between them, “this is good for me, because I’d never been to a carnival until the other night because that’s just … not how I grew up. Before I was doing this job, my brother was doing it, and before that my father was, so … I don’t really know anything but business and it’s fine , but … it’s nice doing things with someone else. I don’t … go for lunch with people unless it’s a business meeting, and I don’t meet friends outside my office and hug them. I’m starting to realise that maybe I should take more time off.”

     

                “Okay,” Kara murmured, still somewhat stunned as she took Lena’s arm and turned her back the way they’d come. “Well … I’ll just- I’ll keep thinking of things to do.”

     

                A laugh burst out of Lena as she hung her head, hiding her smile as her cheeks still looked rosy against her pale skin. “You don’t have to-”

     

                “I like hanging out with you too . It’s just … surprising, is all.”

     

                “Yeah, I don’t think there’s really a good way to tell someone who you are if they don’t already know.”

     

                “I should’ve Googled you,” Kara snorted, “I thought you might’ve been in the … I don’t know, handmade soaps or organic skincare products industry or something. Not- not the owner of a giant tech conglomerate. I mean … that’s very young.”

     

                With a wry smile, straightening slightly with pride, Lena shrugged nonchalantly, “the numbers are better than they’ve ever been, so anyone who doubted … well, they soon learned when to be quiet.”

     

                They walked past L-Corp again, Kara looking at the soaring building with renewed awe as Lena latched onto her with her head ducked and turned aside, hoping she went unnoticed, which Kara found endlessly humorous. Crossing two city blocks, they made a right and Kara glanced sideways at Lena.

     

                “So … does this mean you’re like … a genius?”

     

                With a sheepish smile, Lena bit her lip as she shrugged, “kind of. I mean, I’ve got two doctorates and I did join MENSA, but it’s mostly just business.”

     

                “Two- you need to stop talking,” Kara laughed, gently bumping shoulders with her, “what did you study?”

     

                “Bio-engineering and computer science.”

     

                With a low whistle, Kara walked them around a patch of uneven sidewalk and raised her eyebrows at Lena. “Impressive.”

     

                Shrugging off the compliment, Lena quickly tried to steer the conversation to other topics, and Kara was tactful enough to notice her evident discomfort and comply. They soon arrived outside a worn restaurant, the faded sign in Mandarin and the door sticking for a moment as Kara forced it open. The narrow shop held a row of tables along one side and an open hatch to the kitchen at the far end, the smell of ginger and soy perfuming the air. A young guy was seated behind the short counter off to the right and looked up at their arrival, a rickety fan clicking above his head as it wafted the stagnant air of the room around and around.

     

                Recognition lit up his eyes at the sight of Kara and he handed them two laminated menus, free to choose their own seats. Only two other tables were occupied at the time and they sat near the window, a yellowed tint to the old glass as blinds masked them from the worst of the sun. A tepid pitcher of tap water was set on the vinyl covered table, nicked and scarred from years of use and Kara gave her a crooked smile.

     

                “This place has my favourite takeout in the entire city. I’m not even kidding, I come here like … three times a week when I’m home on leave.”

     

                Lena ordered the hot and sour soup and egg rolls, while Kara ordered Kung Pao chicken and dumplings. The portions were generous and the stifling heat made Lena’s shirt stick to her back as the spice spread a slow flush from her stomach to her face, her skin prickling. 

     

                “How is it?”

     

                “Really good,” Lena earnestly replied.

     

                Cheeks dimpling with a smile, Kara’s eyes crinkled and Lena arched an eyebrow at her, waiting for her to include her in the joke. Wrinkling her nose in an endearing manner, Kara’s eyes took on a mystified look as a pucker formed between her eyebrows.

     

                “You have a very serious face. You don’t smile a lot and it’s hard to know what you’re thinking.”

     

                “Really?” Lena asked, her brow furrowing. 

     

                She’d thought that she’d been smiling quite a lot recently, and she didn’t have to look further than right in front of her to know why . People had a tendency to think she was a bitter person, and maybe they were right, but Lena had never reflected much on it. They also called her antisocial, which she took to mean she wasn’t overly keen on people, instead of taking it literally, which she wholeheartedly did agree with. More often than not, Lena simply just didn’t like engaging in small talk.

     

                “Well, I suppose in comparison to you nobody would smile a lot,” Lena wryly teased her. “And maybe I just don’t have many reasons to.”

     

                Giving her an apologetic smile, Kara ducked her head over her chicken as she poked at it, “sorry, that was probably rude of me to point out. I didn’t mean it as a criticism, only that … I like how serious you look. It makes me think that you’re … reliable.”

     

                “Reliable?” Lena quietly snorted, giving Kara a grin, “don’t apologise though; you are right. I’m not a very optimistic person, I don’t really see the point in it. Not that I’m a pessimist, more of a realist actually. I don’t know, I just- I’m not … attached to people.”

     

                “Don’t you get lonely?”

     

                With a grim smile, a flash of sadness in her green eyes, Lena shrugged a shoulder, “sometimes, but I don’t really have time to dwell on it. Besides, I’ve always been … independent. I guess that some people just aren’t built for love.”

     

                “I don’t believe that; I think … you just have to find the right person.”

     

                “Let me know how that works out for you.”

     

                “What, you don’t believe in true love now?”

     

                Squeezing her eyes shut as she laughed, Lena shook her head and softly groaned, “true love? I haven’t heard that since I was a kid. God , no. True love is- is a thing made up by the romance industry because deep down … it’s what everyone wants, isn’t it? To be loved by someone so much that they believe it’s … fate, or some bullshit like that.”

     

                “Come on,” Kara said in a wheedling voice, pouting slightly, even as her eyes glimmered with mirth, “ why are you so cynical? Haven’t you ever loved someone?”

     

                “Never,” Lena firmly replied before she scoffed, “and I’m not cynical .”

     

                At Kara’s chuckle, Lena flushed with indignation, bristling. “I’m not!” she exclaimed defensively, “I just don’t share your optimism. But I do find it …”

     

                She trailed off, waving her hand as she tried to think of the right word to describe it. With a lopsided smile on her face, Kara cocked her head to the side, eyebrows raised.

                

                “Naïve?”

     

                “No,” Lena sighed, “I don’t know … endearing?”

     

                “Endearing?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena said with more conviction. “I find you endearing, because … it’s nice to think that there are some people who haven’t let the world stomp their joy and love of things out of them. But me? I don’t think like that.”

     

                “And how do you think?”

     

                Lips pressed in a flat line as she glanced up at the spackled ceiling, her fork in hand as her expression darkened with a pensive look. Humming, her lips thinned and she spoke slowly.

     

                “I don’t … trust people. If you let someone in, give them the power to hurt you, they always end up doing exactly that . And maybe it’s just the way I was brought up, but … I can’t imagine owing anyone anything.”

     

                Looking disturbed by her thought process, Kara frowned, “you think that to love someone is … to owe them something?”

     

                “I mean … yeah, isn’t it? You owe them your love and honesty and comfort and safety. That’s part of the deal, that you try your best to make someone else happy with you and I just- I don’t know. It seems like it’s a weakness.”

     

                “It’s a strength ,” Kara countered, “when you’ve seen firsthand the … horrible things people can do, you want to look for the better things. I don’t think I’d ever think I was weak because I love my sister and I love my friends and my mom and trusted every person I’ve ever spoken to. It’s not a failure on my part if they take advantage of it, so …”

     

                “I guess that’s true as well. Maybe I’m just too selfish.”

     

                She said it with a rakish smile, picking up her fortune cookie on the plate that had been brought to their table, turning it over in her deft fingers. Kara grimaced at her words though, fixing her with a searching look.

     

                “I don’t think you’re selfish at all.”

     

                “Or maybe I’m nicer to you than to everyone else.”

     

                Kara let out a quiet laugh, reaching for her own fortune cookie. “Seeing as we hardly know each other … I find it hard to believe I’m getting special treatment. You know what I think? I think you’re shy.”

     

                She snapped the fortune cookie in half and slipped the strip of paper out, rasping between her thumbs as she straightened it out to read it. Lena raised her eyebrows expectantly as Kara cleared her throat.

     

                “A part of us remains wherever we have been. I like that one,” Kara smiled at Lena before jerking her chin at her. “What does your one say?”

     

                Cracking open her own, Lena shifted forward, hunching over with her elbows on the table, “love- oh come on!”

     

                Kara laughed at her outburst, eyes crinkling at the corners as her cheeks dimpled, and Lena gave her an exasperated look.

     

                “Love is like oxygen; you need it to survive.” 

     

                “I think it’s trying to tell you something; you should listen to it.”

     

                “I think … you and the cookie are conspiring against me,” Lena sourly muttered, pouting as she folded the strip in half and slipped it into the pocket of her pants.

     

                Kara teased us relentlessly and Lena couldn’t help but laugh and smile, even as she fought them back and scowled and scoffed, enjoyed herself so much that she had to text Jess to cancel her next meeting.

     

                Just watching Kara talk was fascinating to Lena. Never had she seen someone so animated , her face lighting up with eagerness or excitement as she told a story, and by the time they finished their lunch and were able to move, they knew more about each other than when they’d walked in. Kara insisted on paying for their meal and as they waited for the check, she counted out bills and casually brought up the baseball game again.

     

                “So, I know I said the baseball game was this Saturday, but … if you’re not busy, maybe we could do something else before then? Dinner? Drinks? Anything other thing you’ve horrifyingly never done before? Bowling? The zoo?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena grimaced, “I actually haven’t been to the zoo before. I’m not really a fan of them unless they’re like … conservationist or rehabilitation programs.”

     

                “You’d love the one here then.”

     

                “Sure, let’s go.”

     

                “Really?” Kara asked, sharply looking up with surprise as she put the bills on the table. “You don’t think it’s silly?”

     

                Lena’s face softened and she smiled faintly, “of course it’s not; who doesn’t like animals, right?”

                

                “Right? And they even have this little hole at the otter enclosure where you can hold their hands, it’s really sweet.”

     

                A slow grin spread across Lena’s face, wider than before, revealing her dimples to Kara. “I’ve never seen someone so excited to hold an otter’s hand before; this must be good.”

     

                Climbing to her feet, gathering up her bag, Kara gave Lena a hopeful look, “okay, great, well … let me know when you’re free.”

     

                Shrugging, Lena arched an eyebrow, “how about right now?”

     

                “Right- right now?”

     

                Glancing down at her watch - just past three o’clock - Lena shrugged, “sure, why not? What time does it close?”

     

                “You’re not busy? You don’t have … meetings? I don’t know what you really do.”

     

                “Nothing that’s important. I could do with a day off, to be honest.”

     

                “Okay,” Kara slowly said, “okay, let’s go now then.”

     

                Giving her a winning smile, Lena slung her bag over her shoulder and made for the door, thanking the waiter on the way out, hoping he appreciated the tip she’d left on top of Kara’s money, and held the door open.

     

                “I have a feeling like you’re going to make me live out an entire childhood worth of activities, aren’t you?” Lena asked as they walked back towards L-Corp to fetch her car.

     

                With a sheepish smile, Kara shrugged helplessly, “there are just some things you have to do in life. You’ll thank me for it one day.”

    Chapter 5

                Lena parked outside the zoo, on the outskirts of the city, tucked into the beginnings of the foothills with a surprisingly mundane appearance as Lena eyed the front entrance. The walls were tall and solid, an abundance of trees and vines and plants growing there, and the smell of animals, hay and manure hung in the air as they climbed out of the car.

     

                As they crossed the parking lot, Lena’s phone started ringing and she glanced down at the number, stomach sinking at the sight of Jack Spheer’s name lighting up the screen. With a weary sigh, she gave Kara an apologetic smile.

     

                “Would you mind if I got this?”

     

                “Go ahead.”

     

                Accepting the call, Lena pressed her cell phone to her ear, meandering along to the ticket booth as she spoke, trying to keep the irritation out of her voice.

     

                “Jack, hi.”

     

                “Lena. Is now a bad time.”

     

                “It’ll have to be quick. Sorry.”

     

                “No, no, don’t apologise. I just wanted to discuss the acquisition before dinner on Monday. Are you free Saturday night? We could get drinks.”

     

                Grimacing, Lena peered sideways at Kara, clearing her throat as she lowered her voice to a murmur. “Saturday? I can’t, sorry. If there’s an issue with the proposal, I can call my lawyers and-”

     

                “No, it’s nothing like that. I just want to know who I’m selling my company to.”

     

                “You already know who,” Lena stiffly replied. “If this is because of my- nevermind. I have to go. I’ll see you at the meeting. Monday. Don’t be late.”

     

                Jack’s chuckle irked her, despite its warmth, or maybe because of it, as if he found her brusque manner amusing. Hanging up on him, Lena shoved her phone into her bag and rummaged around for her purse, pulling out her credit card before she looked up and saw Kara studying her.

     

                “You’re busy,” she murmured, a look of understanding in her eyes as she jerked her head to the car, “come on, let’s go. We can come-”

     

                “No, no,” Lena blurted out, seizing Kara’s arm as she stepped in close, feeling her face flush at the desperation. Letting go as if she’d been burned, Lena cleared her throat and stepped back. “It’s fine. It wasn’t anything important; I just have a meeting on Monday and they’re being pushy.”

     

                “An important meeting?”

     

                With a harried air about her, Lena tossed her ponytail and smiled thinly, “I’m trying to acquire a company that deals in nanotechnology. I think it’d help push L-Corp’s environmentally friendly projects to the next level in sustainability and … well, I won’t bore you with it. But it’s a big deal.”

     

                Lena’s smile was shy and Kara gave her arm a squeeze, “you’ll be great.”

     

                “Yeah? The board is hedging their bets about how this will turn out. But … right now, I have some hand holding to do.”

     

                Kara thread her fingers through Lena’s and swung their entwined hands slightly before her expression dropped and she gave her a mildly panicked look. “You meant with the otters, didn’t you?”

     

                Laughing, Lena squeezed her hand as Kara tried to let go, leaning in close, “I did.”

     

                She dropped her hand as they stepped up to the ticket booth and paid for them both, the woman handing over two tickets and a large paper map to direct them around the enclosures. Pushing through the turnstile, Lena unfolded the map and shook it out, narrowing her eyes as she took stock of the enclosures.

     

                “The otters are this way,” Kara said, taking hold of her arm and gently tugging her with a playful smile on her face.

     

                Folding the map, Lena smiled and allowed herself to be dragged down the paved path, overgrown trees shading the way, before they came to a large tank with windows revealing the scene inside. Standing side by side, Kara still clinging to Lena’s arm, they watched the otters slip in and out of the water, twisting and playing as they went. Kara dragged Lena over to a little hole in the side of the enclosure, away from the pool of water they splashed in, her face lighting up with excitement as she turned to face Lena.

     

                “If you put your finger in here, they come and hole it,” Kara explained, stooping over and poking a finger through. 

     

                She quietly laughed, the sound full of fondness as an otter reared up, whiskers twitching as it made a squeaking noise and wandered over to see. It gripped Kara’s finger and she spoke to it in a quiet, cooing voice before she pulled back and gestured for Lena to try. Sticking her finger through, Lena laughed as the otter grabbed her finger too, eyeing its little hand with surprise.

     

                “They have human hands, that’s so weird,” Lena said, glancing up at Kara as she grinned.

     

                Lingering a while, enjoying watching the otters as the sun warmed their backs and Kara talked and talked, never seeming to tire, they eventually wandered further into the zoo. At the sight of each enclosure, Kara would grab Lena’s hand and enthusiastically pull her forward, pressing up against the glass as she pointed out the creatures within, from lazy lions to chattering monkeys, and then she’d let go to take photos, reloading new film into the polaroid camera while Lena read the signs full of information and facts. 

     

                A quick reader, while Kara was patient and particular about her photos, Lena always ended up standing back and watching her. She could’ve watched Kara all day, taking note of the minute changes in her facial expression, the pinched look of concentration that made her eyebrows screw together slightly, the crinkling smiles that always graced her face.

     

                At the giraffe enclosure, Kara gasped as they watched the tall creatures strip the leaves from branches with their long tongues, and she craned her neck upwards as she snapped a photo of the closest one.

     

                “Look at them! They’re gorgeous, aren’t they? I love giraffes.”

     

                “You love a lot of things, don’t you?”

     

                Lena noticed that Kara used the word freely, seemingly in love with everything she encountered. It humoured Lena, who could think of perhaps a handful of times she’d tried the word out as a child, it never quite sticking, always feeling wrong , like she was supposed to say it but her feelings didn’t really hold the weight of it.

     

                “Don’t you think that overusing it kind of … detracts from the meaning? Like when you say you love Chinese food, or you love baseball and animals … doesn’t it make the word less special when you say you love your sister?”

     

                Brow knitting together in a baffled look of light-heartedness, Kara let out a quick laugh. “Of course it doesn’t! Why shouldn’t I love everything?”

     

                Lena shrugged, unable to come up with a good enough objection to that question, feeling stumped as she pursed her lips together in a contemplative manner. Why shouldn’t that be a good enough reason for her? Lena didn’t know, but it made her uneasy to sit with the feeling, as if she was wrong, which was a rare thing that always bothered her.

     

                “Haven’t you ever loved anything? Like … I don’t know, work?”

     

                Rolling her eyes at Kara’s teasing, Lena let out an exaggerated, withering sigh as she folded her arms over her chest. Scraping the sole of a heel along the concrete, her mouth thinned for a moment before she looked up at the giraffe, squinting against the sunlight, which was starting to turn a faint orange, the sun sinking lower and ushering in the golden hour.

     

                “Yes,” Lena softly replied after a long moment, feeling Kara’s attention drawn to her. “I loved my brother. Once.”

     

                Looking down, meeting Kara’s sad gaze, Lena snorted and shook her head, “you don’t have to pity me, he-”

     

                “You don’t have to explain to me.”

     

                “No, it’s fine. He just- he stopped being my brother a long time before that. Even when I was younger there was something … unnerving about him. He was smart, God, he was so smart, and I wanted to be just like him. Things were fine until I got old enough for it to be apparent that … as smart as he was, I was smarter. And God , how he hated me for that. I guess it wasn’t really surprising when he went off the rails. I don’t know what he … what he was trying to do. I don’t know if he knew the building would collapse like that, with … all those people inside. If he was just making a point and it went wrong . Either way, he’s still the man who blew himself up, along with all those people, but the man that died wasn’t the brother I loved.”

     

                “It still must’ve been hard for you.”

     

                Kara’s hand found hers, squeezing it in silent comfort, and Lena swallowed thickly, thinking about the wreckage of the company, of the scorn heaped onto her, a pariah in the tech industry as she tried to cobble together the remains of the company. It had been difficult, especially being so young, but the move to National City, the shiny new office building with no memories attached to it, a brand new name … it all made it a little easier. 

     

                But still, they judged her from afar, not knowing she condemned her own brother for what he did as much as they did. Perhaps even moreso, for Lena had been a victim of his volatile moods, his mad rants and frustration at failed plans long before he’d brought down thousands of tonnes on his head.

     

                “It is what it is,” Lena wearily sighed, “and maybe that made it harder for me to love than it already was. If there’s one thing I’ve learned growing up in my family, it’s that love only tears you apart.”

     

                “Maybe,” Kara murmured, giving her hand a squeeze, “but it’s love that puts you back together again.”

     

                Moving on, from the topic and the enclosure, they watched as a crocodile was fed a large haunch of meat and a panda methodically chewed its stick of green bamboo, and after a stint through the reptile room, they were back at the entrance. It was late, the shadows lengthening and blurring, and Lena’s lack of sleep the night before was catching up with her as they dawdled towards the exit. 

     

                “So, has this been an enlightening experience for you?” Kara asked, looping her arm through Lena’s in a manner that was becoming startlingly casual.

     

                “Oh, definitely,” Lena grinned, “I’m a changed woman after holding hands with an otter. Completely different.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara gave her a withering look, fighting back a smile, “okay, but did you at least have fun?”

     

                “With you? Always.”

     

                Feeling pleased with herself as Kara ducked her head with pink cheeks, biting her lip as she was overcome with a brief bout of shy silence, Lena’s eyes snagged on the souvenir shop near the exit. Gently bumping Kara, she raised her eyebrows suggestively as their eyes met.

     

                “Souvenir?”

     

                “I can’t say no to that.”

     

                They stepped inside the small shop, browsing aisles of stuffed animals, children’s books and animal print pencils, mugs and t-shirts and all manner of cheap mementos. Kara picked a keychain from the selection, a little otter holding a sign saying National City Zoo and Lena hefted a bag of compost from the arrangement near the desk.

     

                “Compost? Really?” Kara sceptically asked.

     

                “It’s for my herb garden,” Lena shrugged, as if it was obvious.

     

                “You have a herb garden?”

     

                “Of course. It’s … well, it’s new . I’m trying to become more sustainable, right? Reduce waste, less plastics, cleaner energy. It’s part of my rebranding for the company, so I’ve started with a herb garden. Hopefully I’ll work up to a vegetable garden at some point, but we’ll see how it goes. You should try something from it; I never used to use fresh herbs in my food, but I’ve recently started using a lot of mint and it’s actually really good.”

     

                Mild surprise crossed Kara’s face as Lena paid and they stepped outside, “you can cook?”

     

                Stomach lurching with panic, Lena opened and closed her mouth. “I- well, I- I can . I’m not … a chef, but, well, if you- if you want, you could come over for dinner.”

     

                Already silently cursing herself, Lena was in too deep to take it back, to tell Kara that cooking was a very generous term, and the most Lena could cook with heat was a microwaved meal or a slice of toast. Anything else that wasn’t supposed to be eaten raw was far out of her realm of talents, but Kara seemed to perk up at the thought of Lena making her a meal with some of her freshly picked herbs, and how was she supposed to say no to that? She made a mental note to ask Jess to pick up some cooking books so she could at least have a guide.

     

                Exiting the zoo, they walked back to Lena’s parked car and climbed inside, the compost safely stored in the trunk while Kara fiddled with her house keys as she attached the new keychain, holding it up with delight for Lena to see. In the confines of the car, Lena felt exhaustion wash over her, her feet sore from so much walking, yet it was a content feeling and she wasn’t sure if she was ready to part with Kara just yet.

     

                “Do you … want to go anywhere else?”

     

                “Oh, no, it’s okay,” Kara said with a slight smile, “you look tired.”

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, Lena’s eyes creased as she raised her eyebrows, “what a polite way to tell me I look awful.”

     

                “No, I- that’s not what I meant, I just-”

     

                “Relax, I’m teasing you,” Lena murmured, reaching out to touch Kara’s hand, enjoying how flustered she was.

     

                Blushing harder as she rubbed at the back of her neck, Kara stared straight ahead through the windscreen. “You just- you could never look awful. For the record.”

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena self-depricatingly replied, her voice light with teasing, “you haven’t seen me in the mornings.”

     

                Kara snorted at her joke, shaking her head before she relaxed into the seat, the car smelling of heated plastic and the smell of faux leather as Lena started the car and pulled out of the parking lot. The city was a web of lights as the sunlight dwindled, and they breathed in the sweet aroma of the desert as they drove away from the foothills, the wind warm for early spring.

     

                As a compromise, they stopped for coffee on the way home, and Lena parked outside for a while as they sipped their drinks and talked, before Kara finally said goodbye. Climbing out, she smiled at Lena and told her to get home safe, and Lena didn’t think anyone had ever cared about her enough to say that to her. She thought about it the entire way home.

    Chapter 6

                Saturday rolled around with overcast skies and the muggy closeness that made Lena feel like she couldn’t breathe, although that might have just been the panic of trying to choose an outfit for a baseball game. Having never watched a game before, Lena wasn’t overly excited about the match, and her knowledge of how the game worked could have barely filled a teaspoon, but she’d done her research the night before so she could at least follow along and understand Kara’s excitement for it. 

     

                Mostly, she was just looking forward to seeing Kara again, their lunchtime coffee on Wednesday feeling far too long ago for her liking.

     

                She insisted on having her driver take them to the game this time, to skip the trouble of looking for parking, and they pulled up outside Alex’s apartment in the sleek black towncar to find Kara outside, leaning against the brick wall with a shirt over her arm. 

     

                Lena opened the back door and poked her head out, a smile on her face as she lifted her sunglasses. “Kara!”

     

                Attention caught, Kara’s eyebrows rose as she pushed off the wall, loping towards the car and slipping inside. Shutting the door behind her, she buckled in as she looked at the driver in the front seat with mild surprise.

     

                “You weren’t kidding about the driver, huh?” she smiled at Lena before leaning as far through the open partition so she could greet the driver.

     

                Watching with thinly veiled amusement, Lena raised her eyebrows as Kara settled down on her seat, “how’re you?”

     

                “Excited,” Kara grinned, gesturing to her outfit, a white shirt with navy blue piping, emblazoned with a logo of a shark. She was wearing a matching blue cap and Lena couldn’t help but smile. “I even stole my sister’s jersey so you … could match.”

     

                She held up the shirt that she’d brought with her, an identical copy to the one she was wearing, which Lena took to mean they were the official uniform of the National City Sharks. With a mild look of amusement, Lena reached out and took the shirt, holding it up to eye it before she smiled and slid the partition up. She’d decided on a pair of cropped jeans and loafers, with a plain white shirt, and Lena quickly unbuttoned her shirt, catching a glimpse of Kara’s mouth clamping shut as she quickly busied herself looking out the window.

     

                Fighting back a smile, Lena slipped the shirt off and the baseball jersey on, buttoning it up and turning to Kara, leaning across the empty middle seat. “How do I look?”

     

                Turning back around, Kara smiled brightly, her cheeks still faintly pink and set the blue baseball cap on Lena’s dark head, tugging it down snugly and fixing her hair. “Perfect.”

     

                Smiling to herself, Lena leant across the seat and whispered, “you too.”

     

                Not only for the satisfaction of seeing Kara’s cheeks redden further, but because she meant it. With a quiet laugh, Lena hesitantly touched the back of Kara’s hand, wondering to herself if it was okay to do so, if she would know that Lena wasn’t teasing her, only enjoyed the flustered look on Kara’s face.

     

                “I like it when you blush like that,” Lena admitted after a moment, a pleased smile spreading across her face as she teased her. “Are you embarrassed?”

     

                “I- no,” Kara scoffed, “trust me, in the army … you see everything . I just didn’t want to stare.”

     

                “Well that’s the first time I’ve heard that.”

     

                Giving her a withering look, Kara rolled her eyes as her little finger brushed against Lena’s on the seat between them. “Another first,” Kara murmured with a droll smile.

     

                The conversation went back and forth, full of light teasing and witty remarks, the city passing by as Lena’s driver navigated the way through each block, towards the stadium that rose up amidst the skyscrapers across the harbour bridge.

     

                It was heaving as the towncar pulled over as close as possible and Lena thanked him, both women slipping out and joining the throngs of people dressed in blue and white, or the occasional red and yellow jersey for the opposition. The line was long and they chatted as they waited, Lena’s hand finding Kara’s so they didn’t lose each other in the crowd along the way.

     

                Inside, they stopped to buy beer in plastic cups and a loaded fries to share before they made their way to their seats. They were towards the back of the stadium, the field a small square of green and Lena felt packed in like sardines with the rest of the crowd, the noise so overwhelmingly loud that she had to lean in close to Kara to make herself heard.

     

                “How long do these games usually last?”

     

                “Three or four hours,” Kara said, leaning in close, “I figured a day game would be better so we could eat afterwards.”

     

                Nodding in agreement, Lena watched as Kara fished her camera out of her bag, holding it up with a hopeful expression on her face. “Just one, I promise.”

     

                Agreeing with only a slight pout, she nestled up beside Kara, who put her arm around Lena’s shoulders and pressed her head up against hers. Lena hated having her photo taken, mostly due to a few bad experiences with the press, but she smiled widely for the camera as Kara clicked the button and the film started printing.

     

                Tucking it into the pocket of her jersey, Kara waited for a few minutes, both of them sipping their mercifully cold beer as the sweltering heat beat down on them from over the rim of the stadium roof. It would set within an hour or so, but Lena was grateful for the cap Kara had brought for her.

     

                After a few minutes, Kara pulled the photo out and held it up to show Lena their smiling faces, and Lena handled it delicately before Kara safely tucked it in her bag. Leaning in close, Lena’s lips brushed Kara’s ear as she spoke.

     

                “Why do you never take photos on your phone? I mean, the polaroids are cute but it would be easier.”

     

                Shrugging, Kara gave her a crooked smile, “yeah, it’s easier but it’s just not the same. I have a few cameras for work - film and digital - but there’s something magical about film. There are no do-overs; it’s permanent.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara’s face briefly clouded before she patted the bag by her feet, “and this camera was my dad’s. It’s one of the few things I have to remember him by.”

     

                “Shit, sorry. I really do like the polaroids though, I was just curious.”

     

                “It’s a fair point,” Kara replied, brushing off Lena’s concerns, “film isn’t nearly as popular these days, but … I don’t think I would’ve had a love for photography if not for this camera.”

     

                “Then I’m glad you have it.”

     

                Giving her a bright smile, Kara picked up a fry from the paper tray and popped it into her mouth. It was another twenty minutes before the game started but Lena was perfectly content to sit and drink her cheap beer, masking the bitter taste with barbeque sauce as they shared the fries, until players streamed onto the pitch.

     

                Although she’d researched it, Lena would’ve picked up the rules quickly anyway, finding the statistics easy to follow as batters took their turns, running around the pitch as the ball was sent wide. The atmosphere was the best part, and while the game wasn’t exactly riveting, it was interesting and the excitement of the crowd was palpable.

     

                During the seventh inning, they bought more beers, drinking them in the heat as they roasted, Lena feeling uncomfortably warm on the plastic seat. They finished them quickly while waiting for the game to resume, chatting over the noise, when a loud cheer cut them off and Lena’s eyes landed on the giant screen showing the audience.

     

                Watching with curiosity as couples and strangers leaned in to kiss, Lena leaned in to Kara, “why are they all kissing?”

     

                “It’s a kiss cam! The cameramen single people - usually couples - out in the crowd to make them kiss. It’s a bit of fun.”

     

                As the next couple kissed, Kara added her voice to the cheers, laughing as she shook her head, and then Lena’s eyes went wide with surprise as she saw the next unsuspecting person show up on the screen. It was Kara.

     

                Lena frowned slightly as she jerked back to stare at her, her glance moving to the guy on the other side of Kara who turned to face her, raising his eyebrows suggestively. Lena didn’t know how to explain the sinking feeling in her stomach as her insides writhed with jealousy. Turning back to the screen, Lena couldn’t bear to look at Kara directly, feeling flustered and irritated at the stranger sitting on the other side of her. She knew it was all fun, but it left her disgruntled, clenching her teeth as she tried to ignore the uncomfortable feeling. 

     

                And then she felt someone tapping her and her head whipped around to face Kara, who was looking at her with a helpless smile, shrugging slightly as her eyebrows raised. Lena’s eyes darted down to Kara’s lips as her own parted, and whatever the look on her face was, Kara understood because she leant in and captured Lena’s lips with her own. Taking them both by surprise, Lena pushed back against her, eyes closed as she grabbed a handful of Kara’s shirt, the dull roar of the crowd washing over her as she felt herself flush.

     

                It was only a moment, but Lena couldn’t move, couldn’t speak, couldn’t do anything but stare at Kara with parted lips as she watched her raise her hand in a wave as the crowd whistled and cheered. Lips tingling and her heart pounding, Lena felt hot all over and noticed that Kara was blushing furiously too.

     

                The guy on the other side of Kara seemed as shocked as Lena felt, and as soon as the camera had moved on, Kara leant in, her nose wrinkling apologetically. “Sorry, I didn’t want to leave the camera hanging.”

     

                “Oh, yeah, no, it’s- it’s fine. That was … yeah.”

     

                Glancing sideways at Kara, Lena shifted in her seat and tried for an air of nonchalance as she squeezed her empty plastic cup, wishing for more beer. She couldn’t think straight for the rest of the game, the Sharks cinching a win as the stadium cheered, and as they joined the flow of foot traffic out the exits, Lena said yes when Kara asked if she wanted to grab a drink.

     

                They found the nearest bar, the folding windows open to the bustling street to alleviate some of the heat from too many bodies packed in, while fans worked overtime to dispel the stuffiness. Sitting on stools near the windows, a small round bar table to themselves, Lena ordered a gin and tonic for herself and a tequila slammer for Kara, sneaking a shot of vodka at the bar to calm her nerves before she carried the drinks back.

     

                Loud music was drowned out by loud voices and Lena had to shout as she gave Kara an unsteady smile and set her drink down in front of her. “One tequila slammer.”

                

                “Thank you! What did you get?”

     

                “Gin and tonic. Would you like a sip?”

     

                Leaning in closer, Kara took a sip from the straw Lena angled towards her and hummed as she lowered herself back down onto her stool, “not bad. Want to try?”

     

                Trying her drink, Lena agreed that it was good and they finished them quickly, followed by another round. So engrossed in their conversation, the drinks going to their heads, so dehydrated from sitting in the sun for hours that both of them quickly became tipsy, and with that, Lena grew loose-lipped and more relaxed, laughing and at ease, despite the lingering panic at the fact that Kara had kissed her.

     

                It was just shy of midnight when they finally left the bar, without even meaning to stay out so late as time passed them by while the rest of the world carried on, and Lena called her driver to come and pick them up from the street corner they lingered on. Pacing back and forth beneath the orange glow of a streetlight, the night still warm as music spilled from an all-night shawarma and cars blew past, their headlights blinding as they washed the two young women out for a brief moment. Kara was telling Lena about her friends in the military while she balanced along the edge of the curb with her arms outstretched for balance.

     

                “So, Winn is in communications - he’s like … really good with computers. James and Lucy are dating, but Lucy works as a prosecutor, so she’s mostly in Metropolis, but James is a photojournalist in Afghanistan with me. Alex is dating his sister; she’s an ex-military psychologist. I’ve got a few friends here too; Nia was a freshman in college when I was graduating and she’s kept in touch. And there’s her boyfriend, Querl.”

     

                “And what does Alex do?”

     

                “She’s a pharmacist. Our mom is in medicine, so she followed after her.”

     

                “Interesting,” Lena said with a short laugh, “my mom is also in medicine. She runs a lab now, with a focus in biomedical engineering.”

     

                “Oh, that’s interesting. They’d probably get along then.”

     

                Wincing, Lena gave Kara a pained look, “oh, no. If your mom is anything like you, I would never wish it upon her to be within a hundred feet of my mother. She makes me look downright warm.”

     

                “I think you’re warm.”

     

                “You might be the only one.” 

     

                Scoffing, Kara stopped her balancing act and stepped away from the edge of the road, gripping the streetlight and slowly swinging around it as she grinned like a child. “Well, from what they’ve heard from me , my friends can’t wait to meet you.”

     

                A guarded look crept into Lena’s face as her eyes flickered with wariness, stomach tying itself into knots. “You- you … told them about me?”

     

                “Of course! They’ve been giving me shit about it since we met. ”

     

                “You want me to meet them?”

     

                Opening her mouth, Kara quickly closed it as her face crumpled with the dawning realisation that maybe Lena wouldn’t like that. “Well … you don’t have to, I’ve just told them so much about you - nothing personal, of course - that they’re … interested. And Alex has a knack for picking up on this sort of thing.”

     

                “What thing? Secret friends?”

     

                “When I like someone,” Kara softly admitted, a certain shyness to her as she spoke the words, the orange glow softening her features. 

     

                Lena didn’t know what to say, standing in the circle of light as she opened and closed her mouth, thinking of the kiss, thinking of how she’d wanted to kiss Kara before that. It confused her that Kara might have thought that too, and not just because of the kiss camera.

     

                “You … like me?”

     

                Groaning, Kara winced as she wrinkled her nose, “ignore me. Please. I know, I know. We barely know each other, you’re too busy, we’re just friends . And … I’m a little bit drunk right now and I’m going to be mortified in the morning, so ...”

     

                “So … when you kissed me it was because … you like me?”

     

                Throwing her head back, Kara covered her face with her hands, “oh God , it sounds so much worse when you say it out loud.”

     

                Face crumpling with confusion, unsure of what to make of it all, considering the fact that Lena liked being alone, liked to remain detached and aloof. But also liked that Kara might like her too. She felt conflicted even as a warmth spread through her chest, and Lena reached out to pull Kara’s hands away from her face.

     

                They stared at each other for a long moment, the silence between them weighted as the air felt charged with tension. Standing in the halo of light from the lamppost, the edges of her mind pleasantly blurred, Lena didn’t know who moved first, only that one moment she was staring at Kara, her fingers gripping her wrists in her clammy hands, her heart in her throat as she tried to articulate her thoughts.

     

                And the next, she was kissing Kara, one of them - or both - bridging the space between each other, their lips brushing gently as if to test it. Her eyes were squeezed shut and Lena stiffened slightly, hardly daring to believe it as she felt Kara’s fingers brush her cheeks, the side of her neck, the collar of her borrowed shirt. She pushed back against her, grasping a handful of Kara’s shirt as she let out a quiet gasp, her lips parting, and reached up to cup the back of her neck.

     

                The night had taken a turn that neither of them expected and when they separated, Lena’s eyes were wide and her lips tingling as she found the air close, leaving her breathless. Kara was pink-cheeked, and there was an almost curious look in her eyes, as if she didn’t quite comprehend what had happened, neither of them speaking. 

     

                Before she could muster the courage to speak, to take a step towards Kara and take her hand, to kiss her again, soft and sweet, a car pulled up in the light of the streetlight and Lena turned her attention to the towncar. 

     

                Kara turned around and her shoulders drooped as she watched the driver climb out and open the door. Murmuring her thanks, she slipped into the backseat, leaving Lena on the sidewalk, staring at the empty space she’d occupied as something inside her felt jittery and tight. Blinking herself out of it, Lena ran a hand over her face and climbed into the car, buckling up and sitting rigidly in her seat as the driver took Kara home. And the entire way there, all she could think about was that kiss; Lena knew that she’d remember it for the rest of her life.

    Chapter 7

                Lena didn’t see Kara for the rest of the following work week, swamped with so much work that she barely had time to sleep before she was back at the office, the dinner with Jack on Monday night a success that had her pushing to close the deal by Friday. It was going to be a big acquisition for the company, sinking in a fortune that would potentially double their profits with the schematics Lena had in place for their future technology. 

     

                In anticipation of closing the deal, she sent Kara a text inviting her to dinner at her house on Friday night, having Jess pick a recipe from one of the cookbooks Lena had her pick up but hadn’t had time to crack open. As busy as she was, she was still intent on cooking dinner herself, as disastrous as it undoubtedly would be, and was out of the office just before the masses clocked out, riding the elevator down alone, away from the stares and whispers that she knew had been circulating. 

     

                One of the tasks she gave Jess was to keep an ear out for office gossip, anxious to know if she was doing a good job at handling things in each sector. The only time her name had passed lips recently amongst the lower level employees was to talk about the fleeting mention of Lena’s dating life in the tabloids with a blurry photo of her and Kara on the kiss cam at the baseball game. It wasn’t the first time Lena had appeared in a magazine, occasionally stalked by the paparazzi when something big was happening at the company - although she didn’t know why people were so invested in the life of a billionaire who barely qualified as a celebrity - but it was the first time in recent months that it had been without the slanderous comments that had dogged her steps for a while now.

     

                It normally didn’t bother her, but when Kara was involved, it made her chafe at the scrutiny and hoped it would die off soon. Pensive on her drive home, listening to the radio as she caught up with the news, Lena beat traffic hour and was flagging by the time she made it home, her eyes burning from too many late or sleepless nights.

     

                Punching the espresso button on the coffee machine, she sipped from the little cup, hoping the caffeine would carry her through the dinner, before she made her way upstairs to shower. Changing into a beige linen shirt and cream cropped jeans, Lena padded barefoot down to the kitchen and cracked open the cookbook to the page with the little sticky note Jess had placed there for her. It was a recipe for creamy herb chicken, reading relatively easy as Lena frowned, poring over the steps. 

     

                Everything had been ordered and delivered and Lena put the kitchen to use for the first time, the patio doors open to the warm afternoon as she boiled potatoes and dipped the chicken breasts in the onion and garlic powders and added them to the frying pan with oil. Cooking them five minutes either side, as instructed, she set them aside and added garlic cloves with freshly picked parsley, thyme and rosemary before adding the cream. Stirring it until it was thick, Lena eyed the bubbling pan of sauce until the potatoes started boiling over and stole her attention.

     

                Things only seemed to get progressively worse as she tried to juggle the cooking, her face flushed from the steam and the still air outside that only served to make the kitchen more humid, and by the time Kara knocked on the door at six o’clock, Lena was woefully unprepared. Something definitely smelled like it was burning.

     

                Wearing a pristine apron, Lena swore as she quickly put on her lipstick and fixed her hair before walking towards the door. Pulling it open with an uneven smile, she took in the sight of Kara, wearing a worn red and navy striped polo rugby shirt and holding a bouquet of flowers. 

     

                “Hi!” Lena said, drawing in a deep breath and exhaling fully as she tried to calm herself, “come in.”

     

                “Hi,” Kara murmured, a wariness in her eyes as she held the flowers out, “these are for you.”

     

                Heart stumbling in her chest, Lena reached out to take them, a soft look of wonder on her face. It was the first time anyone had ever bought her flowers. “They’re beautiful. Thank you.”

     

                Catching her hand, Kara eyed the band-aid on Lena’s finger and raised her eyebrows, “cooking up a storm?”

     

                Flushing, Lena gestured for her to move into the foyer, watching as Kara’s eyes went round as she looked around the place. It was modest, given Lena’s hefty bank account, but it was understatedly luxurious inside, from the brocade walls to the crown moulding on the ceilings, to the trifling decorations that only the wealthy would waste money on; marble busts of Greek philosophers and artfully arranged coffee table books that would’ve sat there collecting dust, if not for Lena’s housekeeper. Feeling self-conscious, Lena retreated deeper into the house with Kara in tow.

     

                Nerves knotted Lena’s stomach - not least of all because of the kiss hanging unmentioned between them - and she could hear Kara’s footsteps behind her, slow, and knew she would be taking everything in with wide-eyed wonder. Leading her through to the kitchen, Lena cleared her throat and turned around, flowers in hand.

     

                “So, how’ve you been?” Lena asked as she took a vase off the kitchen counters and filled it with water, adding the flowers and adjusting the arrangement.

     

                “Oh … um, good, yeah,” Kara slowly replied, looking mildly surprised as she tore herself away from studying Lena’s home. “And yourself?”

     

                Grinning widely, Lena tried to keep the smugness out of her voice, “good! You’re looking at the new owner of Spheerical Industries. As of today.”

     

                Eyebrows rising, Kara’s mouth fell open, “you- you closed the deal?”

     

                “Mhm,” Lena smiled, fetching the bottle of champagne from the fridge where she’d left it to chill. “I thought we could celebrate with something nice tonight.”

     

                “Champagne?”

     

                “I’ve been waiting to drink it and tonight seemed perfect.”

     

                Brow furrowing, Kara wrinkled her nose faintly, “does … something smell burnt to you?”

     

                “Shit,” Lena swore, setting the bottle down and turning to her bubbling sauce, “um, no, everything’s fine. I’ve just been … a little scattered this week. Not a lot of time for sleep.”

     

                Letting out a strained laugh, Lena was glad her back was to Kara as she flushed, stirring the creamy sauce, which she could feel was sticking to the bottom of the pan. Raking a hand through her hair, Lena cleared her throat.

     

                “Um, I’ll just … turn this off until we eat. Do you want to sit outside?”

     

                “Sure.”

     

                Snagging the bottle, Lena gave Kara a sheepish smile and gestured for her to make her way out onto the patio, leaves skittering across the wide paving stones as a light breeze disturbed the early evening. The lights strung between the house and the trees that were technically Lena’s property cast a homely glow over the small table she’d set up, champagne flutes and linen napkins and the cutlery all neatly arranged.

     

                While Kara took a seat, Lena popped the cork on the champagne bottle and filled the flutes before setting the bottle down. She settled down on her own seat and took a sip, the taste light and sweet and cool as she swallowed, and she studied Kara, who was looking up at the facade of the house.

     

                “You live here all by yourself?”

     

                Tilting her head to the side as she smiled, Lena twirled the stem of her glass between her fingers, “I do.”

     

                “It’s … gorgeous. ”

     

                “Mm,” Lena hummed in agreement, “I had it restored when I bought the place. I prefer something more … modest .”

     

                “Modest?” Kara choked. “It’s- it’s got four floors!”

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena rolled a shoulder in a half-hearted manner, “if you- if you knew where I grew up … this is … well, the townhouse we have in London for business trips is more ostentatious.”

     

                “Jesus.”

     

                “Do you want a tour?”

     

                Hesitating, Kara bit her lip, “is that … okay?”

     

                “Sure.” Setting her glass down, Lena pushed herself to her feet, beckoning for Kara to follow after her. “Come on.”

     

                Kara quickly climbed to her feet and followed after her as Lena took them back in through the back door. Waving a hand at the spacious kitchen, which Kara had already studied, they went through to the dining room, decorated in the same muted tones, the white walls and wooden floors and minimalist paintings. Crossing the foyer, Lena took Kara into the living room, cream cotton sofas facing each other, a white fireplace with the white plastered wall showing a large patch of red brick above it. A large TV dominated the wall opposite it, and the tall windows let in the last of the buttery spring sunlight, painting the room yellow. 

     

                Walking around the room, Kara eyed the paintings and brushed a hand across the back of the camel leather armchair tucked in by the window, eyed the crystal decanters of whiskeys and scotch on a sideboard, and the marble chess set on the coffee table, before her eyes landed on the wide cabinet at the far end of the room. A wooden record player sat on top, with a long row of vinyls neatly catalogued in the unit and she glanced over at Lena.

     

                “What’s the last album you listened to?”

     

                Giving her a self-conscious smile, Lena moved over to her side and plucked an album from the long row, turning it over in her hands to reveal the black and white cover. “Billie Holiday. I’ll Be Seeing You.”

     

                Reaching for it, taking note of the 1944 on the cover and realising how old it was, Kara raised her eyebrows with a hopeful look on her face. “Can I?”

     

                She gestured to the record player and Lena nodded, watching as Kara raised the plastic cover of the machine and then carefully slipped the red record from its sleeve. The tinkling sound of piano keys lightly played throughout the room from the small speakers, before the sound of the trumpet swelled and the rich vocals started singing.

     

                “It’s good,” Kara said after a long moment of the two of them standing in silence. “You like old music?”

     

                Shrugging, Lena smiled slightly, “I just like what I like. Classical. Eighties synth. Pop. Rap. Rock. You have to try everything once, right?”

     

                They moved on to another sitting room at the back of the house, lacking the same personal, lived-in feeling as the other rooms in the house, with a large, worn cello propped up in one corner of the room like a bizarre decoration. Kara pointed to it with a perplexed look on her face.

     

                Letting out a loud laugh, Lena clapped her hands together, “ah, I was a very proficient cellist at one point. And I hated it. Mostly because my mother refused to let me quit, but also because I just really had no interest in playing instruments. I mean … who plays the cello , right? Anyway, I played it for eight years before I caused such a fuss that I was allowed to stop. I used to saw at the strings for hours, just a … horrible grating sound, and I guess it eventually drove her insane. Now … I have fond memories of my cello.”

     

                Covering her mouth as she tried to stifle a laugh, Kara gave her a reproving look, “you were a troublemaker?”

     

                “No. I was actually a shy child. Smart, obviously, and stubborn as hell, but I didn’t really cause that much trouble. I just- if I didn’t want to do something, no one on earth could make me. Nothing’s changed.”

     

                “That’s good.”

     

                “I think so.”

     

                Taking her to the bathroom and then downstairs to the home gym, the brick walls and polished concrete, floor mats for her weekly Muay Thai and boxing lessons with her personal trainer, a spin bike and treadmill and various weights and bands and balls. A rack of rolled towels and a fridge of water bottles and plants breathing life into the room, while at the far end stood a small sauna and a plunge pool.

     

                One the first floor, she opened and closed the doors to various spare bedrooms, made up with piles of sheets and blankets, all neutral shades of pale greens and greys and beige and cream with complementing furniture and knick-knacks to make them seem homely, even though Lena hadn’t set foot in them since the first time she’d nosed around her newly furnished house. There was another bathroom and a reading nook, and then they were on the third floor, Lena’s bedroom only showing signs of being lived in in the stack of books and magazines on the bedside table. 

     

                “And now, my favourite place in the house,” Lena said, already mounting the staircase to the fourth floor as she smiled over her shoulder at Kara before hesitating, “and perhaps the most boring too.”

     

                Kara looked around with interest as she stepped out into the wide office, the place more lived-in with schematics still pinned on the drawing board, the large table a web of sticky notes and scrawled writing in the margins of the documents piled there, disassembled pieces of equipment and the corners of large blueprints weighed down with heavy textbooks and fine-tipped tools. 

     

                “This is your office?”

     

                “Mhm,” Lena smiled uncertainly, “if I’m not at the office … I’m usually here.”

     

                With a burst of laughter, Kara shook her head at her with a bemused look, “do you ever stop working?”

     

                “Not really. Too much paperwork. All the time. I barely have time to sleep half of the time.”

     

                “You look tired,” Kara noted, her voice softening as her eyes roamed over Lena’s face, taking in the bruised shadows beneath her eyes.

     

                Running a hand over her weary face, Lena smiled ruefully, “I was up all night finalising the proposal for the deal today.”

     

                “Wait, you- you haven’t slept yet?”

     

                “I’m a bit of a night owl,” Lena waved away her concerns, “most of the time I can’t sleep, which is why I spend so much time on paperwork.”

     

                “You should have invited me on a different night so you could’ve slept,” Kara gently scolded her.

     

                Waving a hand, Lena gave her a shy smile, “I wanted to celebrate and I … well, I know I’ve been busy this week and we haven’t talked much, so I- I wanted to see you.”

     

                “You- you did?”

     

                “Yeah.”

     

                “Oh. It’s just that- nevermind, we should eat, right?”

     

                Surprise slowly dawned on Lena’s face, a gentle look that kindled confusion inside her, her stomach knotting uncomfortably as her eyes tried to pierce the restless evasion of Kara’s body language, her shoulders taut beneath her polo shirt as she fiddled with her fingers.

     

                “Right,” Lena said after a moment, feeling the conversation slip through her fingers, unable to catch the end of it and reel it back in. She felt like she was missing something and it left her feeling hollow with worry.

     

                Making the trip back downstairs, Lena sent Kara outside with a fleeting smile and turned her attention to their dinner. Two plates were set out and Lena scooped the mashed potato onto them before adding the chicken she’d set aside and scooping sauce over it. As she scraped the bottom of the pan, black bits were mixed into the sauce, which was more like a paste than cream, and she quietly swore, panic settling in as she untied her apron.

     

                Carrying the plates outside, she set one down before Kara and took her seat, shaking out her napkin and refilling their champagne as she watched Kara like a hawk, waiting for her to take the first bite as she complimented the look of it. Cutting through the chicken breast, Kara chewed and gave Lena a crinkly smile, which alleviated some of the tension enough for her to take her own bite.
