                Chewing her mouthful, Lena slowed, coughing slightly as she covered her mouth, and forced the lump of food down. Watching as Kara took a slow sip of champagne, her cheeks turning rosy, Lena narrowed her eyes and set her knife and fork down.

     

                “How is it?”

     

                “It’s good.”

     

                “You’re lying.”

     

                “No, I’m not.”

     

                With a short bark of laughter, Lena picked up her cutlery and cut through the chicken breast to reveal the centre, still a little pink, while the outside was crispy. And the mash … lumpy. Not to mention the burnt sauce. Groaning, Lena set her cutlery back down and covered her face as Kara looked at her innocently.

     

                “You’re a bad liar. I know, because I’m a good liar and I know when I’m being lied to. And you’re clearly very bad at knowing when you’re being lied to or you would’ve known the minute I told you I could cook that it was a horrible lie.”

     

                “Hey, it’s not that bad. It’s just … a little undercooked.”

     

                “I might not have cooked chicken before, but even I know it’s not supposed to be pink .”

     

                “I mean … yeah, but-”

     

                “I’ve never used the kitchen before,” Lena blurted out, flushing with embarrassment, “I mean … I use it to heat up food that my- my housekeeper sometimes leaves for me, but I- the most I can manage is toast. But you seemed excited at the thought so I had my assistant buy me cookbooks and I- well … I can’t cook.”

     

                Amusement lighting up her face, Kara stared at Lena with a mild look of incredulity, “you could’ve just said that. We could’ve just … ordered pizza.”

     

                “Let me go and … sort something out,” Lena heavily sighed, abruptly climbing to her feet and whisking both plates away, her shoulders hunched and tense as she felt her cheeks flame. 

     

                The scraping sound of chair legs on stone grated against her ears and Lena set the plates down and gripped the edge of the counter as Kara walked in. Her footsteps were slow and wary as she crept up behind Lena and stood there for a moment.

     

                “Do you want me to go?”

     

                “Wha- I- no . I just- God , I’m not good at this Kara. I don’t know how to- to cook dinner and go to carnivals for fun and have friends. I just-”

     

                “I don’t care about all of that,” Kara scoffed before her voice softened, “I just like talking to you.”

     

                Wincing, Lena closed her eyes, a muscle twitching in her jaw as she clenched her teeth, “I’m not good at that either.”

     

                “Look, I know that I- I kissed you. I’m sorry if you didn’t- if I was reading too much into-”

     

                Turning around, Lena gave her an agonised look, “no, no, it’s not about that.”

     

                Drawing in a deep breath as she leant back, Lena pressed her lips together and stared at the floor for a long moment before she exhaled fully, the tension bleeding out of her. Rubbing at her forehead, Lena swallowed.

     

                “I just … don’t know how to- to have a normal life. Sometimes … I feel like I was born middle-aged and other times I feel like I’m a child. I’m twenty-four and I … have more money than I know what to do with. I mean, I have this house, I have multiple businesses and a whole bunch of degrees when I should still be finishing up grad school … and I can’t even cook chicken . Isn’t that just … stupid?”

     

                A smile playing on her lips, Kara shrugged slightly, “it’s funny.”

     

                “And I like you, I do , and that scares the shit out of me because … I don’t have any friends, Kara. I’m not … good at this.”

     

                Lena’s voice trailed off into a brooding whisper as she reached forward to hook a finger through the loop of Kara’s jeans, gently tugging her forward as she gave her a troubled look. Kara let her, reaching out to cradle Lena’s waist as they stood almost nose to nose, music still softly playing in the background as Lena ducked her head, fiddling with the belt loop as she struggled to speak.

     

                “I really like you though.”

     

                “I really like you too.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose as she smiled slightly, an ache in her chest as she felt her throat constrict, the suffocating feeling that she might cry creeping up on her, Lena tilted her head to the side and looked up at Kara.

     

                “Will you kiss me again?”

     

                Quietly laughing, Kara reached up to brush the hair from Lena’s neck before she cradled the other side of it, thumb pressing into the underside of Lena’s jaw as she leant in and kissed the pale stretch of her skin. Pulling her closer, Lena let out a shuddering breath as she closed her eyes, feeling Kara’s fingertips gently dig into the back of her neck as she kissed Lena’s pulse point, feeling her erratic heartbeat.

     

                Nose skimming along Lena’s jaw, Kara lightly kissed her way to her lips before drawing back and running her fingers through Lena’s hair, staring at her for a moment with a quiet look of wonder.

     

                “You are … the single most interesting person I’ve ever bumped into in this city. I don’t care if you can’t cook, if you don’t have any other friends, or if you spend all of your time working. I already like you as you are so … you don’t have to try for me, Lena.”

     

                “I’m not used to being liked,” Lena thickly murmured, “I’ve … always had to try so …”

     

                Thumbs gently brushing her high cheekbones, Kara gave her a small smile and then kissed her. It was different from their first kiss, and even the second. The third was gentle and expected, both of them coming together as Lena closed her eyes and pressed herself against Kara, wrapping an arm around her waist as she felt Kara bite her lip, the sharp pain jolting her stomach.

     

                Pulling back, Lena eyed her with surprise as Kara’s breath fanned across her mouth, so warm, her lips reddened and slightly swollen, that she looked at her for only a brief moment before she kissed her again. The counter dug into her lower back and Lena could hear her heartbeat in her eyes, thudding loudly, taste the sweetness of the champagne on Kara’s tongue.

     

                She wasn’t sure at which point they’d started stumbling towards the stairs, dinner forgotten about as wrapped up in each other as they were, but next thing she knew, she was being ushered up the steps, her lips still on Kara’s as she stumbled up each one blindly. Until Kara picked her up with surprising ease, eliciting a gasp from Lena as her eyes flew open, staring into Kara’s, which were bright with mischief, and was carried up to the second floor.

     

                “Which room?” Kara murmured, kissing the corner of Lena’s mouth as she ran her fingers through her hair.

     

                “Any.”

     

                Lena didn’t tell Kara her room was up a floor, and she couldn’t say why she didn’t, but perhaps some part of her knew that it would mean more in her bed where she slept. Instead, she pulled Kara by the front of her shirt and slipped into the nearest spare bedroom. Lena got the curtains as Kara eased the door shut and then they looked at each other for a moment, daring each other to make the next move.

     

                In a fumbling rush, they undressed, the act interspersed with kisses, and Lena felt her earlier doubts abate until they were nothing but fading thoughts on the edge of her mind and she forgot what had made her feel so anxious only minutes beforehand. And afterwards, lying amidst the pile of pillows and blankets as sweat dried on her skin and her pulse slowed, Lena felt too comfortable to move, her eyes leaden and the room stiflingly warm.

     

                “Was it okay?”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena turned her head to the side to meet Kara’s eyes, her hands fumbling across the blankets to brush against Kara’s fingers as she smiled unevenly. “Yeah. Yeah it was … perfect.”

     

                Softly smiling, a pleased curl to the corner of her mouth, Kara turned her hand over beneath Lena’s touch to lace their fingers together, and neither of them moved, quietly breathing as they lingered in the moment as it stretched out around them, enveloping them, the rest of the world quiet and distant outside of the bedroom door. Lena could’ve fallen asleep right there.

     

                “Lena?”

     

                “Mm,” she hummed.

     

                “I’m going to go,” Kara said after a moment, “you look tired; you should sleep.”

                

                Peeling her eyelids open, Lena pushed herself up onto her elbow as a crease formed between her eyebrows, “no, no, don’t go. We haven’t even had dinner yet. Let me … order pizza or Chinese. I’d cook for you again, but I don’t think either of us want to repeat that so soon.”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Kara studied her face for a moment before pushing herself up and climbing out of bed. Picking up her clothes, she dressed quickly while Lena pursed her lips with a sinking feeling in her stomach. Aware of the fact that Lena hadn’t moved, Kara glanced over at her as she buttoned her jeans up.

     

                “Come on.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “I’m going to cook you dinner.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena bared her teeth in a rueful look, “you don’t have to do that. Honestly. I’ll order us something.”

     

                “I want to. I came all the way here for your herb garden and I’d be sad if I didn’t get to try something from it.”

     

                Blushing slightly, Lena got out of bed and dressed, hopping after Kara as she struggled with one leg in her jeans. Following her downstairs, ruffling her tangled hair, Lena stepped into the kitchen to find Kara rummaging through her fridge, perfectly at ease as she made a pile in her hands. Smiling brightly at Lena, seeming younger without her glasses on, Kara moved over to the counter and set her armful down.

     

                “How does steak sound?”

     

                “Oh, um, perfect.”

     

                “How do you like yours cooked? Please say medium-rare.”

     

                With a chuckle, Lena nodded, moving to take the plates with her own cooking and quickly scrape away the evidence of it into the trash. She loaded the dishwasher and fetched new plates and cutlery, eyeing Kara out of the side of her eye as she confidently moved around the kitchen, opening cupboards to look for pots and knives and bowls.

     

                The kitchen was soon filled with the smell of meat cooking, Kara spooning melted butter over the filet mignon as it cooked with garlic and rosemary, plucked from Lena’s herb garden. She’d also been sent to gather parsley and basil, and as the steaks seared, Kara deftly chopped cucumber and avocado while Lena washed lettuce leaves in the sieve.

     

                Dinner was ready in no time, Kara setting a steak on each plate, beside the herb salad, sprinkly snow pea sprouts on top and drizzling on the lemon and mustard dressing. The sun had fully vanished and cicadas sang in the underbrush below the patio, stars speckling the sky overhead, and they ate in the glow of the string lights, drinking the whole bottle of champagne between them as they talked. Lena’s chest felt lighter, the knot of unease gone in wake of the admission, both of them understanding each other a little better now, she hoped.

     

                Even then, Lena found herself more willing to open up to Kara, sharing a few stories from boarding school, her birthday, her favourite colour (moss green) and the first time she’d broken a bone, when she’d fallen off her horse at nine and fractured her wrist. It was perhaps the most she’d shared with someone in a long while, perhaps ever, outside of her family, of course, but it didn’t feel like it left her vulnerable, providing the weaknesses for Kara to use against her. Instead, it felt like the most effortlessly natural conversation she’d ever had, both of them giving and taking as they cleared their plates. 

     

                And after, eating pistachio gelato from little bowls, Lena caught Kara staring at her with a mystified look in her blue eyes, made darker by the dark, and while she found no judgement there, it was an unfamiliar expression.

     

                “What is it?”

     

                “Nothing,” Kara said, smiling down at her bowl as she scooped up a spoonful, “I- you’re just … a lot different than I expected.”

     

                “Really? How?”

     

                With a breathless laugh, Kara shrugged helplessly, shaking her head, “I don’t know. The first time I met you … you seemed so serious. And you are , but I thought you were so mature, so good at everything, but … you have a herb garden and you have The Hunger Games on your bedside table and you can’t cook. You feel … very real to me.”

     

                “Real? I feel real? How did I feel before?”

     

                “Too good to be true. Maybe you still are, I don’t know, but … it’s funny to see you in your own home. You’re still just as witty and- and warm -”

     

                “Warm? I don’t think that’s something I’ve ever been called.” 

     

                “Maybe they just didn’t take the time to get to know you better,” Kara gently replied, a smile on her lips. 

     

                A slow smile curled one side of Lena’s mouth and she fiddled with her spoon, letting her hair fall in a dark sheet around her face. “Maybe I didn’t want them to. Until you.”

     

                “Why me?”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena couldn’t even begin to fathom what exactly it had been about Kara that had just felt so comforting. It wasn’t just her kindness - Lena knew many kind people - or the fact that she’d been brave enough to interrupt Lena’s work, something that would ordinarily have irritated Lena. It wasn’t that she was so approachable, so earnest and her smile put you at ease, it was everything about her. 

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena honestly replied, a bewildered look on her face as her voice dropped to a low murmur, “all I know is that my walls are five feet thick, and you didn’t break them down, you just- you walked right in like you had the key. And that … scares the shit out of me and makes me want to cry, all at the same time.”

    Chapter 8

                Monday morning was grey and muggy, a thin haze lingering over the city as Lena made her way to the office. She’d woken up at five to work out and then gotten ready for work, beating the heavy traffic, but not the lone photographer linger outside L-Corp, snapping photos of her as she swept into the building with a disgruntled look on her face. The office was quiet and Jess wasn’t there yet when Lena stepped off the elevator and swept past her assistant’s desk.

     

                Hanging up her coat and stowing her bag, Lena was halfway through the influx of emails that had been pre-screened and colour-coded according to importance by Jess when her assistant stepped into the office, a newspaper tucked under her arm as she held a green juice and a tablet.

     

                “Good morning, Miss Luthor.”

     

                “Morning, Jess,” Lena said, looking up from her screen, “good weekend?”

     

                “It was quiet. I have a kale and green apple juice for you today, and here’s your schedule for the day. The weekly meeting with the department heads has been scheduled for lunch today; I’ve ordered catering from that sushi bar you like.”

     

                Nodding, Lena extended a hand for the newspaper that Jess was holding, taking in the uncertainty on her assistant’s face as Jess nervously shifted. “Thank you, Jess,” Lena pressed, “and the newspaper?”

     

                With a quiet sigh, Jess handed it over and Lena unfolded it to find her face on the cover, small at the top right of the page, alongside a photo of Kara in her military dress uniform, standing before the American flag. Biting back a curse, Lena tore open the newspaper to find the page number displayed on the front, and was greeted with the title Lovestruck Luthor , along with a reprint of the photo of her and Kara kissing. It seemed inevitable that the local news would find out from the gossip sites, although Lena still didn’t find it newsworthy, and it bothered her that they’d figured out Kara’s identity.

     

                Sometimes, she forgot that her life was so public, her every business decision scrutinised and anticipated by business journals and news sites, but it had never really crossed over into the realm of relationships before. Only her family’s private life had ever been under the microscope, and Lena could understand why, but this was something new and she wasn’t sure that she liked it.

     

                Heart racing, she pressed a clammy hand to her forehead, eyes scanning the article before she swallowed, her mouth dry, and looked up at Jess. Composing herself, Lena tossed the newspaper onto her desk, folded in half and hiding their faces, and cleared her throat.

     

                “That’ll be all,” Lena murmured.

     

                Jess was the same age as Lena, and it left her feeling uncomfortable at times, to know that the lives they led were so different, that Jess could’ve been her friend if Lena hadn’t been her boss, hadn’t been the boss of everyone in the company. She could see a flicker of what could’ve been in her assistant’s eyes as Jess hesitated, looking as if she was about to say something comforting, or perhaps encouraging, before she remembered her place and ducked her head in assent before backing out of the room. 

     

                Sipping her juice as she debated whether or not to tell Kara - would it freak her out? Or should Lena prepare her? - her phone vibrated on the desk and Lena glanced down, finding Kara’s name on the screen as if she’d summoned her. Setting her drink down, she picked up the phone and answered it.

     

                “Good morning,” Lena quietly murmured, a smile in her voice even as she stared at the newspaper with a twisting discomfort in her stomach.

     

                “Hi. I, uh, I know you must be busy, but I- Alex told me about some newspaper article.”

     

                Grimacing, Lena sighed, leaning back in her chair, “I’m looking at it right now. I should’ve warned you last week, but some gossip rag was running a story with the photo. I guess it’s picked up enough interest to make the local news.”

     

                “You … don’t sound mad.”

     

                “Mad? Why would I be mad?”

     

                “I just know how private you are.”

     

                With a small smile, Lena raked a hand through her hair, “I mean, yeah, I wish they hadn’t , but … I mostly care that they’re going to latch onto you now. After my brother … well, I don’t think any articles would be able to top what they were saying about me then. I had reporters and photographers outside the Metropolis office for weeks.”

     

                “Oh. Well, don’t worry about me . I can handle it.”

     

                “It’s fine, Kara. It’s not the first time I’ve been photographed kissing someone. I’m used to it. We’ll just have to be more careful next time; I’d rather not have to deal with it if I didn’t have to, and if my mother hasn’t already seen it, I’d prefer not to give her more chances to find out.”

     

                “Next time?”

     

                “Well … I was hoping it wasn’t just the one time.”

     

                “When can I see you again?”

     

                Lena’s lips twisted into a smile and she bit her lip as she picked up a pen and idly tapped it on her desk, thinking. “How about dinner tonight?

     

                “Dinner? At a restaurant or are you-”

     

                Letting out a laugh that was more of a groan, Lena put her face in her hand as her shoulders shook, “please don’t remind me again. I’m never cooking again!”

     

                “Well … if you don’t want to order take-out, I can cook.”

     

                “You don’t have to cook.”

     

                “Are you kidding? I’m dying to get back into that kitchen; it’s so big and I bet your pantry has never been touched.”

     

                “I mean, I definitely only go in there for the wine.”

     

                “Such a waste,” Kara softly chided her, clicking her tongue.

     

                With a quiet laugh, Lena took a sip of her juice, a slow feeling of tenderness spreading through her as she listened to Kara’s voice, still a little rough from sleep. “Let me know what you need and I’ll get it delivered. I can leave a little bit early, so … shall we say five?”

     

                “Five is perfect.”

     

                Glancing up as her office door opened and Jess stepped inside before halting at the sight of Lena on the phone, Lena’s stolen moment of light-heartedness amidst the harrying routine of business came to a close and she let out a soft sigh as she nodded at Jess.

     

                “You have to go,” Kara guessed.

     

                Straightening up in her seat, Lena set her drink down, “as much as I’d love to spend my morning talking to you, my first meeting is about to start.”

     

                “Tonight then. I hope you have a good day.”

     

                “You too.”

     

                And with Kara’s orders, Lena resolved to at least try and enjoy herself, smoothing out her skirt as she presented herself for her first meeting, Sam stepping into the office and raising her eyebrows at the unfamiliar smile on Lena’s face.

     

                She wasn’t as aloof in her meetings and lingered a few minutes after the meeting over lunch to talk to the department heads about their weekend’s, and sent Jess home early for a change while she rushed through some spreadsheets and made note of which to revisit tomorrow. Lena was out of the office early, right in time for the rain that offered no relief from the humidity.

     

                Peeling off her wet coat and heels at the door, she had a quick shower and dressed in a thin turtleneck and pressed slacks, putting her damp hair up as she moved through the house, putting on Blue by Joni Mitchell and deliberated over wine’s as she eyed the ingredients that had been delivered and wondered what Kara was making. 

     

                Sitting in the armchair in the front living room, Lena distracted herself with The White Album, a volume of essays by Joan Didion as she listened to the rain pelt the tall windows, the sunlight weak as the house creaked and groaned and held a chill to it that was welcome, if only because National City was uncomfortably warm and Lena had started missing the cold and rain. She slid one of the windows up a fraction to breathe in the aroma of sweet peaches and lemon from the magnolia trees outside.

     

                There was a knock on the door right on time at five o’clock and Lena let the armchair hold her page as she pushed herself to her feet. Stepping into the long hallway of the foyer she pulled the door open to reveal a soaking wet Kara, smiling brightly with a damp paper bag peeking out from the top of her raincoat as she held it protectively against her chest and a small potted plant in hand.

     

                “Hi!” Kara said, grinning on the stoop as flecks of rain speckled her glasses. 

     

                “God, you’re soaked,” Lena tutted, opening the door for her to come in, “did you walk?”

     

                “No, I got a cab. Well, I did walk, but only from the closest bakery. This is for you; I noticed you didn’t have fennel.”

     

                Kara kissed Lena’s cheek and handed her the little pot, and Lena felt a funny twinge in her chest as she watched Kara shed the thin parka, revealing a damp Levi’s t-shirt, faded with a hole in the collar, and removed a bag of pastries. 

     

                “Thank you,” Lena said before her expression clouded, “you should’ve called me to pick you up.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively as she kicked her boots off and tucked them in beneath the coat rack, Kara brushed her wet hair out of her face. “It was fine. The rain is warm here and I miss it when I’m gone.”

     

                “Well at least have a shower; you can’t sit here in wet clothes all night. Let me get you something dry.” 

     

                Directing her to the bathroom, Lena rushed upstairs and rifled through her clothes for something that would fit Kara’s taller frame, coming up with a navy sweater and her loose cashmere pants before she made her way back downstairs and rapped her knuckles on the door and opened it.

     

                The bathroom was steamed up, a wall of heat hitting her from the shower that pounded on the slate floors, and Lena set the clothes down on the counter as she shouted over the sound of running water, “clothes are next to the sink.”

     

                “Thank you!”

     

                Retreating, Lena shut the door behind her and walked to the kitchen to put the pot of fennel out in the rain until she could plant it alongside the other herbs, smiling as she watched the feathery leaves bowed beneath the raindrops. 

     

                Leaving the doors open, the air still warm despite the rain, Lena dithered in the kitchen until Kara emerged, rosy-cheeked in Lena’s clothes, towelling her hair dry as she squinted slightly without her glasses. She looked softer, younger even, and Lena couldn’t describe why she liked the sight of Kara in her clothes, or why exactly she’d picked a colour that made her eyes look cerulean against it.

     

                “I need a pair of these pants,” Kara said, wrinkling her nose with a smile, “I don’t think I’ve ever worn something so soft.”

     

                Quietly laughing, Lena made a note to order a pair for her and moved to take the towel from Kara as she lowered it, holding it uselessly in her hands. “Here. What did you do with your clothes?”

     

                “I hung them on the towel rack. Hopefully they dry before I go.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena smiled faintly, “I’ll have them dry cleaned and returned to you.”

     

                “No, no, you don’t need to do that.”

     

                “Do you need anything there for tomorrow?”

     

                “Well … no.”

     

                Taking the towel, Lena gave her a look that broached no room for argument, “then I’ll have them sent to your apartment tomorrow afternoon.”

     

                Relenting, Kara gave her an exasperated look, “you’re going to make me forget I’m not rich if you keep this up with your chauffeurs and dry cleaners and housekeepers.”

     

                “You’ll just have to get used to it. Convenience is better. ”

     

                “I’m not complaining,” Kara said, holding her hands up before she smiled, “right, I’d better get started on dinner.”

     

                “What are we having?” Lena asked, her tone bewildered as she ducked into the bathroom and tossed the towel in the laundry basket with Kara’s clothes, “I tried to figure it out but, honestly, I was clueless.”

     

                “Paella. You like seafood, right?”

     

                Rounding the corner to the kitchen, Lena nodded complacently, “mhm, seafood is good. Let me see what wine pairs well with that.”

     

                Clucking her tongue as she shook her head, Kara rummaged through the drawers and pulled out the pristine apron, tying it around her waist as Lena gave her an expectant look. “What’s so funny?”

     

                “I’ve never been friends with anyone who pairs wines .”

     

                “Friends?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara gestured vaguely, “you know ...”

     

                “It makes the food taste better, Kara.”

     

                “But does it actually?”

     

                “Yes! You’ll see. Let me Google what’s good.”

     

                Kara pulled out a large skillet and a chopping board, before eyeing the sharpness of a knife and putting the pan on the heat with some oil. She washed her hands as Lena hummed to herself and then disappeared into the pantry, returning moments later with a bottle of white wine.

     

                “Albariño,” Lena said triumphantly, putting it in the fridge to chill.

     

                “Mm, my favourite type.”

     

                Lena flipped her off over her shoulder as they laughed, before she drifted over to Kara with hesitation, eyeing the spread of ingredients. “What can I help with?”

     

                “You,” Kara said, drying her hands and then taking Lena by the shoulders, spinning her around, “can help by sitting down and telling me about your day.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena grimaced as she reached for a knife, “I know I’m a shit cook, but I’m not completely useless.”

     

                “No, no,” Kara protested, catching her hand and slipping the knife from her fingers before she kissed her knuckles and prodded her away, “sit. Grab a drink. Talk.”

     

                “You really want to know about my day?” Lena slowly asked, fetching two seltzers from the fridge and setting one down nearby for Kara before she climbed onto a stool.

     

                “Of course I do,” Kara lightly asked, her expression softening as she read the uncertainty on Lena’s face.

     

                Lena had never once in her life come home to someone who wanted to hear about her day, someone who was genuinely interested, and she didn’t know where to begin as she sat before Kara, who was patiently chopping chorizo. There was no pressure, even as the moment dragged on, no discomfort at the stretching silence, and Kara seemed as if she had all the time in the world.

     

                “Oh … well, I mean … it was good. I had a few meetings, finished some paperwork, made the front page of the local news. A standard Monday.”

     

                Kara smiled at Lena’s feigned nonchalance, looking up to raise her eyebrows in a sheepish look, “should I apologise for that? Maybe a public kiss cam moment wasn’t the best idea.”

     

                Waving her hand dismissively, Lena twisted the bottle cap off and took a sip as her brow furrowed, “please, don’t even worry about it.”

     

                “You’re sure that it’s okay?”

     

                “If it bothered me, I’d tell you. Believe me. If there’s one thing I know how to do, it’s avoid people and you’re in my kitchen , cooking me dinner so ...”

     

                “Is that a big thing for you?”

     

                “You’re the first person who isn’t here for some sort of work.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “No friends, remember?”

     

                Brow puckering as she turned and moved over to the stove, scraping the chorizo into the pan, Kara turned back around and started thinly slicing the squid into rings. “But … that’s a choice, right?”

     

                Lifting one shoulder in an indifferent shrug, Lena nodded as she took a sip of her carbonated water. “Yeah. Yeah, it’s a choice. Kind of.”

     

                Nodding as she silently mulled the admission over, trying to parse through what it meant that Lena chose to push people away, and what it meant that she was standing in her kitchen, Kara cooked, the faint notes of music drifting through the house as the smell of cooking sausage, and then seafood filled the air, mingling with the smell of rain.

     

                Lena watched her cook, the easy way Kara sautéd the onion and garlic, browned the chicken, measured the Valencia rice and put in the prawns and mussels, seeming to take comfort in the routine of cooking. After months away from home, she probably cherished the chance to have home cooked meals, and Lena resolved to take her out for dinner more often.

     

                They talked as Kara cooked and Lena got up to change the vinyl to its B side, and Kara told her about her day and it all felt so normal , so domestic, that Lena couldn’t comprehend that they’d only known each other for a month, that this was all surreal to her when it already felt habitual. 

     

                Once dinner was ready, Kara carried two heaped bowls to the dining room where Lena had set the table, and the bottle of Albariño was fetched from the fridge. Lena was pleasantly surprised at how good the paella was, telling her as much as she opened mussel shells and delicately pulled the heads off the shrimp. Kara even agreed that the wine was a perfect complement and once they were finished, Lena convincing her to leave the dishes piled in the sink, they took the rest of the bottle into the front living room.

     

                “What’re you reading?” Kara asked as she snagged the book from the arm of the chair and eyed the cover.

     

                “Joan Didion. Some of her essays about living in California, seeing as I’m a resident now.”

     

                “How do you like it here?”

     

                She set the book down and looked up at Lena for her answer. Sinking onto the sofa, Lena set the bottle of wine down, while Kara put down the plate with the two raspberry and custard cream mille-feuille she’d brought for dessert. Crossing her legs, Lena tipped her head to the side.

     

                “It’s nice. I think I like how relaxed it is here.”

     

                “Because you’re known to relax a lot.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena took a sip of wine, “I mean the city. It’s warm, there are palm trees , and everyone seems more laid back. Everyone at work goes … hiking and to spa retreats and vineyards on the weekend. Metropolis is still freezing cold this time of year - although, I’m not sure how I feel about it being warm all year round.”

     

                “We get a few rainy days, like today,” Kara said, looking towards the windows where the rain still pattered against the window panes and the curtain fluttered from the slight breeze wafting through the gap.

     

                “Were you born here?”

     

                Shaking her head, Kara’s eyes creased at the corners, “Tennessee. And then we moved to Newport in Oregon for my dad’s job. My adoptive family are from Midvale - it’s an hour’s drive north of Newport. Eliza worked at the hospital there as a general surgeon when they brought me in.”

     

                “When did you move to National City?”

     

                “Alex came first for college. I followed after high school. We went backpacking around Europe during the summer break and I’ve been here ever since.”

     

                The music stopped playing as the album came to an end and they both dwelled in silence for a moment, Lena torn between asking the dreaded question on the tip of her tongue or leaving it for another time. Climbing to her feet, Kara crossed over to the row of albums and crouched down.

     

                “What else have you got in here?”

     

                Lena watched her rifle through them, eyeing the covers, before she pulled one out with a crow of delight. “Oh, man, I can’t believe you have this!”

     

                “Which?”

     

                “L.A. Woman!” Kara grinned, showing Lena the sleeve, “my dad used to love The Doors. I haven’t heard them in a while.”

     

                “Put it on then.”

     

                She smiled as Kara carefully put Blue back in its sleeve and set the new record on the player, delicately dropping the needle onto the vinyl. Returning to the sofa as the first notes of The Changeling started playing, she picked up her wine and smiled, eyes closing slightly as if she was transported back in time, to a different place, before her eyelids snapped open again, her eyes so blue against the sofa as she took a sip.

     

                “Which song is your favourite?”

     

                “On the album? Riders on the Storm.”

     

                “A good choice.”

     

                They made it to the B side of the album, eating their dessert as they shared the plate between them, scattering flaky pastry all over the cushions, and finished off the bottle of wine. Lena was full and relaxed, her mind pleasantly fuzzy around the edges as she made them green tea and Kara started a fire in the empty grate, even though the chill in the house wasn’t unbearable. The smell of woodsmoke was comforting as they watched the crackling flames, and Lena’s head tilted to the side, her arm along the back of the sofa as she reached out and gently let her fingers follow the vein along the back of Kara’s hand.

     

                “Kara? Can we talk about something?”

     

                Her voice was small and soft and Kara’s eyebrows rose a fraction, her expression tender as she propped her cheek in her hand, leaning against the back of the sofa, and stared at Lena.

     

                “About the other night?”

     

                “Kind of,” Lena murmured, “and … your job.”

     

                “You want to know when I'm going back?” Kara guessed.

     

                With a wispy sigh, Lena looked down at her lap, picking at the balls of lint on the edge of her sweater as she pressed her lips together. “I just- I know it’s only been … just over a month. But I want to know … if this is- I don’t know. I don’t know what to expect from this; I don’t do relationships, in any capacity … but I like you.”

     

                Exhaling as her shoulders slumped, Kara ran a thumb above her eyebrow as she closed her eyes, “I was gone for nine months this time. I’ll be home for … maybe a year. It could be less, or more - they can’t guarantee anything - but I’ll be back to work again soon, at Fort Rozz. Working behind a desk all day until they ship me off again, unless I’m home through to October. But … you don’t have to do anything you don’t want to. I like being around you, that’s all.” 

     

                “How long are you enlisted for? How did you- why the army? I keep coming back to it and I just- I can’t think of why someone like you would want to go out there.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Kara gave her a pained look and Lena’s stomach clenched. Reaching out to rest her hand on Kara’s knee she gave her a faint smile.

     

                “You don’t have to talk about anything you don’t want to.”

     

                Nodding, Kara pressed her lips together for a moment before setting her tea down and clearing her throat. “I … was nineteen. I was smart in high school - not like you , but I was - and I knew I wanted to major in journalism even then. I ran the school newspaper in senior year. But my family … we’re pretty middle-class, you know? I had a good childhood, I was given everything and more, but … my mom could never afford to pay for college for me. And journalism would never pay well; I didn’t want to spend my whole life paying off student loans. Alex is still paying off the interest , and I just … I didn’t want that to be my life. My adoptive father was in the Marine Corp and I think … when they came recruiting at our high school, it seemed like a solution. I went travelling with Alex, and when I got back, I enlisted just after my nineteenth birthday. They’d pay for my degree, they’d train me as a journalist if I was offered that role. You have to actively enlist to be eligible for the grants … they tell you it’s a four year contract, but it’s eight.”

     

                “So … you’ll be done soon?”

     

                A muscle jumped in Kara’s jaw as she looked away, “not exactly. They … let you remain on active duty and attend college full-time, if you’re lucky. Some of their programs help with that, but … I got stuck in a longer active duty contract. After the four years, you go into the reserves, but I picked six active, and then an extra year, so I could finish my degree faster. I still didn’t graduate until last year; I was taking online classes but when I was deployed … all of that got put on hold.”

     

                “How many times have you been deployed?”

     

                “Five. The first time was only a month in Kosovo to report on the guard duty there. I did two months each in Iran and Iraq. The last two were in Afghanistan - seven and nine months. Pushed my classes back a bit, and on top of training and advanced individual training, I’ll be done with my seven years soon, if- if nothing else comes of it.”

     

                “October … that’s when your seven years of active duty are up?”

     

                “Mhm. I turn Twenty-six in September.“

     

                “If you make it that long …”

     

                “Unless they desperately need someone, I’ll spend my last year in the reserves.”

     

                “So, you might not even get deployed?”

     

                With a wan smile, Kara feebly shrugged. “It’s possible.”

     

                Pursing her lips slightly in a thoughtful manner, Lena ran her fingers in gentle circles over the back of the sofa, a pucker between her eyebrows as they furrowed together. She tried to work out a way to phrase her thoughts, a trembling in her chest as she swallowed thickly.

     

                “If- if you stayed … you and I, would we …”

     

                “Whatever this could be … I know you said you’re not looking for anything, that you don’t think it- well, I don’t expect you to sit around and wait for me. I can’t offer you anything concrete, and if that’s not good enough …”

     

                “I don’t like not being in control of everything,” Lena admitted, “I’m not in control when I’m with you and that … frightens me. But I like you and if you’re only home for … a couple of months, then I think that’s worth a shot, right?”

     

                “Is that optimism?”

     

                Letting out a choked laugh, Lena ducked her head, her lips twisting in a wry smile, “I don’t know, maybe it is. Maybe you’re already changing me.”

     

                “Don’t change too much,” Kara murmured, her hand landing on Lena’s, warm and solid, “I like you just the way you are.”

     

                “Yeah, I like you too,” Lena murmured, “I don’t normally like being around people this much. And I think about you a lot. I don’t know if I can just be friends with you, Kara. Even if it’s only for another week or month.”

     

                Looking at Kara, her eyes dropping to her lips as her stomach clenched, pulse quickening, Lena realised she’d never wanted to kiss her more than she did then. And maybe it was the glasses of wine, making her more vulnerable, more honest, but Lena didn’t care. The feeling in her stomach was enough to convince her; she didn’t know how to be close to someone, but she didn’t want Kara to leave. It was too early to tell, but it was enough for now.

     

                Reaching for Kara’s cup of tea, wedged between her legs, Lena set it down on the coffee table and shifted closer to her on the sofa, on one knee as she balanced herself with her other foot on the rug. Her fingertips brushed Kara’s cheek, tracing her cheekbone and down the side of her neck, running beneath the collar of Lena’s sweater as she breathed in the sweet floral smell of the pink clay soap Kara had used in the bathroom.

     

                Kara didn’t move, staring up at her with owlishly round eyes, lips parted expectantly, and as Lena leant down to kiss her, she smiled slightly. Hair still the slightest bit damp was clutched in Lena’s hand as she cradled the back of Kara’s head and she slipped a hand up the sweater, her fingers splayed across Kara’s spine, feeling how soft her skin is, how warm.

     

                Pulling back a few moments later, her breath shaky as she pressed her forehead to Kara’s, their noses brushing, Lena let out a breathless laugh and Kara joined in too, her lips a faint brush against Lena’s as if reluctant to let it end. Disentangling her hand from Kara’s hair, Lena pulled back.

     

                “I- do you want to go upstairs?

     

                Gently kissing Lena, once, and then again and again, Kara smiled in the way that Lena was quickly beginning to love, her eyes screwing up as her lips curved. “Yeah.”

    Chapter 9

                Another two weeks passed by, interspersed with dinner’s at an Italian bistro and Iranian restaurant, Kara showing up at L-Corp one night with phở and goi cuon as Lena worked late and Kara poked around in awe at the office. They went to the open air markets on Sunday, browsing stalls of homemade jams and leather wares, Lena buying herself a new moleskine and flowers for Kara. 

     

                The weekends had never excited her before, just another day to work from home instead of the office, to sleep in a little bit later and fit in the workouts with her personal trainer, but they were occupied with Kara now. Lena thought she would fall behind on her work, as distracted as she was, seeing Kara six times within the last two weeks, but, if anything, she felt more motivated than ever.

     

                On the following Saturday, they had plans. Kara wouldn’t tell Lena what, exactly, but her ensemble required casual clothes and comfortable footwear, which Lena took to mean there would be something physical involved. She settled on a half-zip olive green running top, grey leggings and her running shoes, putting her hair up and eyeing herself in the mirror with scepticism. 

     

                Kara pulled up outside at nine o’clock, driving a silver hatchback and texting Lena to meet her outside. Stepping out onto the stoop, Lena locked up and jogged down the steps, slipping into the passenger seat as she smiled at Kara. 

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                “Hi,” Kara smiled, leaning across the centre console to kiss Lena’s cheek before she held up a plastic cup. “I got you one of those juices you like. Carrot and ginger.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Taking a sip as Kara pulled out onto the street, nudging her glasses up her nose, Lena leant against the door and stared out the windscreen.

     

                “So … are you going to tell me where we’re going yet?”

     

                “It’s a surprise.”

     

                “Did I at least dress okay?”

     

                Giving her an appraising once-over, Kara beamed at her, “perfect.”

     

                She was wearing a faded Eagles t-shirt and shorts, a plaid shirt tied around her waist and battered sneakers. Lena wasn’t sure what to make of the ensemble but figured there would be some amount of walking involved and left it at that. The weather was nice, regardless, they sky azure and cloudless, the air the kind of dry that left her grateful for her juice as they took the exit ramp to merge onto the highway, after a series of stops and starts that left Kara grimacing apologetically. She was not, in fact, a very good driver, a fact that seemed to amuse Lena.

     

                “So, I, uh, I got the news that I go back to work on Monday,” Kara said as she indicated to shift lanes, the news playing over the radio as they had the windows rolled down to let in the breeze. 

     

                She had her elbow propped up in the open window, her skin tanned and an air of nonchalance about her that belied the tension in the set of her shoulders. Lena slowly sipped her juice before setting the cup in the holder and clearing her throat as she shifted in her seat.

     

                “Oh? That’s- that’s great. So, um, where are you stationed?”

     

                “Fort Rozz,” Kara said, biting back a smile.

     

                “That’s not too far, right? I mean … we’ll be able to see each other on the weekends, won’t we?”

     

                “It’s only forty minutes out in the desert so I’ll be staying with Alex.”

     

                Relief flooded through Lena at the prospect of Kara staying close by in National City, and she felt the knot in her stomach unclench as she smiled. 

     

                “That’s … perfect. We should go out for dinner after work.”

     

                They talked the whole way there, brainstorming ideas for dinner, Lena listening while Kara explained some of the work she would be doing on-base, basking in the warmth of the sunshine as enjoyed the drive. They were heading north, through the hills crowded with mansions that paled in comparison to Lena’s childhood home, and through to the stretch of national forest just north of the city.

     

                Eventually, Kara turned off the empty highway and drove for another twenty minutes down a road that was so cracked and pitted and covered in sand, that Lena thought she was driving them out to the desert. Pulling over on the side of the road at a seemingly ordinary spot, Kara smiled brightly.

     

                “We’re here.”

     

                “And where is here?” Lena asked, glancing around at the sand and dirt, rocks and trees; native sycamores and black walnuts, cottonwoods and grey pines and even a few of the hardier desert plant life, ponytail palms and palo verde trees. 

     

                “We’re going on a picnic,” Kara proudly declared, unbuckling her seatbelt and climbing out of the car.

     

                “A picnic?”

     

                Lena’s eyebrows rose as she hurried out of the car, and Kara smiled at her over the roof, uncertain as she judged Lena’s expression. “Yeah, I mean … I didn’t know if you’d ever been on one before. I like hiking out here when I’m home, and I haven’t managed to make it out here yet, so I thought I’d take you to my favourite spot.”

     

                A smile curled the corner of Lena’s mouth, crooked and tender with mild surprise, “that’s … really thoughtful. Thank you.”

     

                Kara’s shoulders dropped with relief as she smiled brightly, moving to the trunk. Lena met her at the rear of the car and looked into the trunk, taking in the bulging backpack that Kara slung onto her back before slamming the trunk and locking the car. 

     

                “We’ve got a bit of a hike, but it’s worth it. Trust me.”

     

                And Lena did, more than she thought was possible, given the short while they’d known each other, but she did all the same. Letting Kara take her hand, reassuring and guiding, they set off through the trees, taking an unmarked path up a gentle incline.

     

                Lena was quickly lost, her sense of direction all but non-existent amidst the trees, offering sparse reprieves from the harsh sunlight as the canopy overhead cast fractured shadows on the dirt track, but she was content to listen to the birds singing around them as they flitted from tree to tree. It was hot and she soon had to take her running shirt off, tying it around her waist as sweat stuck the polyester tank top to her back.

     

                “So … have you been on a picnic before?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena shook her head, “no, I didn’t have that … kind of childhood.”

     

                “What kind did you have?”

     

                Silent for a long while, carefully picking her way over roots as she balanced herself against warm tree trunks, keeping a hold of Kara’s hand with the other, Lena thought for a moment.

     

                “I … was sent to boarding school as soon as they would take me. We went skiing every Christmas to somewhere around the world, and we’d fly back after one day once one of my parents got sick of it. I took … fencing lessons, and Latin and cello, my dad was always away on business trips and my mom was always at work. They never … had time for me. I was my father’s favourite, as much as that meant, and my brother was my mother’s. I think … most people would envy it, you know, with the- the money, the luxury of doing whatever I wanted, of having no parents around. But … I- this is going to sound a bit ridiculous.”

     

                Lena let out a breathless laugh as a spasm of pain crossed her face and Kara squeezed her hand, looking away to give her a moment. She was grateful for that, her throat dry as she inhaled the dust they kicked up, leaving the breath hitching in her throat as she tried to compose herself.

     

                “I just wanted them to like me, you know? I wanted parents who … put me on the soccer team and came to my matches, showed up at recitals and parent-teacher conferences. I wanted to stay at home and have my mom make something for a- a bake sale and a dad who taught me how to ride a bike and drive. My childhood is just … blank . I don’t have any moments where it felt like they liked me , as a person. They gave me everything I wanted … and I still feel … neglected. It’s like they put me in boarding school and forgot I existed, and I just … didn’t get to feel … loved.”

     

                “That’s not ridiculous at all,” Kara murmured, a hoarseness to her words as she squeezed Lena’s hand again.

     

                “What was yours like?”

     

                Kara opened and closed her mouth before remaining silent, her mouth a flat line as she forged ahead. It was all the answer Lena needed, a quiet chuckle making its way past her lips as she smiled ruefully.

     

                “It was everything mine wasn’t,” Lena surmised.

     

                “It’s not fair. I got two sets of parents who loved me; you deserved at least one. I’m sorry.”

     

                “I think having more money than I know what to do with takes the edge off the bitterness.”

     

                They both knew it was a lie, but she liked that Kara was too polite to call her on it, letting Lena wallow in that bitter part of her heart that still resented the things she’d had to beg for that had still been denied her. She couldn’t help but wonder what Kara’s childhood was like though, amidst the losses and struggles, if her family went camping and ate dinner together every night and if that was how she’d learned how to cook.

     

                Filing away those thoughts for later consideration, Lena walked onwards until, nearly an hour later, they came out onto a small, half-moon meadow shaded by the trees, purple needlegrass, june grass and foothill sedge growing in tufts, interspersed with wildflowers. It was only a dozen feet across at its widest point, before it gave way to a steep, twenty-foot drop to a slow-moving stone blue river, narrow as it carved a path through the layers of sediment, greenstone and metavolcanic rock.

     

                Nothing moved as she stared across the wide gap at the wall of trees opposite, a lone kestrel circling overhead, and it was so quiet that she could hear the cicadas in the shrubs as she breathed in the fresh smell of life. There was the dankness of the muddy river below, the dusty earth and the heavy richness of clay, dried grass and weeds scorched in the heat. 

     

                “It’s beautiful,” Lena said, closing her eyes as a gust of wind whistled through the trees, tugging at her ponytail.

     

                “I found it accidentally when I was hiking one time,” Kara said, a smile in her voice as she playfully tugged the end of Lena’s ponytail and slipped off the heavy backpack.

     

                “It was certainly worth the hike.”

     

                She moved closer towards the edge, a sense of vertigo washing over her as she peered down below and then quickly jerked back. Turning around, she watched as Kara removed the rolled blanket from where it was buckled on top, shaking it out and spreading it in a shaded patch of grass. 

     

                Kneeling on it, Kara rummaged around inside and pulled out a variety of little containers and boxes, spreading everything out as Lena joined her, baffled amusement softening her face as she took stock of everything spread out around them. Kara handed her a bottle of water with a smile.

     

                “I wasn’t sure what you liked, so I thought I’d pack a variety. Chicken and avocado sandwiches - that much I do know you like - some chopped vegetables, fruit salad, deviled eggs, banana bread and oatmeal cookies. Oh, and I made a peanut butter and jelly sandwich for you, just in case you’ve never tried one. It’s like … the childhood snack.”

     

                Lips twitching slightly, enjoying her own private joke, Lena leant back on her elbows and stretched her legs out before her, listening to Kara list off half a dozen more snacks. Lena was touched at the effort she’d gone through, taking in the neatly cut sticks of carrot and cucumber, the ice packs wedged in alongside the stacked containers to keep it cool, the attention to the little things she’d picked up on, like how Lena liked her banana bread with walnuts and didn’t like mango.

     

                “Thank you for going to so much trouble,” Lena said, reaching out to take Kara’s rouch hand, running a thumb across her knuckles, “it all sounds delicious. And you’ll be pleased - and shocked - to know that I’ve never had a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. How about we save that for last?”

     

                Grinning, Kara opened her own bottle of water and took a sip as they dwelled in the serenity of the meadow, the quiet sound of running water below, the rustling of the leaves and muffled buzzing of a nearby bee.

     

                “It’s so peaceful up here,” Lena murmured after a moment, her eyes closing as she listened, picking up on more sounds as the silence filled itself in.

     

                “Mm, it’s nice to get out of the city sometimes.”

     

                Opening her eyes, she found Kara studying her with her head tilted to the side, an open look of curiosity in her blue eyes, and Lena flushed beneath the scrutiny, sitting upright and crossing her legs in a self-conscious manner as she raised an eyebrow.

     

                “You’re staring.”

     

                “I like looking at you,” Kara said, somewhat shyly as she fiddled with her bottle cap and Lena’s stomach swooped with delight, “you’re … very beautiful. It seems very … plain to say that but it’s true. I’ve never met anyone like you before.”

     

                “Oh? Go on.”

     

                Groaning as her cheeks turned red, Kara put her face in her hands, “I don’t know, this is embarrassing. I haven’t met anyone I liked this much in a really long time and I’m still trying to figure you out. You’re a mystery to me.”

     

                “Me?” Lena asked, surprise flashing across her face, “oh, no, with you … I’m an open book. I can’t keep anything from you.”

     

                “Really?”

     

                “I don’t know why. You just have one of those faces, I guess. You make me want to tell you everything.”

     

                “I want to know everything,” Kara murmured, putting the bottle cap on and setting her drink aside, “I was to know everything about you. Your- your favourite song and what you’re afraid of and what you think about the conflict in the Cold War and what your thoughts are on building a colony on Mars. Is that stupid?”

     

                With a burst of laughter, Lena tugged at one of Kara’s knotted shoelaces, shoulders hunched as she considered it, “no, it’s not. What else do you want to know?”

     

                She looked up, eyebrows raised and a wary look of interest on her face and Kara’s lips twitched with a smile. “Did you always want to run your family’s business? Which countries have you been to? Do you have a favourite artist?”

     

                Lena’s grin slowly grew wider, until her cheeks dimpled and her eyes creased and she was holding Kara’s hand in hers, fiddling with her fingers as she eyed the pale nicks of scars and the rough calluses on her palms and fingertips. 

     

                “So many questions,” Lena teased her with feigned exasperation, but she didn’t mind the easy questions, it was the other ones that Kara seemed to sense she wanted to avoid, but would eventually have to come up, that worried her. “I was actually getting into manufacturing equipment for genetic engineering. And then everything happened with my brother two years ago, and my mom put the idea to the board as a way of keeping it run by someone in the family without her having to be the one to do the heavy lifting.”

     

                “At twenty-two. How did you even know what to do.”

     

                “Honestly, I think a part of her was hoping she was setting me up to fail. I quickly bought another company and made the CFO there the CFO of L-Corp - she’s probably the closest thing I have to a friend; you’d like her - and she relocated with me a couple of months ago after helping me rebrand and rebuild. I’ve been … to every country in Europe, all the East Asian countries, and India and Sri Lanka. Australia and New Zealand. Most of South America and a few in North Africa too. My favourite artist is Vija Celmins, a Latvian photorealist painter. Her art makes me feel peaceful. Do I get to ask you any questions?”

     

                “That depends.”

     

                “On what?”

     

                “Can I kiss you first?”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Lena pulled her closer and Kara eased her down onto her back as she bore down on her, suspending herself over Lena as she cocked her head to the side, a v between her eyebrows.

     

                “What’s so funny?”

     

                “You don’t have to ask.”

     

                “I like to make sure,” Kara murmured, leaning down to kiss Lena, her lips warm and soft as they pressed against her mouth and then trailed down to her jaw. Pausing, Kara raised her head again, a wary look in her eyes as she hesitated. “Sometimes … you seem like you don’t want to-”

     

                Reaching up, Lena gripped Kara’s arm as her expression clouded with dismay, “it’s not- no, no, I just … I’m not used to it.”

     

                “Does it bother you? How affectionate I am?”

     

                “No, no,” Lena quietly assured her, a smile in her voice, “I like it; it’s good for me. I just- I’ve never … dated anyone who wanted to hold hands and go to the zoo and on picnics. My experiences were just … dinner, drinks, sex. It wasn’t bad , but it wasn’t … personal. No one’s ever wanted to know what my thoughts on a colony on Mars are before.”

     

                Lena choked out a laugh as she pressed her lips together to hide a smile, bemused mirth flashing in her green eyes as she stared up at Kara. There was a faint flush in her tanned cheeks and her blue eyes were gentle and kind and Lena felt the breath catch in her throat as she reached up and stroked her thumb along Kara’s cheekbone.

     

                “Your eyes, they’re incredible.”

     

                Kara let out a quiet laugh, surprise flashing across her face before she leant down and kissed Lena, stretching out on the blanket as she propped herself up on one elbow, her hair tickling Lena’s cheek. When Lena pushed back against her lips, Kara pulled back, a mischievous gleam in her eyes that elicited a frustrated sigh as Lena leant back on her elbows, a withering look on her face.

     

                Leaning in slowly, Kara kissed her again, the tickling brush of her fingertips on Lena’s collarbone as goosebumps rippled over her skin at the sensation, and Lena cupped the back of Kara’s neck so she couldn’t pull all the way back. Their lips were a hairsbreadth apart when Lena spoke, her voice a low murmur.

     

                “Teasing isn’t very nice.”

     

                Pulling Lena up with her as she sat back on her knees, Kara brushed the stray flyaway hairs off Lena’s neck and pressed a kiss to the soft skin behind her ear, smiling against her skin as she heard the quiet intake of Lena’s breath.

     

                “Did you bring me here for a picnic or to just frustrate me?”

     

                “Hmm, maybe both?”

     

                Letting out a scoff of laughter, Lena rolled her head to the side and Kara kissed the underside of her jaw before pulling back and reaching for a container of sliced cantaloupe. Offering it to Lena, who took a piece, they both basked in the dappled sunlight, the day warm and clear, picking through the food that Kara had packed for them. They talked about work and the countries they’d both been to, the art gallery Kara had been to before her last deployment and the first Christmas after her parents died, Lena’s favourite holiday (she didn’t have one; each one was spent like any other day) and the various charity projects she’d created. 

     

                Her curiosity got the better of her and the conversation turned to Kara’s job, how it worked, what she did. The military was a foreign area to Lena, who didn’t supply them with any of her technology, environmental specs and computer software so far removed from their mission that she’d never even given it a second thought about what it entailed. She knew the basics, of course, like anyone else, but she wanted to know more about the process.

     

                “You enter as Private, which is an E-1 rank - the lowest - and then complete ten weeks of basic training. Everyone, no matter what area you go into, has to complete it.”

     

                “Was it hard?”

     

                “So hard. You’re in full gear sometimes, which can be a hundred pounds, getting yelled at while you run miles and miles. Every part of you just aches for all ten of those weeks. It was … awful. It’s necessary, of course, but tough. Then you go on to do your advanced individual training based on what you picked from your offers. I was lucky to get offered what I wanted; it was four months of training for it, and once I finished that I advanced to E-2, which is Private 2. It took … nearly eighteen months for the next promotion to Private First Class, which was a bit longer than usual, but I was also studying full-time so it was … a lot to handle. It was three years of active duty before I made it to Specialist, and I’ve been stuck in that pay grade for a while. The promotion thing gets … tricky after E-4. They have unlimited spots until then, but hitting E-5 means they need an empty spot somewhere to promote up the chain, and there aren’t really a lot of reporter command positions that open up often. They promoted me laterally though, to Corporal. It’s still not an officer’s position, but … it kind of primes you for a promotion, so ...”

     

                “You’ll be out by then though, right?”

     

                Scrunching her nose, Kara smiled, “yeah, I mean, maybe. Who knows?”

     

                Kara was stretched out on her stomach, plucking wildflowers from the grass and threading them together, her fingers moving in quick, deft movements, and for all her casual posturing, Lena could see the tension in her shoulders beneath the thin cotton of her t-shirt. Resting a hand on her back, feeling uncertain as she felt Kara’s chest expand with each breath, Lena watched her for a moment before tactfully changing the topic.

     

                “Did you bring your camera?”

     

                Face lighting up, Kara rummaged around in her backpack and pulled out the old Polaroid. “Of course!”

     

                Taking it from her, Lena smiled as she spoke, turning the camera over in her hands. “Here, smile.”

     

                She raised it to eye level and pointed it at Kara, who groaned, covering her face with a hand. “No,” she lamented, tipping her head back, “I don’t like having my photo taken - unless it’s with other people.”

     

                 “Oh, come on,” Lena encouragingly coaxed, “you’re always taking photos.”

     

                “I like being behind the camera.”

     

                “Just one; you look beautiful. No one else has to see it if you don’t like it. I’ll … throw it in the river. I mean, I won’t, because that’s littering, but mentally I would do that for you.”

     

                “Fine. One photo. And after, I get to take one of you.”

     

                Rolling her eyes exaggeratedly, Lena agreed and pressed her eye against the viewfinder. Snapping the picture quickly, before Kara could change her mind, she turned it upside down to let it develop while Kara raised the chain of daisies and set it on Lena’s dark hair before taking the camera and taking a photo as Lena scoffed with veiled amusement at the flowers. 

     

                Heads crowding together as they peered down at the photos, Lena picked up the one of Kara and smiled. “Do you mind if I keep this one?”

     

                Face furrowing with a perplexed look, Kara shrugged indifferently, “sure, if you want to.”

     

                Smiling with satisfaction, Lena tucked it safely in the zip pocket of her running top and picked up a pitted olive, her eyes creasing with a smile as she bit into it. She didn’t have any personal photos - in her house or office - and she liked the idea of having one, even if only to tuck inside her journal to look at in secret, reminding her of the feeling of comfort at being around someone whose company she enjoyed.

     

                They stayed all afternoon, lounging on the blanket as the hours stretched out before them, passing by so quickly that noon came and went and they were still so engrossed in their conversation and their picnic that they hardly noticed. Lena found her laughter quick to come, each one as surprising as the last, and when all that was left was crumbs, Kara took a few photos of the meadow, of the forest and the slow-moving river below, while Lena propped her chin up in her hands and watched her.

     

                Leaning precariously over the edge as she crouched, Kara snapped another photo and was in the midst of plucking the square film from the mouth when she let out a cry of dismay. “No!”

     

                Snapping herself out of her staring, Lena scrambled to her feet and rushed to Kara’s side, her hands instinctively grabbing her to make sure she had her balance. It wasn’t an extremely large drop, but Lena had no idea how deep the river was, or if there were rocks or rotting trees or debris below that could hurt her.

     

                “What’s wrong?” Lena brusquely asked, a stern look on her face as she gave Kara a once-over.

     

                “I dropped my camera!”

     

                She looked at Lena with utter devastation, her blue eyes bright, even though she blinked rapidly to keep the tears at bay, unwilling to cry in front of her. But Lena knew how much the camera meant to Kara and hesitated, lips pressed together as she thought for a moment.

     

                “Wait here,” Lena said, her hand lingering on Kara’s back for a second as she frowned down at the grey river and then tore herself away and unknotted her running shirt from around her waist.

     

                “What are you doing?”

     

                “Um … I don’t know yet.”

     

                Giving her a rakish smile over her shoulder, Lena strode towards the edge of the meadow and set off through the trees, ducking beneath branches that left scratches on her pale arms, swatting mosquitoes and gnats as she stumbled over rocks and roots, the ground a sloping decline as she stuck to the edge of the cliffs.

     

                Fingers muddy and scraped on the rough bark of paperbark trees, she was finally at a point where the cliff was only a six foot drop, the layers of rock and sediment offering a few uneven shelves for her to lower herself down. Kicking off her running shoes and shedding her clothes at the top, Lena lowered herself precariously over the edge, her bare feet finding the warm stone that held beneath her weight as she gripped the rock by her fingertips.

     

                From the shelf, Lena lowered herself into the water, cold despite the warmth of the sun heating the surface, and she grit her teeth as she slipped into it. Weightless as she paddled, the water surprisingly deep as she found herself unable to touch the bottom, Lena ducked down beneath the surface and came back up, her dark hair slicked back as she shivered slightly. 

     

                Getting her bearings, she set off upstream, against the gentle current of the river, and watched as the sloping cliffside grew steeper on both sides of her, until Lena felt as if they were closing in on her from either side, blotting out more of the sunlight that dappled the surface a bluish colour while her breaststroke disturbed the silt and sand below her. 

     

                It took her fifteen minutes of laborious swimming before she spotted Kara high above her, shading her eyes as she looked towards the way Lena had gone and then back to the water, and then back to the trees. Treading water, Lena cupped her hands around her mouth and shouted to get her attention, watching as surprise flashed across Kara’s face.

     

                “What are you doing?” Kara’s voice drifted down to her.

     

                “I’m going to see if I can find it for you!” Lena shouted back, “it’s not that deep!”

     

                Despite the gritty dirt that muddied the colour, the water wasn’t entirely opaque, the cloudy water allowing her to see the dark bottom below as she dove beneath the surface. It took her a dozen tries, holding her breath and angling sharply for the riverbed, her hands scrabbling over algae-slick rocks and branches, old weeds tangling in her fingers as she came upon old rusty cans and plastic bags, slimy to touch, canvassing the area near the base of the cliff where she thought the current might’ve towed that camera as it sank down to the mud below.

     

                And then after another dive, she spotted it, a dark lump in the dimness of the muddied water, the hard plastic a satisfying feeling in her hand as she snagged it from the bottom and resurfaced in a spray of water. Holding it aloft, Lena grinned triumphantly, feeling smug as she pushed back to the middle of the river and waved her arm.

     

                “I got it!”

     

                Kara was too high up for Lena to clearly make out her expression, but she heard her astonished laugher and could envision her smile, the way her eyes creased, how her nose would wrinkle, and it filled her with pleasure as she let the current aid her back down the river where she’d slipped in. 

     

                The climb back up was trickier with the camera, but Lena finally managed to haul herself over the lip of the cliff, grains of dirt and dust clinging to her wet skin as she wrung out her hair and gathered up her clothes. Her eyes were sore from the clouded water and she blinked rapidly, standing in the sun for a few minutes. Her shivers abated quickly, save for her damp hair, which she’d freed from its ponytail, and she set off back through the forest, rocks and sticks digging into the soles of her bare feet, as loathe as Lena was to put her dry clothes and shoes back on when she was damp and dirty.

     

                Breaking through the treeline, clothes and shoes bundled against her sports bra with the camera safely nestled on top, she couldn’t help but smile at the look on Kara’s face as she rushed over to her in excitement.

     

                “One slightly soggy camera,” Lena imperiously replied, an almost haughty manner to her words even as she smiled and held it out to Kara.         

     

                 “Thank you!” Kara said in quiet awe, grinning as she turned the camera over in her hands.

     

                It was ruined - that much was apparent - but it was the sentimental value that meant more to her than anything else, and she couldn’t hide her smile as she held it tightly, as if to assure herself that it was safely returned to her. 

     

                Looking back up, Kara smiled shyly and leant in to kiss Lena, brushing a damp strand of hair off her pallid cheek. A tremor ran through Lena at the mild breeze that rushed through the trees, and Kara pulled back, her eyes round with surprise, eyeing Lena’s state of undress as she bit her lip to try and hide her smile.

     

                “Come on, let’s get you dried off.”

     

                Quickly shifting all of the empty containers and their rubbish into the backpack, Kara shook off the blanket and turned the clean side inwards before draping it around Lena’s shoulders, fussing over her while Lena let her, her arms rubbing up and down her arms as she tried to infuse some warmth into her. The day was hot though and the cold, clammy feeling of Lena’s wrinkled skin was soon gone. Still, Kara packed up everything else, tucking her ruined camera safely away and zipping everything up.

     

                “We should probably get you home. The sunset isn’t far off and it’ll be cold with you in your wet clothes.”

     

                Touched by her concern for her wellbeing, Lena quietly agreed and pulled on her exercise gear, the polyester sticking to her skin as she struggled to pull it on, and then she rolled up the blanket and tucked it under one arm.

     

                The walk back to the car was quicker, the ground sloping away, the heat and the sun less intense, even with the weary slump of both women’s shoulders from the long day spent lounging in the sun. Lena imagined she’d sleep early that night, perhaps even at midnight, and was looking forward to a warm shower and dry clothes.

     

                At the car, she let Kara dig her out a bottle of water and a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, Lena not having the heart to object, and she buckled herself into the passenger seat and laid her head back against the headrest. The shadows were growing long as the day slurred into night, a purplish tint to the light as the sky was streaked lavender and violet as the sun dipped lower, a ball of orange inching towards the horizon.

     

                She ate slowly on the drive back to the city, the radio playing static at first before it tuned into the local radio stations, and Lena tried to muster her enthusiasm as the peanut butter stuck to the roof of her mouth and made her throat constrict.

     

                “Do you like it?” Kara asked, glancing sideways at her as she switched on the headlights and watched Lena swallow the last bite.

     

                Humming in agreement, Lena gave her a thin smile, brushing crumbs off her lap as she felt her lips start to tingle. Taking a tepid sip of water, Lena cleared her throat and gave her a brighter smile.

     

                “It’s … interesting.”

     

                Kara just laughed, the highway flashing by as they hit the suburbs and then the outer-city limits, a darkness descending as the sky turned indigo and the streetlights glowed orange as they streaked past them.
