                Lena snorted and gently elbowed her, Kara unwinding her arms from around her as Lena flipped the other one. “I mean, we’ll see. I think they’re pancakes, but who the fuck knows?”

     

                Kara laughed as she fetched mugs and poured the fresh coffee into them, leaving Lena’s black as she set it down on the counter beside the stove. They moved about each other in quiet companionship, gravitating around one another in a practised dance as Kara set the small table with plates and cutlery, while Lena moved back and forth from the fridge, setting butter and syrup down.

     

                Rousing Alex and Kelly, the four of them crowded in the small kitchen as Lena made a steadily growing pile of pancakes, and insisted everyone start eating as she manned the skillet. Tired and quiet, there wasn’t much conversation until they were all a cup of coffee in, and it was with wry amusement as she swallowed her first bite that Kara’s eyes glimmered and she laughed.

     

                “Congratulations, you’ve graduated to four ingredient recipes.”

     

                “You’ll make a chef of me yet,” Lena snorted, transferring the fresh pancakes to the plate in the middle of the table.

     

                Joining them as the last one finished cooking, she spread butter and drizzled syrup and listened as the conversation turned towards the trip to Midvale. Swallowing, Lena gently cleared her throat and took a sip of her fresh cup of coffee.

     

                “So, how are we getting there? We can take my jet if you want to fly.”

     

                Alex choked on a mouthful of coffee as Kara opened and closed her mouth, giving her a sheepish smile as she shrugged. “I mean … we usually just take the train. It’s quicker than driving and we don’t have to take turns.”

     

                Quietly scoffing, Alex shook her head as she cut her pancake. “I shouldn’t be surprised, I really shouldn’t, but of course you have a private jet.”

     

                “You can fly commercial if you’d prefer,” Lena replied, coolly arching an eyebrow.

     

                Kelly laughed as Alex grinned, pressing a hand to her heart. “I’m actually very grateful to have a friend with a private jet, who’s generous enough to take me to Fiji for it for my birthday.”

     

                “Oh, so we’re friends now, huh?”

     

                “Don’t let it get to your head; I know having friends is a shock for you,” Alex quipped.

     

                Sighing heavily, Kara rolled her eyes, “you two are pains. Can we skip the teasing and actually plan this?”

     

                Lena was grinning when her phone vibrated. Pulling it out of her pocket, her expression soured as she saw who was calling her. Rejecting it, she sighed as a text message came through next. Her stomach knotted with irritation and Kara brushed her shoulder as she cocked her head to the side.

     

                “Everything okay?”

     

                Looking up, Lena smiled thinly as she took in the innocent, questioning look in Kara’s blue eyes. Raking a hand through her hair, her lips turned downwards at the corners as she set her phone down.

     

                “It’s my mom,” she clucked, rolling her eyes. “She’s at my place.”

     

                “I thought she’d left town already,” Kelly said, her brow furrowing with confusion.

     

                Shrugging in reply, not keeping tabs on her mom’s comings and goings well enough to know where she was or what she was doing, Lena leant back in her chair. After a moment, she shook her head to clear it and then picked up her knife and fork again, digging into her breakfast as she buried thoughts of her mother at the back of her mind.

     

                No one broached the topic again, and after helping Alex clean up in the kitchen, Lena took a hasty shower and borrowed one of Kara’s shirts. With the whole day to themselves, she put half a dozen suggestions forward, including the art museum to let Kara see the exhibition of her favourite paintings before they left, which they eventually decided on. 

     

                First, they had to make a quick stop at Lena’s home for her to drop off her paperwork and overnight bag, and as Lena pulled down her street, her stomach dropped at the sight of her mother’s Audi parked in her spot outside the brownstone. Gritting her teeth, Lena pulled in close behind it and cut the engine, climbing out as her eyes flashed with annoyance behind her sunglasses.

     

                As she grabbed her bags from the trunk and made for the steps, the car door opened and her mom climbed out, unfolding herself to her full height, elegant and regal as she primly crossed over to the stoop. Folding her arms over her chest, Lillian gave her a once over and glanced at Kara before turning her attention back to her daughter.

     

                “It’s nice of you to keep me waiting,” Lillian brittly greeted her, disapproval colouring her words.

     

                “I didn’t know you would be here. Obviously,” Lena said as she slowly mounted the steps, fishing her key out and unlocking the door.

     

                She dumped her belongings in the foyer and barred the entrance as her mother crested the top step. Kara lingered at the bottom, an apprehensive look on her face as she tried to remain unobtrusive.

     

                “If you’d answered my calls or texts-”

     

                “I’ve been busy,” Lena interrupted, shrugging dismissively.

     

                “Well, you’re here now; aren’t you going to invite me in?”

     

                “We’re on our way out.”

     

                Lips thinning, Lillian’s eyebrows drew together in a disgruntled look of dismay. “I thought we could see each other while I’m in town.”

     

                “We never have before; why start now?”

     

                “Maybe we could go out for lunch and talk,” Lillian suggested, ignoring Lena’s nettling tone as she stepped back outside, forcing her mother down a step as she firmly slammed the door behind her.

     

                “I’m busy.”

     

                “There are things we should discuss.”

     

                Exhaling forcefully, Lena brushed past Lillian and grabbed the iron railing as her footsteps thundered down the steps. She could feel her shoulders growing tenser with each passing minute, her jaw aching as she clenched her teeth and a trembling feeling in her chest.

     

                “Mom, I don’t have anything to say to you,” Lena sighed as she reached the bottom and looked back up at her. “Really. I don’t know what you want me to say, but … what’s there to talk about?”

     

                “Lena,” Lillian tersely replied, her heels clicking on the stone steps as she descended. “I’m worried about you. About you being here all alone, so far from home.”

     

                “Yeah, well, that was kind of the point, mom,” Lena snapped, her eyes bright with anger. “And I’m not alone; I have Kara. This is the least alone I’ve ever felt.”

     

                Scoffing, Lillian stepped onto the sidewalk and Lena shook her head, turning to make for the car, for Kara who was now lingering beside the door. She stopped in her tracks as her mother snagged the sleeve of her shirt, turning to raise her eyebrows expectantly.

     

                “I’m trying to look out for you,” Lillian softly murmured, a conflicted look in her eyes as she frowned. “You might see me as this terrible person, but I do care about you. I don’t want to see you get hurt, and this- this relationship … it’s not going to end well, Lena.”

     

                “You don’t even know what you’re talking about.”

     

                “I know she’s getting deployed,” Lillian called after her as Lena walked off, freezing as her mother’s words hit her. “I have a friend in the military who looked her up for me.”

     

                “So?”

     

                “What about when she doesn’t come back?”

     

                Lena flinched as the blood drained from her face, her eyes flat with anger and terror as her bloodless lips pressed into a thin line. The shallow breath she dragged in was a struggle, her vision dimming at the edges, and she could barely manage to speak, the words choking her up as her chest constricted.

     

                “Leave.”

     

                No one moved for a moment, and then Lillian unfroze, slowly turning and making for her car as Lena stood rooted to the spot, her hands curled into fists as her fingernails gouged crescents in her palms. Drawing in a ragged breath, Lena felt a lump form in her throat as her eyes stung with tears, her fear vocalised, leaving her shaken. 

     

                She jumped as Kara’s hand fell onto her shoulder, a gentle touch that made Lena swallow thickly and turn, the sound of her mother’s engine purring as she pulled away from the house. Reaching up to brush Lena’s dark hair out of her face, Kara ducked her head slightly and gave her a gentle smile.

     

                “Don’t listen to her.”

     

                Letting out a choked laugh, Lena smiled ruefully. “I never thought I’d say it, but she’s right though.”

     

                “No, she’s not,” Kara lightly but firmly corrected her. “I’ll come back to you, even if I have to crawl home.”

     

                Lena’s throat constricted at the promise but she let Kara wrap her in her arms for a moment anyway, choosing to drop the topic, her bilious mood making her restless with agitation. Pulling back, Lena gave her a ghost of a smile and pushed her glasses up her nose.

     

                “Now, I believe I promised you some art.”

     

                “We don’t have to go,” Kara murmured, taking her hand. “We can just stay here.”

     

                “I’m not letting my mom ruin our plans,” Lena scoffed. “And I know you really want to see Lê’s photographs.”

     

                She insisted, leaning in to give Kara a quick kiss before towing her towards the car. Forcing a brighter smile on her face, Lena opened the door and gestured with a flourish before rounding the front and slipping behind the wheel. Exhaling fully, she deflated in her seat and buckled herself in before starting the car and turning to give Kara another smile.

     

                “Let’s go and see some art!”

    Chapter 19

                Sunday came with golden sunlight as they rose late, and Lena grinned at Kara as she sipped her green tea, eyes bright as she watched Kara move around the kitchen, adding feta and sundried tomatoes to the eggs she was scrambling in a pan.

     

                “What?” Kara asked as she caught her staring.

     

                “I have some errands to run today, if you want to join me.”

     

                “Sure. What’re we doing?”

     

                “I asked Jess to arrange a few showings for apartments yesterday. You know, because you said you were thinking of looking for a place.”

     

                Kara gave her an uneven smile, raising her head as she arched an eyebrow. “I think my budget is going to be a lot lower than your standards. We’re talking bars on the windows and electrical wiring from the thirties.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena tilted her head to the side. “We can still go and look. It’ll be fun.”

     

                “Sure. It’ll be better if I line up a place first before telling Alex; she won’t feel so guilty if I make it my choice. I know she’ll never do it otherwise,” Kara mused as she scraped eggs onto two plates. “When’s the first showing?”

     

                “At eleven. There are only four of them.”

     

                Nodding, Kara took a seat beside her and they ate their breakfast in the warm kitchen as sunlight pooled golden on the floor. It was going to be a sweltering day and Lena changed into a plain cap-sleeved linen dress after showering, pinning her hair up in a loose chignon and donning oversized sunglasses as she waited for Kara to finish getting ready.

     

                Putting the address into maps, Lena drove them to the first apartment, in a modest neighbourhood of high-rise buildings with vegan café’s, boutiques and a dog park on the corner. Kara frowned as she climbed out of the car and followed Lena to the glass doors, agitated as Lena pressed the buzzer and conferred with the man who answered before they were let inside.

     

                The apartment was on the third floor, a studio empty of any furnishings. It was modern and clean, the floor dark wood and the walls painted a soft cream that glowed yellow from the sunlight flooding in through tall windows. Lena poked around, curious as she looked around the bathroom and looking up when Kara touched her elbow, a clouded look on her face as her cheeks turned pink.

     

                “Lena,” Kara whispered, “I can’t afford a place like this.”

     

                “Don’t worry,” Lena assured her, giving her a small smile. “Just see if you like it.”

     

                “I do like it, but … what’s the rent?”

     

                “Twenty-four hundred a month.”

     

                Kara balked at the prospect and Lena grimaced slightly. Fiddling with her fingers, Kara listened as the man droned on about the facilities and the rental agreement, before Lena politely thanked him and steered them out. 

     

                The second one was on a grungier street, a karaoke bar two buildings down, graffiti brightening up the alleyways and tattoo shops and adult film shops dispersed between the drugstore and 7/11. This apartment was a shared one, a young woman interning at a local law firm showing Kara the spare shoebox bedroom amidst the clutter of her own belongings. The rent was half the price of the other place and she could see Kara considering it before she whisked them away to the third one. It was a one bedroom, a little cramped but more private than the studio, despite the aged seventies feeling of the place.

     

                “Okay, ready for the last one?”

     

                Nodding, Kara looked out the window as Lena drove them through the inner city traffic, an agonisingly slow process, until the neighbourhood started growing familiar, the wide streets of terraced brownstones and upscale designer stores nestled amidst towering skyscrapers shining in the sunlight. Frowning, Kara turned to Lena as they pulled onto her street.

     

                “Did you forget something?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “What about the other apartment?”

     

                Lena pulled into a parking spot in front of her house, right behind a shiny grey Porsche that made her beam as she turned the car off. Getting out, she couldn’t stop smiling as she walked up the steps to the front door and unlocked it, revealing an envelope on the floor. Opening it, she pulled out a key fob and turned around, stepping back outside.

     

                “Whose car is that?” Kara asked, standing near the Porsche and eyeing it with quiet awe.

     

                “Mine.”

     

                “Yours?”

     

                With an airy wave of her hand, Lena smiled sheepishly as she descended the steps, “I’ve been eyeing it for a while so I decided to get one. It’s electric too, and I thought … well, I wanted an upgrade and you don’t have a car so … well, here.”

     

                She extended the key card for the Tesla and Kara frowned as she reached out instinctively to take it. “What?”

     

                “The Tesla. You can have it.”

     

                “Lena,” Kara sighed, “you can’t give me your car.”

     

                “I have lots of cars. I’ve got two right here. Besides, it’ll all be registered in my name; you can just drive it so you don’t have to take Alex’s or mine.”

     

                “But-”

     

                Gently folding Kara’s hand over it, Lena gave her a pleading smile. “Please, just take it. There’s something else I need to show you first.”

     

                “The fourth apartment?”

     

                Holding onto her hand, Lena walked backwards and towed Kara along with her, nerves making her smile waver as she neared the bottom of the steps. “Okay, so … the fourth is actually a house.”

     

                “I can barely even afford an apartment , let alone a house,” Kara exclaimed as a bubble of laughter welled up inside her chest and fell from her lips.

     

                Digging in her bag, Lena pulled out a small key and inhaled deeply before holding it out. “The best part is it’s already paid for … because it’s my house. And I have lots of room for your things - too much, even - and you stay here almost every night anyway, so I was thinking … well, if you didn’t like any of the apartments we saw today … maybe you’d like it here. If- if you wanted to move in, that is.”

     

                Kara blinked in surprise, pulling back slightly as her lips parted, her eyes landing on the key nestled in Lena’s palm. The sunlight caught the stray feathery hairs and turned them to spun gold as her mouth opened and closed for a moment, and when she spoke, her voice was gravelly, thick with emotion. She cocked her head to the side and looked confused.

     

                “You … want me to move in with you?”

     

                Letting out a self-conscious smile, Lena rubbed at the back of her neck. “I know maybe it’s a bit rushed, and maybe- maybe we haven’t known each other that long, but … yeah.”

     

                Reaching out, Kara picked up the little silver key, staring at it for a moment before she wrapped her fingers tightly around it. With a pained smile, her shoulders slumped and she gently touched Lena’s cheek.

     

                “Can you just … let me think about it for a minute?”

     

                Blinking as slow surprise dawned on her, Lena swayed back slightly, a wounded look of confusion in her eyes as the smile on her lips dimmed. “Oh, um, of course.”

     

                “I’ll … go and pick up lunch for us, okay?”

     

                Lena nodded, her eyes bright and her smile tight, before watching Kara retreat down the steps with the key card in one hand and the house key in the other. Shutting the door behind her, Lena pressed a hand against it and exhaled slowly, feeling her shoulders knot with tension. She’d thought Kara would immediately say yes, and would be lying if she said it didn’t sting a little that she hadn’t, but, resolved to be mature about it, Lena moved through the house, leaving belongings strewn in her wake as she made for the patio.

     

                Spending ten minutes lovingly watering her plants in the sunshine, she ended up retreating to her office once she finished, curling up in an armchair with a book that she couldn’t concentrate on as she sought peace in the eaves of the old building. The attic was still, the house groaning slightly as it settled, dust motes spiralling through shafts of sunlight, and Lena checked her phone twice while she waited.

     

                When the sound of the door shutting drifted up three flights of stairs, she straightened in her seat, the book splayed in her lap as she waited. Kara mounted the top step a few minutes later, immediately making for the office in the attic without pausing to scour the other rooms first, knowing it was Lena’s refuge in her own home.

     

                She smiled as she crossed the room, cheeks dimpling and eyes creasing softly at the corners as she set down a Big Belly Burger paper bag on the coffee table and the drink tray beside it. Without breaking her stride, she crossed over to the armchair and sank down to one knee before her, reaching up to cup Lena’s cheek in her rough palm.

     

                “Sorry,” Kara exhaled, her mouth thinning into a grimace as her blue eyes shone. “I, uh, I know that you were hoping I’d say yes right away, but I just- I needed a minute to think about it. I’m not ashamed to admit that I can be a very proud person at times, and that makes me stubborn, and the thought of moving in without contributing anything-”

     

                Lena clicked her tongue and shifted forward, covering Kara’s hand with her own as she frowned. “I don’t care about things like that-”

     

                “I know you don’t, but I do, ” Kara lightly murmured. “That’s part of the problem, because you just- you already own a house worth more than I’ll ever make in my life, and you can buy a car on a whim, and I don’t have any money and … I’m too proud to take a handout.”

     

                “It’s not a handout, Kara,” Lena said with dissatisfaction as her mouth turned down at the corners. “I want you to move in with me. You could just as easily stay with Alex, because we both know she would never kick you out, but I want you to move in because it benefits everyone. And you stay here so often anyway, and you’re going to be gone soon, so it just- it doesn’t change anything, does it?”

     

                “I know.”

     

                “I don’t mean to make you uncomfortable with the way I just throw my money around, but if I can help someone I love … well, I’m going to do it.”

     

                “I know,” Kara repeated, a little exasperated as she let out a short laugh. “And I would love to move in with you.”

     

                Pausing, Lena’s brow creased and she tilted her head to the side, blinking in surprise. “Really?”

     

                Face creasing with a soft smile, Kara nodded, her lips curling at the corners as her nose crinkled. “Really. I think … I don’t want to waste any time. Typical soldier behaviour of me, right?”

     

                Lena let out a shuddering laugh, her face flushed with happiness, and no small amount of relief, and she brushed Kara’s hair out of her face, her fingertips light as they brushed over her cheekbone. Leaning it, Lena pressed a lingering kiss to her lips before resting their forehead together.

     

                “So … how long were you planning that?”

     

                “I’d thought about it before, when you said about Alex, but when you brought it up again on Friday I dug my spare key out and got Jess to arrange the showings just in case.”

     

                “What if I’d said yes to one of those?” Kara chuckled.

     

                Cracking a smile, Lena shrugged and pulled back. “I guess I’d be signing the paperwork to buy the building and give you suspiciously cheap rent. After I’d still asked you to move in, of course.”

     

                Humming, Kara narrowed her eyes slightly. “I wonder what Alex is going to say.”

     

                “Honestly, that apartment is tiny; she’ll probably be glad to move into Kelly’s place.”

     

                “Mm, psychologists make a nice salary; maybe I should’ve studied that instead.”

     

                Cradling her face between her hands, Lena chastely kissed her lips and then the tip of her nose before ushering her up to her feet. “Studying what you enjoy is always the better idea.”

     

                Scoffing, Kara flopped onto the armchair next to her and leant forward for the greasy bag, fishing out a wrapped burger and handing it to Lena with a rakish smile. “It’s only a better idea until you can’t get a job from it.”

     

                “Well, you don’t have to worry about that until you’re back in one piece.”

     

                Sighing softly, Kara murmured in agreement, palming off an order of fries and setting a drink down before Lena. “It shouldn’t be a long deployment, which is good at least. Maybe a couple of months, unless the tensions rise.”

     

                “It’s still a couple of months,” Lena shrugged, her mood souring as she took a bite of her cheeseburger.

     

                “It goes fast,” Kara earnestly reassured her. “Honestly. I’ll be back before you know it.”

     

                Giving her a droll smile, Lena swallowed and arched an eyebrow sardonically. “You know, I’ve gotten so used to having someone around that even a day without you seems strange.”

     

                “I’ll call,” Kara promised, looking so childishly insistent that Lena couldn’t help but smile sadly. “Every day. And you’ll be too busy with all of your meetings to miss me too much.”

     

                Lena snorted and shook her head as Kara grinned at her. The talk of her leaving when she was seated a few feet away made Lena’s chest ache and she untactfully steered the conversation away as they ate. Kara chattered about plans to box her things up and move them in, and they talked over the plans for Midvale with a growing apprehension twisting Lena’s stomach.

     

                Clearing her throat as she set her Coke down, Lena feigned nonchalance as she glanced at Kara. “So, um, just checking, but your mom knows about me right?”

     

                Eyebrows rising in a surprised look, Kara smiled with confusion. “Of course she does.”

     

                “No, I- well, I figured that you would’ve mentioned me, but like … she knows about me, right? That you and I- we’re a couple?”

     

                “Yes, Lena, my mom knows I like girls and that I’m bringing one home,” Kara said with thinly veiled amusement, crumpling the burger wrapper and tossing it into the paper bag. She climbed to her feet and took Lena’s trash from her before dropping a kiss on top of her head.

     

                “Good, good,” Lena murmured to herself, worrying at her cuticles as she stared into space with a furrowed look of anxiety on her face.

     

                Pausing, Kara cocked her head to the side and studied her for a moment, smiling as Lena blinked herself back to the present and raised her head, her eyes softly creasing as she smiled.

     

                “Are you worried about meeting my mom?”

     

                Letting out a strained laugh, Lena shrugged dismissively, panic flashing in her green eyes. Resting her elbow on the arm of the chair, she chewed on her nail for a moment, shoulders taut, and then sighed as she looked at Kara with mournful worry.

     

                “Well … yeah, of course I am. I mean … what if she doesn’t like me?”

     

                “Eliza likes everyone,” Kara shrugged, unbothered.

     

                “Yeah, but this- this is different . She can’t just like me - not the same as she likes everyone else. And I clearly don’t have much experience with mom’s - I can’t even make my mom like me-”

     

                Stepping forward and reaching down, Kara pressed a finger to Lena’s mouth to quiet her as her concerns devolved into uncharacteristic nervous rambling. “She,” Kara murmured, removing her finger to cup Lena’s chin, her thumb gently stroking her lips, “can’t wait to meet you.”

     

                “Really?”

     

                “Of course. She’s curious to meet the person I never shut up about.”

     

                Lena let out a snort of laughter and Kara grinned as she resumed her cleaning up. Climbing to her feet, Lena gave her a sceptical look. “Never shut up about, huh?”

     

                “There’s just so much to tell.”

     

                “Now, that’s concerning.”

    Chapter 20

                Lena’s driver pulled up outside Alex’s apartment at nine o’clock, idling as the CEO made her way upstairs to the apartment, taking the stairs with the elevator in the lobby out of commission, audible voices drifting through paper thin walls before she’d even made it to the front door. She knocked twice, listening to Kara’s voice grow steadily louder as she approached, and raised a questioning eyebrow as the door was yanked open.

     

                “Morning,” Kara said with a rough sigh as she rolled her eyes and dropped a kiss on Lena’s lips. “You’re so lucky you don’t have a sister.”

     

                “Mm, so much worse than a mass-murdering brother,” Lena agreed as she eased the door shut. “Is everyone ready?”

     

                “No. Leave it up to her to oversleep and pack before we leave.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose faintly, she sank down onto the sofa and picked up the autobiography splayed open on the coffee table to pass the time as Kara and Alex shouted back and forth. It was a comfortable banter that she imagined was normal for the sisters, and Lena looked up to nod at Kelly as she gave her a commiserating look and joined her with her morning coffee.

     

                “All packed?”

     

                “Ex-military,” Kelly said, pointing at herself. “Of course I am.”

     

                Nodding, Lena delved back into the book of essays, wondering whose book it was as she flicked through the pages, picking up snippets as she let the din wash over her. Eventually, Alex emerged with a bulging duffle bag and snapped her fingers as she looked around.

     

                “Sunglasses, sunglasses.”

     

                “They’re on your head,” Kelly called out without looking.

     

                “Ah,” Alex muttered, patting the frames resting on her hair. “Keys.”

     

                “Coffee table. Now can we go? We’re going to be late.”

     

                Clicking her tongue with annoyance, Alex snatched up her keys and spread her hands helplessly as she raised her eyebrows at Kara, who had her backpack on and the front door open. “Your girlfriend owns the plane - you did catch that right?”

     

                “We still have to be on time .”

     

                “Then next time don’t steal my phone charger and maybe my alarm will go off.”

     

                “You said I could have it.”

     

                “Alright, let’s go,” Kelly interrupted, pushing herself to her feet and ushering Alex out the door as she snatched up her own bag.

     

                Lena followed them out and let Kara lock up before she shadowed Kelly to the stairs. “Do you have any sisters?”

     

                “Oh, God no, thankfully,” Kelly snorted. “But my brother and I used to argue like crazy when we were younger. We eventually grew out of it - unlike these two.”

     

                A small smile pulled at the corners of Lena’s mouth as Kara and Alex’s bickering and questions and comments filled the stairwell as they made their way down to the lobby. Filing out into the warm day, the driver climbed out of the car to help stow their bags in the trunk, and Lena found herself in the front seat of the town car as they pulled out into traffic and made out of the city.

     

                The plane was at a private airstrip that her family owned, forty minutes north of National City, already brought out of the hangar and waiting on the sun baked tarmac. It was a small thing, sleek and a glossy obsidian colour with the L-Corp logo on the side of it, solely used for Lena’s business trips - she didn’t go anywhere else to make use of it, and it was a tax write-off in the company’s name.

     

                “Well, shit, I thought you were kidding,” Alex noted as the car came to a step a dozen feet from the small jet.

     

                Lena snorted and let herself out of the car, watching as a set of steps descended. Nodding at the private pilot, situated on the tarmac in uniform, Lena murmured a quick hello as she gripped the railing and made her way up into the aircraft. It was made to fit twelve people, surprisingly spacious given its deceiving size from the outside, and was upholstered in cream leather in a comfortably modern look.

     

                Bottles of San Pellegrino were nestled in a bucket of ice, packets of mixed nuts - no peanuts included - and an assortment of tiny patisserie cakes laid out on a silver tray, and an air hostess stood by with an open bottle of Dom Pérignon as she waited to pour it into glasses for them. Lena murmured for them all to leave their bags and took her customary seat, a copy of the Financial Times already waiting for her on the table. Kara flopped down across from her, eyes wide and face alight with wonder as she reached for her buckles.

     

                “This is better than First Class. Did you pull out all the stops, or is this how you usually travel?” she asked, quickly thanking the air hostess as she was handed a glass of champagne.

     

                Lena echoed the sentiment as she accepted her own glass and gave Kara a crooked smile. “Unless it’s a last minute trip. It’s a new electrical prototype L-Corp developed so it’s better for the environment. It’s still not in mass production but … you know, it is safe, coming from someone who hates flying.”

     

                “Ah, of course. So it is a special treatment.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena smiled faintly, “only the best for you.”

     

                “I could get used to this,” Alex said with satisfaction, one arm slung around the back of the bench she’d sat on, her champagne in hand as she looked around with interest. “I don’t think I’ll ever be able to fly coach again; look at all this legroom.”

     

                Feeling a prickle of pleasure that her decision to fly them all to Midvale had gone over so well, Lena relaxed into the soft Italian leather of her seat and glanced at the headline of the newspaper before tossing it aside. She’d usually use a flight for the opportunity to catch up on the business world, pinpointing new stocks to invest in and businesses to add to her conglomerate, if not trying to put a dent in the endless paperwork and emails and texts, but this time she was determined to enjoy herself.

     

                They’d been in the air for forty minutes, eaten half of the cakes and pastries and finished the bottle of champagne, by the time Lena had won her fifth hand of poker. Kelly had thoughtfully packed a deck and pulled it out, the four of them crowding around the table as they held their hands fanned out before them and a crumpled pile of bills and loose change grew before Lena. As another card was turned over and all hands were shown, Kara and Alex groaned in unison, tossing their cards down as Lena chuckled at the flush laid out before her.

     

                “She’s cheating, right?” Alex asked, glancing at Kelly and then Kara as she waited for them to back her up. “She’s way too good at this to not be.”

     

                “I happened to be one of the best at card games at boarding school,” Lena smugly confessed, shuffling cards as she split the cash evenly to deal everyone back in. “Mostly because I learnt how to count cards and could memorise patterns, but still.”

     

                “Oh, you conveniently forgot to mention that, didn’t you,” Kara laughed. “I thought you said you didn’t have any friends at school; how’d you become so good at cards?”

     

                “Most of them were always older than me by a few years - at least when I first got sent away - so they had no interest in babying me, but … well, they liked money well enough. Hated losing it though, so they stopped letting me play after a while. I’m a bit rusty, but, well, no offence, but none of you are good.”

     

                Scoffing, Alex shook her head and picked up her next hand, “remind me to never actually bet anything big against you, or you’ll end up with the keys to my apartment at this rate. Don’t worry, I have every intention of thrashing you at Monopoly tonight though.”

     

                “You know I’m a businesswoman, right? Isn’t that the point of the game?”

     

                “Well, it’s a matter of pride now.”

     

                Lena cracked a smile before composing herself and picking up her hand and letting Kara flip over the first card. She cast her girlfriend a sideways look as she tried to decipher if she’d mentioned anything about moving out of her shared apartment with Alex yet, but didn’t want to broach the topic if Kara didn’t want to bring it up yet.

     

                She ended up winning that hand too, and the next three, before they finally packed up. It was past lunchtime, the sky a cerulean blue beyond the oval windows of the plane, and all four of them were getting a little restless at being cooped up on the plane - granted, they had more legroom than they’d ever had on a flight before and stretched their legs in turn as they lounged about for the last hour of the trip. Kara was flipping through a book as Lena questioned Kelly about her work and Alex stretched out, taking a quick nap.

     

                Their descent into Oregon was quick, blue skies and a few puffy clouds stretching out over a wide expanse of pines and firs, black cottonwoods and aspens. They landed at a private airport in Forest Grove, a small airstrip in a densely forested area a forty minute drive from Midvale, and found a car waiting for them. It wove through shaded roads and made west for the coast, and finding herself squashed into the middle seat in the back as the staticky radio tuned in and out of a music station, Lena found herself nervous as her skin prickled and chest constricted.

     

                It was warm outside, the leather car seats sticking to exposed patches of skin as the air conditioning worked to keep the interior cool, and Lena felt suffocated as she ran through a thousand possible scenarios in her head for meeting Eliza. As if sensing her worry, Kara squeezed Lena’s knee and gave her a warm smile that helped that tightness in her chest abate for a while.

     

                To occupy herself, Lena stared out the window, past fields and small towns as they neared the coast. It was a hilly place, the rugged landscape of the Pacific NorthWest on full display as rocky outcroppings covered in moss and lichen and so much greenery made the air hold a green quality to it, tinting the filtering sunlight. It reminded Lena of business weekends in Vancouver, of wetter climates that evaded National City and its arid heat. 

     

                Still, even the beauty of nature couldn’t dissuade the tension that grew in her body, muscles taut and tendons straining as she clenched her hands and hunched her shoulders, fighting off a tremor in her fingers. It was with a sense of horror that they slowed on a sloping street and the driver indicated at the foot of a steep driveway. Atop it was a white clapboard house, modest and welcoming, situated on the very edge of the ocean, soft, rolling sand dunes giving way to gentle seagreen waves.

     

                As soon as the car door was opened, the smell of salt air and damp and greenery slammed into her, fresh and invigorating and alive. Lena slid from the back seat and shaded her eyes against the sunshine as she eyed the house, taking in the small balcony on the second floor, overlooking the forest, the small porch at the front with the front door opening to a blonde woman, starting to grey at the temples and smiling widely.

     

                Lena looked away, pale and stricken, at the gentle nudge of Kara handing over her bag, which she quietly thanked her for, plucking at the front of the striped cuban shirt she’d opted to wear with jeans and wondering if her first impression would be good enough for Eliza to at least try to know her. Reaching out, Kara took Lena’s free hand and squeezed it tightly, a sympathetic look of understanding softening her face as a smile tugged at her lips.

     

                “Ready?”

     

                “Mm,” Lena hummed, unable to make herself say anything else.

     

                Dropping her hand, Kara squeezed her shoulder and her smile widened, genuine happiness shining in her eyes as she jerked her head up the driveway. “Come on, time to meet my mom.”

     

                Mouth dry and a sceptical air about her as she tried to aim for aloof, trying to convince herself that it didn’t matter , Lena lingered back as she slowly followed the trip toward the front door, where Kara had already engulfed Eliza in a warm hug. Glancing back over her shoulder, she watched the car back out of the driveway and turned back around, tuning into the conversation.

     

                “It’s so good to see you,” Eliza said, her eyes shut as she held Kara close. “How are you? How was the flight?”

     

                “I’m good! I’ve missed you; I wish I could come and visit more often.”

     

                “I know,” Eliza softly sighed, patting Kara’s cheek before she held her arm open to hug her other daughter.

     

                Alex dutifully allowed her mother to hug her, exasperatedly answering questions and promising her she wasn’t working too much, that she’d try and visit sooner next time. Lena was a little more relieved as she watched Eliza kiss Kelly’s cheek, embracing her as warmly as her daughter’s, that knowledge that she wasn’t the first to have been brought home a small comfort. But still, once Kelly marched inside after Alex with her bags, Eliza’s blue eyes landed on Lena and brought back her nervous fear anew. 

     

                “And you must be Lena,” Eliza warmly greeted her, lines radiating from the corners of her eyes as they creased with a smile.

     

                “It’s nice to meet you, Mrs Danvers,” Lena earnestly replied, a tentative smile managing to grace her lips as she felt a prickle of heat in her cheeks.

     

                “Call me Eliza.”

     

                Lena blinked as she was briefly embraced, and swallowed thickly. “Right. Um, thank you for having me.”

     

                “You’re very welcome! Come in, come in. Make yourself at home, please.”

     

                Opening the screen door, Kara held it open and ushered Lena inside after Eliza before bringing up the rear. It bounced shut and Lena took in the white walls of the hallway, the dark stain of the cedar floorboards and the clutter of family photographs and knick-knacks in the hallway. 

     

                “I’ll take your bag up,” Kara said, easing it from Lena’s tight grip.

     

                Shooting her a fearful look at the thought of being left alone, even momentarily, Kara winked quickly and vanished upstairs, taking them two at a time as her heavy tread disappeared up the staircase. Softly clearing her throat, Lena hovered in the hallway as she watched the trio of women disappear through an open doorway to the long kitchen.

     

                It was as light and homely as the hallway, notes of blue amidst the white and worn wood. An open window let in the roaring sound of waves and crying gulls, and Lena breathed in the smell of salt that permeated everything. Lingering in the doorway uncertainly, she watched as Kelly dragged a chair out and took a seat, answering one of Eliza’s questions, and Lena watched with fascination as she watched Eliza lovingly trail her fingertips across Alex’s shoulder, laughing as she scooted behind her daughter to make for the sink.

     

                “Coffee? Tea?” she called out. Her gaze slid to Lena, pale eyebrows rising as she smiled, “Lena? What will you have?”

     

                “Oh, um, tea, please,” she murmured. 

     

                Too much caffeine seemed like a bad idea, given how jittery she already was, and she hoped for something herbal and soothing to take the edge off. She wasn’t used to being so shy - quiet, yes, but shy wasn’t something Lena was typically used to, although her cold detachment was often attributed to that. 

     

                Drawing in a deep breath, Lena took a step into the kitchen, fiddling with her fingers as she raised her heavy eyebrows slightly in a politely questioning look. “Can I help?”

     

                “No, no,” Eliza waved her away, “take a seat. Go on, now, make yourself at home.”

     

                Alex dragged a chair out, the legs grating across the floor, and gestured for Lena to sit with a knowing smile curling her lips. Smiling faintly in response, Lena took a seat beside her and shifted it in closer to the table, her eyes darting around as she took the decor in, listening to Kara’s approaching footsteps thundering downstairs. She materialised in the doorway, looking gentle in a worn white shirt and light denim, tanned and golden and wary as she assessed the mood in the room.

     

                “So, Lena, Kara tells me you’re in business.”

     

                Blinking, she opened and closed her mouth, glancing at Kara before her gaze drifted to the back of Eliza’s denim shirt as she set on a pot of coffee and filled an iron kettle.

     

                “Oh, um, yes. It’s a family business.”

     

                Snorting, Kara moved over to her mom and snagged a few mugs from the cupboard overhead, none of them matching and all of them emblazoned with some logo or pattern. “Family business is an understatement .”

     

                “It’s impressive,” Eliza hummed in agreement.

     

                Lena flushed slightly and shifted in her seat as Alex quietly chuckled, not unkindly, and nudged her gently. “Not as impressive as her private jet.”

     

                “Or her personal driver,” Kelly said with an amused smile.

     

                “I’m not nearly as prissy as they’re making me out to be,” Lena said, rolling her eyes good naturedly.

     

                Eliza laughed, the kettle whistling faintly on the stove with increasing pitch until she snagged it off the heat and poured boiling water into a mug. She set it down in front of Lena with the teabag steeping, the smell of bergamot drifting up from the cup of Earl Grey in a cloud of steam, and Eliza gently squeezed Lena’s shoulder.

     

                “You poor dear, I bet you’ve had them teasing the life out of you.”

     

                “Don’t worry, she gives as good as she gets,” Alex assured her mother.

     

                “I’m surprised you haven’t frightened her off yet,” Eliza said, shaking her head and fetching the other two cups of tea, setting one down in front of Kelly before taking the seat beside her. 

     

                Kara made coffee for herself and Alex and took the seat perpendicular to Lena, squeezing her knee under the table. “She doesn’t scare that easily.”

     

                Lena smiled around the rim of her mug as she took a scalding sip of tea, warm air blowing in off the ocean and the smell of lavender growing in the garden making for a heady perfume as bees lazily wafted past. The conversation washed over her as she leaned back in her seat, cradling her mug and contributing when someone asked a question, but otherwise, Lena was perfectly content to listen to everyone catch up, keeping pace with new stories and new people and the tangled web of small town gossip. 

     

                After they’d finished their drinks, Kara dragged Lena away from the table to give her a tour of the house, leading her through to a long living room stretching the length of the house at the back. An L-shaped sofa was situated before a TV, the windows behind it overlooking the sea, blue waves limned in silver where the sun caught the white crests, and they ducked into another sitting room at the front of the house, which doubled as a study with a sturdy wooden desk overlooking the small flower beds beneath the windows and held a wall of bookshelves housing everything from crime fiction to medical journals to children’s fantasy. 

     

                Lena drank it all in with curious eyes, pausing to stare at photos of Kara, young and blonde with braces, smiling next to a younger Alex, on vacation in Seattle and shading her eyes in her military fatigues. There were clippings of her newspaper articles from high school, yellowed with age but framed with care, and remnants of a man in the heavy fleece still hanging on the hook in the hallway, in the signed baseball on the desk that Kara told her had been her adoptive father’s most prized possession. 

     

                They made their way upstairs and Kara pointed out doors to Eliza’s room, the guest bedroom, the bathroom and then Alex’s bedroom and her own. Kara eased open the door to her childhood bedroom with a sheepish look on her face and let Lena step inside to see. The walls were painted a duck egg blue, a double bed pushed up against one wall and made with forget-me-not patterned bedsheets. A patchwork knitted blanket was folded over the foot of it.

     

                Against the wall with the door was a dresser, cluttered with framed polaroids, these ones older and slightly worn from the sunlight spilling through the windows, the souvenirs and trinkets of a teenage girl, sticky ring stains from long gone bottles of cheap perfume, and a dusty soccer trophy for participation. The wall opposite the bed held a desk with a bookcase wedged in alongside it, teen magazines alongside compilation books of photojournalist’s works, alongside chemistry textbooks and a battered set of Twilight with the edges curling up. Lena ran her hand over the spines of the books, taking in framed certificates from school, half-burned candles and a lopsided unglazed mug filled with pens and markers, sitting atop a stack of composition notebooks and a clunky desktop computer.

     

                “Well … this is it,” Kara said with wry amusement, “sometimes I feel like this was the last time I ever really felt like I had a home. I’ve never had to pack it up and move it somewhere else; it always had a sort of … enduring feeling to it, that no matter what, I’d always have somewhere to go.”

     

                “It’s … so normal,” Lena said with a bewildered note to her words. “I mean … you have posters of NSYNC.”

     

                “Ah, I probably should’ve taken those down,” Kara self-consciously muttered, rubbing the back of her neck.

     

                Chuckling, Lena looked around with fascination, sinking onto the edge of Kara’s bed and glancing at the photo on the nightstand. One edge of it was singed, but there was a young blonde girl - unmistakably Kara - in between a greying man with glasses and a brunette woman with the same eyes, even if they were brown instead of blue.

     

                “Your- your parents?” Lena hesitantly asked.

     

                “Yeah, it’s the only photo of them I’ve got,” Kara softly replied, sinking down on the mattress beside her. “If I didn’t … I think I would have forgotten what they looked like by now. I already have a hard time remembering what they sounded like.”

     

                Her laugh came out a little sharp, the pain in it clear and pitiful. Lena squeezed her knee and then set her chin on Kara’s shoulder, her arm around her waist as they lingered in silence for a moment. Inhaling, Lena slowly breathed out and smiled slightly before kissing Kara’s shoulder.

     

                “I like your mom.”

     

                “Yeah? I think she likes you too.”

     

                “Does- does she know … about my brother?”

     

                Kara stilled for a moment and it was all the answer Lena needed as she slowly closed her eyes and swallowed. “It’s not something that would ever change her mind about you, you know. It wasn’t even your fault. She’s just happy that I’m happy, and she does like you, really.”

     

                Running her palms over the thighs of her jeans, Lena nodded, “right. I’m just nervous.”

     

                “It’s alright,” Kara said with a crooked smile, “come on, how about some late lunch?”

     

                Eliza had gone grocery shopping in anticipation of their arrival and they picked at slivers of smoked salmon, wedges of Camembert cheese and stuffed olives trying to decide on dinner. The ultimate winner was pizza and as Alex placed the order over the phone for later on that evening, Kara convinced Lena to go for a walk along the beach with her. It was inching towards late afternoon, the sun already sinking lower, although it would stay light for hours yet, the later summer months not yet yielding to autumn.

     

                Still, Lena donned one of Kara’s fleeces before stepping out, a sharp edge to the breeze blowing in off the coast. They walked out onto the back porch, wooden outdoor furniture situated to face the waves, and Lena followed Kara down the bleached steps before kicking off her sandals. 

     

                The sand was warm beneath her feet, and soft as they crested the mounds of sand dunes, beachgrass, marram grass and sea oats rippling with each gust of wind. Leaving gouges in the dry sand, Lena ducked her head and half slid down the sloping dunes before her feet found harder sand, rough and damp and packed together.

     

                Looping her arm through Lena’s, Kara closed her eyes and tipped her face up to the sun as she inhaled deeply. A smile played on her lips and they drifted down to the wet sand where the waves rushed up the shore in a thin blanket, leaving shells and seaweed and pieces of driftwood in its wake.

     

                “It’s good to be home,” Kara murmured with satisfaction.

     

                “When was the last time you were here?”

     

                “As soon as I got back; I always come home first. Straight from National City to Midvale.”

     

                “It’s nice here,” Lena noted, shading her eyes with her sandals as they walked parallel with the sea, tiny shells and glass worn smooth from years of being caressed by the sea spackling the shoreline. She watched as a little crab scuttled into the water and smiled softly. “I’ve never spent much time near water.”

     

                Kara looked at her with surprise, “no?”

     

                “I never told you how my mom died, did I?” Lena said with a wan smile, shaking her head as a pang of sadness and confusion knifed through her. “I don’t remember much of it … I was only four and I guess- I blocked out as much as I could. She drowned. I was there. I couldn’t tell you what happened, or if she meant to, but … ever since, I’ve hated the water. Baths are just about all I can handle; anything deeper than that, bigger than that …”

     

                Lena suppressed a shiver and Kara squeezed her arm, a sympathetic look on her face. “I know how you feel. It was years before I could stand to be around a campfire afterwards. The smell of smoke, of being in the house … it’s not something I’ll ever be able to forget.”

     

                Sighing, Lena grimaced and gently bumped into Kara, “what a pair we make.”

     

                “Yeah,” Kara weakly chuckled, “I guess I was never going to settle for someone normal.”

     

                “Mm, was it too much to ask for someone without mommy issues?” Lena replied, giving her a sideways glance as she grinned.

     

                “You know, I think I should meet her again. I didn’t really get a chance to talk to her both times; I was kind of just there .”

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena let out a strained laugh, “honestly, that was enough. The next time I’ll have to see her will be … I don’t know, Christmas? For the annual fundraiser. Maybe the next board meeting - if she shows up, which I’m sure she’ll try her damn best to.”

     

                “Yeah, I got the sense that she didn’t like me much.”

     

                “Don’t take it personally - she doesn’t even like me . Granted, I’d be pissed if my husband brought home someone else’s kid, but … still. What kind of person is a dick to a four-year-old?”

     

                “Have you ever talked to her about it?”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes. “Yeah, so, we didn’t really talk about things in my family. You just- you pretended everything was fine, avoided each other, for the most part, and then moved away and only saw each other for holidays. What a loving environment to raise such well-adjusted people. Not like this place; Eliza adores you.”

     

                Letting out a resigned sigh, Kara raked a hand through her hair. “Yeah. Yeah, she does. I’m lucky.”

     

                Tugging her to a stop, Lena raised her eyebrows in a gentle question. “What’s wrong?”

     

                Giving her a weak smile, Kara shrugged quickly, her shoulders slumping as she looked out over the water. It shimmered in the light and they watched a fishing boat trundle past out beyond the surf. Her lips twitched as she thought for a moment before speaking.

     

                “Do you ever feel like you’re disappointing someone?”

     

                “Literally all the time. You’ve met my mom, remember?”

     

                “Right, well … I feel like … sometimes I’m disappointing my mom too. I know she didn’t want me to follow after Jeremiah, and that it- it’s hard for her whenever I have to leave, and it just- it makes me feel guilty. I feel like I’m hurting so many people with my choice.”

     

                “To be honest, Kara, what kind of person wants their kid in the army?”

     

                “I know, but … they don’t tell you what it’s like. They make it seem like you’re doing it for your country but that’s- that’s not what it is, and I know I’m there to write stories on what I see there, but it still feels … dirty. It feels like I’m disappointing Eliza and Alex - and you - by going back there, and when I have to- to come home and say goodbye to my mom … I can feel that disappointment. I’m letting her down, Lena.”

     

                Reaching up to cup Kara’s cheeks, Lena gave her an uneven smile. “Look, I won’t pretend that anyone wants you to go, or is happy about it, but … you’re not a disappointment. You’re not. It’s just- it is what it is, and it’s almost over, so …”

     

                Wilting slightly, Kara gave her a grim smile, “I’m going to miss you, you know.”

     

                Lena felt the stinging pressure of tears behind her eyes and dropped her hands before looping her arm through Kara’s and towing them onwards. Her voice was a little rough when she replied, “yeah, me too.”

     

                Their walk was overshadowed by their conversation after that, Lena’s heart not quite in the novelty of tide pools riddled with darting silverfish and starfish and mussels clinging to moss-slick stone. They must have walked for an hour one way though, through the shade of dune willows growing in a patch of damp grass where the beach narrowed to a sliver of damp, earthy sand, passing by an elderly man with an exuberant Labrador chasing after a tossed stick of driftwood.

     

                Eventually, they turned back and slowly walked home, the sun sinking lower and the shadows deepening a fraction, even though dusk was far off. Kara was quiet, lost to her own thoughts, and Lena was content to let her dwell as she let herself unwind away from the office and her workload. She’d taken the week, giving up her control for once as she resolved to enjoy herself without the worry of work. If anything important came up, Sam had her personal cell phone number and would let her know, but otherwise, Lena was completely unplugged.

     

                The food arrived not long after they got back to the house, Alex prying the bottle caps off bottles of beer as they scattered across the sofa and armchairs in the living room, watching Jeopardy as they ate pepperoni pizza and called out answers. So far, Lena was on par with Eliza for the most correct answers and found herself relaxing into the cushions as the sky slowly darkened, a washed out indigo descending as the sun lingered.

     

                “I’ve got the night shift,” Eliza said after she’d finished eating, “so, I’m going to fit in a few hours before I get going. What’re you girls going to do now?”

     

                “Do you know where the Monopoly set is?” Alex asked, already rubbing her palms together as she grinned at Lena, elbows on her knees and looking eager.

     

                “In the closet upstairs - above the camping gear, I think. Why?”

     

                “Lena’s never played before and she kicked my ass at poker on the way here, so fair is fair.”

     

                Eliza shook her head and rubbed Alex’s back as she walked past, off in search of the board game. Smiling exasperatedly, Eliza picked up empty beer bottles, the brown glass clinking in her hands, and Lena quickly stood up to help stack empty pizza boxes. She carried them into the kitchen and deposited them on the counter where Eliza indicated and found herself nervous to be alone with the other woman in the shadowed dimness of the kitchen.

     

                As if sensing her unease as she hovered, Eliza wiped her hands as she turned to smile at her. Reaching out, she gently squeezed Lena’s arm. “It’s nice to finally meet you,” she softly told her.

     

                “You too,” Lena murmured.

     

                “Well, I’ll see you tomorrow. Hopefully we’ll have more time to get to know each other then.”

     

                A small smile twitched Lena’s lips as she ducked her head in a quick nod. “Have a good shift.”

     

                Gently patting her arm, Eliza’s eyes creased at the corners with a smile. “You sleep well, honey. You look tired.”

     

                Lena blinked in surprise, her cheeks warming slightly, from the concern and the observation, and followed Eliza out into the hallway. She made left, for the door at the end that led back into the living room, while Eliza rounded the end of the stairs, bumping into Alex who came charging down with a box in hand.

     

                “Goodnight, sweetheart. Make sure you girls keep the noise down.”

     

                Alex ushered Lena down the hall and back into the living room, switching on lamps and light switches as she flooded the room with warm golden light. Kara shifted half-finished pizzas off the coffee table while Kelly snagged the unfinished beer bottles, making way for the board that Alex unfolded.

     

                “Okay, I’m banker,” Kelly interrupted before anyone could speak. “All of you are cheaters; I don’t trust you.”

     

                Kara squawked in protest but Alex and Lena just laughed. The game seemed to go on for hours, beer making Lena’s head faintly fuzzy, the sour taste unpalatable but welcome all the same as she found herself running out of cash, landing lucky sixes more often than not, and claiming half of the board as hers before Kelly managed to snag a win with the most hotels and bankrupting Kara. 

     

                It was fun and so ordinary that Lena wondered what it would have been like to grow up in a family that played board games together, that ate dinner together and shared beers and teased each other. It left a warm feeling in her stomach, a reluctance to move as she dwelled in the moment, and when they packed up just past eleven, she gave Kara a tired, contented smile.

    Chapter 21

                Lena opened her eyes to the white ceiling of Kara’s bedroom, the glow-in-the-dark stars still faintly glowing as dawn arrived early beyond the curtained windows, leaving rectangular outlines of golden light to break up the darkness. It was quiet, a faint ringing in her ears at the lack of traffic that always permeated even the quietest neighbourhoods in the city centre of National City. Instead, Lena listened to the house settle, quiet creaks and clicks interspersing the gentle rush of the ocean just beyond the back door.

     

                No one stirred downstairs, and she assumed Eliza had left for work hours earlier. Kara was still fast asleep, sprawled out with her face buried into a pillow and Lena rolled onto her side to watch the gentle rising and falling of her chest. She would have been content to stay there all morning, wrapped up beneath the pilled blankets, but, eventually, Kara’s eyes fluttered open and she pushed herself up onto her elbows, blearily blinking as she reached out for her glasses on the nightstand. Pushing them onto her face, she blinked again and then her face creased with a sleepy smile as she looked at Lena.

     

                “Morning,” she hummed, leaning over to kiss her sweetly, voice thick with sleep.

     

                “Did you sleep well?” Lena murmured, pushing hair out of Kara’s face so she could kiss her cheek, the underside of her jaw, the soft spot beneath her earlobe, smiling against her tanned skin as she listened to the breath hitch in Kara’s throat.

     

                “Mm. You?”

     

                “Like a baby.”

     

                It was true, and Lena felt well-rested as she stretched her limbs out, feeling her muscles roll beneath the skin. The stillness of the night, the routine of sleeping early, had left her feeling refreshed, and she climbed over Kara to slip out of bed, her bare feet hitting the cold floorboards and sending goosebumps rippling across her skin.

     

                “Breakfast?” Kara asked, stifling a yawn as she swung her legs over the side of the bed, mismatched socks landing on the floor as she hunched forward for a moment, rubbing at her tired eyes.

     

                “Sure.”

     

                Lena shooed Kara away from the bed, insisting that she would be able to make it by herself, even if she couldn’t manage those crisp hospital corners drilled into Kara by her superiors in the army. Parting the curtains, Lena let early morning sunlight filter in and then followed the smell of brewing coffee down to the kitchen as she crept past closed doors.

     

                The kitchen was warmed by the sunlight spilling in wide swathes across the room, a crisp quality to the day outside as birds twittered in the pines and a nearby neighbour mowed their lawn. Walking up behind Kara, Lena wrapped her arms around her waist and propped her chin on her shoulder, cold fingers digging into the soft skin of Kara’s stomach, warm to the touch.

     

                “Scrambled eggs?” Kara asked, turning her head slightly.

     

                “Sure. Anything I can do?”

     

                Nodding at the fridge, Kara lifted the steaming coffee pot and pulled two mugs closer. “Eggs are in the top of the fridge. There should be cream in the door.”

     

                Fetching them, Lena traded off for a cup of coffee, letting the heat seep into her palms as she gently blew on in and leaned back against the counter, watching as Kara cracked eggs with rhythmic ease. Sipping her coffee, Lena listened to the sounds of nature and let her shoulders drop, so used to the tension of being rushed off her feet that a few minutes of dwelling in the kitchen with nothing to do and nowhere to be left her feeling a little off-kilter.

     

                “You okay?” Kara intruded after a minute.

     

                “I was just thinking about how nice it is to not have anything to do. I mean … I have a lot to do, but it’s nice to know that I’m not touching it for a week.”

     

                With a chuckle, Kara gave her a sceptical look, “I give you two days, max , before you’re sneaking in emails on the side.”

     

                “Ha ha,” Lena sarcastically replied, rolling her eyes. “Is our week going to be that boring?”

     

                “Boring? No. Uneventful? Probably.”

     

                “Good. I could use a trip where absolutely nothing demanding of me happens.”

     

                “I may demand some of your time to walk into town for pie,” Kara gravely told her before her face crumpled into a smile. “The best pie you’ll ever try.”

     

                Nodding, Lena scuffed her foot along the floor, a faint curve to the corners of her mouth. “I think I could make time for that.”

     

                “Good. I thought maybe we could head in for lunch at the diner today. Just the four of us.”

     

                “Sounds good.”

     

                “What’s good?” Kelly asked, stepping into the kitchen as she hid a yawn behind her hand.

     

                She stepped past Lena and pulled a mug out of a cupboard, mumbling her thanks as Lena topped the cup up and Kara filled her in as she scrambled eggs in a pan. Alex wandered down just before breakfast was ready, and Kara rolled her eyes as she put more bread down to toast and set about cracking more eggs to feed everyone.

     

                Lena shook sriracha out of a bottle and watched as everyone ducked around each other and talked over one another, the kitchen bursting with personality and bodies, despite the space. It felt the same as when she spent the night at Kara’s place, everyone packed into one place and making it feel like home. 

     

                “Diner, later?” Kara asked Alex once everyone was seated, raising her eyebrows in an expectant look.

     

                “Pie?”

     

                “Pie,” Kara agreed.

     

                “What’s so special about this pie?” Lena exasperatedly asked Kelly.

     

                She shrugged in response, a crooked smile curling her mouth as she set her coffee down. “It’s just good pie.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena finished off her breakfast and then started on the dishes while she waited for everyone else to catch up. Kelly and Alex dried and put them away while Kara called first dibs on the shower, monopolising the bathroom for half an hour as Lena unpacked her clothes and poked around Kara’s room a little more. She found the yearbook from her senior year of high school and sank onto the edge of the made bed as she flipped through, reading all the kind messages scrawled in the pages, her expression softening at the sight of Kara, much the same but a little younger, something more naïve in her shining blue eyes, not yet subjected to the harshness of war and cruelty that had knocked the edge off her gullibility.

     

                Once Kara stepped into the room, blonde hair damp and curling, a towel clutched around her and her glasses fogged up in one hand, Lena slipped out and followed Kara’s directions to fish a clean towel out of the closet. Trying not to use up all the hot water, Lena was brief, Kara’s familiar bodywash a cloud of sweet florals as she let the hot water cascade over her skin. Hastily brushing her teeth, she slipped back into Kara’s room and changed into jeans and a starched shirt, rolling the sleeves up and spritzing herself with perfume as she let her damp hair air dry.

     

                There were still a couple of hours to kill before they planned on leaving, giving everyone enough time to get ready, so Lena retreated to the back porch with a book of feminist essays and a fresh cup of coffee. Wind chimes hung from the eaves of the porch and they tinkled quietly in the breeze as Lena took a seat in one of the wooden deck chairs and crossed her legs, mug balanced on the arm of the chair and the warm air wrapping around her.

     

                Kelly joined her there a while later, quiet so as to not intrude on the peacefulness of the moment, and they listened to the loud voices of the two sisters from inside the house and the rasping of pages as Lena read. Eventually, the screen door squeaked open and Alex stuck her head outside, sunglasses covering her eyes as her eyebrows rose.

     

                “Ready?”

     

                “Are you?” Kelly wryly shot back, pushing herself up from her seat.

     

                Lena dog-eared the page and picked up her coffee mug before trekking inside, emptying the cold dregs into the sink and taking her book upstairs. She fetched her handbag and donned some sunscreen, coaxing Kara into letting her apply some to the back of her neck and chest while she did her face before they walked downstairs and out the front door.

     

                The air was thick with the warm smell of pine needles, mown grass and sweet flowers, cut through by the salt of the sea, and Lena lingered in the shade of the porch as she waited for Kara to lock up. The four of them set off down the sloping driveway before setting off down the street, sticking to the patches of shade the towering trees offered, and made for the centre of town. The good thing about such a small place with only a few thousand residents was that everything was within walking distance and it didn’t take them longer than thirty minutes to walk from their house into the main strip of stores on offer.

     

                Charmed by the quaint feeling of the small town, she walked hand-in-hand with Kara as kids rode bicycles past them and residents stopped to chat to each other. The main street was a thoroughfare of neatly spaced trees and colourful awnings and shopfronts, all the doors open to the warm day as people drifted in and out. It was a place where people stopped on their way up or down the coast, usually coming from or going to Portland, with the small fisheries nearby offering most of the local trade exports. 

     

                Kara pointed out buildings to her - the local library, the mayor’s office and the place where they printed the town’s gazette - and they ambled along behind Alex and Kelly. Venturing into a small bookshop, the stacks narrow and towering, the four of them perused the selection before Alex and Kara fell into conversation with the owner and Lena picked out a couple of books that caught her eye. 

     

                She paid for them and took her paper bag with thanks before stepping out onto the street, away from the musty, close smell of paper and leather and ink. Lingering in the shade as she browsed the selection set out on the trestle table, she was rejoined a few minutes later before they ducked into a small diner, old and worn with faded signs and the greasy smell of a business that had been operating since their parents were young and had never truly been clean since.

     

                Sliding into a cracked booth in the far corner, in the yellow tinted light of the grease-stained windows, they were quickly greeted by an older woman in uniform with a cheerful smile as she set down sticky menus before them. Kara and Alex made amicable conversation with her for a few moments before she whipped out a notepad and poised her pen.

     

                “Now, what can I get for y’all?”

     

                “Coffee, please,” Lena murmured.

     

                Alex and Kelly followed suit before Kara put in a request for a strawberry milkshake and they were left to browse the menu for a brief moment before she returned with clean cups - albeit a little worn and chipped - and a jug of coffee. Lena took hers black and quietly thanked her as she cradled it between her palms, deliberating over what to choose from the menu.

     

                “Are you getting pie?” Kara asked, leaning in to point at the list.

     

                “Are we not having a real lunch first?”

     

                “Pie is a real lunch.”

     

                “I was going to get a salad.”

     

                Alex made a choked sound and gave Lena a severe look. “You are not getting a salad from a diner . You’ll just be disappointed, trust me. We’ve been coming here since we were young and their pie is incredible but everything else, save the breakfast foods, are either greasy, soggy or just bad.”

     

                “Pie it is then,” Lena said with a decisive nod.

     

                She ended up with a wedge of blueberry pie, ice cream on the side and tiny crystals of sugar dusting the top of the pastry. Kara and Kelly both ordered apple while Alex got a slice of pumpkin. Lena was pleasantly surprised as she took her first bite and hummed enthusiastically as she swallowed.

     

                “It’s good, right?”

     

                “Mm, really good.”

     

                Kara beamed at her and stole a bite of hers before offering up her apple pie for Lena to try. It was equally as amazing and she was soon too stuffed to move as she leaned back in the booth and let her food settle in between sips of coffee.

     

                Before they left, she caught the waitresses attention and ordered a full chocolate and pecan pie to go before setting a hundred dollar bill beneath the napkin dispenser and ushering everyone outside without waiting for her change. Kara carried the white box with a delighted look on her face and towed Lena along by the crook of her elbow as they walked along the rest of the street.

     

                “Well, this is pretty much it. The rest of it is mostly just neighbourhoods. And obviously there are the schools and the hospital and stuff, but that’s a small town for you.”

     

                “I’ve never been to a small town before; I like it.”

     

                Snorting, Kara smiled faintly, “I’ve never really lived anywhere but a small town, until National City. I don’t remember living in Tennessee; we moved when I was still too young to have any memory of it. What about you? Was it always Metropolis?”

     

                Letting out a weary sigh, Lena ruffled her dark hair as her brow creased slightly. “Yeah. Just outside of the city. It’s … a family home.”

     

                Kara cocked her head to the side and eyed her for a moment, a searching look in her blue eyes that Lena avoided, focused on where she was walking as she waited for the inevitable questions. “I- I know you don’t like talking about your family … but what was your childhood actually like? You don’t have to tell me if you don’t want to.”

     

                Expression softening with amusement at Kara’s quick assurances, Lena hummed as she pursed her lips, choosing her words carefully as memories assaulted her. She didn’t quite know how to put some of it into words - sometimes, she thought it sounded silly to be so hurt by insignificant things. With so much money, what could have been that bad that a fortune couldn’t soften the stinging blow left behind?

     

                “I love you, Kara, and- and I do want to share things with you,” Lena murmured, keeping her voice down to not be overheard by Alex and Kelly, who were a short way in front and deep in their own conversation. “It just- it sounds so … trivial . The worst thing in my life is that I watched my mom die-”

     

                “That’s a big thing to watch, Lena,” Kara murmured, a pained note in her voice as she winced.

     

                “Yeah, but that’s just it. I don’t really remember it so it’s not the worst thing to me. I was four when I was brought home to my new family; I don’t even remember what my life was like before, without a dad and a brother, with a different mom. That should be the worst thing, but instead … I remember being terrified - all the time - of my dad; he was an angry man and he always took it out on me last, because I was his favourite. But that only went so far.”

     

                “Is that- Lex …”

     

                Nodding curtly, Lena swallowed as her lips curled ruefully. “He was funny, you know. And clever. And so patient with his new little sister - he was so much older than me that I didn’t understand I was treated like a pet until I got old enough to realise. My father was always at work, and so was my mom, but when they were home - when he was home - there would be fights. Always fights. We lived in a big house, but even that couldn’t quieten the shouts. He would be that loud, ripping into my mom or my brother after too much to drink, and then me if neither of them were around.”
