She wondered if Alex had left it there for her, or if Kara had laid it out in preparation for her to find the next time she went in there. Either way, Lena avoided it for the time being, her ears ringing faintly as she drew in a shallow, strangled breath and ducked into the bedroom.

     

                Turning the shower on, she stripped off her clothes and stepped into the steam and heat, closing her eyes and swallowing dryly. The body wash that smelled of Kara was enough to take the edge off her misery, familiar and sweet and convincing enough to make Lena pretend she was just in the other room. It was a cold comfort, but she took it all the same, stepping out of the shower smelling like Kara, fishing out one of her faded t-shirts and shrugging it on over her too-long sweatpants, enveloped in the smell of her detergent.

     

                Once she was ready for bed, skincare routine complete and teeth brushed, although she couldn’t muster the energy required to blow dry her hair, Lena stopped putting off the inevitable and climbed beneath the heavy covers. Pulling the photo album and letter toward her, she set the envelope aside and drew in a deep breath before flipping open the cover to the first photo.

     

                On the first page was the photo from the coffee shop, sunlight hitting one side of Lena’s face as she looked into the camera. On the white trim at the bottom, Kara had scrawled ‘The day we first met’ with the date next to it. A small sob caught in Lena’s throat as she traced a fingertip over the writing. Flipping to the next page, there was a photo of Lena from the back as she walked out of the movie theatre, a rumpled ticket stuck on beneath it and another caption. ‘First movie date’.

     

                Next was Lena biting into a hotdog, her eyes creasing at the corners with amusement and faint embarrassment, one hand blurred in motion to stop Kara. ‘The hotdog experience’ with another date beside it. On and on it went, with photos that Lena didn’t even realise Kara had taken of them and their days together. Some of them had both of their faces wedged into it, Kara holding the camera at arm’s length, some obviously taken by Alex or Kelly, who made a few appearances as well, from dinners and nights at bars and trips hiking together. In most of them, Lena was oblivious to it being taken, and those ones with Kara were her favourite, both of them wrapped up in their own bubble, their love for each other shining through in the way their faces softened slightly with a look.

     

                Finally, she reached a photo of them that morning, Lena opening the door to the coffee shop and then one with Kara’s face cut out, where Lena had stolen it for her locket, and realised that she was at the end. The album wasn’t finished, but it was the last photo. She was crying by then, her cheeks wet and nose running and her breaths hitching and shallow as she caressed Kara’s face in each of them, the message clear - she would be back to fill the blank pages up with more photos. Lena would be counting down the days until that moment.

     

                And then, there was the letter. She tore the envelope open with shaking fingers and unfolded a few sheets of lined paper, taking in the spots where the ink from a cheap ballpoint pen had bled through the pages and smudges in others from Kara’s apparent tears. She’d cried while writing it.

     

                Eyes racing through the words, devouring each one like she was starving, Lena finished it and was left wanting more, even though she felt as if her heart was breaking. At that moment, she was irrationally angry at Kara, irate as she wiped at her cheeks with a scowl on her face and the pages of the letter scattered in her lap. Wiping her face on the t-shirt, she suppressed a pitiful sound that built in her chest and turned the lights off, crumpling the pages as she rolled over beneath the blankets and drew them up over her head. 

     

                It had been years since she’d done that, the thin veil offering protection from the outside world, where things hurt and frightened her. Misery overwhelmed her and she clutched the pages in a trembling hand as she finally broke down, in a way she hadn’t since before her father had died. So much of Lena’s personality had come from the meticulous suppression of anything that stung, but it was like opening the floodgates on so many things that had built up over time, waiting for a moment of weakness when she would be blindsided by something she couldn’t help but feel.

     

                Lena cried until her throat was raw and scratchy, her eyes sore and bloodshot from rubbing them too much, and her chest eventually felt lighter. It was like a heavy weight had been lifted off her, weeks of worrying about the inevitable finally culminating and coming to pass, and now that it had and she’d cried it all out, she just felt drained. So incredibly tired . But even exhaustion couldn’t make her anxious mind slow down enough for sleep to take root, and it was three o’clock when she finally slipped out of bed.

     

                The house was still in the early hours of the morning, shadowed and occasionally making clicking noises as the old bones adjusted. Her feet were silent as she padded downstairs, the lights dimly coming on in the kitchen as she poured herself a glass of water from the filtered jug. It was cold, almost painful, to her tender throat, and she sipped it slowly as she stared out the window above the sink, taking in the shadowed outline of the rustling trees.

     

                “Can’t sleep?”

     

                She dropped the cup into the sink, glass shattering, at the sound of the voice, and whirled around as her heart hammered in her chest. Raking a hand through her hair as she clutched at the front of her shirt, Lena grunted noncommittally and sighed as she turned around, plucking shards of glass from the basin.

     

                “It’s funny, I’ve been alone for my entire life, slept alone every night, and then your sister comes along and now …” Lena’s bottom lip wobbled and she let her dark hair fall around her face as she moved over to the bin, shards of glass tinkling as they fell into it. “Now, I can’t sleep because she’s not beside me.”

     

                “It’s okay to miss her,” Alex said, drifting further into the kitchen, a weary look on her face as she ruffled her undercut. “It’ll be a big adjustment for the first few days; no one’s expecting you to just get over it. You’ll probably spend most of the first week crying.”

     

                “You heard that, huh?” Lena muttered, embarrassment washing over her.

     

                “I was coming to check on you. But … it just takes time, but it will get easier, I promise.”

     

                With a scathing sound at the back of her throat, Lena curled her lip derisively. “Everyone keeps saying that but it won’t make her come back any faster.”

     

                “Look … the best thing you can do right now is look after yourself . You need sleep.”

     

                Humming in agreement, Lena rubbed her hands over her face, blinking back the burning in her eyes from two nearly sleepless nights in a row - the whole week, really - and let out a small laugh. Shooing Alex out of the kitchen, Lena followed after her and turned the lights off, their footsteps slow and heavy as they made their way back upstairs.

     

                Alex was on the second floor, and Lena rounded the end of the staircase, watching her silhouette make for one of the closed bedroom doors. “Hey, Alex? Thanks.”

     

                “Get some sleep, Lena.”

    Chapter 24

    Lena,   

     

    I know that it probably won’t make you feel better to come home to this, but there are a lot of things I don’t know how to say to you. I’d probably cry before I could even get a word out and I didn’t want to make it any harder than it had to be. I know I could just as easily have emailed you, or called you as soon as I got here - I still will - but some things are better said when they’re written down. I thought that maybe the photos would help show it; they’re just a few of the hundreds that I’ve taken over the past seven months, and a few out of the thousands I plan on taking in the future.

     

    Truthfully, I’m dreading going back. More than I ever have before, because this time I’m leaving you behind too. I didn’t think it would feel any different, but this time it’s especially bitter, because I love you and I’m the one that’s hurting you. It hurts me too, even though I know it’s not forever. It’s only nine months, which seems like forever right now, but it’ll go faster than we think. The thought of coming home to you will be all I need to get through it - and I will come home, I can promise you that much. 

     

    I guess I just wanted to let you know how grateful I am to you for the past seven months. I never got to tell you how grateful I was because we thought we’d have more time, but I really am. Because of you, I have truly known what it’s like to be loved and I will be grateful for that forever. Thank you. 

     

    I know I made you do all those silly things you’d never done before, and I want you to know that it has meant the world to me that we could do them together. Maybe a part of me was being selfish and wanted those moments for myself too, knowing that this would happen and wanting to feel like we had a year in a handful of months. I’ll cherish every memory of those days and all the moments we spent together in between. The photos are a testament to that.

     

    For so long, I photographed all the beautiful things I saw and all the ordinary moments that I didn’t want to take for granted. I wanted to appreciate the hand that life dealt. But you - you’re the most beautiful thing I’ve ever photographed and I wanted to leave you something to prove that. No matter what happens, we have proof that we loved each other, and in these pages, I won’t ever let you go.

     

    I know there’s no point in telling you not to worry about me, because that would be like telling me not to worry about you. I know you probably won’t be sleeping and you’ll be at work all the time, but you should try and enjoy life a little bit more - for me. Just know, I’ll be fighting every day to come home to you because we still have a lifetime to spend together and nothing can take that away from us. Not even silly little stories on what’s going on over here.

     

    You can probably tell that I’ve been crying while writing this - hopefully you can still make out what I said. There’s so much more to say but I’ll end it here. Just know that I love you more than you even know and I’ll never stop - I’m certain of it. This is going to be hard, I know that, and I’m dreading it, but please hold onto the hope that I’ll come home. Once I’m back, I’ll never have to leave again. I still have the empty pages in the album to fill up with our new memories.

     

    Yours always,

     

    Kara x

    Chapter 25

                Waking up early the next morning, Lena made her way downstairs to the gym, dressed for a workout and puffy eyed from a lack of sleep. Even after her talk with Alex it had taken her another hour to doze off, and she’d slept fitfully for a few hours before rising, brimming with too much pent-up energy, despite her exhaustion. 

     

                Whaling on a boxing bag until her wrapped knuckles hurt and her arms felt rubbery and on fire, Lena climbed onto the treadmill for a two mile run before she collapsed down on a gym mat and stretched, feeling her muscles twinge and her heart rate slow as she forced in steady lungfuls of air. Sweat dried on her skin and snagged a small towel from the rack and wiped her brow as she made her way upstairs. 

     

                She heard movement in the kitchen but headed upstairs for a shower first, scrubbing herself clean and wincing at the tenderness of her scraped knuckles. Dressing for work in an oyster grey pencil skirt and a silk blouse, Lena did her makeup and sprayed on perfume, glancing at the clock and noting how much time she had. It was just after seven and she didn’t have any meetings until nine-thirty, according to the schedule Jess kept updated.

     

                Padding downstairs barefoot, she carried her heels and handbag, a thin trench coat thrown over her arm and left on the narrow bench in the hallway before she stepped through the open archway and through to the kitchen. Alex raised her eyebrows at her appearance and Kelly glanced over her shoulder, a coffee cup in hand, frowning slightly.

     

                “You’re working today?”

     

                “I’ve already missed enough meetings over the last couple of weeks,” Lena muttered, making for the coffee machine.

     

                “Give yourself a day before you throw yourself back into it,” Alex chided her.

     

                Shrugging, Lena watched strong espresso drip into the tiny cup and pursed her lips slightly, her back to the other women as she swallowed thickly. “There’s an upcoming annual shareholder meeting I need to prepare for.”

     

                Alex softly swore, shaking her head, and Lena turned, espresso cup pinched between thumb and index finger before she knocked it back, leaving a smear of red lipstick on the rim. She cleared her throat and set it down in the sink.

     

                “I should get going.”

     

                “At least eat something before you go,” Alex pressed.

     

                Suppressing a sigh, Lena rolled her eyes, giving into her fussing, if only to avoid the hassle. She hadn’t imagined that she’d be subjected to being pestered while Kara was gone, being babysat by Alex and Kelly, who clearly didn’t think she could look after herself well enough without their supervision. Lena supposed that Kara had been smart to leave her with the two of them; she did have the bad habit of skipping meals and sleep in favour of work.

     

                Pouring a small portion of granola into a bowl with Greek yoghurt, Lena leaned against the counter and shovelled it into her mouth without really tasting anything. She dumped her bowl into the sink once she was done and fixed the cuff of her shirt before giving Alex a pointed look.

     

                “Alright, I need to go. Are you guys good to lock up? Kara gave you her key, right?”

     

                “Mhm.”

     

                “Okay. Um … thanks for last night.”

     

                They both smiled slightly and nodded and Lena slowly rubbed her palms together. Reaching out, Alex gave her a sympathetic look and squeezed her arm. “No problem, just try and take it easy today.”

     

                “Yes, boss,” Lena said with a wry smile.

     

                She had every intention of throwing herself into her work, to drown out any thoughts of Kara, if only for a moment. It was being home alone that troubled her, knowing that she wouldn’t be able to avoid missing her in the empty house. Throwing herself into blueprints and statistics and project proposals would be a welcome reprieve, and Lena had every intention of utilising it as much as possible. 

     

                “Well, I’ll see you both soon,” Lena hesitantly said.

     

                Her brow creased faintly with a cautious look. She wasn’t really sure when they would see each other, but she assumed Kara had asked her sister to keep tabs on her, so maybe they’d catch up for coffee in a week or so. Still, Lena felt uncertain as she awkwardly lingered for a second longer before making her way out to the hallway.

     

                Slipping on her heels and donning her coat, she checked her lipstick in the mirror and double checked her laptop and keys were in her bag before snagging the car keys off the console. “Bye!”

     

                She heard the same echoed back at her from in the kitchen and smiled slightly as she stepped out onto the stoop, pulling the door closed behind her. Unlocking the Porsche, she slid behind the wheel and drove to L-Corp, the underground parking lot cool and smelling of damp concrete as she nodded to the security guard and stepped into the elevator.

     

                Jess was there, newspaper, fresh juice and tablet ready for her as she swept in, keeping pace with Lena as she rattled off a list of updates. Taking a seat behind her desk and thanking her, Lena brought the computer monitor to life and gave the front page a cursory read while sipping her juice. There was a stack of manila folders arranged to show the titles printed on labels and arranged by importance, and Lena familiarised herself with the media rollout for quantum batteries, press talking points and an outline for the speech she’d have to give at the launch. It was one of their closely kept secrets that would revolutionise the tech industry as well as benefit the clean energy image. Lena was expecting to secure numerous contracts once the project was launched, projected profit margins increasing by thirty-six percent.

     

                Briefing herself for her first meeting, she was silent through most of it, knowing that the media campaign had been fine-tuned for weeks, with every possible pedantic thing she’d picked up on ironed out until it was perfect . Lena wouldn’t settle for anything else, and knew that those high up enough to be in the same room as her were of the same mind; they didn’t need her input to know that it was perfect and so she offered minimal input to the conversation as it washed over her. Her silence was uncharacteristic though and without her pressing questions and penchant for poking holes in things until they were airtight, the meeting wrapped up quickly.

     

                Poring over numbers in her office as she highlighted important points for the meeting, Lena wallowed and picked at the lunch Jess had delivered to her desk as noon rolled around. She was too distracted by thoughts of what Kara was doing - it would be night time in Afghanistan, she would have arrived already, but so far she hadn’t heard from her. Lena didn’t know what the protocol was with calling home and she felt stupid for sitting around waiting for her phone to ring.

     

                After a few minutes of toying with a slice of orange in her salad, Lena set the fork down and pushed the button on the phone, calling through to Jess, who picked up immediately. “Miss Luthor?”

     

                “Hey, can you come in here for a second?”

     

                She put the phone down and straightened up in her seat before dumping the salad in the trash. Wiping her fingers on the napkin, she watched the door swing open and her assistant warily come inside. It was no secret to Lena’s employees that she’d been seeing someone, Jess sheepishly keeping her informed on all of the gossip that was rife in the different departments, and Jess knew the circumstances of their relationship better than anyone else in the building, having been the orchestrator of many dates, outfits and gifts. 

     

                Lena frowned slightly as she tapped a pen on the desk, chewing thoughtfully on her bottom lip as Jess hovered before her desk, fiddling with a ring on her fingers. With an uncertain smile, Jess arched an eyebrow. “Ma’am?”

     

                Blank look smoothing into a pleasant look, Lena’s lips twitched with a smile, “I need you to do something for me. I’m trying to think about how to get you to ask.”

     

                “Oh. Well, I’m sure anyone will say yes to you.”

     

                With a scoff of laughter, Lena gave her a droll look, one side of her mouth curling up with mirth. “Literally anyone else would.”

     

                She was silent for a moment longer before tossing the pen down and shaking her head. “Can you- can you just call my mom for me. Or better yet her assistant, if she hasn’t fired the last one yet. Ask them to dig out some of my childhood photos and send them to me. Please.”

     

                “Oh,” Jess murmured at the strange request. “Right, of course. I’ll … do that now.”

     

                “Thanks, Jess,” Lena called out to her assistant’s retreating back.

     

                Alone, the sunlight streaming in through the wall of windows behind her and warming her back, Lena tapped the armrests for a minute as she waited. When Jess poked her head in to say that Lillian’s assistant had taken a message, she decided to stretch her legs to dispel some of the tension in her shoulders and curtly thanked her assistant. Donning her coat and grabbing her cell phone and purse, Lena swept out of the office and made her way to the elevator, riding it down to the lobby and stalking across the marble floors without paying the curious looks any mind.

     

                There was a coffee shop in the lobby of the building next door and she queued behind a gaggle of men in crisp suits, opening unread texts and ignoring them all until it was her turn to order. She ordered two dirty chai lattes - one with oat milk - and lingered on the sidewalk for a minute, pacing back and forth as she sipped her drink and then made her way upstairs. Passing by Jess’s desk, she set the spare drink down on the counter and met her dark eyes, shrugging slightly.

     

                “You drink chai, right? With oat milk?”

     

                “I- yes. Um, thank you,” Jess said, blinking away her surprise as she rose from her seat.

     

                Nodding, Lena swept back into her office as her phone started ringing in her pocket. The door slowly swung shut behind her and she all but dropped her coffee in her haste to set it down onto the coffee table, hand scrabbling in her coat pocket as her purse bounced on the couch cushions. Her heart hammered in her chest but her stomach plummeted a moment later as disappointment knifed through her and her lips twisted with bitter disdain at the name lighting up her phone’s screen.

     

                “I’m busy,” Lena greeted her mother, too emotionally drained to muster up the energy to deal with Lillian right now.

     

                “Planning for the shareholder meeting, I know. I just wanted to let you know I’ll be in town in a few days for it-”

     

                “I’m the majority shareholder now,” Lena interrupted, “there’s no need for you to come.”

     

                “Nevertheless, I have a vested interest so I’ll be there. I’m bringing the photos you asked for with me.”

     

                Lena paused, lips twitching as she slowly sank down onto the sofa, crossing her legs and leaning back. Suspicion curled at the edges of her mind and she sucked on her teeth for a moment. “What’s the catch?”

     

                Her mother sighed but was forthcoming. “I’ll give them to you over lunch.”

     

                “Lunch?” Lena said with a snort of laughter. “You’re going to blackmail me with lunch?”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Lillian replied with vague amusement, “really, Lena, only you would see lunch as blackmail. I thought it might be nice to catch up.”

     

                “Catch up?” Lena stressed, her eyebrows rising sceptically.

     

                “Is that really so hard to believe?” Lillian softly asked, a brittle edge to her words as if wounded by Lena’s disbelief.

     

                “Uh, yeah, kind of. But … fine . I’ll see you then.”

     

                “Perfect.”

     

                Lena hung up without another word, tossing the phone onto the coffee table with a clatter before raking a hand through her hair. Shaking her head, she muttered to herself and pursed her lips, rankling at the thought of seeing her mother. Absorbed in her sulking thoughts of lunch with Lillian, she groaned softly as her phone started vibrating a minute later, heaving a sigh as she reached for it to ignore her.

     

                But then her eyes landed on the name and she upset her drink, coffee and chai spilling across the coffee table and onto the cream rug as she pressed the green phone. “Shit,” Lena swore, shooting to her feet as she held the phone, the screen dark, and grabbed a handful of tissues from the box to mop up the mess. “Fuck’s sake.”

     

                “I thought you’d be happy to see me.”

     

                She froze at the sound of Kara’s voice and let out a breathless laugh as she took in the pixelated screen, slowly glitching into focus as the video call connected. Tears springing to her eyes, Lena sank down to the stained carpet and gave her a yearning look as a tentative smile curled her lips.

     

                “Hi,” Kara said, looking exhausted as a tired smile graced her face and she propped her cheek up in her hand.

     

                “Oh, ” Lena softly said, the air rushing from her lungs, drinking in the sight of her as she touched the screen with a trembling fingertip. “Oh , it’s you. It’s- God, I didn’t know when you were going to call. Hi. I miss you so much. I love you.”

     

                Kara laughed at Lena’s babbling, her eyes creasing at the corners, even as they shone with tears. Shifting forward, sitting on the edge of a cot, the sandy wall of a tent behind her, she softly sighed.

     

                “Sorry. This is the first free moment I’ve had since I got here.”

     

                “It’s okay. I figured you’d be busy. I just- I’m so relieved to see your face; I can’t stop thinking about you.”

     

                “Oh, yeah?” Kara grinned, “I can’t stop thinking about you either. I think I cried the whole bus ride and on all three legs of the flights.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena swallowed thickly. “Yeah? Well, I had this letter left on my bed to read right before I went to sleep. In case it’s not obvious, I didn’t get much sleep.”

     

                With a loud laugh, rocking back slightly, Kara smiled widely. “Yeah, sorry about that.”

     

                “No,” Lena murmured, her expression softening as she sobered up, “I loved it. And the photos.”

     

                “Good.”

     

                “I will be holding you to your promise that you’ll be back to fill the rest of the pages, though,” Lena sternly warned her.

     

                “Of course.”

     

                There was a momentary pause and Lena let out a breathless sob that shook her shoulders, her face crumpling as she jutted her chin forward in a petulant manner. “Seriously, Kara. I mean it. I swear to God, you better come home or- or I’ll fly there myself and drag you back.”

     

                “I always keep my promises.”

     

                “Good. Have you spoken to Alex yet? Eliza?”

     

                “Not yet. I had to see your face first; I wanted to make sure you were okay.”

     

                “I’m … managing,” Lena said with a wan smile, gesturing vaguely as she shook her head, running her fingers through her hair.

     

                They both knew she was putting on a brave face, aiming for levity as they made the most of their quick call. Underneath it all, all the false bravado and nonchalance, she was heartbroken and feeling that loneliness she’d thought she’d sworn off after meeting Kara.

     

                “You should call your mom and your sister,” Lena said after a moment. “Let them know you got there safely. I don’t want to hog you.”

     

                Kara smiled, wrinkling her nose as she leaned forward. “Every inch of me is yours, Lena Luthor. But … you’re right, I should call them. I’ll call you as soon as I can, okay? Hopefully tomorrow.”

     

                “Call whenever, okay? It doesn’t matter if it’s four in the morning, as long as I get to see your face.”

     

                “Yes, ma’am. I love you.”

     

                “I love you too. Please, stay safe.”

     

                Kara gave her a lazy salute and they both sat there staring at each other for a moment, waiting for the other to hang up so they didn’t have to. Letting out a snort of laughter, Lena shook her head and waved before she hung up for her. The screen went black, leaving her staring at her own reflection, and although her chest twinged with missing Kara, she felt better now that she’d spoken to her, looked at her. It was oddly reassuring, even though circumstances hadn’t changed. If she really tried, Lena could almost pretend that she was just talking to Kara like she usually did at work, when they’d call each other on their lunch breaks. 

     

                With a sigh, she finished mopping up as much of the spilt drink as she could, dumping the wad of wet tissues into the trash, along with the empty cup, and then stood at her desk, staring down at the files. Exhaustion stooped her shoulders and after a moment of deliberation, Lena decided to call it a day. Packing everything into her handbag, she grabbed her phone and purse, fished her keys out of her bag and stepped back out of the office.

     

                Jess looked up at her appearance, taking in the coat and her bag and realising that she was leaving. Clearing her throat, Lena fumbled for her sunglasses to hide her bloodshot eyes, although they hadn’t escaped Jess’s notice, and slipped them on.

     

                “I’m done for the day,” Lena quietly informed her. “You should go home; there’s no reason to stay.”

     

                “Oh, well … I could always double-check the schedule for the rest of the week.”

     

                Waving a hand as she cut her off, a faint smile lifting one side of her mouth, Lena shook her head. “No need. It’s only the stockholder meeting that matters; I’m sure the others will manage if I don’t show up.”

     

                “Right.”

     

                “Have a good night.”

     

                She went straight home after leaving the office, the drive leaving her far too much time to think as she slowly moved through each intersection. Lena needed something engaging , something that would distract her from her own thoughts, and as soon as she stepped into the empty house, she changed into something more comfortable and went up to her office. The perfect distraction from Kara seemed to be writing a letter to Kara, and as she sipped a glass of lemon water, Lena slowly let her looping writing cover the piece of personalised paper. She quite liked the idea of them writing letters back and forth to each other; not only was it something to occupy her time, but she would be able to take her time to write down things that happened, things she might forget or have trouble putting into words during their talks.

     

                Once she had finished writing it, she folded the pieces of paper up and put them into an envelope of matching, creamy paper. The set had been a gift off her mother once she’d assumed the position of CEO at L-Corp, and while Lena had scoffed at the gesture at the time, leaving it untouched at the bottom of her desk drawer, she was oddly grateful for it in that moment, and had to admit that it was nice stationery. 

     

                Spending as long as she could fussing over the letter, leaving it to be posted as soon as she got Kara’s address, Lena ventured downstairs and onto the back patio. Sipping her lemon water, she enjoyed the fresh breeze on her skin and spent a good while watering the herb garden with loving attention, pulling a few weeds and taking a few clippings to propagate them. 

     

                The sound of the door opening brought her inside a few minutes later, apprehension written on her face as she cautiously padded through the kitchen, setting her empty glass on the counter as quietly as possible. The sound of Alex’s voice reached her ears a moment later and Lena let out a held breath as she boldly stepped into the hallway, arms crossed and an eyebrow arched.

     

                “What are you doing here?”

     

                “See? I told you she was home,” Kelly said, nudging Alex.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex grimaced, “well, she usually lives at the office.”

     

                “My car’s parked out front.”

     

                “You have multiple cars.”

     

                “Touché, but I very much did leave in that car this morning. Did you come to rob me?”

     

                Alex let out a quick laugh as Kelly shut the door, holding a bursting bag in her arms. They trekked further inside, making for the kitchen and setting down their grocery shopping. Quickly unpacking things, Alex looked up and met Lena’s confused eyes.

     

                “What?”

     

                “I’m just … a bit surprised that you’re here,” she said slowly.

     

                “Oh. Well, I think Kara was worried you’d starve if you had to fend for yourself, so we thought we’d cook dinner tonight. Kelly makes a mean chili con carne.”

     

                Snorting, Lena looked on with amusement as she shook her head. “She knows that I survived on my own for six years, right? Like, I fed myself and everything.”

     

                “Yeah, well, you can’t cook for shit so you’re stuck with us.”

     

                 Chewing on her lip as she furrowed her brow, evidently perplexed, Lena watched on in silence until Alex sighed and gave her a pointed look. “What?”

     

                “Nothing, I just- I’m grateful for the company but … I’d resigned myself to spending the next nine months alone, so I guess I’m just … kind of confused. I figured that … well, Kara was the middle person and we wouldn’t really … hang out while she was gone.”

     

                Surprise flashed across Alex’s face, softening into a slightly wounded look of offence as she scoffed. Quiet understanding lit up Kelly’s eyes as she set down a tray of ground beef, pity making her shoulders drop.

     

                “You- you thought that we were being nice to you for Kara’s sake?”

     

                Shrugging as she self-consciously laughed and rubbed the back of her neck, Lena smiled sheepishly. “I mean, yeah. ”

     

                “Kid,” Alex sighed, giving her an exasperated look, “you’re family now. So, tough. You’re stuck with us.”

     

                A bubble of happiness expanded in Lena’s chest as a lump caught in her throat. She didn’t even have it in her to reply to that, but the mournful look of bewilderment eased into a tender look of delight as she went to rummage in the fridge for seltzers as she tried to hide her floundering surprise. In so many ways, this was as new to her as her relationship with Kara, and she hadn’t anticipated earning herself a family in the process. Lena was glad all the same.

     

                After dinner, they stayed a while, talking over beers and filling the empty house with life and noise for a little while, until they eventually left. Lena knew they were trying to keep her company for as long as possible, giving up their evenings to help fill the void, because Alex had Kelly but Lena had no one else. 

     

                When they left, the hour late and the city still very much alive, she changed into Kara’s pyjamas, breathing in the clinging smell of her, and lay in the middle of the bed, taking up all the space that should’ve been split between the two of them. She cried again - just for a little while - clutching the photo album to her chest until she wore herself out enough to sleep.

     

                As the following days stretched on, Lena started going back to sleep in the mornings, after rising early and going for a run on the treadmill and boxing until her knuckles were mottled with bruises and her limbs were burning with the effort. She dozed on top of the blankets in her gym clothes, letting the mild breeze of late July blow in through the open window until it was time to get up for work. She would feel the morning coffee still pushing through her veins, but sink into sleep with relief and gratitude.

     

                At the end of the week, the shareholder meeting was scheduled and Lena was in a foul mood from the moment she woke that morning. Not only was she about to end the week with lunch with her mother, but it was her first weekend without Kara and she was anxious to get through it, to have it over and done with so she would be able to throw herself back into work on Monday. As it was, Lena anticipated a busy weekend with paperwork until she died of boredom.

     

                Washing and styling her hair, she brooded in the mirror as she applied her makeup, aiming for the appropriate amount of maturity to be taken seriously and adding a slash of red lipstick to her mouth as an act of revolt. Opting for wide-legged navy pants and an ivory silk shirt, Lena accessorised accordingly and wolfed down a banana and scalding green tea before driving to the office.

     

                She was early, which was an unavoidable nuisance because it meant there was a window of opportunity for her mother to prey on her unsuspectingly. Checking her teeth for red lipstick stains in a small compact mirror, she snapped it shut as the elevator doors dinged at the top floor and parted to spit her out. 

     

                No sooner had she stepped out of the elevator before Jess was upon her, a wince on her face as she lowered her voice to a hush as Lena gave her a bewildered ‘good morning’. “Miss Luthor, your mother-”

     

                Letting out a scathing sigh, Lena’s lips twisted ruefully and she gave Jess a mollifying look, cutting her off with a gentle touch on her arm. “Don’t worry about it.”

     

                Throwing her shoulders back and jerking her chin up slightly, Lena strode into her office, all business. Lillian was sitting on the sofa, flipping through a magazine, and glanced up as her daughter burst in. There was almost a mildly amused hint to her mother’s emotions that automatically put Lena on edge, playing the defense before she even knew what the attack was, and that morning was no different as she shot her a wary look and moved over to the hidden cupboard in a wall panel to stow her bag and jacket, fishing out her keys, laptop and notebook in the process.

     

                “You’re here early,” Lena stated.

     

                “I’m still on Metropolis time; I thought I may as well come in and try and catch you before the meeting.”

     

                “I’m not sure why.”

     

                “You still drink cappuccinos, don’t you?”

     

                Lena glanced over her shoulder and watched as Lillian nudged one of the coffee cups on the table forward an inch. Her lips twitched and she scornfully replied, “I take it black now.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                Still, she walked over to the coffee table and stooped down to pick up the cup, the thought of making it through the meeting without caffeine even more unbearable than the stilted conversation with Lillian. Lowering herself onto one of the square ottoman’s situated across from the coffee table and cast her mother a cautious look.

     

                “Thank you,” she awkwardly said after a moment, taking a sip of coffee.

     

                Nodding, Lillian continued to flip through the magazine as the tension built and the moment stretched on. After a few minutes with no conversation forthcoming and the discomfort making Lena’s stomach tie itself into knots, she cleared her throat and climbed to her feet.

     

                “The meeting’s going to start soon; I should make my way in.”

     

                Lillian nodded again, setting the magazine down on the coffee table and following her daughter to the conference room in silence. Lena was too occupied talking to Jess, who was laying out a stapled stack of papers before each seat, to make small talk with her mother and it wasn’t long before a series of people in suits started trickling in, ready for it to be open so they could go about their weekend playing golf or visiting Napa Valley.

     

                The meeting seemed to drag, but Lena was grateful for the time it ate up as she wearily painted a picture of the future for L-Corp, clicking through a presentation on the giant screen as she plotted out the points and strategies to achieve it. Her mother was silent but watchful and it was all Lena could do to ignore the prickling feeling of her eyes on her skin as she answered questions and made confident assurances. Eventually, the meeting adjourned and she shook hands in the hallway outside, giving them thin smiles and nods as the stream of men and women flooded into the elevators.

     

                “Lunch?” Lillian pressed her, arching an eyebrow as she materialised at Lena’s side, accepting her coat and handbag off Jess.

     

                “Let me get my things,” Lena muttered, walking into her office as she resigned herself to it.

     

                Slipping on her coat as they climbed into the elevator, she pushed the button and added a touch more of red lipstick to her lips as they lurched down through the building. Looming beside her, ever as dominatingly tall and elegant, Lillian looked up at the numbers, watching it descend.

     

                “I made a reservation at a new French restaurant in town.”

     

                “Fine.”

     

                “The meeting went well, don’t you think?”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                Lillian let out an exasperated sigh and shook her head as she gave up on any attempts at conversation. They walked through the lobby with numerous attracted looks, a rare day to see both Luthor women together, and Lena had to fight the urge to hunch her shoulders and shrink away from the attention. Her mother had a driver, smoking idly against the side of the car as the older man waited for her return, and he quickly exhaled a cloud of grey, crushing his cigarette underfoot and lunging for the door.

     

                They sat on opposite sides of the car, Lena resting her cheek in her cupped palm as she looked out the window and watched the city pass by. They came to a stop outside a five-star hotel a few blocks from L-Corp, stepping into the perfumed lobby and making for the carved stone doorway to a restaurant.

     

                Inside, it had a curved wall of windows overlooking the street and was decorated in neutral tones, thick creams and natural wood giving it a modern but grand air, reminiscent of the elegance of Paris but without the opulence. Their coats were taken at the door and they were escorted to their table without the necessary introductions, waiters in trim waistcoats and starched shirts pulling out their chairs as they sat.

     

                Lillian ordered a Kir for herself as an apéritif while Lena opted to wait for the paired wine menu with their lunch. It was a set menu of three half dishes with cheeses and dessert and Lena knew they’d be staggered over an agonising hour at least , her mouth thinning as she grimly looked around the place, arms folded sulkily over her chest as she leaned back in her chair almost goadingly.

     

                “So … how are you?” Lillian asked as soon as her drink was placed before her.

     

                Lena’s lips twitched faintly as her face creased with amusement. A quiet huff of laughter was expelled from her as she looked aside, a muscle twitching in her jaw. “We don’t have to do this part.”

     

                “I’m curious.”

     

                “You’re fishing.”

     

                “I know she was deployed. Kara , isn’t it? At the start of the week.”

     

                Indignation made Lena bristle as she shifted up straighter in her seat and leaned forward, keeping her voice down as she quietly fumed, cheeks red with embarrassment. “Stop spying on me.”

     

                Scoffing with a patronising laugh, Lillian shook her head, “I’m not spying. But I wouldn’t have to go through all the effort to know how you are if you’d answer any of my calls.”

     

                “I answered your call the other day.”

     

                “Don’t be pedantic,” Lillian chided her, clicking her tongue as she set her fluted glass back down.

     

                Lips twisting ruefully, Lena scowled at the sunlight seeping in through the curved windows. Lillian chuckled, which made Lena flush at the sound of it, and then let out a soft, resigned sigh as she leaned across the small table, eyes glancing around at the near-empty restaurant as the quiet murmur of conversation and lunch surrounded them.

     

                “Is it so hard for you to believe that I may actually want to know my own daughter?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena slowly replied, her tone clipped and haughty. “It is, actually.”

     

                “Go ahead,” Lillian urged her, leaning back and raising her glass to her lips. “Be angry at me.”

     

                Her calmness only served to infuriate Lena more and she seethed in silence. The minutes ticked by and she found her frustration growing as if she wanted a fight that Lillian wouldn’t provide. It was childish, perhaps, but Lena wanted her mother to prove her doubts right, to give her that vindication when her feelings were hurt again. It was familiar, comforting, even, in its own twisted way, and Lena didn’t know how they were supposed to have any relationship that didn’t revolve around that.

     

                “We have the warm young partridge and foie gras pâté, with bitter salad and Périgueux sauce. Paired with a Côtes de Gascogne .”

     

                She looked up at the waiter who appeared at her elbow, setting down a wide plate with a small serving plated up. Another was set down in front of her mother while another server poured the wine. Murmuring her thanks, Lena shook out the napkin and draped it in her lap as Lillian sniffed the wine and held it up to let the sunlight catch the greenish tint of it. Taking a small sip, Lillian hummed appreciatively.

     

                “You’ll like that one. It’s sweet.”

     

                Lena gave her a scornful look and cut a sliver from her plate. The food was good but her appetite was lacking, and despite the small portion, she barely ate. Her mother observed her, curious, as she ate her own and Lena hated to admit that she did like the wine as she took a timid sip.

     

                “You promised me lunch,” Lillian said after a couple of minutes. “Eat.”

     

                Mouth thinning, Lena gripped her knife and fork tight enough to turn her knuckles white before she cut another bite from her plate and chewed quickly, as if the faster she finished, the sooner she’d be able to escape the nightmarish luncheon.

     

                “You know I regret how things turned out between us. Really, I do, Lena. I don’t blame you, of course; I know I was never a good mother to you. I would like to … make it up to you though.”

     

                Freezing, Lena was silent for a moment before letting out a hoarse bark of laughter as surprise flashed across her face. “And how exactly do you plan on doing that?”

     

                “I was hoping you would tell me that,” Lillian slowly replied, wary uncertainty flickering in her pale eyes as she set her fork down and sipped her wine. “My efforts so far haven’t been very effective. I’ve hardly seen you at all since you moved out of home.”

     

                “And why is that?”

     

                “You resent the attention I denied you. That I blamed you for your father’s mistakes. You have every right to, but … you’re all I have left. I don’t want to lose you too.”

     

                Lillian’s voice softened with sadness and a pang of longing that made Lena blink in surprise. Mouth opening and closing, she set her knife and fork down and reached for her glass. She slowly drained the rest of her wine, watching her mother over the rim with untrusting eyes.

     

                “Can I ask you a question?” Lena asked as she set her glass back down, looking at her mother with a guarded expression. At Lillian’s slight nod, she forged on. “Why didn’t you kick me out? When dad died, why didn’t you cut me off?”

     

                Surprise rippled across her mother’s face and Lena could see that she truly had caught her off guard. She watched as Lillian’s throat bobbed and she idly stroked the stem of her wine glass, her shoulders slumping as she avoided Lena’s hard stare.

     

                “You’re my daughter - I would never have done that,” Lillian firmly told her, her eyebrows drawing together in a displeased look as she spoke quietly. “I may not have shown it well, but I do love you, Lena. Most of what I did was to protect you - you were just too young to realise it.”

     

                “How can you say that?” Lena spluttered, wounded as she looked away, her anger simmering as she fought back the urge to grab her things and go; she still needed those photographs.

     

                “Do you want to know why I never favoured you?” Lillian snapped, her eyes flashing with old pain and shame too, if Lena wasn’t mistaken, as she leaned across the table to keep her voice down as they bickered back and forth. “Your father was a cruel man. I’m sure you understood that when you were older, but he was like that from the minute I met him. It was just Lex and me for a long time before he brought you home - who do you think he took all that anger out on, hm?”

     

                Her mother was proud, Lena knew that very well, but it made her stomach twist nauseously as Lillian laughed hollowly, her eyes glimmering with wry amusement. “And then he brought you home and you were his darling girl, and he loved you oh so much. I knew what that love would cost you if I stepped in, tried to pull you closer to me. He would’ve taken it out on you too - taken it out on you more . I did what I could, even if it wasn’t enough, and … by the time he died, knowing the kind of man he was, you already resented me.”

     

                Lena was silent, slumped in her chair with her knife and fork in hand as she looked at Lillian blankly, absorbing her words. They were a stunning blow that cut her deeply and she didn’t quite know how to process it. She knew undoubtedly that Lillian wasn’t lying to her, because it fit too well; the only thing her mother had ever done was orchestrate the rift between them, too big to span, big enough to fit the years they’d gone with minimal contact. Even the truth wouldn’t be enough to fix all of that, but it left a sour taste in Lena’s mouth as she set her cutlery down on the plate at an angle.

     

                “May I take your plate, madam?”

     

                “Thank you,” she murmured to the waiter who had appeared out of thin air, their plates and glasses whisked away without another word.

     

                “I’m … sorry,” Lena haltingly started after a moment, her throat constricting around the words. “I’m sorry that things aren’t different between us, but I just- I can’t pretend like the past never happened.”

     

                “I don’t expect you to. All I want is the chance to make some things right.”

     

                Lena was preoccupied with her thoughts, a part of her shockingly torn. She knew without a doubt that it was Kara’s fault, that over the months, Lena had managed to lower her defences without having to compromise her boundaries, finding some middle-ground for trust and love, despite her mistrust of people. If Lillian had asked her for a chance at the start of the year, it would have been an outright no , but Lena was considering it. Only just.

     

                They were interrupted by the arrival of the second course, a crispy blue lobster with fennel and cherry, paired with a Chardonnay, and Lena picked at the tender flesh as silence shrouded their table. After a few minutes, Lillian cleared her throat and turned the conversation in a safer direction.

     

                “So … the photos. Can I ask what you want them for?”

     

                Lena chewed slowly and swallowed before shrugging nonchalantly, avoiding Lillian’s eyes. “I promised I’d try and dig up some photos of me as a kid.”

     

                “For Kara?”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “And? How is she?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena tersely replied. 

     

                Her phone started vibrating in her handbag then and Lena set her fork down against the edge of her plate as she fished it out. Her stomach lurched at the sight of Kara’s name on the screen and she tried to hide her eagerness as she grabbed the napkin from her lap and scooted the chair back.

     

                “Excuse me,” Lena murmured, “I have to take this.”

     

                Lillian nodded, reaching for her wine. “Give her my best.”

     

                Shooting her a suspicious look, Lena made for the lobby of the hotel, tucking herself away in a corner as the video call connected and Kara’s face lit up the screen. She smiled as she waved, her face alight with happiness. “Hi!”

     

                “Hi,” Lena murmured.

     

                Loitering in the corner, the lobby seemed cavernous and still, as quiet as a library and she watched Kara’s brow crumple with confusion at the unfamiliar backdrop. “Where are you?”

     

                “Oh, um, I’m having lunch with my mom. She, uh, she actually said to give you her best.”

     

                “Your mother?” Kara echoed, eyebrows rising in surprise. “Why?”

     

                “It’s in return for a favour. It doesn’t matter now. Anyway, how’re you? How was your day?”

     

                “Exhausted. Tiring. Full of missing you.”

     

                “I miss you too.”

     

                “Are you okay though?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena shrugged half-heartedly as a sad smile graced her lips. “I’m managing. Your spies have been keeping an eye on me.”

     

                Choking on a quiet laugh, Kara grinned impishly, “hopefully Alex isn’t being too bossy.”

     

                “She’s lovely,” Lena murmured, “they both are. I just- I didn’t imagine that I wouldn’t be alone. I thought with you gone- well, it makes it a bit more bearable.”

     

                “Good.”

     

                “I think you’ve had a bigger impact on my life than I originally thought,” Lena mused. “I mean, I’m having lunch with my mom.”

     

                “Yeah, that’s … surprising. Just- remember to put yourself first, okay? Don’t let her guilt you or whatever.”

     

                Rubbing at the back of her neck, Lena’s brow puckered as she grimaced. “She, uh, she actually wants a fresh start. There were some things she told me; it put things in a new light for me, so … I don’t know.”

     

                “Oh. That … that must be a shock. That’s big. Do you know if you even want to work things out?”

     

                Letting out a withering sigh of frustration, Lena shrugged. “No. I don’t know. Maybe. I know we had some good times - it wasn’t all bad - but I just don’t know if it’s a good idea, you know? Maybe I’m just better off sticking to my new start in National City and leaving everything to rest.”

     

                “I won’t tell you what you should do,” Kara slowly replied, “you know what’s good for you and what’s not, but … if you’re considering it, if it’s something you want, it might be worth a shot. At least you’ll know for good and get some closure. Just … put yourself first, okay? I don’t want you to get hurt again.”

     

                Smiling softly, Lena nodded, a thoughtful look on her face. “Yeah, you’re right. God, it hasn’t even been a week yet, how am I going to get through the rest of the time when I already don’t know what to do without you?”

     

                “Mm, you’re going to make me bad at my job; I can’t stop thinking about you.”

     

                “That makes two of us.”

     

                Someone shouted in the background and the sound of an engine rumbling filtered through to Lena’s end and Kara winced slightly as she glanced over her shoulder. “Sorry, it’s pretty loud here. Too many people.”

     

                “It’s fine. As long as I get to look at you, I don’t care. I know you’re safe. But you’re okay though, right? You’re sleeping okay? You have everything you need?”

     

                “I’m fine. Really. I think it’ll take me a while to adjust to a shitty cot and constant noise, but I’ve been through it before. I’m sure lugging around my body weight’s worth of equipment all day will wear me out enough to sleep soundly. I think I’m good for now though; maybe some lip balm? I forgot to pack some. Another pack of film for my camera too - I’ve already gone through one.”

     

                Lena laughed at her sheepish look and made a mental note. “Alright. I’ll put together a care package for you. Let me know what else you want - anything at all - and I’ll make sure it gets to you.”

     

                “Don’t go overboard,” Kara sternly cautioned her. “The only thing I really want is you.”

     

                “You already have me, you’ll just have to come back for it.”

     

                “It won’t be long.”

     

                “Every second is too long,” Lena scoffed, pouting slightly.

     

                “Is this the first time in your life you haven’t been able to get your own way? How’re you handling it?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena’s lips twitched at the corners. “It’s not fair. How do normal people deal with not being able to have everything they want? It sounds exhausting.” 

     

                “Welcome to the real world, sweetheart.”

     

                “The real world is shit; I prefer mine.”

     

                “The one where you’re having lunch with your mom?”

     

                Grumbling, Lena gave her an exasperated look and Kara let out a light laugh. “You should get back to your meal.”

     

                “You’re probably right, but I don’t want to. But you should call Alex or Eliza, so I will. I’ll speak to you soon.”

     

                “Mhm. I love you. Try not to worry.”

     

                “Well, that’s not going to happen. But, I love you too. Stay safe and out of trouble. Do you hear me, Kara?”

     

                “Yes, boss. Wait for me; it won’t be long.”

     

                Promising she would and wrapping up their goodbyes over the next few minutes, Lena was left alone in the lobby, clutching her phone to her chest as she lingered a moment longer to pull herself together. Finally, she made her way back into the restaurant and took her seat. They’d taken her lobster and wine glass and no sooner had she taken her seat did the delayed third course arrive. Grilled silk grain veal with sea lettuce, citrus and spruce oil, paired with Pinot Noir.

     

                “Things are well, I presume?” Lillian asked, arching an eyebrow.

     

                “Mm,” Lena hummed without elaboration, taking a sip of wine and then shifting closer to the table as she ate.

     

                They were silent through the third course, and once the plates had been swept away for the matured cheeses to arrive shortly after, Lillian reached into her handbag and drew out an envelope. Setting it down on the pristine tablecloth, she slid it across to Lena, holding it in place for a moment as she judged her daughter’s expression.

     

                “Here. As promised. So, you can leave whenever you wish.”

     

                Lena hesitated before nodding and reaching out to slip the envelope from beneath her mother’s fingertips. Lillian relinquished her hold and sat back as Lena blinked back her surprise at the thickness of it. Frowning, she unwound the string from around the washers and let a stack of photos fall into her hand. She’d expected three or four, miniature prints of the awful staged things that had been hanging in the Luthor house when she’d left; there were dozens, more than she’d ever known existed.

     

                Curious now, Lena shuffled through them with a clouded expression on her face, head ducked down and lips pressed into a flat line as she flipped from photos of herself from the age of four until her first college graduation, barely fourteen and swamped by the cap and gown. A few were family photos, but most were candid ones of her playing chess, on horseback or at a cello recital.

     

                Shifting uneasily in her seat, Lena cleared her throat and set them back down on top of the envelope as she unfolded her legs. “Thank you,” she muttered, giving her mother a hard look of suspicion.

     

                Lillian nodded and then smiled slightly as she leaned across the table, tapping a manicured fingernail on a photo from the splayed stack. “This one’s my favourite.”

     

                Lena was surprised by the genuine warmth in her mother’s voice, affection in the soft curve of the smile as she pulled the photo loose. Looking down at it, Lena found herself staring at a photo not long after she would’ve been taken home, looking serious and reserved, as ever. She was dressed in a plaid pleated skirt, a shirt tucked in with a cardigan over the top and woollen tights. Her dark hair was pushed back with a headband and she was sitting on Lillian’s lap on a wingback armchair, staring into the camera with wide green eyes, still scared and shy as her mother loosely held her and looked into the camera with her piercing stare.

     

                “This was the day I signed the adoption papers. Your father had already been put down on the birth certificate, of course. I thought it would be a good idea to have some photos of you taken, and you fought me on it. Stubborn little thing. You never liked me much then - nor I, you, to be honest. I was still holding onto the resentment; I knew about you, of course, but I didn’t expect you , and we hadn’t decided what to do with you yet when he just … brought you home.” 

     

                She broke off and was silent for a moment, her lip curling ruefully. “You didn’t like me, and I hadn’t really made much of an effort to change that. But, I signed the papers and called the photographer, and right before this was taken, you ran and you hid. Lex couldn’t find you, your father couldn’t find you - thankfully - but I found you under your bed. I was annoyed. I didn’t have the patience for little kids anymore - I don’t think I ever really did, but I agreed you’d be good for Lex - and I told you to come out right now. You said you were scared.”

     

                Lillian let out a quiet chuckle, lips twitching as she looked at the photo with an amused look on her face, while Lena frowned. She didn’t remember that day. Memories of her younger childhood were mostly a blur, vague snatches of tears and lessons and loneliness all lacking any definition as one melted into the other.

     

                “I had to get on my knees and crawl halfway under the bed myself before you would even look at me. Even then ... you didn’t cry, you just looked at me and you said you missed your mom. You sounded so Irish; you were so much like her. I- I wanted to hate you even more for it. I told you if you came out, you would have a new mom and a new family and a better life. It was the first moment that you trusted me - maybe the only one. You crawled out and took my hand and you wouldn’t let go to have your photo taken, so I- I sat there with you and we took it together.”

     

                Reaching for the photo, Lillian took it from Lena and ran a thumb over their seated pose, a resigned slump to her shoulders as she let out a regretful sigh.

     

                “For that hour, I was telling the truth. But then your father and I had an argument that evening about you. My cheek swelled up from how hard he hit me. It was clear that you were his .”

     

                Clearing her throat, Lena looked a little pale, sitting stiffly in her seat as she hoarsely asked, “why is it your favourite then?”

     

                Her lips curled into a smile as a plate of slivers of aged and fresh cheeses was set down before her, and Lillian stared unflinchingly at Lena, the wry smile almost mocking as she replied.

     

                “Because for that hour … you were mine.”

     

                Dessert was baba au rhum , the small, saturated cake filled with whipped cream and served with a tiny cup of espresso, bitter and over-extracted, which they stirred sugar into. Neither of them spoke over dessert, their minds weighed down from the conversation. Truthfully, Lena felt exhausted . Lunch had been stilted and uncomfortable, but not all entirely unpleasant, although her chest felt heavier with the weight of unknown history that had been divulged.

     

                Her mother picked up the exorbitant bill without even glancing at the cost and they were helped into their coats at the door. The sun was shining as they stepped out onto the sidewalk, cars rushing past and the driver smoking yet again as he waited.

     

                “Thank you for the photos,” Lena said as she turned to face her mother. “I appreciate it. And for lunch.”

     

                Lillian nodded, a pleasant look on her face as her eyebrows rose slightly. “Can I give you a ride home?”

     

                “My car is at the office.”

     

                “To the office then.”

     

                Pausing, Lena relented and nodded before following her into the back of the car. Neither of them spoke during the few blocks to L-Corp, but when the car pulled into the no parking zone out front, Lena turned in her seat to look at Lillian. She was still wary, and a little sceptical, but she cocked her head to the side and slowly spoke.

     

                “I’ll call you.”

     

                She caught her mother off guard once again and watched the ghost of a smile twitch the corners of Lillian’s mouth as she inclined her head. “I’d like that.”

     

                Hesitating, on the verge of following a thought, Lena closed her mouth and shook her head minutely as she closed her eyes. With a feathery sigh, she looked at Lillian and gave her a grudging smile.

     

                “Bye, mom.”

    Chapter 26

    Kara,

     

    I’m not sure if you were expecting a reply to your letter, but I have some things to say too, and like you said, some things are better said when written down. Also, I kind of like the idea of writing letters too - it makes it feel like I have a little piece of you here with me, even though you’re a thousand miles away. It’s only been a little over a day, as of the time I’m writing this, so not enough time has passed for me to regale you with any interesting stories about my boring life, so I’ll get some things off my chest instead. I’m not good at talking about my feelings - I quite literally would be a therapist’s worst nightmare with the amount of boxed up pieces of myself - but I’ll try. For you.

     

    There’s so much I could say about my life before you. It was dull and lonely and I never had much time for people or even myself. There hasn’t been a lot of kindness in my life, or much love either, but there were so many opportunities for intellect. I think I never truly understood how stunted I was in so many ways; it always seemed so normal to me that I would work and study and practice and learn. Days of work without eating or sleeping and the manic episodes of intense focus. I never stopped to appreciate the little things, to learn how much a smile could mean, how much a bunch of flowers and a good coffee were worth, how it felt to feel sick on a Ferris wheel and kiss at a baseball game. I don’t say it lightly when I say that you have changed my entire life. I can appreciate the beauty in the simple things now.

     

    I know I’m not an easy person to love and I don’t love easily either. I know you know that - hell, even the fortune cookies knew it - but I need to clear some things up. When we met, I was having a hard time, stumbling through life, not knowing how to manage it all or knowing where I fit. It’s more pressure than I let on - the business and the family and that feeling of inadequacy. I never had much time for love, not much time for dates or not much interest; I’ve been told I’m too emotionally distant for anything more than a one night stand (please let me know if you concur) but I guess I was wrong. It rarely happens, but I was wrong and you were right; you just have to find the right person. I’m glad I didn’t let my aversion for letting anyone in my space turn you away from my table that day.

     

    Kara, it’s almost been a week since you’ve gone. I haven’t sent this letter yet, so I thought I’d add this on while I wait for the mailing address. I spoke to you just a few hours ago while I was having lunch with my mom. You and I both know how big of a deal that is. I’m sure I’ll tell you all about it tomorrow or the next day, but I thought I’d put it down here too. You told me not to let her guilt me into anything, but honestly, I do feel guilty. It’s not something she’s made me feel, but I guess there was just a lot more going on than I remembered from my childhood. I don’t remember much of it but I told you about my father and the kind of man he was, but I guess I just never imagined my mom was put into some bad situations, and that she did the best she could. Maybe she’s been trying for a lot longer than I thought, just in a way that I could never see. I don’t know. 

     

    It makes me think though. Maybe I’ve been selfish in the way I just up and left, or a little harsh, but I know I did it for myself, so it’s okay. It makes me think of you, and the bad situations you’ve been put into for the sake of a couple of stories. People get hurt all the time over there, and I know it’s not in you to be selfish but I want you to know that it’s okay if you only save one person, and it’s okay if that person is yourself. I know it’s selfish, but if it comes down to it, saving yourself is always the right decision.

     

    I think I’ll leave it there for now. We’ll talk soon and I’ll send you your care package as soon as I can get it all together. Who knows when it’ll reach you with this letter, but know that even though it might take a week or a month, I’ll be thinking of you always. I love you. Too many days without you here has left me knowing it without a shadow of a doubt.

     

    Love always,

    Lena x

    Chapter 27

                The first week passed by agonisingly slow but after that, Lena seemed to settle into a routine. The July nights were cloyingly hot and she didn’t sleep well without Kara. Sprawling across the bedcovers, she breathed in the lingering smell of her, until her housekeeper changed the sheets and it was no longer there. She was at the office every day, putting in twelve hours and only dragging herself home to the chidings of Alex and Kelly, and Kara too when they tattled on her. They seemed to think of it as an unhealthy coping mechanism for Kara being gone, and while it might have been unhealthy, it was familiar to Lena - that had been her life for far longer than she’d known Kara.

     

                Lena would go for early morning walks in the borough surrounding her house, when the city was still eerily quiet and the sky lingered in the blue hour of morning. The city’s old buildings seemed tired, or maybe it was just her, dark circles beneath her eyes and her dragging footsteps as she itched to get back in the office. After showering and getting ready, she’d make the drive to L-Corp and stand on the balcony, looking out at the tall glass buildings with all their lights off. Her heart would hurt for what should be vibrant, everything seeming washed of its colour as she lingered in a loneliness she couldn’t stand anymore.

     

                She did take proper weekends though - not out of her own desire for a healthy work and life balance, but so she could appreciate things on Kara’s behalf. On her days off she woke up late - for her - and went to various coffee shops, ordering cappuccinos and reading. She made time for lunch with Kelly and game nights with Kara’s other friends, quiz night at the bar and cocktails on the riverfront after a movie. She had come to appreciate a good movie and frequented the old cinema Kara had taken her too so many months before.

     

                Her favourite time was the evenings though, when she was alone and another day was about to come to a close, bringing her one day closer to Kara. Around seven o’clock, when the light was failing, she would take out a bottle of dry sherry and pour herself a glass, take out a jar of green olives, put on Miles Davis and read in the attic. She didn’t know why it felt so indulgent, but one day Lena realised that ritual was why she had moved to National City - to eat olives and get tipsy and read about people who had done great things while the sun set. She had created a life that was bent in service to living , something she had staunchly refused to do before as she curated a smattering of things and forgot to enjoy them. It seemed almost wrong to have figured out how to live and be left in that colourful world without the object of its source; her grey life before Kara was more fitting to her mood.

     

                Still, she coped as one week became two, filling every part of her waking hours with something to do to distract her. The nights still worried her though, and no matter what she did, Lena would lie awake - for hours usually - filled with dread. She had no more tears in her after that first week. For someone who didn’t cry that often, it seemed silly and trivial to do it every night, something embarrassing that she imagined would be seen on her the next day. 

     

                On her days off, she would take two Ambien and nap to make up for sleepless nights, sprawled out on her bed, freshly showered on the light linen sheets, the floral smell of detergent soothing and the windows thrown open to the heat of the day. She would play Louis Armstrong or Enya and allow the drugs to lull her to sleep as the soft breeze slowly dried her hair, but she never stayed asleep.

     

                The only time she ever felt like she could properly breathe, when that tight feeling in her chest loosened for a short while, reassured by Kara’s face, getting more tanned by the day as freckles spackled her nose, making her eyes impossibly bluer. They spoke most days, Lena holding out for them, slipping out of meetings and breaking off conversations to answer her phone. Those calls were the most important parts of her day and she treasured every moment, but eventually, Kara would have to hang up again and Lena would feel that crushing pressure build inside her chest once more.

     

                On Sunday, two weeks after Kara had gone, Lena woke early to grey pre-dawn light, her gauzy curtains eerily drifting as a humid wind seeped inside. She’d left the windows open to dispel the warmth of the night and a storm had rolled in, muggy and damp as thunder rumbled. Rising from her bed, she shut the creaky window and changed into casual clothes, thin but waterproof, and went for a walk in the rain to a nearby bakery so she could have toast and coffee where there were people, instead of the suffocating silence of an empty house. The storm blanketed the city, grey and dismal as the thunder rippled all around, felt in her bones, but Lena found it comforting; it was cozy in the bakery as fat drops of rain lightly pattered on the windows.

     

                After finishing her breakfast, she almost walked past a bookstore, a tiny, narrow place with stacks obscuring the tall front window, before she ducked inside. She had a pile of half-read books beside her bed and a stack of new ones she’d barely touched, finding herself re-reading old favourites, again and again, seeking comfort in the act of repeating herself these days. But she thought Kara might need something new to read at night and picked out a few new releases that looked interesting before making her way to a local patisserie to pick up petit fours for dinner with Alex and Kelly that night, and a liquor store for a few bottles of wine, which she carried home in a crumpled paper bag, her arms laden and burning from the weight.

     

                The storm broke that afternoon and by the time she knocked on the apartment door at five-thirty, the light was perfect: buttery and dense as it swelled the room as the door was jerked open by Alex. 

     

                “I brought wine,” Lena said, by way of greeting, lifting the paper bag as she stepped inside. 

     

                It smelled of simmering meat and spices, ginger and chilli and the sweetness of coconut, and she hung her coat on the hook and greeted Kelly, who was letting the steam out of a pot. Moving over to the counters, Lena set down the white box on the counter and leaned over to look at their dinner.

     

                “Beef rendang?”

     

                “Mhm. It’s nearly ready.”

     

                “Glass of wine?” Alex asked, already gouging a bottle opener into the soft cork and twisting.

     

                It popped free and Lena fetched the glasses down from a cupboard, setting them down and watching as a stream of blood red Merlot was poured in healthy measures. Sitting at the table, the three of them conversed about their day, Lena skirting around the leisurely actions of her morning and her afternoon spent sheepishly running through a proposal as she ran the dishwasher and sipped tea at the kitchen counter.

     

                “Did you speak to Kara today?” Alex asked as they dug into the heaping bowls.

     

                “Mm. This morning. She seems … I don’t know, happier? Is it wrong to use that word?”

     

                “The first week or two is always the hardest,” Kelly said with a grim smile. “Getting back into the routine, being away from family. But then it gets easier. Kind of like how it is for you.”

     

                Lena’s lips twitched ruefully as she scooped a forkful of rice and beef into her mouth. Chewing as her expression clouded, she cocked her head to the side and glanced at Kelly. “Do you ever miss it?”

     

                Pausing, Kelly was slow to reply as she took a sip of wine. “No. I … I wanted out for a while before I was discharged.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “I was a military psychologist though. Different area to Kara. It’s why I specialise in trauma now, and why I prefer practising back home. You see some things so … besides, it’s nice to settle down somewhere permanent.”

     

                “And I already have to put up with one of you gone,” Alex said, rolling her eyes. “I couldn’t imagine if it was both of you. It’s quiet enough as it is.”

     

                With a weak chuckle, Lena dipped her chin in a small nod. “Yeah, you should live in my house. It’s like I can hear myself thinking.”

     

                “You should get a dog,” Kelly suggested.

     

                “A dog,” Lena snorted, “what would I do with a dog?”
