                “You’ve never had a dog?” Alex exclaimed with disbelief. “Don’t your kind have, like, a dozen purebred hunting dogs or something?”

     

                With a rueful smile, Lena shrugged nonchalantly. “My brother had a dog - this was before I lived with them. I think it was called Ignatius.”

     

                “Yeah, that sounds about right,” Alex scoffed, shaking her head with amusement.

     

                “He had to be put down when he was seven and my mom said that my brother was too sentimental . She wouldn’t let him get another one after that. The most we had after that were horses, but they were only for riding.”

     

                “Your mom sure is … something,” Kelly awkwardly said, giving Lena a wary look. “But you really should consider a dog; you might feel less alone at home if you have someone to look after.”

     

                Snorting, Lena gave her a wan smile, reaching for her wine. “I’m still figuring out how to look after myself properly.”

     

                She wasn’t exactly against the idea though, and she considered it for a moment before the conversation moved on, carrying her with it. After dinner, they ate dessert on the sofa, straight out of the box, listening to music as they laughed and chatted their way through three bottles of wine between them. 

     

                Too drunk to drive, Lena was persuaded to stay the night and collapsed onto Kara’s groaning bed just before midnight, her head swimming and her tongue fuzzy as noise seeped in from outside and upstairs. The sheets still smelled like her and Lena buried her face in a pillow, her skin prickling from the warmth that suffused the cramped space. 

     

                She slept fitfully and woke to harsh sunlight streaming in through the windows as early morning traffic blared outside and a man yelled from the sidewalk. Blinking slowly as she eased herself up, Lena found herself still fully clothed, shoes and all, and put her head in her hands to stop the nauseating dizziness as she curled in on herself. 

     

                Her stomach churned and she lurched out of bed, off-balance and barged through Kara’s door and straight through the bathroom one, breaking the fragile lock as she ignored the sound of running water and dropped down to the tiled floor hard enough to bruise her knees. Retching as she hunched over the toilet bowl, Lena listened to the sounds of protest coming from behind the shower curtain before Alex’s face peered around it, hair spiky and wet as she frowned at her.

     

                “Yuck.”

     

                “Sorry,” Lena hoarsely groaned.

     

                “You look like shit.”

     

                Weakly moaning in agreement, Lena vomited again, placing her clammy forehead in her hand as she sighed listlessly. The water turned off a minute later and Alex reached around the curtain for a towel before yanking the curtain back and stepping out with a grim look on her face.

     

                “Aspirin’s in the cupboard.”

     

                Mumbling her thanks, Lena pushed herself up and flushed the toilet before running the cold water, her skin warm to touch, and stood under the cool water as she washed the sour smell of wine and sweat from her clammy skin. Bile rose in her throat and was washed down the drain, and once she stepped out of the shower, she downed two pills dry and stepped out into the hallway. Looking ghostly pale and rundown, circles beneath her eyes and an owlishly stricken look on her face, she gave Alex a pleading look.

     

                “Do you have anything I can borrow?”

     

                Alex’s laughter followed her down the hallway as she ducked into her room, surprisingly neat and orderly, and fished out a plaid shirt and a pair of sweatpants. Handing them off to her, waving aside Lena’s thanks, she gave her a stern look. “That’s my favourite shirt. Don’t vomit on it.”

     

                “I’ll have it dry cleaned and hand-delivered to your doorstep tomorrow by my assistant,” Lena vowed.

     

                Patting her cheek as she scooted past her, Alex called back over her shoulder, “the coffee’s fresh.”

     

                Changing into the clean clothes in the bathroom, Lena swilled mouthwash and splashed cold water on her face as Kelly stepped inside and wedged in alongside her before the mirror. She was dressed in a v-neck blouse, her hair sleek and looking no worse for wear as she dabbed lotion on her skin.

     

                “What time is it?” Lena hoarsely asked. 

     

                 “Eight.”

     

                “Fuck. I have a meeting first thing.”

     

                Dialling Jess, Lena swallowed the minty taste at the back of her dry throat as she shuffled out of the bathroom and out to the kitchen, snagging a clean cup and filling it with coffee as the call connected.

     

                “Miss Luthor.”

     

                “Jess. Hi. I, uh, I don’t think I’ll be at the office until later,” Lena started, feeling vaguely embarrassed at the admission.

     

                “I’ll push everything to this afternoon.”

     

                “Thanks,” she gratefully replied, massaging a tender spot above her left eye.

     

                “Of course.”

     

                Hanging up, Lena sank down heavily on a chair at the table and sipped the bitter coffee, her head tipped back slightly as she slouched. Slowly, her headache faded as the aspirin took effect and the coffee reinvigorated her. By the time it hit eight-thirty and Kelly had left for work and Alex was ready to go, Lena felt marginally more alive, although she looked worse for wear.

     

                Chuckling as she slung on a leather jacket, Alex arched an eyebrow. “You look green.”

     

                “I only had five glasses,” Lena complained.

     

                “That’s a bottle of wine.”

     

                Following her out of the apartment and down to the lobby, Lena winced at the sharp sunlight, wishing desperately for yesterday’s storm to reappear as she donned her sunglasses. The day was fresh and still a little cool though and she said goodbye to Alex as she made for the parked Porsche. The drive home was slow and frustrating, bile leaving a sour taste in Lena’s mouth as she swallowed frequently, and by the time she reached her home, she was ready to collapse back into bed and call it a day.

     

                She’d barely unlocked the door and stepped inside, closing every single curtain on the ground floor and knocked back a seltzer before there was a knock at the door, cleaving through Lena’s head. Considering ignoring it, she sighed roughly as another knock sounded, and resigned herself to shooing them away so they would leave her in peace.

     

                Flinging the door open, Lena scowled and her stomach plummeted at the sight of her mother standing on her doorstep. Imposingly tall and as regal as ever, Lillian gave her a once over and arched an eyebrow.

     

                “What on earth are you wearing?”

     

                Looking down at Alex’s borrowed clothes, Lena sighed roughly. “I stayed at Kara’s sister’s place last night.”

     

                Her voice was gravelly and Lillian eyed her unflinchingly for a long moment. “Aren’t you going to invite me in?”

     

                “I was actually about to get ready for work.”

     

                “I just came from the office; your assistant said you’re out until this afternoon.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena closed her eyes and stepped aside to let Lillian into the house. Shutting the door behind her, Lena watched as her mother looked around with interest; she’d never been inside Lena’s new place, a sanctuary which she didn’t want her past to taint. Lena eyed her warily, watching as Lillian poked her head into the living room, dim with the closed curtains, and then to the opposite side of the hallway, stepping into the dining room and the opened up kitchen, likewise dark.

     

                She let out a sudden laugh and turned around to look at Lena, taking in the sunglasses and dishevelled look and adding it to the blocked out windows. “A hangover? Really? That’s not very professional of you.”

     

                Flushing as she pulled the sunglasses off and folded the arms, Lena chewed on the inside of her lip and let out an exasperated sigh when no further comments were forthcoming. Gesturing towards her mother, she raised her eyebrows.

     

                “Did you come here for something, or …?”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Lillian gave her a droll look, “straight to business, is it? Not even a cup of coffee first?”

     

                “I’m just surprised you’re in town; there must be a reason.”

     

                “It’s just for the day; I have an interview for a piece in one medical magazine or another. I thought I’d come and see if you wanted to have dinner with me this evening? My flight’s out first thing in the morning.”

     

                “You couldn’t just call?” Lena churlishly asked, lips twitching with annoyance.

     

                “You wouldn’t have picked up,” Lillian pointed out.

     

                Lena ignored the truthful barb of her words and cleared her throat, crossing her arms over her chest. “Dinner? Just dinner?”

     

                Laughing, Lillian shook her head with irate amusement. “You’re always so sceptical. Is it hard to believe I’d like to spend time with you without some ulterior motive?”

     

                 “Well … yeah,” Lena snorted, “it kind of is. There’s usually some criticism, some snide comment.”

     

                “That is not true.”

     

                “Yes, it is,” Lena snapped, bristling with indignation. “You don’t think I do a good job at … anything. Not- not the business, not as a person. You just don’t … like me.”

     

                “You’re my daughter; I love you. And I admit, maybe I haven’t always been vocal about your achievements, but … it’s never seemed to mean much to you anyway. For what it’s worth, I think you’re doing very well with the company.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena gave her a wry smile, “ very well? The numbers have never been this good; the media coverage, the profits, the productivity or anything . I did all of that, no thanks to you. You weren’t even here.”

     

                “And I appreciate that, Lena, but I’m here now. I know I haven’t always been there for you, but Lex … he needed me more than you did.”

     

                “I needed you too!” Lena shouted, two bright spots appearing on her cheeks as her eyes shone with a glassy sheen, her throat painfully tight as she struggled to draw in a shallow breath. “You were my mother too. Everyone needs their mom, and I needed you.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lillian’s face went slack and her voice was quiet and raspy as she took a step towards Lena. “Look, I know, okay? I know . I’m sorry it’s taken me so long but I just- I just want to look out for you. You might think I’m being harsh but I’m trying to help . I don’t want anyone to doubt that you’re not a good CEO; I vouched for you. And now I just want to make up for the rest of it. Was lunch really so bad last week?”

     

                “I just wanted the photos,” Lena defeatedly replied, giving her mom a guilty look.

     

                A smile twitched Lillian’s lips as she let out a quiet huff of laughter, “I know. Don’t worry, I’m not deluded into thinking that you want to spend any more time with me than you have to, but … you said you’d call, so I thought- well, it’s not like you have anyone else. And Kara … what happens if she hurts you?”

     

                “Don’t. Just don’t start with that.”

     

                Backing down quickly, Lillian held her hands up defensively, hearing the brittle steel in Lena’s voice. “Okay. I’ll stay out of it. I have nothing against her personally. I mean, I don’t know her but she seems … nice.”

     

                “Nice?” Lena snorted. “She’s not the heiress you envisioned for me.”

     

                “No,” Lillian hesitantly agreed. “But when were you ever going to settle for someone that I approved of? If I did, it would be the surest way for you to end things immediately. I guess this one’s changed you more than you realise though.”

     

                Arching an eyebrow, Lena quietly snorted. “Oh, yeah? Would you care to enlighten me?”

     

                “You seem happier,” Lillian admitted as her face softened momentarily and then creased with a rueful smile. “And it’s been ten minutes and we’re still having this conversation, which I think says it all.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena rubbed at the back of her neck and looked down. There was a kernel of truth to her mother’s words and Lena was torn between allowing her to be right and spiting herself once more, a terrible habit that she had when it came to Lillian. After a pause of silence, Lena looked up and let out a heavy sigh.

     

                “Well, I can’t do dinner tonight anyway. I’ve already got plans with Kara’s sister and her girlfriend.”

                

                “Why don’t you invite them too?” Lillian asked, grasping at straws with a slight edge of desperation. 

     

                Lena arched an eyebrow at how hard she was trying. “Why?”

     

                “Just … meet me halfway, for God’s sake. I’m trying here and I don’t know when I’ll be back in town next. God knows you’re not going to visit me. ”

     

                “Fine,” Lena relented, mouth thinning, “but I’ll have to ask them first. If they say no, I’m not cancelling my plans.”

     

                “That’s fair. If they say yes, shall we say we’ll meet at seven? I’ll message you the details once they’re arranged.”

     

                Lena nodded tersely and Lillian eyed her for a long moment before she shifted. “Well … I’ll see you tonight then, hopefully. Drink fluids.”

     

                Lillian showed herself out without another word, the front door shutting quietly and Lena let out an irritable groan as she made for the kitchen. Filling a glass with tepid water and sipping it slowly, she frowned and wallowed for a few minutes before fishing her phone out of her pocket and dialling Alex’s number.

     

                She didn’t pick up, so Lena tried Kelly next, listening to it ring three times before it was answered. “Hello?”

     

                “Hi, sorry, I need your help.”

     

                “What’s up?”

     

                “My mom just showed up and asked me to have dinner with her tonight, and when I tried using you as a scapegoat, she told me to invite you as well.”

     

                “Dinner? With your mom?” Kelly echoed.

     

                “Yes! Dinner, as in a fancy restaurant with expensive food and no escape.”

     

                “Okay. That’s fine.”

     

                “No,” Lena quietly exclaimed, “you’re supposed to say you don’t want to go so then I can get out of it.”

     

                “Is that what you really want me to say?”

     

                “Yes. No. I don’t know.”

     

                Softly sighing, Kelly replied with faint amusement in her voice. “Look, Lena, I can’t tell you what to do. You have your own issues with your mom, and you have to figure out what’s right for you. So, if you don’t want to get dinner with her, then don’t - you have no moral obligation to, and you shouldn’t allow her feelings to come before your own. But if you do want to get dinner with her, then Alex and I will be right there with you.”

     

                “Right. Yes, of course. Thanks, Kelly.”

     

                “Just let us know.”

     

                Torn, Lena told her to have a good day and hung up, tapping her phone against her chin as she idly walked around the kitchen in circles, thinking. Pouring fresh espresso for herself and grimly scrambling eggs in a pan, although she had no appetite, Lena picked at thin slivers of prosciutto from a packet with resignation. She scooped pesto out of a jar and slathered it on toast before pouring out her eggs and adding crispy prosciutto on top and had just taken a seat at the table when her phone started ringing.

     

                The sight of Kara’s name made her perk up slightly and Lena answered and set her phone against the side of the mug of red ginseng tea she’d brewed, hoping it would cure her hangover while the coffee kept her awake.

     

                “Hi,” Lena called out as the screen fuzzily connected, cutting a mouthful of food and chewing as she waited for Kara’s face to appear.

     

                “Where are you? Why’s it so dark?”

     

                “I’m at home,” Lena said around a mouthful of eggs. “Too much wine last night.”

     

                “Oh, God. Hangover?”

     

                “It’s not too bad,” Lena said, wrinkling her nose, “I’m going to head into the office a bit later. Sleep it off. How’re you?”

     

                “Not bad. I got your care package today! It got here fast. I haven’t opened the letter yet; I thought I’d save it for bedtime or else I would’ve spent the whole day crying. I did open the photos though and you were so cute! I assume that was the reason you had lunch with your mom last week?”

     

                Giving her a slightly smug smile, Lena hummed in assent before her mouth turned down at the corners in a disgruntled manner. “Mm, and now she wants me to have dinner with her again tonight. Alex and Kelly are invited.”

     

                “Oh, well, that’s unexpected. So … you’ve decided to try and work things out?”

                

                Shrugging half-heartedly, Lena speared a slice of prosciutto on her fork and twirled it idly, brooding as she eyed it. “I don’t know. I mean, I said I’d call her at some point, and she’s only in town for the day, so maybe I should just … get it over and done with and give her one last chance while she’s here and see how it goes.”

     

                “Sounds reasonable.”

     

                “I wish you were here though; it’d be so much more manageable if you were here. I’d probably make more of an effort to be on my best behaviour too.”

     

                “Next time,” Kara promised with a sad smile.

     

                She listened as Kara talked about her day for a while, nothing much to speak on given the secretive nature of the reports she was writing, and then it was time for her to sleep. Reminding her of her letter before she hung up, Lena was reluctant to go but knew Kara would have an early start and needed her rest. With a last warning to stay safe and assurances that she would, they hung up and Lena finished her breakfast in heavy silence before going to get ready for work.

     

                Making it to the office just before eleven, Lena sifted through the stack of reports and called Sam to her office to talk about the financial resources to back a project over lunch that Jess picked up for them. Sam had always been frank with Lena, both of them young for their positions and forging a trusting business relationship out of that - even if Lena erred on the side of caution with the personal side - and she was honest about the pitfalls as Lena hummed and scribbled notes on her tablet, while Jess kept the minutes from the sofa. Suggesting a new strategy that she was confident in from her constant analyses of trends, Sam promised to crunch some numbers and get back to her with a projected budget and a new tactical approach. 

     

                Pencilling her in for another meeting next week, Lena had a few more meetings and a video conference with a subsidiary in London and decided to call it a day as soon as the last meeting finished. She’d knocked back a few aspirin kept hidden in her desk drawer but was grouchy and terse, unable to concentrate as she sipped the green juices she kept sending Jess downstairs to periodically buy. The damp air when the elevator spilled her out on the sublevel car park was cool and welcome and she drove home with the windows down.

     

                After giving Lillian her confirmation that they’d be there at dinner, she was sent through a booking confirmation to a restaurant that turned out to be a very expensive sushi place on Fifty-sixth Street, not far from her office. Her driver picked up Alex and Kelly and dropped the three of them on the sidewalk outside. The restaurant was a hole in the wall, a tiny spartan interior designed through the concept of ma - Japanese minimalism - with only four round tatami cushions arranged around a chabudai made from Hinoki . They were shown to the table through a shoji screen, warm amber light seeping through the translucent paper beyond it.

     

                Lillian was already there, sitting on her low seat, and Lena had to bite back a smile at the sight of her mother’s discomfort at being seated so low down. Rising fluidy, she blinked in surprise and her face softened slightly at Lena’s arrival, as if she’d doubted she’d follow through on her promise to meet her there.

     

                “I’m glad you decided to come.”

     

                Nodding, Lena took a seat beside her mother once her coat was taken, gesturing to Alex and Kelly as they sized her up. “Alex and Kelly.”

     

                Lillian warily shook their hands and they sank down to their tatami cushions across from the mother and daughter duo. They were served sencha to start with, the tea a vibrant yellowish colour with a tint of green as they cupped the clay cups between their palms. Lena sipped hers slowly, giving Kelly a warning look over the rim as Lillian gave them both polite looks.

                

                “So, what is it you both do for work?”

     

                “I’m a pharmacist,” Alex informed her.

     

                “Psychologist,” Kelly said with a cordial smile. “I specialise in trauma; I used to be in the military. With Kara, actually.”

     

                “Oh? Interesting. Is that how you two met?”

     

                Nodding, Kelly glanced at Alex and wrinkled her nose with a smile. “Mhm. I was living in Metropolis after being discharged and came to visit my brother - he’s in the military too; good friends with Kara - and we were introduced at dinner.”

     

                “One good thing to come out of my sister enlisting,” Alex said, raising her eyebrows as she grimaced.

     

                “How long is she gone for this time?”

     

                “Nine months,” Lena muttered.

     

                She didn’t look at her mother, head slightly bowed as she sipped her tea and looked down at the sanded grain of the table. Lillian nodded beside her and Kelly gently cleared her throat, seeing Lena’s unwillingness to dwell on the topic and coming to her rescue.

     

                “So, Lillian, you have your own company too? Lena said it’s in bioengineering.”

     

                “Mhm. I used to be a practising surgeon - cardiothoracic - before I went into the research and development sector as a subsidiary of L-Corp. I’m the CEO of Cadmus, and L-Corp for a brief moment before I stepped down for Lena to take over. Now, I report to her.”

     

                “My mom’s a doctor too,” Alex supplied as an Ishiyaki grilling stone was carefully set down on the table on a wooden board, the volcanic stone saturated with heat as slices of otoro, marinated in soy and sake, were set down beside it alongside a bowl of tosazu dressing. The cuts of tuna sizzled as Lena started grilling them, wielding chopsticks to precision as the conversation washed over her and she let everyone serve themselves. 

     

                They were brought a crystal carafe of sake with ceramic cups to replace their tea, Lena quick to drain hers, the rice wine dry and smooth, the sweet taste lingering on her tongue as the next course of maki was brought out, the rolled seaweed and rice slightly vinegary as she bit through the cucumber and fresh tuna. Next came chilled sashimi with a daikon garnish and then a squid nigiri , and abalone steamed in sake and colourful temari with cured seafood toppings. For dessert, a coconut milk and anko jelly, and another pot of steeped green tea carefully poured into fresh cups.

     

                Lena was relatively silent the whole time, her awkward, stilted efforts to answer her mother’s questions almost painful to bear, and she was happy to let Alex and Kelly carry the conversation with their natural ease. Eventually, their allotted time slot was up and they grabbed their coats, Lillian picking up the check, and swept out onto the street. Lena’s driver was parked right behind Lillian’s, both of them chatting amicably on the sidewalk and snapping to attention at the arrival of their passengers.

     

                Thanking Lillian, Alex and Kelly made for Lena’s car, sliding into the back to give her a moment of privacy with her mother. Lena scuffed the sole of her heel along the sidewalk as she folded her arms over her chest, looking down. The night was humid, an almost soupy quality to the air as sweat prickled her arms and back beneath her coat. Clearing her throat, she peeked up.

     

                “So …”

     

                “Thank you,” Lillian softly said, “for coming tonight.”

     

                Nodding, Lena’s lips twitched with a hint of a smile. “Thanks for dinner. It’s- it’s a nice restaurant.”

     

                “You should bring Kara here when she gets back.”

     

                Lips twisting wryly, Lena nodded absentmindedly as her gaze wandered to the illuminated interior of an art gallery next door, stark white with art nouveau style paintings hanging on the walls. 

     

                “Maybe I will.”

     

                They descended into a tense silence for a moment, a warm gust of wind barely lifting the heat as trash scuttled through the gutters and the sound of idling engines and traffic sounded too loud between them. After a minute, Lillian’s neutral expression clouded into a troubled look as a muscle twitched in her jaw.

     

                “Look, I- I know there’s a rift between us. I don’t know how to bridge that, but … it’s good to see you happy. These girls, Kara … they make you happy. That’s all I want for you; I just- I’m happy knowing that you’re doing okay.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena murmured, blinking in surprise at her mother’s awkward admission. 

     

                “Just … call me if you need anything, okay?”

     

                Her sharp gaze softened momentarily and Lena swallowed thickly as a pucker formed between her eyebrows. She stiffened as her mother raised a hand and reached out with bemused amusement on her face, cupping her cheek with a cool hand for the briefest moment. Her touch was delicate and faint, barely there as she looked at Lena intently.

     

                “I do care about you, you know.”

     

                Before Lena could reply, her hand dropped and she made for her car, sliding into the back as the driver shut the door behind her and climbed behind the wheel. Lena turned with a perplexed look on her face, a funny feeling in her chest as she watched the car pull away, and lingered for a moment longer before shaking herself out of her thoughts and climbing into the back beside Alex.

     

                As the car pulled into motion, Alex looked at her with mild concern, hesitantly speaking. “So … that went well, don’t you think?”

     

                “It … wasn’t so bad,” Lena admitted.

     

                Patting her knee encouragingly, Alex left her to her own thoughts after that and when they pulled up outside her apartment, Lena declined the offer to go upstairs for some beer and a crime documentary. Her driver took her home and she murmured her thanks as she climbed out of the car, keys in hand and walked up the front stoop to unlock the door. The wall of heat from outside pushed into the cool interior as she flipped a light switch to illuminate the expanse of emptiness inside. The house creaked and settled, the plywood and metal ducts and nails all contracting as the old joints of the house cooled after a warm day.

     

                Standing in the foyer for a second, Lena cocked her head to the side and listened before dropping her handbag onto the narrow bench off to one side, imagining having someone to come home to. Maybe she would get a dog after all; maybe just a small one.

    Chapter 28

                Another week passed by - the third without Kara - and every morning, she’d walked and gotten a small cup of coffee at a shoebox of a coffee shop, enjoying it for Kara’s sake as the days grew warm and muggy and watched the sunrise over the harbour from the bridge. The salty air blown in from the mouth of the ocean was fresh and balmy and Lena would linger for awhile before walking home and getting ready for work.

     

                She left the office early the next Thursday, the streets saturated with yellow patches of sunshine as she sat behind the wheel with the windows down, letting in the sounds of traffic and shouts and laughter. National City was teeming with life, with the last boiling days of summer before it turned towards autumn, and Lena basked in the feeling as she idled in traffic.

     

                Arriving home at her house just before lunch, Lena unlocked the door and let herself into the cool interior of the house and paused. The loneliness hit her again at the stifling sound of silence inside. Hovering in the foyer, she swallowed thickly and slowly set her bag down on the console before rifling through it for her phone.

     

                “When’s your next client?”

     

                “I’m about to take lunch,” Kelly replied, following Lena’s lead and skipping the niceties. “My next one’s scheduled for two o’clock, why?”

     

                “I need your help.”

     

                “Sure. With what?”

     

                With a quiet huff of laughter, Lena smiled wryly. “I’m going to get a dog.”

     

                “Meet me at Seventh and Vermont.”

     

                Lena hung up and bundled back outside, slipping her sunglasses down over her eyes against the harsh sunlight, and climbed back into her car. The birds twittered in the branches of the Crape Myrtles as she turned left at the end of her street, fuchsia petals dusting her windscreen as she fiddled with the radio and lazily drove through the midday traffic. She rolled the sleeves of her silk blouse up and thought of lunch and of calling Kara the next morning - preferably with a dog to show off. 

     

                Lena faltered for a moment at the thought of what Kara would say about a dog, considering they’d be living together when she was back, but it was a while away yet, and Lena couldn’t stand the loneliness of those long months in between. It hadn’t even been one month yet, and it was already unbearable as it closed in on her every time she stepped through the front door alone.

     

                She parked in an open space along a quiet street, accounting firms and banks and small, private offices greeting her as she stepped out of the car. Kelly lingered in the shade of a narrow office front and Lena read her name on one of the plaques set on the door, listing the therapists who worked there.

     

                They walked to a little Salvadoran restaurant first for lunch, ordering casamiento, pupusa and tamales at a small vinyl table as the AC unit shuddered overhead; the heat was like an adhesive that even the fan couldn’t shift as sunlight slanted in through the wide windows, yellow-tinted from the laminated posters advertising the menu. They split a tres leches cake before Lena left a few folded bills beneath the napkin stand and they left.

     

                Kelly led them to a nearby rescue centre, the sound of yapping dogs reaching their ears before they’d even opened the door. It was mercifully cooler inside, the smell of wet dog and kibble mingling with the stale air-conditioned smell of bleach and Lena felt her stomach knot as they were led down a hallway and into a room full of cages. Her stomach dropped at the sight: kittens mewling in a pile; dogs listlessly sprawled out on the bare concrete floor, staring at her with dark, liquid eyes; puppies scrabbling at the bars as their tails furiously wagged. 

     

                “How am I supposed to just pick one?” Lena whispered, leaning closer to Kelly.

     

                “This is why Alex never lets Kara and I come here,” Kelly admitted, hooking an arm through Lena’s. “We’d probably come back with five each.”

     

                “I might come home with five.”

     

                Her mouth turned down at the corners as she eyed the cages, slowly towing Kelly along with her, and she knew she’d be leaving with a hefty donation at the front desk and the nagging guilt of not filling her house with every animal in there.

     

                “What sort of dog do you want?”

     

                “I don’t know. Something small?” Lena suggested. “Not one of those prissy ones though; something that’s just … nice and little. Like a lap dog.”

     

                “Mm, right. How about a Corgi? Or a Bichon Frise?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena shook her head and let go of Kelly’s arm, her heels loud on the concrete floor as she walked a little further down. “Do you think a Pekingese suits me?”

     

                Snorting, Kelly gave her a sceptical look. “Absolutely not.”

     

                “Mm, yeah, you’re right.”

     

                She stopped in front of every cage, reading the information - the name, the breed, the age - as she deliberated over the pros and cons. Which one wouldn’t shed much? Which one wouldn’t need much exercise?

     

                In the end, the answer presented itself in such a way that she couldn’t say no. It seemed too perfect - aside from the fact that it was everything she wasn’t looking for, but as she signed the paperwork and swiped her card, a bundle of supplies stacked in a box and her new dog on a leash at her side, Lena couldn’t stop smiling.

     

                “Okay, so, I think we’ve established that you’re a terrible decision maker,” Kelly mused aloud as they retraced their way the few blocks back to her work.

     

                “Isn’t she cute, though?” Lena beamed at her, eyebrows raised as she gestured to the German Shepherd trotting alongside her.

     

                “You said you wanted something small. That’s a horse!”

     

                “She’s not that big!” Lena protested.

     

                “That’s not a lap dog. And German Shepherds shed like … all the time. I would know; we used them in Afghanistan for IED detection. And they need a lot of exercise.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Lena snorted, “oh, well, don’t worry about that. I have a housekeeper and an assistant. Maybe I’ll give them both raises.”

     

                Laughing, Kelly shook her head with amused exasperation and then sighed. “You know, I think therapy would really benefit you, but God , I’m glad you’re not my client.”

     

                Chuckling, Lena shrugged nonchalantly. “I’ll pass on therapy, much to the relief of all psychologists out there.”

     

                Kelly sighed again and clicked her tongue and Lena knew that she was only half-joking. She assumed a dog would help though and was satisfied with her own improvements to her situation, thanking her friend as the box of supplies was shoved into the small trunk and the German Shepherd was bundled into the back of the Porsche.

     

                The drive home was nerve-wracking as the dog shifted around restlessly, and Lena was relieved when she pulled up outside the brownstone to let her out. Groaning at the hair already dusting the leather seats, she shook her head and led the dog up the front steps and into the house before making a trip back to unload the supplies.

     

                Pouring herself a glass of Chardonnay after setting everything up, Lena leaned against the kitchen counters and watched the German Shepherd nervously sniff about, nose to the floor as she took wary steps around the open kitchen and dining room. Noisily lapping up water and wolfing down the bowl of meat, she curled up on the new bed and contentedly lay her head on her paws while eyeing Lena from across the room.

     

                “Well, welcome home, Athena,” Lena murmured, settling down cross-legged across from her and watching her closely.

     

                She was up all night with the dog and finally settled for stretching out on the sofa, reading a book of Richard Siken’s poems by yellow lamplight as she shifted Athena’s bed to the floor beside the sofa so she had some company. Lena woke later than usual to the morning sky, coloured deep peach and amber, while the white curtains from the open windows billowed back and forth without a sound, moved by the breathing of the warm, sun-swept wind.

     

                Athena’s ears pricked up as she shifted upright on the sofa, running a hand over her face and blearily looking around. Raising her head and cocking it to the side, the dog stared at her with dark eyes and Lena smiled softly.

     

                “Good morning. Did you sleep well?”

     

                She didn’t feel quite so mad talking to a dog; she assumed it was better than talking to herself, or Kara who wasn’t there. As her thoughts turned to Kara, she glanced at the time on the screen of her phone and tried calling her, hoping she wasn’t eating dinner or otherwise busy. The call went through and Lena smiled sheepishly as Kara’s face pixelated and then clarified.

     

                “Hi, you!”

     

                “You’re chipper this morning,” Kara said with a wide smile, “gotten over me already, have you?”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes and gave her a dour look. “I wouldn’t go that far. But I have met someone new. She’s cute; I think you’ll like her. She loves long walks and is a great listener and is even ex-military!”

     

                “Ha ha,” Kara sarcastically replied before giving Lena an expectant look. “What’s up?”

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena let out a strained laugh. “Okay, so you know how you love me? Promise you won’t get mad; it’s actually Kelly’s fault. And Alex’s. I hold none of the blame for this - you know that I’m a little impulsive with my purchases.”

     

                “God, you didn’t buy another car did you?”

     

                “No, no new cars. Not yet anyway. This one’s … smaller . So, you know how I told you about the dog conversation?”

     

                “You didn’t,” Kara gasped, eyes widening with delight. “Show me!”

     

                Chuckling, Lena turned the camera around and trained it on Athena, who was still on her bed, tongue lolling and a stillness to her, as if she wasn’t quite sure what to make of the big, quiet house and her new owner. They would have to get used to each other, but Lena knew it wouldn’t take long; she had every intention of spoiling her rotten.

     

                “Lena, that’s not a dog , it’s a horse!”

     

                “That’s what Kelly said,” Lena laughed as she turned the camera back around. “I did want a lap dog, but when I saw her … well, I couldn’t help myself! So, get this, her name is Athena. You know, like the Greek goddess of wisdom and battle strategy? Because … guess what - she was military trained! How perfect is that? Well, I mean almost ; she didn’t complete her training, which was why she was at the shelter because no one took her. Anyway, I just had to take her home.”

     

                “It sounds like she was made for us,” Kara said with a soft smile.

     

                “Right?” Lena eagerly agreed before her expression turned wary. “I still haven’t petted her yet, though; I’ve never had a dog before and she’s a little big. It’s unnerving .”

     

                “Well, we can cross that off my list. I’ve never seen you this excited before. I’m imagining coming home to a whole animal shelter inside.”

     

                 “One’s enough for now. I thought that- well, when you’re home, you can take her on your jogs. And we can take her hiking and stuff.”

     

                “Sounds perfect.”

     

                Lena gave her a loving smile and brought her knees to her chest, propping her chin on top as she held the phone at arm’s length. “So, how was your day?”

     

                “Good,” Kara murmured, giving her a tired smile, her face tanned, but not enough to hide the dark smudges beneath her eyes. “Nothing too exciting.”

     

                “Just the way I like it. You look tired though.”

     

                Kara hesitated and then shrugged, her smile growing a fraction but not quite reaching her eyes. “I’m fine,” she tried to reassure Lena, but failed miserably.

     

                Lena saw straight through her forced optimism and it set her on edge, a panicked feeling in her stomach as her face spasmed with worry. “What’s wrong?”

     

                “Really, it’s nothing. Just … some trouble with the soldiers. It’s not as easy as it seems in training when you get out here and thrown into the thick of it. I used to think that journalism was better than infantry or … whatever, but we’re all still stuck out here, doing the same shit every day.”

     

                Face crumpling, Lena swallowed thickly and her voice was hoarse when she replied. “It’s okay. It’s okay, you’ll be home soon.”

     

                Kara cracked a thin smile and looked down, her shoulders slumped defeatedly as she picked at her nails. “Yeah, but … I might not be me when I come home, baby.”

     

                “Kara, I-”

     

                She was cut off by a loud booming sound that caused the image of Kara to shake. It blurred and Kara’s choppy voice came through in snippets before the call died completely. The last image she was left with of her was Kara’s pale face and wide eyes and Lena sat there frozen for a minute, staring at the home screen.

     

                It took her a minute to process, before her hand started trembling and she felt faint, her breaths coming quick and shallow as a cold sweat broke out on her skin. Terror overtook her, thinking the worst even as she simultaneously tried to squash any thoughts like that, and Lena blinked rapidly as she tried to rein in her panic.

     

                Her first coherent thought turned to Alex. Alex would know what to do. She just had to go and see Alex and then everything would be okay. Abruptly climbing to her feet, causing Athena’s ears to prick up as she climbed to her feet, Lena rushed out into the hallway, cramming her feet into a pair of loafers abandoned by the door and pulling on a coat over her pyjamas before she snatched up the car keys. Whistling for Athena, who bounded over to attention, Lena was outside a moment later, in the car with her dog and on her way to Alex’s apartment.

     

                She parked haphazardly outside and was banging on the door a minute later, far too loud and early for a Saturday morning, earning her a muffled yell from a neighbour across the hall. Alex was likewise irritated as she forcefully yanked the door open with a glower on her face. It smoothed out into one of mild disgruntlement as she raked a hand over her buzzed undercut and squinted blearily, still half asleep.

     

                “Oh. It’s you. What time is it?”

     

                “Something’s happened,” Lena found herself rasping as she forced her way inside, Athena following obediently after her as Alex stared at the dog with confusion and slowly eased the door shut.

     

                “Uh, whose dog is that?”

     

                Lena ignored her again as she paced anxiously back and forth, arms wrapped tightly around herself as she let out a breathless sob, pale and trembling as she came apart at the seams. “I was talking to Kara and- and there was … this loud noise. Like a- a bomb. It was like a bomb went off. And the camera … the call got cut off and I don’t know. I don’t know what’s happening.”

     

                Her eyes filled with tears she stubbornly willed not to fall and she gouged half moons into her upper arms through the wool of her coat as she looked at Alex. Ashen-faced and looking like she’d just had the wind knocked out of her, Alex sank down onto the sofa and buried her face in her hands for a moment.

     

                “Shit. Fuck. No, no, it’s fine. She’s fine. It’s- it’s happened before, it’ll be fine.”

     

                Lena swallowed around the lump in her throat as she stopped packing and looked at Alex, clinging to her words as if they were fact. Drawing in a shuddering breath, she forced herself to nod as she rubbed at her brow.

     

                “Right. She’s fine. Of course she’s fine. She’ll probably call back soon, right? I’m just … overreacting.”

     

                Nodding to herself as she calmed down, the knot in her stomach making her feel nauseous even as she tried to trick her own mind into thinking that everything was okay, Lena sank down to the floor and motioned Athena forward. Hesitantly, she reached out and sank her fingers into the ruff of fur around her neck, closing her eyes as she breathed slowly and allowed the soothing motion of ruffling the fur lull her into a farce of peacefulness.

     

                It was shattered a moment later as Alex shot to her feet and kicked the sofa, letting out an angry shout that made Lena flinch, her eyes flying open as she stiffened. Watching her with wary eyes, Lena’s hands stilled and her flimsy grip on tranquility broke as panic and fear slammed into her.

     

                “I told her not to go,” Alex snarled, fingers clenching and then flexing as she ground her teeth together, brown eyes bright with tears. “I told her not to go back! I’m going to kill her when she comes home, I swear to God.”

     

                Slowly climbing to her feet, Lena stared at her with helplessness, warily picking her way around the sofa and laying a hand on Alex’s shoulder as she guided her back down onto the cushions. For the first time, Lena realised how hard this was for her too; Alex kept herself together a little too well, for the sake of appearances, and it frightened Lena even more to watch her lose that composure.

     

                Uncomfortable, Lena sat stiffly beside her for a moment as they both held their tears at bay, angry and scared and cursing Kara’s name. After a long minute, Lena hesitantly wrapped an arm around Alex, unsure of herself, as unused to comforting other people as she was, and half expected her to shrug off her touch before Alex leaned her head on Lena’s shoulder and exhaled roughly.  

     

                A few more minutes passed by, tense and leaving Lena with that hollow, sickening feeling in her chest, yawning wide open inside her as she dared not give it attention, and then Alex straightened up, running a hand over her face as she seemed to deflate. 

     

                “Sorry,” she hoarsely murmured, looking away as vague embarrassment touched her cheeks. “I think it’ll get easier the more time she goes, but … I just spent the entire time panicking. I meant it when I said she’ll be okay, though. It’s just … one time too many. Ignore me.”

     

                “I’m sorry. I shouldn’t- I shouldn’t have rushed over like this. I just- I didn’t know what to do. You’re the only person who knows how it feels and I- I thought you’d want to know but … maybe I should’ve just waited it out.”

     

                “No,” Alex whispered, patting Lena’s knee. “No, you were right to come here. If anything ever happens, we tell each other, okay? Don’t wait to find out if she’s okay first; don’t wait it out alone.”

     

                Lena nodded and fiddled with her fingers as she stared down at her lap, her heart still hammering in her chest as her stomach clenched painfully. “Should we … call your mom?”

     

                Alex closed her eyes and pinched the bridge of her nose before she finally nodded. Pushing herself to her feet, she exhaled softly. “Yeah. Yeah, I’ll call her now.”

     

                Wiping away an errant tear that hadn’t dried up, Lena blinked back the stinging feeling in her eyes and cleared her throat. “I’ll, um, make some coffee, I guess.”

     

                She shed her coat and discarded it over the arm of the sofa before walking into the kitchen, moving around with familiar ease as she tried to distract herself. Coffee didn’t seem like the best idea, as jittery as her movements already were, but it gave her something to do and the smell of it was comforting. Through the thin walls of the apartment, she could hear the muffled conversation Alex was having in her bedroom, calm and rational, in stark contrast to her burst of anger only minutes earlier.

     

                Lena took a seat on the sofa and set the cups down on the coffee table before texting Jess to cancel her meetings and reaching for the remote. She automatically turned to the local news channel, KPJT News , absorbing the story on an overturned freightliner truck on the highway that had traffic backed up as she waited. The cup of coffee burned her hands as she held it tightly and when Alex stepped out of her bedroom, Lena looked to her immediately.

     

                “My mom’s coming to stay for a couple of days,” Alex quietly announced, shrugging nonchalantly at Lena’s questioning look of panic. “She hates being up there alone when stuff like this happens.”

     

                “Right,” Lena whispered, wondering how often Eliza had flown down from Oregon to sit with Alex and wait to find out if this was the time they’d get the news that Kara wasn’t coming back.

     

                Masking a ripple of pain at her own thoughts, Lena took a scalding sip of coffee and shifted on the sofa. Her eyes landed on Athena who wormed her way through the gap between the sofa and coffee table to sit by Lena’s feet, looking at her with bright intelligence, tongue lolling and ears pricked up.

     

                “What’s with the dog?”

     

                “Kelly didn’t tell you?”

     

                “I worked late last night.”

     

                “Oh, well … the house was a little too quiet so I took your advice. This is Athena; I got her yesterday.”

     

                Alex snorted and ruffled the fur between the dog’s ears. “Cute.”

     

                “Mm,” Lena sceptically replied, still wary of the size of her and the intelligent gleam in her eyes.

     

                Shaking her head, Lena picked up her coffee and took a sip before she checked her phone. The screen lit up with no new notifications - no text messages, no FaceTime or missed calls - and her lips screwed up as she pressed them together in a sombre grimace.

     

                “No news is good news,” Lena muttered to herself before jamming the phone between her leg and the cushions, where she’d feel it if it vibrated.

     

                Alex looked up and gave her a wry smile, “she fed you that line too, huh? She’s not wrong though; every time my mom and I have been sick out of our minds with worry, it’s always turned out okay.”

     

                Giving her a wavering smile, Lena nodded and turned her attention to the TV, chewing on her nail as her leg bounced nervously. She couldn’t help but feel resentful at the fact that she had to feel this way, and that Kara had put her family through it - not once, but multiple times - and she was restless with frustration. She didn’t stop her agitated bouncing until Alex clapped a hand down on her knee and told her to stop, an exasperated look shot her way and a crime documentary put on the TV to pass the time in tense silence.

     

                The hours seemed to inch by, painfully slow and fruitless as neither of them received word from Kara that she was fine. Lena found herself growing more uneasy by the minute, that pit in her stomach filling her with dread until she was almost numb to it. Staring empty-eyed at the screen, Lena chewed anxiously on her bottom lip until it bled and her mind turned over that moment on video over and over again, trying to rationalise it to herself.

     

                At lunchtime, there was a knock on the door and Alex leapt to her feet, a tangle of limbs as she tripped over her feet in her haste and answered the door to a frazzled looking Eliza. She had an overnight bag slung over her shoulder and looked drained from the short flight. Alex hugged her and rubbed at her forehead as she grimly informed her of the lack of news and shut the door.

     

                Lena rose from the sofa and Athena stood to attention behind her, tail thumping against the coffee table as Lena stepped forward, dry-eyed and exhausted as she gave Eliza a quick hug, murmuring vague niceties without even hearing what she was saying.

     

                “You like tired, sweetie,” Eliza commented, patting her cheek.

     

                Waving aside her concerns, Lena gave her a wan smile and sank back down onto the cushions. “I’ve just been working late the past few nights.”

     

                Truthfully, she found herself staying up half the night more often these days, as she hadn’t done in months. Her sleep was so fitful that sometimes it hardly seemed worth the effort, and especially over the last week, she found herself in her office, looking over spreadsheets and emails and contracts and numbers until her head ached and her eyes were dry and shoulders slumped. 

     

                Only once exhaustion bowed her shoulders and she became bone-leaden did Lena drag herself down to that empty bed, because try as she might, it didn’t get easier. She got used to being alone again, but that didn’t make it easier; it just left Lena slowly slipping back into her old habits of sleeplessness and over-working. She masked it well around Alex and Kelly, lying about how many hours of sleep she’d gotten or about working once she’d gotten home from dinner or drinks.

     

                “Coffee, mom?” Alex asked, snagging hers and Lena’s from the coffee table and moving to the kitchen to rinse out the sluggish dregs.

     

                “Sure,” Eliza replied, dropping her bag down beside the arm of the sofa and perching on the edge of the coffee table as she reached out to scratch beneath Athena’s chin. Glancing at Lena, she raised her eyebrows. “Yours?”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Lena shrugged, “the house is too quiet.”

     

                Nodding in understanding, Eliza’s expression clouded, and soon enough it was the three of them squeezed on the sofa with their coffee and their worry shrouding the room as they waited. Alex quietly filled Kelly in over the phone when she finished work, and as the day slipped into late afternoon, the buttery sunlight of the golden hour saturating the tired apartment, the four of them packed into the place and made stilted conversation without any real heart to it.

     

                As the shadows deepened and the noise of the city blared outside, shouts from the 7/11 and honking horns and the shuddering of the AC unit, Lena had finally had enough. It was suffocating, sitting in the tiny living room with the thick tension as no one wanted to voice their fears, and the heat was oppressive, her pyjamas clinging to her skin as she curled up on the sofa, wilting as the day wore on.

     

                Shoving her feet into her shoes and throwing a coat over her pyjamas, Lena raked a hand through her hair and clipped Athena’s leash to the collar before murmuring that she’d be back. Walking around the block, a hot breeze blew the smell of garbage and dollar-slice pizza up off the street, ruffling her hair as she swallowed drily, passing graffitied and shuttered shopfronts and small tattoo parlours and souvenir stands as she tried to catch her breath. Despite the shade of the tall apartment blocks, the air was still thick from the heat of the day, offering no reprieve to the close air of the apartment, and Lena broodingly returned shortly after with bags of Big Belly Burger .

     

                The mood was subdued as she let herself back in, everyone’s attention glued to the TV, although they barely absorbed what they were seeing, and they ate robotically, not even tasting the grease and salt. It felt like ash in Lena’s mouth and it was through sheer will that she forced her burger down. 

     

                The kitchen grew dark as they sat there, but no one got up to turn on the lights. Everything had a blue shadow, soft and indistinct, the furniture simplifying into shapes as their features blurred into silhouettes. Eventually, it was Kelly who switched on a lamp and forced the stiff windows up to assist the struggling AC unit, but the black air wouldn’t move, wouldn’t shift in or out the window as night unravelled.

     

                Lena had intended to go home to her brownstone, but as the hour grew later and there was still no word, Alex convinced her to stay instead. When Kara called, it would be better if they were all there so they could speak to her, so they could all experience that moment of relief together. She agreed but quietly argued with Eliza that she take the sofa, making herself up a bed with a borrowed pillow and blanket while Eliza took Kara’s bare room. 

     

                As they all retreated to their beds, the apartment grew quieter and without the background noise of the TV or the murmured conversation, Lena found her mind free to roam to dangerous thoughts. Sleep eluded her, the groaning springs of Alex’s bed as one of them turned seeming too loud, the muggy air of the apartment making her too hot and sweaty to lay in one spot on the leather sofa for too long before she had to peel herself off, and sound seeped inside through the open windows, a constant dull roar that did little to lift the stillness of the apartment.

     

                Lena stared at the shadowed furniture as she tossed and turned all night, Athena sleeping on the floor beside her head, streetlights and neon shop signs providing a dim glow that only slightly lifted the veil of darkness. Dawn wasn’t too far off by the time Eliza stirred, her silhouette slinking past the sofa, attempting to be quiet as she fetched a glass from the cupboard and filled it with water.

     

                Pushing herself up, Lena rubbed at her burning eyes and mumbled that she was awake; she didn’t bother saying that she hadn’t gone to sleep in the first place, that she’d spent all night with her phone clutched in her hand, the battery on the verge of dying as she waited for a phone call. It was almost a mercy that the sky held a tinge of amber because at least she could give up on the farce and escape the fear of what nightmares lurked in sleep.

     

                Over breakfast, everyone pretended things were normal - as normal as they could - and Alex made scrambled eggs for the dog while Lena texted Jess she wouldn’t be into work that day either. As much as she loved the refuge work offered her, the ability to escape in the drowning pile of paperwork, phone calls and meetings, it would have been unbearable at that moment. Alex and Kelly didn’t have the option to skip work for the unknown, which meant that Eliza was left at the apartment by herself.

     

                “Um, I’m not going into the office today,” Lena quietly informed her, “if- if you’d like to come to my house.”

     

                “Sure, sweetie. That sounds great.”

     

                “Can you just … get the dog out before my landlord gets a complaint?” Alex gingerly asked, scooping eggs onto a plate as Athena’s tail thumped loudly against the table leg and she let out a quiet huff of a bark. “I have a no pets policy.”

     

                Nose wrinkling, Lena gave her an apologetic smile and quickly nodded, finishing off her Lucky Charms with haste and rushing through the dishes while everyone else got ready for the day. They all parted ways in the lobby and Lena somewhat self-consciously led Eliza over to the haphazardly parked Porsche, unlocking it and shooing Athena into the back. The drive was relatively quick, missing most of the rush hour traffic, and Lena parked outside the brownstone and gestured to it.

     

                “This one’s mine.”

     

                “Oh. It’s- well, that’s a nice house.”

     

                Lena smiled wanly and unlocked the front door before gathering yesterday’s mail off the floor. A letter off Kara lay on top and she paused as a tremor worked its way into her fingers. Burying it beneath the junk mail, bills and charity invitations, Lena set them on the console and breathed in the smell of furniture polish and the distinct odour of vacuumed floors. Her housekeeper had come yesterday and tidied up the scattered mess, and Lena was spared the embarrassment of her unkempt panic strewn throughout the house for Eliza to witness.

     

                “Make yourself at home,” Lena told her with a crooked smile, bending down to unclip the leash. “Can I get you coffee? Cup of tea?”

     

                Rubbing Lena’s shoulder as she stepped past her, eyes alight with interest and mild surprise, as if she hadn’t quite realised how well-off Lena was without witnessing the modest four-story home firsthand, Eliza distractedly replied. “Coffee would be great.”

     

                Nodding, Lena kicked her shoes off and padded barefoot through to the kitchen as Eliza and Athena followed after her. Brewing two cups of dark, bitter coffee on the sleek machine, Lena added cream to Eliza’s and then hesitated.

     

                “I might go and wash up and change.”

     

                “Sure,” Eliza smiled, drawing a chair out from the table and taking a seat.

     

                Returning the smile as a flicker of amusement lit up Lena’s eyes at how alike Kara was to her adoptive mother, able to comfortably make themselves at home anywhere, she nodded and slipped up the staircase. The shower reinvigorated her, washing away the dried out feeling in her eyes and the rumpled dishevelment of yesterday, and when she emerged, smelling of lime and bergamot, she dressed in clean clothes and felt more like herself, more in control.  

     

                Lena could rationalise anything to herself, ever the logical realist, and feeling renewed, she was able to tuck away the worry and fear into boxes to delve into later. For now, she had to pretend at least a little as she entertained Eliza and tried to present an image of someone composed and mature, instead of the lost little girl she felt like.

     

                Padding back downstairs, her footsteps silenced by thick cashmere socks as the old steps creaked beneath her weight, she emerged in the kitchen to fetch her coffee and went in search of Eliza. She found her in the back sitting room that Lena rarely ventured into, nursing her coffee as she took in the decor.

     

                “You play the cello?”

     

                “Badly,” Lena chuckled, wincing slightly as she looked at the old instrument propped up in the corner. “And not for years.”

     

                “I don’t believe you could do anything badly,” Eliza said with a faint smile as she cocked her head to the side and watched Lena duck her head with discomfort. 

     

                “Not if I enjoy it, which never included cello.”

     

                Eliza laughed quietly as her eyes swept over the room, a slight furrow creasing her brow, as if troubled by some aspect of Lena’s immaculately curated interior design was found wanting in some way.

     

                “It’s a beautiful house.”

     

                Lena’s lips twisted with a wry smile at the particular choice of word- house , not home - and she dipped her head in silent acknowledgement, knowing her sparse minimalism lacked the typical homely touches of photos and knick-knacks that were useful , and not just decorative.

     

                “Let me show you the rest of it.”

     

                She opened and closed doors, giving Eliza a brief tour, the shy feeling of allowing someone into her home, looking at her things and her interests on neat display making her quiet as they moved up through the levels. In her office, Eliza picked up the framed photo of Kara on Lena’s desk and let out a short laugh, thumbing the glass as she smiled lovingly.

     

                “She’s always been so beautiful, ' she murmured, a pang of sorrow in her voice. “So kind and warm; she’s the type of kid that everyone dreams of adopting, you know? There were so many ways that she could’ve turned out, considering … well, everything, but from the very first day, she wasn’t a problem child , she was just sad and quiet. Until she was warm again.”

     

                “I can’t imagine her not being that way,” Lena said with a small smile.

     

                “You changed her too, you know.”

     

                Eyebrows rising, Lena blinked in surprise, arms crossed over her chest as she tilted her head to the side. “Really?”

     

                “Mm. She was so … closed off. She adapted, she fit into her new family and grew loud and sweet and kind - even when she and Alex didn’t get on, we couldn’t help but love her. Kara’s a people person; she needs to be around people, makes friends so easily and is just … so full of life, but … being over there takes its toll on her. It made her quieter and nervous. She babbles a lot.”

     

                Lena let out a strained laugh at that, knowing all too well how much Kara talked, but she’d never taken it as a nervous habit.

     

                “But, she’s never lost that optimism. She should have, God, she should have, but I’m glad she didn’t. And since she met you … she’s been louder again. Bolder.”

     

                Eliza smiled to herself as she looked at the photo once more and then returned it to the desk, walking over to Lena and looping and arm around her shoulders as she guided them towards the staircase. 

     

                “You love her, don’t you?” Eliza asked after a moment, and Lena was silently stunned as she plodded on downwards, head ducked down and the looming presence of Eliza behind her making her tongue tie itself into knows.

     

                “Yeah,” she whispered to the steps, watching her socks as her cheeks reddened.

     

                A lump formed in her throat too and her voice was scarcely a whisper as she added, “I’m scared she won’t come home.”

     

                Eliza squeezed her shoulder and Lena drew in a shuddering breath as she stepped off the staircase and moved into the kitchen. “Me too. It breaks my heart every time she goes.”

     

                “You said it gets easier,” Lena said, the slight edge of an accusation in her voice as she gave Eliza a brooding look. 

     

                Lips twisting ruefully, Eliza shrugged and set her coffee cup down on the kitchen counter, leaning against it as she bit the inside of her lip. Her blue eyes took on a glassy sheen as she rapped her knuckles on the countertop. 

     

                “I lied. It never gets easier; you just get used to it. The worrying and- and the waiting. I wasn’t going to tell you that though.”

     

                Lena quietly scoffed and rubbed at the back of her neck, the bitter sting of the lie softened by the well-intentioned meaning behind it. She doubted it would have made much difference if Eliza had been honest with her anyway, but she probably would’ve clung to Kara even harder, perhaps begged her not to go and made things more difficult by doing so. At least now she’d had a few weeks without her to adjust.

     

                “She’ll be okay,” Eliza gently reassured her after a long moment of silence. “My girl is tough; all of you are.”

     

                Nodding, Lena drained her coffee and then set both of their cups beneath the drips to refill with fresh coffee. While espresso streamed into their cups, she fiddled with her phone, the battery almost dead and no new notifications on the screen as she turned it in her hands, shoulders tense and a defeated stoop to her posture. She looked younger than she was at that moment, her face bare of any makeup, her eyes wide and doleful and aching as her damp hair left blotches on her thin knitted top.

     

                They drank their coffee in the front sitting room, Lena letting Eliza regale her with stories about Kara and answering questions about work and articles she’d read and what her thoughts on the latest climate change conference was. It helped a little, taking Lena’s mind off of it, even though she was readily aware of what Eliza was trying to do. After a couple of hours, they took Athena for a walk in the nearby private park, which occupied an entire city block, the sprawling series of brownstones in her neighbourhood built around a wild tangle of forest and grass. Through the iron gates built into the towering limestone arches, they walked through the late morning sunlight, past patches of sorels and California poppies as they kept up a leisurely pace, walking beneath the dappled sunlight the overarching rosewood and oak trees as Athena trotted happily along.

     

                Stopping to buy Reubens at a deli on the way back, they returned home and watched reality TV with vapid interest, eating their sandwiches and sipping kombucha as they whittled away the time. Kelly showed up first after work, grave and gentle with ingredients to make peach cobbler to pass the time, and she coached Lena through the process as Eliza insisted on doing Lena’s laundry for her, even though she assured her she’d have it sent out to the dry cleaner’s. 

     

                Alex showed up later, the smell of cheap disinfectant clinging to her white coat as she let herself in without knocking, a bottle of wine in hand and the drawn look of someone who hadn’t gotten enough sleep last night. Lena fetched four glasses and allowed Alex to pour cheap rosé into, the sickly sweet taste of it getting stuck at the back of her dry throat as she nursed it and curled up on the dining chair, keeping her thoughts to herself as she stared at the dark screen of her phone. Surely it shouldn't take this long.

     

                They all stayed at her house that night, the spare rooms put to use as everyone drifted upstairs. Lena didn’t go to bed though, she went up to her office and curled up in the worn leather chair, seeking some comfort in the familiar smell of paper and ink and sanded wood as she nursed a cup of mint tea and listened to the house settle on its old joints.

     

                She was exhausted. After a sleepless night, she was flagging, her eyes looking sunken and bloodshot, her shoulders rounded with terrible posture as she slumped down lower in the seat. Eventually, she couldn’t keep her eyes open, not even out of sheer willpower, and drifted in and out of consciousness while never quite slipping into sleep. Clutching her phone tightly, she dreamt at one point that it vibrated, a droning feeling against her skin as she waited.

     

                Jerking awake, Lena realised that she wasn’t dreaming and blinked owlishly, suddenly wide awake. Straightening up in her seat, she looked at the name on the screen as her hand shook terribly, and felt a stab of fear and panic amidst the ballooning hope. Kara.

     

                Answering it, she cleared her throat and scrubbed a hand over her careworn face, blinking away the burning sensation in her eyes as her heart pounded in her chest. By the time the call connected, her eyes were swimming with tears, and at the first glimpse of Kara’s face, she promptly burst into tears.

     

                “Oh, God,” Lena breathlessly sobbed, swiping her thumb over her closed eyelids as she muffled the choked sound that worked its way up her throat. “You’re alive. You’re okay.”

     

                “Hey,” Kara rasped, a trembling smile managing to work its way onto her lips as she shifted forward. “I’m fine. I’m just … tired.”

     

                Hot tears spilled down Lena’s cheeks, quickly brushed away as she drew in a shuddering breath. Her eyes drank in the sight of Kara as she felt the knot in her chest loosen with the reassuring knowledge that she was there . But she was far from fine . Her tanned skin looked grey from the layer of dust, her hair was frazzled and unkempt and there were small cuts and bruises on her face as she smiled tentatively. The dark circles beneath her eyes led Lena to believe they’d slept the same amount of time since they’d last spoken. 

     

                As relief slammed into her, making her weak and comforted, burning anger took its place and Lena gripped her phone tightly as she hunched over the small screen. 

     

                “Never do that to me again,” she choked out through clenched teeth, her green eyes shining brightly with the threat of her words. It fell short as her voice broke and she let out a choked sob. “Do you hear me? Never. That was … unbearable. I didn’t know if you were coming back.”

     

                Kara’s face crumpled at Lena’s words, at the pain and fear in them, and she nodded as she blinked rapidly, nudging her glasses up her nose and clearing her throat. Her blue eyes shone with tears and her bottom lip wobbled as she inhaled. “I’m sorry.”

     

                “What the hell happened?”

     

                Hesitating for a second, Kara rubbed at her eyes and Lena felt her own sting with tears, listening to the choked reply. “A rocket hit our barracks roof. The power went out, I- I couldn’t hear shit, and there was dust and- and smoke in the air making it difficult to breathe and see. Jeremiah used to tell us … he’d say, if you panic you’re dead. I could hear him in my head saying it. If you panic you’re dead. I couldn’t … it was ...”

     

                “You don’t have to talk about it,” Lena whispered, wiping at her eyes.

     

                “Thanks,” Kara murmured, her voice small and slightly strangled.

     

                Lena let out a pent up breath, choking on a breathless sob as she unfolded her legs and fluidly rose from the chair. “Let me go and wake everyone up.”

     

                “Is my mom there? She normally comes and stays with Alex when I go incognito.”

     

                “Incognito?” Lena snapped, her tone brittle and sharp, watching as amusement lit up Kara’s face and her shoulders shook with laughter. “Don’t you fucking laugh, Kara Danvers. I’ve been out of my mind . I thought …”

     

                They both knew what she’d thought and Kara quickly sobered up, although Lena couldn’t stop the small smile from curling the corners of her lips as she thundered noisily downstairs, knocking on all the bedroom doors until she got responses from the occupied ones. Pushing her way into the one Alex and Kelly were in, she switched the light on and blinded them to much cursing and squinting, as Eliza materialised behind her in the doorway.

     

                Lena passed the phone on, sitting cross-legged at the end of the mattress, content to just listen , to hear Kara’s voice and know that she was okay. They all took turns scolding her and expressing their relief as the phone was passed around, teary-eyed and wide smiles, all of them exchanging fleeting touches of comfort and reassurance and droll looks of their over exaggerations. It all seemed so trifling now, speaking to her and seeing her on screen, a little worse for wear but whole and healthy.

     

                She explained later that there had been an attack on their camp, a few rockets targeting the barracks that she was in as she followed up a report. There were injuries, but luckily no casualties, but it didn’t lessen that stomach-lurching feeling that it was entirely possible she could have died. Needless to say, they were all grateful that the worst she sported was a few bruises and scrapes, and it was with great reluctance that they had to say goodbye.

     

                Kara had to get back to work but promised to call again before she slept later that night, now that they had functioning electricity and the internet was back up and running again. Once everyone had said their goodbyes, Lena took the phone and slipped out, murmuring goodnight to Eliza and smiling shyly, her relief and joy etched in the lines of her face, before she retreated to her room alone to say goodbye.

     

                She must have said it ten times, each one chased with an ‘I love you’ , thinking about that split-second where she hadn’t had time to say anything . And even then, it didn’t quite feel like enough , but still, she reluctantly let Kara go and was greeted with the weightless solace that Kara was okay. For the first time in almost two days, she felt like she could breathe fully, even if those unsavoury of what could’ve happened still lurked in the recesses of her mind. But, reassured, Lena slipped beneath the covers and gratefully sank into a deep sleep, uninterrupted by bad dreams as she clutched her phone to her chest and thought of Kara. Only Kara.

    Chapter 29

    Lena,

     

    Today was a good day. They’re rarer than you’d think, over here, but it was good and it felt like a small victory. It’ll sound silly to you, one of those things that isn’t really funny unless you’re there for it, but one of the Sergeants had a Private walking all around camp for three hours to find his canteen that he misplaced. He had to ask everyone and everything if they’d seen it; I can assure you that in the middle of the desert, watching an adult man ask a car, a rock and a gun if they’d seen his canteen was enough to have everyone slacking off to enjoy it. Can you believe my idea of fun has gone from movie dates and hiking with you to watching stupid people get ordered to do stupid things?

     

    It was a good day, but it made me miss you more because of it. Right now, I’m writing this outside with a flashlight as I look up at the stars. They’re the same ones as they are back home, and I never thought I’d find the Big Dipper comforting, but it is. It makes me sad that we’re not looking up at the same sky though; it’ll be before noon there. 

     

    Lena, it’s so hot these days. I wonder how you’re doing. I hope you’ve eaten breakfast. I hope the people around you know to make sure you’ve eaten, that you don’t stay cooped up in your office all the time. You tell me you’re sleeping when we talk, but there’s a part of me that knows you’re lying. You look tired and I know I should tell you that, but I hate to waste our calls nagging you over it. Look after yourself for me, okay? It makes it more bearable to know you’re doing fine without me. 

     

    I can’t tell you much, but there’s talk of some big operations and I don’t want you to worry.
