I know I’m in the thick of it, trailing after everyone with a notepad to write down what’s happening, but things are going well this time. I don’t think I’ve ever been further away from the fighting in all of my deployments as I am now. I hope that makes you worry less. Knowing you, it probably won’t, but I want you to know it’s boring stuff. Without the books you send and endless games of solitaire and gin rummy, I think I would’ve lost my mind by now.

     

    But it’s almost a month in now. I’m sure you know that, but I’ve been ticking it off on my little calendar, and aside from talking to everyone back home, it’s the highlight of my day. Each cross in each box brings me one day closer to seeing your face and holding onto you as tight as humanly possible. Eight months feels like a lifetime away, but just think about how fast the past few weeks have gone (just pretend, for me - I know they’ve dragged) and think about how soon we’ll see each other again. 

     

    Just think, there’s going to be a point in our lives where we wake up beside each other every morning, where we wake up in our house with our dog and our little life, and this will all feel like a bad dream. Until then, I’ll have to miss you every day. I know I still get to see you on the screen, but it doesn’t feel the same, and as beautiful as you are, I don’t think the camera does my memory justice. Neither do the photos I brought with me, the ones I keep in my pocket, right next to my heart so I can feel like you’re with me. I’ve enclosed some that I’ve taken here, of the camp and the boys and the desert. It’s all boring and dry and we’re all getting by, but I like taking them all the same, in case anything happens. I want the people I love to look back and see evidence of my life, of it being lived, loved and celebrated. That’s why I take so many of you when I’m home. You’re proof that I haven’t always been completely alone in this world.

     

    I should probably sleep now, or I’ll be the one getting yelled at in the morning and being made to do stupid things for the amusement of other stupid people. At least when I wake up, I’ll have another box to cross through and I’ll be one day closer to the day I’m home for good. Please say you’ll wait for me to come home. I love you.

     

    Yours always,

    Kara x

    Chapter 30

                Eliza stayed an extra day before returning to Midvale and her small town of patients and life resumed much as it had for the past three weeks, with Lena slogging through each day, trying to make the most of it and failing miserably. The palpable tension between the trio left back in National City eased up by the end of the following week, the danger feeling like it had passed - for the time being - and life resuming, much as it had before. 

     

                Lena wrote letters to Kara and slipped them into care packages filled with toothpaste and candy and extra sunscreen and new socks. She slumped on the sofa, staring at eddying dust tumbling across the hardwood floor as she whittled away at the chunks of time she was left alone, Athena staring dolefully at her as the TV droned on and she drank glasses of limoncello and vodka, the sticky heat of July giving way to August’s cooler days. 

     

                Halfway through the month, she took a business trip to Hong Kong, messing up her sleep schedule to talk to Kara at their usual time for the few days she was there before closing a deal and heading straight back to National City. After days of deliberating, Lena convinced Sam to arrange a meeting with the Human Resources manager to give her staff a raise, earning a small kernel of satisfaction at the act and inviting Sam out to dinner with Alex and Kelly in a spontaneous, almost unheard of gesture of friendship.

     

                The days still blurred together though, her waking hours consisting of a sort of murkiness, in the dim place between the real world and dreams. She tried hiking by herself, driving the Porsche out through the immense, arid mountains, their sprawling bulk dominating the skyline in shades of sage green and umber, desert shrubs and native trees crowding along the side of the rodes and the sloping hills, Athena eagerly adventuring off ahead of her until Lena felt lost and sunburnt and turned back. She never did figure out where Kara had taken her that one time. During a particularly bad storm, she sat outside on the back patio and let the rain soak into her clothes as she listened to old moody music blaring through the open kitchen door and watched lightning arc across the sky, the rain deliciously warm and cleansing the city before she watched a gleaming pink sunrise appear once the storm broke.

     

                All in all, Lena was bored. She’d never felt bored before, never had those moments of reprieve from work and the weight of her baggage to have time for herself, and now that she did, she struggled to find ways to fill it. Work was always there, waiting for her, but she was making a conscious effort to leave the office, to take days off and delegate her work to others and take advantage of the time to figure out the things a twenty-four year old should have been. For so long, Lena felt like she’d skipped ahead of her life, missing the young years where she should have been making mistakes and patching them up and repeating it all over again. She should have been confused about her career and living in a shitty apartment and planning on going home for Thanksgiving, but she lingered in the city with her daily coffee and walks through the streets, keeping to her own odd hours as she allowed Kara’s family to slot in around her schedule.

     

                September was on the verge of arriving, the turn of the seasons bringing a burst of colour to the trees, the warm hues of autumn brought out in the brownstones and the reddish bricks that comprised the older parts of National City. The days still held the amber warmth of sunshine but there was a cooler edge to them, the air not quite as stifling and the sky not quite cerulean anymore. Lena had a trip to Metropolis booked for a launch of the latest L-Corp operating system and was sitting behind her desk at the office, teeth worrying at her red bottom lip as she hesitated, frowning down at her phone.

     

                It took her over an hour before she finally decided to bite the bullet and press the name of the last woman she could imagine herself turning to for help. And yet, some part of her had decided to give it a try. For all that Lillian had told her, Lena had decided recently that she would no longer hold resentment or blame towards her mother for the things Lillian had never been able to control. It had been weeks of frustrated talks with Kelly over wine for her to accept that she couldn’t change the past, only understand why she felt the way she did and how to help herself despite it. Calling her was the first decisive choice Lena had made of her own free will. It was no surprise when her mother picked up after two rings.

     

                “Lena?” Lillian brusquely greeted her, her voice laced with anxious surprise. “Is everything okay?”

     

                “Um, hi, mom,” Lena slowly mumbled, her stomach twisting itself into knots as she rubbed at her forehead and turned her back on her desk, staring out at the pale blue sky and the weak sunlight reflected off a thousand windows below. 

     

                For a brief moment, she wondered whether she was making a mistake, but pushed her doubts aside as she forged onwards. The worst that could happen was that things would peter out and she and her mother would return to their cold and stunted relationship of haughty conversation at board meetings and galas. She’d been through it before; it had been the crux of their relationship for most of Lena’s life, and she could handle it again. Lena had armoured herself against hoping for anything positive or pleasant when it came to her family, and she wouldn’t lapse into unsuspecting complacency that easily.

     

                “Everything’s … fine,” she haltingly replied. “I mean, um, I’m going to be in town in a couple of days.”

     

                “For the launch?”

     

                Silent for a moment as a prickle of guilt needled her heart, Lena softly cleared her throat, scuffing the red sole of a Louboutin across the tiled floor of her office as she gingerly winced. “Yeah, for that. I’ll be there a few days beforehand to check on everything and do a run-through, and I thought … maybe we could get dinner while I was there. Maybe you could give me some … feedback?”

     

                There was a brief pause before Lillian replied, uncertainly. “You want my input?”

     

                “I think a second opinion could be helpful,” Lena hedged.

     

                “Of course. I’d be happy to. When will you be flying in?”

     

                “The launch is on Friday, so I’ll be there Wednesday. Tomorrow morning.”

     

                “Ah, well … I’m sure you already have your apartment made up for you, but you still have your room at the house if you- if you wanted to stay here.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena’s mouth went dry and she struggled to speak for a moment, a lump rising in her throat as she pressed her lips together. “At the house? Oh, um, it’s just-”

     

                “I know you hate it here,” Lillian said with bitter amusement in her voice, “but … I could use the company. Maybe you could too.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena closed her eyes. A spasm of pain ran through her as she was bombarded with so many bad memories of her childhood associated with that sprawling mansion and its dark hallways. The most time she ever spent there was during the holidays - the ones where she wasn’t sent away to a summer camp or overseas - and those would be spent alone in her room, reading books or tinkering with various electronics as she blasted her music just loud enough to drown out the distant shouts downstairs. It was a feeling of isolation and loneliness that she attributed to that house, and she was hesitant to accept her mother’s offer, but found herself warily agreeing, despite her reservations.

     

                Perhaps it was too many days and nights coming home to an empty house, which had only just stopped, on account of the dog she now came home to, but she agreed all the same, surprising both of them. A part of her was already bracing for disaster to strike, for the inevitable breaking down of the fragile peace they’d come to, but if it was inevitable anyway, she would rather rip the bandaid off in one swift motion.

     

                “Oh, I, uh, yeah, I could … try.”

     

                “You will?” Lillian blurted out, completely taken aback by even Lena’s very hesitant agreement. “That- that would mean a lot. If things … well, you can leave whenever, if you feel like you need to.”

     

                “Right,” Lena mumbled in agreement, “well, I should probably get back to work. I have some stuff to finish off before I head home.”

     

                “Okay. Of course. Well … I’ll see you tomorrow then.”

     

                Lena ground out her own awkward goodbye, already feeling antsy and uncomfortable at the thought of going home, and she let out a pent up breath and rolled her shoulders as soon as the line went dead, trying to relieve herself of some of the tension.

     

                “Why did I do that?” she muttered to herself, running a hand over her face.

     

                Shaking her head, she sighed again and went back to work with the rankling knowledge that tomorrow was going to be a very long day. On numerous occasions through the late afternoon as she dwelled at L-Corp, and then the long hours of night as she walked Athena in the dark, puddles of light from street lamps briefly illuminating their forms as they passed by, fetching pizza from the gourmet place three blocks away, and even when she’d gone to bed later on after a few glasses of scotch, Lena considered cancelling. She could feign some excuse that Lillian wouldn’t believe but would let her get away with, with snide, pointed comments that Lena would choose to ignore.

     

                But when her alarm went off at five the next morning, she showered and dressed into the outfit she’d picked out and let her driver load her leather valise into the trunk with Athena’s supplies, and sat on the cool leather seat as they drove through the latent sunrise, the dog’s head in her lap as she ran her fingers through the bristly fur at the nape of her neck. 

     

                The flight was brutally short, something Lena never imagined she’d resent before, and she was silent and grew increasingly tense as the pre-arranged car drove her out towards the acreage of land the big house was situated on. Lena watched as the familiar backdrop of her life flashed past in a blur, the air colder, seeping in through the glass, and the skies greyer as the deciduous trees offered more variety in shade and species, the roads littered with red and orange and curling brown even this early in autumn. She fidgeted nervously as the miles were whittled down to nothing, her nerves fraying as she swallowed and then swallowed again, watching with a plummeting stomach as each turn became increasingly familiar.

     

                Eventually, they approached the tall, wrought-iron gates situated at the end of the driveway, and the driver spoke into the intercom before they parted to admit them. Trees lined the long road up to the house, still obscured from view, and Lena could feel her shoulders aching as they inched up towards her ears. She had to force herself to drop them, to not shrink down in her seat as a cold sweat broke out on her lower back at the dreadful thought of coming home. It had been years.

     

                When the overarching, shadowed branches of the trees finally fell away to reveal the stately house, Lena felt her stomach lurch. Nothing had changed, not even in the slightest , and she stared up at the faded red brick with the limestone trim, the gravel driveway and the two curving staircases that led up to a paved walkway, enclosed with a low limestone wall and periodically lined with large pots of neatly trimmed shrubs. From there rose the house, three stories tall and wide , the square windows all dark and the tall, wooden front doors already open as Lillian waited for her.

     

                The car slowed before the curved double staircases and Lena hesitated for a moment as the driver opened the door for her, before she climbed out, smoothing a hand over her jeans as she stared broodingly at the old stone and the grey sky. A shiver forced her into motion as a frigid wind swept through the estate, trees rustling and a crow’s caw making her skin ripple with goosebumps before she whistled softly for Athena to get out of the car and made for the steps.

     

                Her shoes scraped on the pitted limestone and she felt the faint swooping sensation in her chest as she wavered for a second, cursing herself out for agreeing to do this, despite her better judgement. Still, she caught sight of her mother standing on the doorstep before she crested the last few steps and knew it was too late to back out this early and forced herself across the neat paving stones. Lillian must have seen the scepticism on her face, her smile small and tense, if not a little surprised that she’d actually shown up, and she unfolded her arms.

     

                “Hi,” Lena slowly greeted her, one side of her mouth curling slightly at the corner but not quite making it to a smile, giving her an almost lopsided look of contempt as the driver followed her up with her leather case. 

     

                “Hi,” Lillian said with a little more warmth, but no less awkward and stilted. 

     

                She was dressed in a thin woollen sweater, her caramel hair pinned up and her usually regal posture somewhat ruined by the tense set of her shoulders, high and squared as she slowly rolled her palms together in a restless manner. Lena’s lips twitched at the thought of her mother being nervous and she bit her bottom lip as she stared past her at the house, doubt flickering in her green eyes.

     

                “Don’t just stand there, come in.”

     

                Lillian turned and stepped over the threshold, leaving Lena to linger outside for a moment before the cold ushered her over the doorsill and into the dim house. The driver deposited her bag inside the door and said his goodbyes and Lena stared out at the grey sky and gently decomposing expanse of trees and withering lawn as she listened to the crunch of gravel beneath tires and found one of her biggest fears waiting for her. She was back home, alone with her mother.

     

                Softly whistling for Athena, who trotted inside onto the checkerboard tiles of the foyer, sniffing around with a wagging tail as Lena eased the monstrously big front door shut on creaking hinges. Without the pale sunlight streaming in, the house was dark, the chandelier hanging overhead unable to cut through the dark panelled wood and heavy damask wallpaper, and Lena was hit with a crushing blow of familiarity as she lingered just inside the doorway, finding that nothing had really changed.

     

                “You got a dog?” Lillian asked, her tone brittle as she stepped back from Athena’s adventuring snout.

     

                “I wanted the company,” Lena shrugged, putting her hands in her pockets as she avoided looking anywhere for too long but found herself simultaneously looking at everything.

     

                “Let me know what it needs and I’ll have the housekeeper pick up some things.”

     

                Lena nodded her thanks as her eyes wandered. It was with a flicker of shock that she realised her first assessment of the foyer had been wrong; the walls and the console and cabinets were free of the photos they used to hold. The photos of her and her brother, even the ugly, staged family ones, too. Lillian noticed Lena’s preoccupation with the patches of wallpaper that were a shade darker than the rest of the wall, where the frames that had hung for so many years had left it untouched by the sun’s bleaching effects. Her expression darkened but her lips still curved into a rueful smile.

     

                “I had them taken down afterwards.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, not expecting her mother to touch on anything concerning Lex, Lena looked at her and gave her a disparaging smile as she quietly scoffed. “What? Couldn’t bear to look at him, could you?”

     

                “Yes,” Lillian agreed, her lips thinning as a muscle ticked in her jaw. “The ones of you were already gone by then.”

     

                Her contempt faded into shame and guilt and she ducked her head as rubbed at the nape of her neck, clearing her throat. It made her uncomfortable to know that Lillian had mourned the loss of two children, had lived alone in this big house and had perhaps missed them. It didn’t fit into the image of her mother that Lena had crafted in her mind and she felt tense and uneasy to have a light shone on the truth. 

     

                Eager to move on, Lillian moved towards the staircase, looking back over her shoulder with raised eyebrows. “I had your bed made up for you in your old room. I hope that’s okay.”

     

                “Fine,” Lena curtly replied.

     

                “Do you want to take your things upstairs and get settled in?”

     

                “Sure.”

     

                “I’m assuming you remember the way.”

     

                Lena pulled a disgruntled face at her mother’s lightly mocking tone, and picked up her case before skirting around her and marching upstairs. Once she’d made it to the top, she turned and looked down over the wooden bannister, watching as her mother slipped through the open doorway of a sitting room and through to the adjoining kitchen, Athena following after her, unaware of the tension between mother and daughter.

     

                Turning to look down the long hallway stretching out before her, Lena suppressed a shiver at the foreboding feeling it brought. At the far end was a tall window that let in a small bit of light, and sconces lined the walls, emitting a deep yellow glow, but for all its width and height, it felt suffocatingly narrow as she passed by closed doorways and framed paintings and mirrors, vases and consoles and little nooks with a display cabinet or a narrow bench.  

     

                Her bedroom was on the third floor, at the far end, looking north over the neat flower beds and a small stone pavilion, and she took what used to be an old servant’s stairwell up to that floor, coming out three doors down from the closed wooden door of the room she’d grown up in. She stood outside for a full minute before reaching out to grasp the doorknob and turn it. She let the door swing inwards on old hinges as a wave of nostalgia hit her.

     

                It was almost exactly the same as she’d left it when she’d packed her things and vowed to never return, angry and hurt and resolved to carve her own path through the world. If not for the new bedspread on the old mahogany bed and the lack of clutter she’d left behind to been thrown in the trash - scratched CD’s and graded college essays and science fair ribbons and plastic awards - she would have sworn no one had stepped foot in there since she’d left. It was bare of any personal effects but the air smelled of furniture polish and wasn’t stale or dusty and she looked around as if she’d been transported back in time.

     

                The huge bed dominated the room, and there, below the window on the far wall was the desk where Lena had spent hours solving math equations and writing essays and pulling apart machines to put them back together. The bookshelves lining the opposite wall were empty; most of them in her apartment in Metropolis, and a few now rehomed in National City. She walked inside and set her case down on the bench at the end of her bed and sank down next to it, looking around as she felt the ghost of her memories brush against the back of her mind.

     

                Lingering for a few minutes, wishing she could hide up there as she had in her younger days, Lena finally climbed back to her feet and walked back downstairs to join her mother in the kitchen. The smell of fresh coffee hit her first and then the low, murmuring voice of her mother, and Lena walked into the open space to witness Athena being scratched beneath the chin by a stooped over Lillian, who straightened at her daughter’s arrival. Swallowing thickly, Lena looked away, unable to reconcile this version of Lillian with the distant mother from her childhood.

     

                Walking over to the counter and taking the cup of coffee she assumed was hers, Lena leaned back against the cupboards and looked down, softly tapping a finger against the cup as she lounged with her legs crossed at the ankle. She didn’t even know what to say , but the weight of their silence was oppressive, making the hum of the refrigerator that much louder. Awkwardly clearing her throat, Lillian took a sip of coffee and politely raised her eyebrows.

     

                “What’s her name?”

     

                “Athena.”

     

                “Ah. You were always fascinated by the Greek stories.”

     

                “I didn’t pick it,” Lena murmured, “I adopted her.”

     

                Nodding, Lillian pulled out one of the stools at the island counters and took a seat, watching Lena closely with her piercing stare as she cupped her coffee between her hands. Lena could feel her watching her but didn’t look up as she stared down at the slight scuff on the toe of one of her loafers. 

     

                “So … you threw all my stuff out?” Lena eventually ground out.

     

                “Did you want me to?”

     

                Shrugging indifferently, Lena took a sip of her drink, dark and bitter and hot as she felt it warm the cold, hollow part of her stomach that was churning with nerves. “It wasn’t anything I wanted to keep.”

     

                Lillian nodded and bit the inside of her mouth as she studied her daughter’s blank face. Eventually, she let out a soft sigh and cleared her throat. “It’s all in the attic; I didn’t throw it away.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “I thought … maybe you might want it back one day.”

     

                “Feeling sentimental, were you?” Lena snorted.

     

                With a rueful smile and an arched eyebrow, Lillian raised one shoulder in a half-hearted shrug. “On occasion. Sometimes I would go and sit in the armchair next to your bookshelves. For a while, the room still smelt like you; I could almost pretend that you were still away at school.”

     

                “Did you do the same for Lex?” Lena asked, gently pressing on a sore point. She knew she was treading into dangerous territory by poking at her mother’s weakness, at the sore wound of grief that Lillian harboured, but she’d never really had anyone to talk to about him.

     

                Brushing away an errant strand of hair, Lillian swallowed thickly, her throat bobbing as faint amusement graced her sharp features, although Lena wasn’t mistaken into thinking there was any warmth behind the expression. She looked pissed off, annoyed , and was trying to mask it before this shambled attempt at them pretending they were family fell apart before it could even take off.

     

                “Yes,” she eventually replied, clipped and aggravated.

     

                “Sorry,” Lena bluntly replied, “I know he was your favourite. Still doesn’t change anything, though.”

     

                “You think I don’t know that?” Lillian sharply asked, a glint in her eyes as she set her coffee down a little heavy-handedly, sloshing a little on the polished countertop. “It’s every mother’s nightmare to lose their child, and I couldn’t even grieve for mine without feeling … guilty.”

     

                “I know.”

     

                “Do you?” Lillian snorted, rolling her eyes disdainfully. “You didn’t even come to the funeral.”

     

                Setting her coffee down on the worktop she leaned against, Lena folded her arms across her chest and scowled. “And why would I have? Did you honestly expect me to be there? The pariah that you didn’t even want, front and centre for the funeral of the world’s most hated man?”

     

                “He was your brother. ”

     

                “Well, he was a shit one,” Lena snapped, “he only liked me for what I did for him; you know that. That’s more than I can say for you, though, isn’t it?”

     

                Sighing, Lillian hunched over the counter and rubbed at her temples, a sort of weariness to her posture as she closed her eyes. Regret flashed through Lena quickly but she bit back an apology and sipped her coffee, waiting for that feeling of vindication to come sweeping through when Lillian shot back a stinging retort.

     

                “I’d rather not spend time dwelling on the past, thank you,” she replied, firmly but with a sharp edge. “If you- if you could just tell me how to fix it ...”

     

                “What do you want me to say?” Lena asked, her words filled with resignation as her shoulders slumped and she gave her a mother an aching look of defeat. 

     

                “What do you want from me?”

     

                “Absolutely nothing,” Lena said with a bittersweet smile, tight and cold and making her heart twinge. “I didn’t come here for anything, okay?”

     

                “So, what? That’s it, then? There’s nothing I can do to make it right?”

     

                Heaving a sigh, Lena ran a hand over her face, feeling out of sorts from the flight and off-kilter from being back in the house. She groaned softly and shook her head before draining the rest of her coffee and firmly setting the cup back down, pushing off the counter and standing boldly in the middle of the kitchen as she gave Lillian a flat look.

     

                “I don’t know what you expect me to say. I wanted a mother - I can admit that much. I wanted a mom who would hold me when I cried and look after me when I was sick, watch movies and order Chinese food and- and show up . You never showed up for me. You shipped me off to boarding school the minute you could, and then to college when I should’ve been starting high school. You just- you took away any sort of normal life I could’ve had so … I don’t know what you can do to make that right. Anything I have to say about this family … it’s well deserved.”

     

                Looking pale and ashamed, Lillian opened and closed her mouth, her knuckles whitening as she clenched her bony hands into fists. “I’m trying my best. I’m trying.”

     

                “Yeah, well, you don’t have to, mom,” Lena replied, an agonised look on her face as she bared her teeth in an uncomfortable smile, shrugging one shoulder. “It’s just … it’s the way it is and that’s fine .”

     

                “Then why’d you come here?” Lillian challenged her, climbing off her stool and standing tall and imposing as she demanded an answer.

     

                Lips twitching ruefully as they turned down at the corners, Lena couldn’t meet her eyes. “I just- I don’t want to be that person who blames everything on what happened to them instead of just … trying to get better.”

     

                With a loud scoff, Lillian’s lips curled into a smile. “Did the psychologist tell you that?”

     

                “Kelly.”

     

                “I remember her name,” Lillian curtly replied, “but these people don’t know you, Lena. They don’t know what it was like for us, the way it was here. I’m glad that you’re happy with your new life, but I’m not happy with mine; I wish you could see that I really do want to try and get better too, instead of blaming it all on your father.”

     

                Blinking back the burning feeling behind her eyes, Lena nodded, her mouth dry, and found herself unable to form a reply as her throat tightened. Without another word, she made for the back door, unlocking it and stepping out onto the patio, holding the door open just long enough for Athena to eagerly bolt outside after her. It was too cold for her to be outside in her thin sweater but Lena didn’t have it in her to bend her pride and go back inside for a coat, and resolved to hug her arms to herself and hunch her shoulders against the chill air as she walked out onto the lawn.

     

                The grass was short and spiky and the covered outdoor furniture gave way to two tiers of grass with wide limestone steps cutting down through them, old statues posed amidst square plots of land with low hedges fencing them in. She walked down the two short staircases, looking out over the low hedge maze that stretched out at the foot of the steps, old willows and oaks and maples crowding around the edges of the sprawling garden, and took in the still fountain in the middle of it all, ten feet wide and collecting dried leaves as late-blooming flowers providing started to wilt in the neat, geometric flower beds radiating outwards from it. 

     

                Walking along the gravel path winding through the maze, Lena scowled and blinked furiously, bristling with frustration and anger - mostly at herself - as she let her feet take her along the familiar route through the chest-high hedgerows. Storming out into the open centre, she walked loops around the amaranthus and dahlias, verbena and chrysanthemums, ignoring the autumn beauty of the place as she sought solace in the quietness of the outdoors. Sitting on the edge of the wall encircling the fountain, she plucked an aster and angrily plucked at the lavender petals, tossing them into the murky green waters as she brooded. 

     

                Athena sniffed around and tried biting the heads off a few roses and Lena watched her with a grim look on her face, the tension slowly receding as the cold seeped into her and she got lost in the fresh smell of the air, free from exhaust fumes and garbage and greasy takeout stores. There was the faint smell on the wind that made her suspect that it was going to rain soon, and she lingered outside until it started spitting, before hurriedly retracing her way back through the maze as the drops became fatter as they splattered onto her shirt.

     

                Letting her back in through the kitchen, she wiped her feet on the bristly mat outside and found the open space empty, their coffee cups still sitting on the counters, abandoned. Wariness crept up on Lena and she shook it off as she slipped silently through the house, damp and cold, and made her way all the way up to her bedroom, where she gently closed the door behind herself and sank down onto the high bed while Athens sprawled on the rug. If she’d thought her house was too quiet, it was nothing compared to the deafening silence of the mansion.

     

                It was still relatively early in the day, although the time difference put her forward a few hours, and it was only just hitting noon when she fished out her phone and called Kara. Stretching out on the fresh sheets, the lemony smell of detergent wafting around her, she waited expectantly for the video to connect and smiled tiredly as Kara’s face eventually appeared. The tension suddenly fled her body, and in the draughty room at the top of the house, Lena finally felt some semblance of happiness and peace.

     

                “Hi,” she murmured, her eyes scouring Kara’s appearance for any signs of injuries, something that had become a habit after the bombing.

     

                “Hey, yourself. You’re there then?”

     

                Lena gave her a tight smile and made a sound of agreement, rubbing at her forehead as her chest tightened. Sensing her discontentment, Kara cocked her head at the side and gave her a sympathetic look, aching and tender.

     

                “Is it that bad? Being back home?”

     

                “It’s … difficult,” Lena managed to grind out, her throat constricting as she looked around the bare room, sadness welling up inside her. “Things are mostly the same, it’s just- it’s odd . I don’t like it here. And my mom … God, I can feel myself turning back into a sulky teenager every time we speak. I think … it was a bad idea.”

     

                “You can leave.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena hummed faintly, picking at a loose thread on the seam of her jeans as she brooded. “I know. I figured I should probably at least give it the day.”

     

                “I hate the thought of you being someplace you tried so hard to get away from,” Kara murmured, a grimace thinning her lips.

     

                “It wasn’t all bad. At least my mom’s trying now; that’s new. And my dad’s dead so … no shouting. It just- it feels … empty. I can’t stand the quiet anymore. I wish you were here with me.”

     

                “Me too. Maybe … if things go well and you want to go back, you could take me there one day.”

     

                Lena’s lips twitched with a fleeting smile and she stared at Kara with warm adoration on her face. “Mm, maybe.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara gave her a sheepish smile, full of barely concealed excitement. “Can I see it?”

     

                Eyebrows rising slightly, Lena let out a snort of laughter. “The house? Sure, why?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara grinned impishly. “I just want to see where you grew up. I don’t know what I’m supposed to be picturing.”

     

                Pushing herself up, bed springs groaning beneath her weight, Lena climbed to her feet. “Sure. Hold on. This- this is my room. Well, it was - it doesn’t really have anything in it anymore. Except the furniture. See?”

     

                Lena turned the camera around and panned the room, showing the old grandeur of the solid furniture and decor. Slipping out into the hallway, Lena skipped over the paintings and opened a few doors to show her the interior - the bathroom next door, the library stocked with old leather volumes, the parlour room with its colossal pool table and Chesterfield sofa - slinking from room to room as Kara commented on the extravagance of it all. That part was lost on Lena as her mood soured with the rooms she passed through - here, where her father had struck her brother one Christmas, there where her brother had smashed a vase and blamed Lena for it, there where she’d walked through the mudroom in her riding gear in tears from a hard kick from her pony, greeted by Lillian’s cool indifference.

     

                She opened the door to the plush office that had been her father’s, mid-laughter at something Kara had said, before she abruptly stopped in the doorway and sobered up at the sight of Lillian sitting behind the desk, looking at her over the top of the laptop she was typing away on. Her amusement evaporated as if she’d been doused in cold water and Lena cleared her throat awkwardly as she hovered in the doorway, one hand still on the doorknob as the other that held the phone dipped slightly. 

                

                “Oh,” Lena muttered, “sorry, I was just giving Kara a tour. I didn’t realise you- I thought this was still empty.”

     

                “It’s my office now,” Lillian informed her.

     

                “Right. Well … I’ll leave you to it.”

     

                Beckoning her in as she glanced back at her screen, Lillian cleared her throat and shifted in her seat. “You can show her around. I’m just going over an article.”

     

                “Right. Um …”

     

                “Hi, Mrs Luthor,” Kara called out, trying to diffuse the tension, for Lena’s sake.

     

                Gratitude washed over Lena and she glanced down at the screen, staring at Kara’s face as her cheery tone made a smile grace the corners of Lena’s mouth. Lillian blinked in surprise as she looked up, a pucker between her eyebrows before she leaned back in the tall leather chair and tilted her head slightly to the side, amusement curling her lips.

     

                “Hi, Kara. I hope you’re doing well over there.”

     

                “All good on this front! You have a beautiful home.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Lena quickly panned the camera around, stifling the annoyance that flared to life inside her, still rooted to the spot in the doorway, before she cleared her throat. “I’ll, uh, leave you to it then.”

     

                Lillian nodded absent-mindedly and Lena quickly stepped back out into the hallway, jerking the door shut and pausing for a moment before she shook her head. Once they were a few doors down, Kara smiled slightly on the screen.

     

                “She seems happier than last time.”

     

                “Oh, yeah?” Lena snorted. “I don’t think she’s the type of person to be happy.”

     

                “Maybe she likes that you’re staying with her.”

     

                “Maybe she does,” Lena reluctantly agreed, passing through the kitchen with a quick glance around the place before she stepped outside into the fine drizzle. Walking down the two flights of steps, she turned and squinted up at the house through the misting rain and tried to fit it all into the frame as Kara let out a crow of shock.

     

                “Oh my God! That’s not a house; that’s a mansion.”

     

                “Mm, it’s … a bit big,” Lena hedged as her forehead creased slightly.

     

                “And was that a maze? Who has an actual maze in their garden?”

     

                Laughing, Lena did a quick three-sixty and then started back up the steps as the cold assaulted her, stepping back into the kitchen and holing herself up in a small sitting room that barely fit an armchair, a large, vacant fireplace and a cabinet holding various expensive vases and figurines from around the world. It was cold in there, but Lena liked that sitting room as it overlooked the front of the house and the lawns that gave way to trees, and curled up in an armchair for warmth as she listened to Kara talk to her about her day.

     

                She evaded her mother during lunch and managed to get away with hiding herself upstairs to work on her speech for the launch through the rest of the afternoon before she found herself sitting across from her mother at the dinner table, making stilted small talk over a dinner prepared by Lillian’s chef. It was fine, for the most part, with one of Lena’s favourite dinners, as if Lillian was making a point that she did remember some things about her daughter, even if they were from a decade ago, and aside from a few awkward pauses, dinner passed by without event.

     

                After dinner, she considered sneaking away upstairs but there was still most of a bottle of wine to finish and she trailed her mother into the main living room and sipped at the shiraz as she curled up on a sofa and sat through a medical documentary on an LA emergency room. Lillian ran through the procedures aloud, pointing out mistakes and planning treatments before the doctors could get to it, and Lena supposed it was her attempt at sharing an interest with her daughter, but it just made the wine taste sour to Lena; there had been a point in time where Lillian had wanted her to be a surgeon too. 

     

                When it finished, Lena made a quick escape and changed into one of her old MIT shirts and a pair of Kara’s pilled grey sweatpants, pooling around her ankles, and climbed under the covers. She wasn’t sure if she felt better or worse for being back home, because while it brought back the childhood she would’ve rather left buried and untouched, it took her mind off missing Kara. In a way, the emptiness of her room as she lay in the bed felt so different to her modest but luxurious bedroom back home in National City that she felt even further away from Kara; there was nothing of her there in Metropolis.

     

                In the end, it always came back to Kara. Lena would miss her every moment she was away, and there was nothing she could do to stop it. She thought of her in every reminder of her, and thought of her in the absences too, clinging to the thought that she would come back and then there would be no without anymore.

     

                Her sleep was restless that night, barely a few hours snagged before dawn broke, pale and cold across the estate. Still in her pyjamas, her hair rumpled and her face indented with the seams of the pillows as she lay there, willing sleep to take her, Lena padded downstairs, the tiled floor freezing underfoot as she stepped into the kitchen, stifling a yawn.

     

                “What on God’s earth are you wearing?” Lillian drawled, the newspaper she held sagging in half as she arched an eyebrow.

     

                “They’re called pyjamas,” Lena snidely replied, tugging at the hem of her college t-shirt a little self-consciously. It was a little short for her now, considering it had been worn by her as a teenager who still had a couple of inches of growth left in her. 

     

                “You look like you’re homeless.”

     

                “Not everyone sleeps in Carine Gildon pyjamas, you know,” Lena snorted, making for the coffee machine and setting a fresh cup beneath the filter. 

     

                “Well, you used to. And you never complained about it, either.”

     

                 Lena shrugged and kept the real reason she wore the faded sweatpants to herself, despite the fact that her silk or cashmere loungewear and pyjamas would’ve been more comfortable. It was a simple answer that never would have crossed Lillian’s mind; the pants were Kara’s and she liked the way they felt, worn thin from years of use.

     

                Taking her coffee over to the table set before the wide windows overlooking the garden, Lena dragged a chair out and Lillian clicked her tongue at the grating sound before tossing the newspaper down in front of her and rolling a pen across the tabletop. Lena quickly skimmed over the news articles and the numbers in the business section before she picked up the pen and silently started filling out the crossword puzzle.  

     

                “I wondered if you still did that,” Lillian mused, nodding her head to the puzzle as Lena glanced up.

     

                Shrugging, Lena was silent as she made her way through it, the chef wandering in and quietly cooking breakfast for them as she filled out the squares with ease. At a question that stumped her, Lena hesitated. “What’s the town at the eighth mile of the Boston Marathon?”

     

                “Hm? Oh, it’s Natick.”

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                “What time would you like to go into the office?” Lillian asked as Lena filled in the supplied answer.

     

                “I don’t know. Around ten, I guess.”

     

                “Maybe we could have lunch together afterwards.”

                

                The pen slowed in its movements and Lena only paused for a brief second before ducking her head in agreement. “Sure.”

     

                Satisfied, Lillian ate her eggs benedict at perfect ease with the silence as Lena picked at her own plate and finished off the crossword. After, she went upstairs to shower and change, spending a good hour in front of the mirror as she scrutinised herself and hated every second of it, before making her way downstairs. Lillian drove them in her sleek Jaguar and Lena spent the ride into the city staring out the window, watching the tall buildings materialise out of a haze of fog.

     

                Walking through the front doors of the Metropolis office, the duo monopolised the attention of the employees, surprise and interest flashing across faces as they made straight for the elevator bank. Lena hadn’t been back there since moving the L-Corp headquarters to National City as part of the rebranding, so it was a rare sight to see more than one Luthor in the building, let alone two. Still, it was all very familiar to Lena and she pushed the button to take them upstairs to the conference rooms where she’d used to command the presence of everyone at various meetings, finding everyone already waiting for her, despite them being ten minutes early.

     

                Shaking hands and taking seats, a bottle of Perrier set before her, she sat beside Lillian and the two of them watched the presentation on the wide screen with the same critical stare. Their bearings were similar, despite the rift between them, and Lena could feel the desperation of her employees in the air as they waited for her opinion as she jotted down notes and critiques. 

     

                She was impressed with the presentation, a little sceptical about the few bugs they had with the computer software, but gave her approval for the release of Friday on the expectation that they would be working around the clock to iron out as many kinks over the next thirty hours. Thanking everyone as they left, she lingered in the conference room with her mother as she navigated the new operating system on one of the company laptops, pleased with herself.

     

                “I’m not so sure I think it’s ready,” Lillian slowly said after a few minutes, sitting on the edge of the long conference table as Lena clicked through a few apps and folders.

     

                Stiffening, Lena glanced up at her as a muscle twitched in her jaw. “It’s fine.”

     

                “Yes, it’s fine, but it’s not great, and you always strive for the best; it’s how you were raised. The bugs they mentioned … they’re not the best.”

     

                “They’re fixing them. It runs well enough for a launch. The best way to find bugs is to let more people use it and complain about it until we figure out a patch.”

                

                Silent for a long minute, the air between them charged with the tension, Lillian straightened up and smoothed a hand over her dress, glancing down at her daughter with a disgruntled look on her face. “If you’re not going to listen to my advice, then why am I here?”

     

                Sighing, Lena leaned back in her seat and pinched the bridge of her nose as she sank down and angled herself towards her mother. “I was trying to be nice. ”

     

                “Nice?” Lillian echoed, letting out a sharp laugh.

     

                “It’s my company now. I run it. I decide when our products will be released.”

     

                Her tone left no room for argument and Lillian scoffed quietly, shaking her head as cool amusement graced her face. “So, you’re just going to ignore my opinion?”

     

                “It wouldn’t be the first time, would it?”

     

                “Well … it’s obvious you’re just going to do what you want, like always.”

     

                “What do you mean ‘like always’?” Lena defensively asked, her expression darkening as she looked up at Lillian with an expectant look on her stubborn face.

     

                Her mother’s face tightened, her usual icy demeanour taking over as she let out a cold laugh. “You’ve never listened to a single thing I’ve told you in your life,” Lillian bitterly replied, her tone caustic and haughty as she drew herself up. “Every single time I’ve ever tried to help you, you’ve just … pushed me away. You get angry, you get defensive. You act like a child.”

     

                “You never say anything to just help. You’ve never once been supportive of me, never once allowed me to make my own decision. If I pushed back the release you would have said I was being too cautious or- or too much of a perfectionist. I just can’t win with you!”

     

                Sighing melodramatically, Lillian rolled her eyes and gave her an exasperated look as she folded her arms over her chest. Her perfume was light and sweet and Lena resented the familiarity of it in that moment, the cloying smell making her seethe as she sat rigidly in her seat, scowling up at Lillian with bright eyes. 

     

                “That’s your problem; you always take everything so personally,” Lillian chided her, her mouth turning down at the corners. “This isn’t personal, Lena. It’s business . If you can’t handle someone disagreeing with you, maybe you’re too young to be the CEO of the company.”

     

                Abruptly shooting to her feet, Lena’s face paled as she squared her shoulders and curled her hands into fists, bristling with anger. “I can handle a lot of things, mom, but being around you isn’t one of them. I don’t need you to tell me how to handle running a company; you couldn’t even handle raising two kids.”

     

                Snatching up her bag, Lena streaked for the door, two high spots of colour on her cheeks as she stormed out, ignoring the sound of her name being called behind her as the door softly hissed shut and sealed the sound inside. She brusquely took her coat from the closet and rode the elevator down to the lobby, spilling out into the cool August day and making a left.

     

                Cabs passed by, but Lena walked, feeling the cool wind soothe her flushed cheeks as she buried her hands in her pockets and walked fast, burning off some steam as she left her mother behind. She walked block after block, until the heels made her feet ache, and stopped for a coffee, the paper cup scalding in her cold hand as she sipped at it and walked past old familiar haunts, reminiscing over lonely days and wishing for the company of her friends in National City.

     

                Lilacs shed as she walked the bridge that spanned the harbour, grey choppy water churning below her as she stopped halfway and leaned against the tarnished railing as cars sped past behind her with freezing gusts of wind. Her phone buzzed twice and she turned it off, looking out at the dreary city, drab and miserable and bursting with people who didn’t know the warmth that still drenched the streets back west. 

     

                Eventually, she grew too cold to linger outside any longer, listening to the low, endless blaring of ship horns as she watched them navigate the harbour, and she flagged down an empty cab and gave them the address for home. A part of her was vindictive enough to consider going to her apartment at the top of one of the endless skyscrapers, but she’d left Athena at the estate and knew her mother would swoop in on her at some point with her clinically cold dismissals and contemptuous comments that always managed to touch on Lena’s sensitive spots.

     

                The cab dropped her off outside the gate and Lena was left to trudge the long gravel driveway up to the house alone, shedding her heels and walking on the damp grass to spare her feet as she moved through the shaded cover of the trees. The front door was unlocked when she reached it after walking up the curved staircase, and she wiped her wet feet on the bristled mat and eased it shut. 

     

                Sneaking upstairs, she changed into casual clothes and tied her hair up before washing her face of the makeup and sitting cross-legged in the middle of her bed, staring down at the picture of Kara she kept in her locket. Lena missed her more than usual at that moment, self-pitying sorrow washing over her as she sat slumped and defeated.

     

                An hour later, a gentle knock sounded on the door, and although Lena didn’t reply, it still creaked open. Lillian was cast in shadow as she lingered out in the hallway, a wary look on her face as she hovered uncertainly.

     

                “I thought you’d be gone by now.”

     

                “I considered it,” Lena admitted.

     

                Nodding, Lillian rubbed at her arms, the strain between them uncomfortable as it dragged on. Eventually, Lena let out a weary sigh and raised her eyebrows, putting an end to the discomfort.

     

                “So … is there a reason why you’re here?”

     

                “I wanted to apologise,” Lillian slowly said.

     

                Waiting for a moment, Lena gestured vaguely, “was that the apology?”

     

                Fixing her with a withering look, Lillian stiffly replied, “no. I’m sorry.”

     

                Nodding, Lena chewed on the inside of her lip for a moment, head bowed and shoulders taut beneath the sweatshirt, before she managed to swallow her pride. “I’m sorry too. I was acting childish; you just- you bring it out in me. I was hoping that … maybe this time you would’ve been on my side.”

     

                “I am on your side, Lena,” Lillian frustratedly replied, crossing the boundary of the room as she crossed the space in long strides, sitting on the end of the mattress as a vexed crease formed between her eyebrows. “I wish you would believe that. Even when it’s not what you want to hear, it’s in your best interest.”

     

                “But it’s not what I think is the best decision,” Lena quietly argued. 

     

                “Well, then just ignore my input like you always do!” Lillian exasperatedly told her, throwing her hands up in defeat.

     

                “There you go again with the always. It’s always my fault, right?”

     

                Sighing heavily, Lillian fixed her with a disapproving stare that made Lena wilt slightly. “Don’t put words into my mouth. I’m not one to mince words; if that’s what I meant, I’d say it. You’re just … always pushing me away. It feels like you don’t even want to try.”

     

                “Well, maybe I don’t,” Lena snarkily retorted, sounding petulant and juvenile as she hugged her knees to her chest.

     

                Letting out a defeated sigh, shoulders drooping, Lillian gestured towards the door. “Then go. I don’t want to argue with you, I just want you to be safe and happy. I watched you go to National City to get away from me and this place and the bad memories in it. I know it’s hard for you to be here, so if being in National City is what makes you happy then go . Please. You’re the most important thing in my life now, and if being as far away from me as you can get is what makes things easier for you, then do it.”

     

                Lillian let out a short laugh, flat and a little wounded, and Lena’s eyebrows drew together in a clouded furrow as she took in the weary blankness of her mother’s face. “You would really let me go? That’s that? No more trying to contact me or prying?”

     

                Shrugging slightly, Lillian’s mouth thinned with displeasure. “If that’s what you want.”

     

                “What I want … is to not feel like a huge disappointment to you, to not feel second best. I know I’m making it harder for both of us, but … I am trying too. I promise you that. I just- I can’t get past all the times you made me feel like I was failing at everything.”

     

                Tears stung her eyes and Lena quickly turned her head, resting her cheek on her arms as she stared at the nightstand and felt Lillian studying her. Embarrassment tinged her face pink as she swallowed around the hard lump in her throat, feeling stupid for getting upset over old wounds she’d resolved to not let bother her anymore as she sealed them shut deep inside her heart. It was easier said than done though, and she found those memories laid bare to her now.

     

                “I never meant for you to feel that way,” Lillian regretfully replied. “I told you why, and I know that’s not a good enough excuse for pushing you aside. I’m sorry for that. I’ll never forgive myself for letting him come between us.”

     

                “I just want my mom,” Lena said in a small voice.

     

                She sounded like a child and Lillian’s aloof demeanour fell away as she let out a soft sigh. Hesitating for a moment, she shifted across the mattress, closing the gap between them, and wrapped an arm around Lena’s shoulders, trying to draw her into a hug. Lena resisted for a moment, stiffening at the gesture, but let her mother hug her all the same, for the first time in well over a decade. After a moment, she unfroze and allowed herself to sink into the circle of Lillian’s embrace, her head resting on her shoulder for a brief moment. It wasn’t long, and was surely uncomfortable for them both, and when Lillian withdrew her arm, Lena stared down at her lap, her hair falling around her face in a dark curtain as she fiddled with her fingers.

     

                “I truly am sorry for the way things worked out. If I could do it all over, I’d make different choices,” Lillian solemnly murmured as she brushed Lena’s hair out of her face and ducked her head slightly to look at her, insistently.

     

                “I know,” Lena murmured, tears stinging her eyes. “I’m sorry too.”

     

                She lingered for a moment longer before letting out a soft sigh and pushing herself to her feet. At the door, she paused and glanced back over at Lena, her face softening minutely, unseen by her daughter, who was trying her hardest to avoid looking in her general direction.

     

                “I’ll be downstairs if you need anything.”

     

                No sooner had Lillian left did her phone start ringing. Staring down at Kara’s name on the screen, Lena frowned as it connected as a phone call and pressed it to her ear. 

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “Hi! Sorry, I can’t video call you, I accidentally dropped my tablet and it shattered the screen.”

     

                Lena smiled faintly at the irritable sigh that Kara let out, the wheedling disappointment in her voice banishing Lena’s frustration and bitterness as a warmth took root in her chest.

     

                “Ah, I was wondering about that. I’ll have a new one sent to you immediately; I can’t not see your face, can I?”

     

                “Have I ever told you you’re the best? Because you are,” Kara said with a small laugh, slightly sheepish at having to let Lena waste money on a new tablet for her. She swallowed her pride though, because they couldn’t spend months not seeing each other’s faces.

     

                “Once or twice,” Lena replied, her voice low and warm, “but I love to hear you say it.”

     

                Stretching out on her bed, Lena pulled her locket out from beneath her shirt and opened it to reveal the tiny picture of Kara. Starting down at it, she smiled softly and let out a small sigh. “I wish I could see your face though.”

     

                “Me too. But how’s your day?”

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena closed her eyes and forced herself to relax, sinking into the mattress as her body went limp with exhaustion. She ran a hand over her face and let out a heavy sigh.

     

                “I went to the office with my mom earlier, just to double-check the new software. You know how I like to approve it all myself, in person. And … that was a bit of a disaster. My mom, not the software. I think it’s ready to be launched.”

     

                “And … she doesn’t?”

     

                “No,” Lena moodily muttered, “we had another argument over it, but it’s fine though. We sort of … patched things up. She hugged me, it was really weird, actually.”

     

                “She hugged you?”

     

                “Mm. First time in at least ten years, I think,” Lena said with a frown as her mouth turned down at the corners.

     

                It wasn’t just Lillian; her family were just never big on affection. It was all of them. Lena was as likely to hug her mom as Lillian was to hug her , and as she’d grown, she’d only become further closed off to such displays. From the age of ten, Lena didn’t think she’d so much as gotten a proud pat on the shoulder for anything, or a genuine smile. On the rare occasion that affection and praise was poured onto one of her children, it was always onto Lex.

     

                “Yikes. How did that go? I know how you are with people touching you.”

     

                “I mean … I sort of hugged her back. It was just for a second, which is still kind of a big thing for us ... I don’t know. Arguing aside, we’re kind of getting our footing. But, it has mostly been arguing, so that’s not saying much. It just feels good to be honest instead of having to bottle it up. Still, what I wouldn’t do for a hug from you right now.”

     

                She let out a wispy sigh, full of longing, and listened to Kara’s sad huff of laughter on the other end. “Anything. I’m not sure about you, but I’d give anything.”

     

                “Are you okay?” Lena murmured, concern jolting her stomach at the strained sound of Kara’s wobbly voice.

     

                “Yeah, I’m fine. I just- I miss you more today. Like more than usual , which is saying a lot. I-”

     

                Lena sat up, cross-legged in the middle of the bed as she cupped the back of her neck and swallowed around the lump that formed in her throat. “What’s wrong?”

     

                “Sorry. I just- I’m tired. I’m sick of waking up alone. Sometimes, I still wake up and reach for you before I remember I’m all the way here on this shitty cot. I miss falling asleep next to you and how you grind your teeth in your sleep. Did I ever tell you that you do that? I don’t think I did, and I don’t know if you even know that you do it, but you do and I love it. I just miss you.”

     

                “I miss you too,” Lena murmured, tears spilling down her cheeks as she quickly wiped them away with the cuff of her shirt, hearing the thickness in Kara’s voice that told her that she was crying too. 

     

                “I’m sorry. I don’t mean to make you cry, I just-”

     

                “Sh, it’s okay. It’s been nearly six weeks now; we’ve made it this far. I promise I’ll … eat peanut butter for you when you’re back, and I’ll complain about how you leave your shit everywhere and how insufferably hot National City is and I’ll … nag you for all the sugar you eat. I’ll do whatever you want me to. Ask for it and it’s yours.”

     

                Kara choked on a laugh and it made Lena’s heart swell slightly with gratitude. “Anything? I just want you.”

     

                “You already have me. Until you’re sick of me.”

     

                “I’ll never get sick of you. Not now, and not in a million years. Nothing could ever change that.”

     

                “Of course not,” Lena murmured in agreement. 

     

                Their conversation turned to light teasing and weak attempts at jokes to make each other laugh, and Lena stayed on the line for longer than she should have, knowing that Kara needed her that night. She wouldn’t let her go to bed upset, even if it meant Kara would be exhausted the next day. Instead, they talked about their days and the photos Kara took and what the weather was like and whether they should take a vacation to Bora Bora when Kara was home, painting a nice picture of the future that Lena promised to give her.

     

                When she finally made Kara hang up, it was with the knowledge that she was at least a little less upset, and with the promise that she’d stay safe and that she loved her, Kara hung up the phone. Lena sagged with the miserable feeling that washed over her as she finally allowed herself to stop putting on that mask for Kara’s sake and she padded downstairs for water and some Aspirin for the headache forming at her temples.

     

                As she started back up the left wing of the double staircase, Lillian materialised at the top and her eyes widened a fraction at Lena’s slightly puffy and bloodshot eyes. She hesitated as they closed the gap between them, Lena’s shoulders hunched as she ducked her head.

     

                “Is- is everything okay?” Lillian haltingly asked.

     

                “Fine.”

     

                She brushed past her mother without further explanation but slowed at the gentle touch of Lillian’s hand on her shoulder. It made her tense, her mother’s touch cool and uneasy. Lena didn’t turn around, and Lillian said nothing else, dropping her hand a moment later and letting Lena continue to plod upstairs.

     

                Stopping in a bathroom on the second floor, she splashed cold water on her face and then made for the library to pick out a book to distract her. She never made it to the library though, her eyes catching on her brother’s door and drawing her over to it. After a slight hesitation, Lena turned the handle and eased it open.

     

                It was exactly as she remembered it. He’d always been messy, his room cluttered with books and papers and obscure models for designs that he always gave up on before he finished, and as she looked around the room, it felt like stepping back in time. Where Lena’s room had been cleared out, Lex’s still lingered in the disarray it had always languished in, stacks of long abandoned papers strewn across the wide oak desk, blueprints taped over the dark panelled walls and wires, screws and tools left on the nightstand, the floor and the chest of drawers amidst polished dress shoes and creased shirts and a half-filled carafes of liquor. Unlike Lena’s room when she’d left, Lex had intended to come back. Until he hadn’t.

     

                Crossing the room, Lena sank down onto the bed, a puff of dust rising from the rumpled sheets. She smiled sadly as she saw the white knight chess piece on his nightstand and reached out to pick it up. She had the family set at her house now, and this piece was from a different set, but it still brought back fond memories of thrashing her brother at the game. As she reminisced, with that strange heaviness of a guilt she barely even felt - and perhaps that was why she felt it at all - a flicker of movement from the corner of her eye caught her attention. 

     

                Looking up, Lena saw Lillian standing in the doorway, holding a cup in her hand as she stared at the mess of the room. It was like she’d seen a ghost, as pale and stiff as she was, and Lena slowly set the knight piece back down on the nightstand, feeling as if she was trespassing somewhere she shouldn’t have been.

     

                “I haven’t been in here in years,” Lillian softly murmured, hesitating before crossing the threshold of the room. She sank down onto the dusty covers beside Lena, coughing slightly as she fanned the air before her face and held the cup out to the side. “I thought you might like some tea.”

       

                “Thank you,” Lena warily replied, reaching out to take the cup, leaching the warmth from the china as she breathed in the scent of Chamomile.

     

                Lillian nodded and they sat there in silence for a few minutes. Lena could almost still smell his cologne beneath the stale mustiness of the airy room, and she resisted the urge to sneeze as she shifted and let loose another cloud of dust, shafts of light through the uncovered windows highlighting the spiralling motes as they hung in the air.

     

                “You should think about getting rid of his things,” Lena eventually said before she climbed to her feet and turned to look down at her mother’s bowed figure.

     

                “I know,” Lillian quietly agreed.

     

                Escaping to the library after that, Lena dwelled there all afternoon, making a call to Sam and arranging for Jess to buy and send a new tablet to Kara before she spoke to Kelly at length and sipped her tea. She didn’t see her mother again until dinner and they tactfully steered clear of any talk of the launch tomorrow, although Lena suspected Lillian would have agreed with her this time, even if only to show that she could support her daughter’s decision.

     

                Afterwards, Lena joined her in the living room again, stretched out on the sofa with the book she’d plucked from the library. It was a Charles Dickens one she’d never gotten around to reading and it lulled her to sleep as the night dragged on, the TV droning in the background and the exhaustion of a long week and a boring book luring her into a light nap. She dreamt that a woman was stroking her hair and a heavy blanket covered her and woke to Lillian shaking her awake near midnight, telling her to go to bed. It wasn’t until she sat up and a blanket pooled around her waist that Lena realised through a fog of sleep that it had been Lillian, and she blinking owlishly, her face creased with sleep and confusion as she mumbled a goodnight and vanished upstairs to collapse into her own bed.

     

                The next day passed by quickly, Lena practicing her presentation to her reflection in the bathroom and then leaving early for the convention centre for the tech expo she was announcing the launch at. She lingered backstage in her own dressing room and was still as two women did her hair and makeup before changing into her stylish black ensemble in the garment bag and waiting for her turn.

     

                The spotlight on the stage was glaring and hot and she leisurely paced the stage, gesturing with her hand as she cast cursory glances at the teleprompter to stay on track. The dim audience listened to her list the new features, the prototypes for new models and the nuclear batteries to be implemented in future hardware, the long spiel about green energy being the future of L-Corp winding up the presentation as the screen behind her dimmed. 

     

                She made a polite stop by the cocktail party afterwards, fielding congratulations from familiar faces - Jack Spheer, Andrea Rojas - and likewise commending them on their own proposed ventures for their respective businesses. Lena didn’t linger long though and as she rode home in the back of the towncar with her mother, Lillian turned to her and gave her a thin smile.

     

                “You did very well tonight. You should be proud of yourself.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Pausing, Lillian pressed her lips together before gently clearing her throat. “And I’m proud of you too.”

     

                A wry smile twitched Lena’s lips and she nodded before staring out at the city that flashed past, glowing street lights and neon signs giving way to rolling suburbs and then then bigger estates and mansions set on plots of land. She felt a flicker of smugness inside her at the fact that it had gone well, although it wasn’t without her mother’s words getting to her, ensuring Lena came down hard on her coders to have the bugs worked out as quickly as possible before midnight, when it would go live.

     

                Still, she was satisfied and her mood was marginally warmer to Lillian as they stepped into the illuminated house and Lena kicked off her heels, ducking to coo over Athena as she welcomed them at the door. Clearing her throat, Lillian gave Lena an uneven smile, a hopeful look on her face as she raised her eyebrows slightly.

     

                “I was thinking that perhaps we could get breakfast before you leave tomorrow.”

     

                “Sure,” Lena agreed, a faint smile on her lips as she picked up her heels and made for the stairs.

     

                “Wait,” Lillian called out after her, and Lena turned around, arching an eyebrow expectedly. “I was- we should celebrate.”

     

                “Celebrate?” Lena snorted, with a dismissive laugh, “it was just a new operating system; it’s not that big of a deal.”

     

                Smile faltering slightly, Lillian’s expression became strained. “Well, I- I ordered us dinner. I thought that … well, it deserves some recognition. If not for the work, then just … to you.”

     

                Biting her red lip, Lena hesitated before relenting, softly sighing as she nodded. “Fine. Let me get out of this suit first.”

     

                She swept up two flights of stairs and changed into something more casual before jogging back down to find her mother in the living room, a spread of white takeout boxes on the coffee table and two champagne flutes beside it all. Lillian was working the cork out of a bottle of Dom Pérignon and Lena slowed as she walked in, confused.

     

                “I, uh … what’s with all the food?”

     

                “Chinese food. And you can pick the movie,” Lillian nervously replied.

     

                The breath caught in Lena’s throat and it took her a moment to reply, a painful twinge in her chest. “You don’t-”

     

                “No, I do ,” Lillian murmured, a firm note in her voice as she managed to pop the cork off, quickly filling the first flute before it spilled on the rug. “It’s time I made the effort to be the mother I should have been. So … pick a movie, Lena.”

     

                Feeling a little embarrassed at her outburst a few days beforehand, and that Lillian had taken it to heart well enough to give her what she’d vulnerably divulged, Lena sank down onto the sofa and picked up the remote, switching to Netflix and clearing her throat.

     

                “Have you seen Pride and Prejudice? It’s quite good.”

     

                “I haven’t.”

     

                Nodding, Lena found it and turned it on before accepting the flute that Lillian held out to her. They sat on opposite sofas with the coffee table full of food between them and Lena returned Lillian’s strained smile with a wan one.

     

                “To you, then,” Lillian said, raising her glass slightly in a toast.

     

                “Right,” Lena muttered, taking a sip and feeling oddly grateful for the expensive bottle Lillian had decided on, the faint taste of peach sweet on her tongue as her eyes drifted towards the screen. 

     

                Picking up a carton of lo mein, Lena dug in and let the notes of the piano soothe the anxious feeling in her chest as she ate with her mother and felt, perhaps for the first time, that things were normal between them. If not normal, as close as it could ever get between two people with so much difficult history. It should have been insurmountable, perhaps it would have been even a few months ago, but Lena felt like she could breathe a little easier for trying at least.

     

                Once she’d eaten her fill from half a dozen cartons, Lena sipped from her refilled glass and shifted slightly, turning her attention from the TV to her mother. “Thank you,” she murmured.

     

                Lillian nodded, her eyes still fixed to the screen, and Lena tried again as her stomach tied itself into knots. “Not just for this, I mean- well, the past couple of days … thanks for trying. I- it means a lot and I know … it’s not great, but I do appreciate it.”

     

                “I’m glad you do,” Lillian said with a small smile, surprise flashing in her eyes as she looked at her daughter.

     

                Lena shrugged self-consciously, trying to quell the mortifying feeling of revealing that she actually cared about how things were between them. Then again, if she hadn’t cared at all, she would never have found herself sitting there in that situation to begin with. It diffused some of the tension between them and they made occasional conversation as they watched the movie and sipped champagne, and Lena basked in the surprised feeling that she was having a real conversation with her mother and was enjoying it. Somewhere in the midst of the last three days, things had stopped feeling quite so strained and had mellowed out into something that was almost comfortable. 

     

                “So, what’s next for the company?” Lillian asked at one point.

     

                “I’ll be heading to Tokyo at the start of next year, hopefully with something to show for the nanotechnology of the nuclear batteries we’re developing. I think it could be useful in all parts of tech development, not just for batteries. You know, computer hardware, phones, cars, tablets, but also environmental sciences and how we manage water filtration and food resources. I think it would even progress medicine a lot too; I’ve been looking into biomedical equipment and how we could revolutionise it on a molecular level. It’s … ambitious. We’re already leading the race, and that’s potentially billions of dollars in revenue, but it’s all about innovation, and, with the wide scope … well, it’ll be hard.”

     

                “Well, you’d be hard-pressed to find someone more innovative than you. I don’t think I ever thanked you properly for getting the company back up on its feet; you did what I couldn’t and I’m grateful that you stepped up. I know it’s not what you envisioned for your own path.”

     

                Sighing heavily, Lena grimacned and drained her glass before setting it down. “He really fucked things up for us, didn’t he?”

     

                “I’m not sure if you’re talking about your father or your brother,” Lillian bitterly laughed, “I think it applies to both of them.”
