                With a snort of laughter, Lena gave her a rueful smile, “I guess so. At least the bar is pretty low for me though. Is that why you suggested to the board that I take over as CEO? Like … no matter how bad I was, I couldn’t be that bad, all things considered.”

     

                Lillian shook her head and chuckled quietly, and Lena found herself joining in. “Well, you’re not wrong. But, for what it’s worth, I never doubted your ability to run the company. I wasn’t setting you up for failure. You were always smarter than Lex.”

     

                “I know.”

     

                Perhaps it was the effects of the champagne, or maybe it was that she’d never really gotten to know her mother at all, but Lena felt at ease as they talked, the movie soon forgotten about as Lillian told her about her work and Lena told her about the things she’d gotten up to in the missing years between them. She listened to her mother tell stories of Lena’s childhood that she was too young to remember, an odd feeling in her chest at the warmth and amusement in her voice and the distant fondness in her eyes. 

     

                They ended up going to bed late and Lena stayed awake, thinking about how there were two conflicting versions of her mom in her head. She liked the new one more, but it was still largely overshadowed by the old, but there was that spark of hope that maybe it wouldn’t be all bad from now on. Lena would go back to National City and perhaps there would be more space between them for things to be amicable, without the pressure to perform well at meetings and meet some invisible standard.

     

                When she woke the next morning, she packed her things and drove into the city with Lillian for breakfast, city before the wide windows in an upscale café as they were waited on and lingered in the remaining couple of hours before Lena’s jet was scheduled to leave. Clearing her throat, Lillian took a sip of tea and set it back down on the saucer before giving her daughter a shrewd look.

     

                “I’ve been thinking.”

     

                “Oh?”

     

                “It … it hasn’t been so bad for you, has it? Coming home, I mean,” Lillian asked, uncertainty flashing across her face.

     

                “I mean … no, it hasn’t. I, uh, I actually found that I have some good memories too. They just … got a bit lost in all the bad, so I’m glad that I had the chance to remember them.”

     

                “Good. I’m glad.”

     

                They lapsed back into silence for a minute and Lena arched an eyebrow at her, a droll smile curling her lips as she spoke. “So, uh, was that it? That was what you were thinking about?”

     

                Inhaling sharply, Lillian looked down at her plate and rotated the cup on the saucer, shifting restlessly in her seat. “Well, no. I was wondering how you would feel about coming back.”

     

                “Coming back?”

     

                “When Kara comes home. I’d like it very much if you’d come and visit again, and maybe bring her next time.”

     

                “Oh!” Lena softly exclaimed, relief slamming into her as she deflated in her seat, letting out a strained laugh. “Oh, you want me to visit again? I thought-”

     

                “Don’t worry, I’m not asking you to move back home,” Lillian said with a bark of laughter. “I’d just like it if we could see each other a little more often. I’m grateful that you came, and it means more to me than you know, so … I’d like it if you’d come again. Not just for a reason.”

     

                “Oh, I, uh, yeah. Of course I can bring Kara. I’m sure she’d love to see the place. And … well, I think maybe I’d like that too.”

     

                Resting her hand on top of Lena’s for a brief moment, Lillian smiled warmly. “Thank you.”

     

                Breakfast passed by quickly and Lillian drove her out of the city, towards the private airstrip where her jet waited, and they both lingered on the tarmac as Lena’s luggage was loaded and Athena was led onto the jet.

     

                “I guess I’ll see you next time, then,” Lena said with a fleeting smile.

     

                “Next time,” Lillian agreed, her expression clouding with uncertainty for a moment before she continued. “Would you mind … texting me when you get home? Just so I know.”

     

                “Oh. Um, sure.”

     

                “Good,” Lillian nodded, a pleased look on her face. “Well, you’d better get going.”

     

                “Right.”

     

                Lillian reached forward and seized her hand quickly, giving it a hard squeeze before dropping it just as quickly, and Lena gave her a small smile. “Thank you, Lena. Really.”

     

                Nodding, Lena whispered a goodbye and turned towards the steps, climbing up them and hesitating in the open doorway to give her mom a small wave before disappearing into the cabin. She took her usual seat and couldn’t see the car through the oval windows, but she had the nagging suspicion that Lillian waited just a minute longer before leaving.  

    Chapter 31

    Kara,

     

    I’m having a hard time writing this one, as I sit in my old bedroom at the desk I spent so many hours studying and inventing, in the room I used to hide in while I imagined all the ways I’d escape this house one day. Somehow, I’ve ended up back here and it’s caught me off-guard. I don’t know if it’s good or not. The thought of you keeps me distracted from that rabbit hole though, and as I sit here and write this letter, I consider myself lucky; the girl that used to sit in this chair never imagined a future where she’d have someone she loved enough to make being in this house bearable, because she’d be thinking of her while writing letters.

     

    I worry though. I’ve never been one to worry about much because it always seemed so simple to me; if I didn’t like something, I got rid of it or fixed it. There was never anything to worry about, never a problem I couldn’t fix or something I wanted that was out of reach. Maybe I’m too spoilt, and maybe I’d be able to bear it better if I wasn’t, but I worry about you every second of the day. To be honest, I’m terrified. Those two days you went radio silent gave me a new perspective of life, and it wasn’t a good one. For almost two days, I was slapped with the very real possibility of a world without you, and I finally know what real fear is.

     

    I finally understand what love is too, and I’m convinced it’s the bravest thing you can ever do. It takes so much faith because you never know what can happen, you just have to hope that it’ll last forever, and I’m not good at hoping, but I’m trying really hard for you. I’m trying really hard with my mom too, and I think that’s because of how much I love you and how much you love Eliza, and seeing what it’s like to be surrounded by love. I’m learning that there are different kinds and Lillian loves in the capacity that she’s able to, so maybe it’s not all bad. It still scares the shit out of me though. I don’t know if I’ll ever be able to give it as freely as you do but I can only try.

     

    So, while I try over here, you have to try for me too - you have to try and stay out of trouble. I know you always say you’re fine when we talk, but I also know there are things you won’t tell me and it hurts my heart to think of all the things you keep to yourself. When you read this and we talk, I know we’ll pretend again that everything’s fine, but I want you to know it’s okay to be honest too. I know the reality of it is worse than I can even imagine, but you’ll be home soon. That’s something, isn’t it? It almost sounds like I’m being optimistic; isn’t that a funny thing. I think I worry and miss you too much for any real optimism though. Hurry up and come home to me, I’ll be waiting impatiently.

     

    Love always,

    Lena

    xxx

    Chapter 32

                August cooled the muggy city and brought overcast skies with it as a breeze shifted the stagnant air and autumn managed to creep into the trees and the shortening days. It was nearly over before it had started and Lena spent most of it parked behind a desk or sharing tapas and movies and hours around the pool table at a dive bar with friends. It wasn’t just Alex and Kelly on those nights at the bar; Nia and Brainy and Sam joined them often, and one night two weeks after she got back from Metropolis, the six of them went to see Raiders of the Lost Ark together at that rundown theatre Kara had taken Lena to.

     

                Lena found she didn’t resent their company as much as she’d anticipated, allowing herself to be pulled from her wallowing more often than she would have liked, but was all the more grateful for it when she found herself laughing until her stomach hurt, despite the ache of longing in her chest. She realised that to miss Kara didn’t mean an empty void of waiting in her life, and she was glad that she let Alex and Kelly’s stubborn determination to turn her into a social butterfly slowly work its charm. Perhaps not as much as they would have liked, but Lena was cut down to barely two late nights at the office a week now, a stark contrast to the entire weeks when she’d trek home in the early hours of the morning, only to return to her office mere hours later.

     

                As August rolled into September, she booked Alex and Kelly a weekend getaway to Joshua Tree out of gratitude, and to give them some time to themselves - and Lena would have been lying if she didn’t say she just wanted one weekend to herself. They left on Thursday and Lena enjoyed the quiet night in with Athena, working through the meeting minutes with a project manager from the engineering department as a documentary played in the background.

     

                On Friday night, despite her promise to herself that she’d stay home and do minimal work, she found herself at the office late, staying behind to inspect a prototype and indulge in the empty workshop. She had her own lab, of course, but there was something about walking through the open workshops that made her long for the days she’d spent on her own research, the practical aspects that didn’t revolve around arduous meetings and mountains of paperwork or the constant conversations about money and KPI’s and working out which projects to proceed with. She didn’t miss the long hours spent coding computer programs, nitpicking through strings of letters and symbols for tiny mistakes, but she missed the careful work of soldering and connecting wires and assembling fiddly pieces.

     

                Most of her time now was spent signing off for other people to do that sort of work for her, hiring hundreds of people to create the products L-Corp sold throughout their various divisions, but she spent a couple of hours that night, dismantling the prototype for an image-guided robot and poring over blueprints as she inspected the parts of it. It was an upgrade of an old model Lena had designed, trying to implement nanotechnology through nanosensors and fine-motor mechanics with its own self-renewing energy source, but so far it had been unsuccessful. She knew that once they cracked the key to it, it would be a staple at the forefront of modern medicine and engineering, making quick, precise work that human hands made errors of.

     

                On the street below, cars inched past the dark building, dinner patrons making their way to the fine restaurants along the river at the end of the block while late commuters headed home. Above them, the setting sun smeared the sky red and gold and pink, the palm trees and cypresses swayed in the cool breeze. The hours got lost on her as she worked, the office emptying and the smell of grease and metal clinging to her blackened fingertips as she happily played away, knowing that she wasn’t providing anything valuable to the effort but content to see for herself how the work was progressing.

     

                It was past eleven when she finally became aware of herself, of the ache in her stiff shoulders from hunching over for hours, of the dry, burning sensation in her eyes and the gnawing hunger in her stomach that let her know she’d forgotten about dinner. Lena could’ve stayed there for hours, but she’d already broken her promise to not stay late and caved, deciding to call it a night. She had half a mind to go and get dinner first though and checked to see if the nearby Thai place was still open. 

     

                Placing her order online, Lena decided that the short walk would do her some good, stretching out stiff legs in the cool night air, and fetched her coat and handbag and rode the elevator down to the dim lobby. A few security guards nodded at her, surprised as she let herself out through the locked sliding doors and set off on foot. She was looking down at her phone, reading emails - a short one off Kara that made her smile as she hunched over the screen - and didn’t see the dark shadow peel away from the dark shadows of a tree shading the sidewalk. 

     

                She didn’t notice the antsy behaviour as they followed her, hand in their pocket, past the dark office buildings and businesses onto the next block. The orange glow of the streetlights made Lena unafraid - she didn’t even consider that it was late and that she was alone or someone might have a reason to follow her. She was too busy typing out an email back to Kara to find once she’d finished work to pay any attention to her surroundings. 

     

                Perhaps it was that she’d never had any cause to walk alone late at night or that she’d always felt safe at the top of her soaring office with the security downstairs, but Lena paid little attention to her surroundings until a deep voice called out from behind her. She looked up and half-turned, mild surprise lifting her eyebrows with polite indifference. 

     

                “I have something for you,” he said, his rough voice laced with anger and an edge of amusement.

     

                Raising a hand, Lena’s lips twitched faintly. “No, thank you.”

     

                She watched as his face darkened with a flush of rage and fully turned, standing a few feet from the open mouth of a dark alleyway, the fetid smell of old food and urine making her nose wrinkle slightly as she frowned slightly, confused. He moved towards her, hand in his pocket and Lena felt a flicker of wariness.

     

                “You have a good night, though,” she murmured, turning to go again.

     

                Pulling his hand out of his pocket, in the darkness between streetlights, Lena couldn’t see what he held, only that he held something. He raised it then and she knew without being able to see it clearly that he was pointing a gun at her. Her mouth went dry and fear slithered up her spine, but for some insane reason, her mouth spoke of its own accord, her bristling snark spilling from her lips before she could bite back the words.

     

                “What’re you going to do?” she laughed, raising an eyebrow in a mocking manner as she spread her hands slightly. “Shoot me?”

     

                “This is for my sister.”

     

                Confusion flashed across Lena’s face and she opened her mouth to reply but choked on the expelled breath as the sound of the gun firing shattered the night and searing pain tore through her stomach. Stumbling back, Lena’s phone slipped from her grasp and clattered onto the asphalt in the alleyway and her ankle twisted as the stiletto of her heel gave way beneath her. Gasping for air as she fell back heavily onto the cold ground, white-hot pain blinding her, Lena watched as the shadowed man quickly retreated, gun hidden in his pocket. Pressing a hand to her stomach, she felt the warmth of blood, slick on her fingers as she drew in a shallow breath, feeling faint and hollow.

     

                It was a quiet slip of a street that she was on, full of day-time businesses that would be empty at midnight, and through the haze of pain, Lena was starkly aware of the fact that she was alone. No one was going to help her and blood was welling up from the wound, soaking into her satin shirt with an alarming sized patch of red. Lips trembling and eyes smarting with tears, Lena crawled for her phone in the alleyway, a sob hitching in her throat at the pain in her stomach. Scraping her hands and knees, she picked it up, her hand shaking so violently as she tried to bring the shattered screen to life that she could barely dial 911.

     

                Sagging against the base of a grimy, graffitied wall, her numb lips chattering as shock slammed into her, Lena didn’t even feel the frigid brown water of the puddle she was sprawled in seeping into her clothes. Eyes half-lidded and grey face twisted into an agonised grimace, she held the phone to her ear and drew in short, sharp breaths as the operator’s voice soothingly washed over her without Lena making any sense of the words.

     

                “I- I’ve been- I’ve been sh-shot. He- he … shot me. He shot me.”

     

                “Can you tell me where you are?”

     

                “I don’t know,” she sobbed, her voice pitifully small as hot tears welled up. “I’m in an- an alley. A few blocks … east of L-Corp. West Cordova. It’s on- it’s on that road.”

     

                Her vision furred at the edges with darkness and she swallowed the sour taste of bile, feeling her world pitch. A slightly hysterical laugh bubbled up inside her and the phone fell from her limp hand, clattering into the pool of water as she sank into unconsciousness, the tinny voice on the phone speaking to the silence.

     

                “EMT’s are enroute, just stay on the line with me, okay? Ma’am, what’s your name? Ma’am? Is he still there with you?”

     

     

                She dimly became aware of herself moments before her groggy mind was able to comprehend that she was awake. A listless breath slipped through dry lips and her tongue felt heavy in her cotton wool mouth, stiff sheets and a stiflingly hot sensation cocooning Lena as her eyelids remained heavily shut. Her limbs were heavy and unresponsive but she felt safe , buoyed by the warm feeling of weightlessness as she listened to the muffled beeping sound that was nearby.

     

                It became rather irritating after a moment and her face furrowed as a small groan worked its way up her throat and she managed to open her eyes to narrow slits. The sound of rustling fabric and a creaking chair caught her attention and, gripped in the euphoric haze of morphine, the flash of movement that she dimly became aware of made her sigh softly, content and happy. Blonde . A flash of blonde hair. Everything else was indistinct, unknown to her as she drifted.

     

                “Kara,” she mumbled, the oxygen mask over her nose and mouth muffling the sound of her voice.

     

                “Sweetie? It’s Eliza.”

     

                Trying to force her eyes open, the drugs she was on leaving her drowsy and dazed, Lena made a sound of confusion at the back of her throat. She tried to push herself up, but her body was unresponsive, clumsy and heavy, and a dull ache in her stomach flared up.

     

                “Don’t move,” Eliza murmured, her voice low and gentle.

                

                Lena felt her hands on her shoulders, easing her back against the thin pillow she rested on. Humming disconcertingly, Lena tried again to open her eyes, feeling some of the fogginess receding as she fought heavily against sleep. Clarity slowly crept up on her, the droning of the harsh fluorescents overhead, the sharp, antiseptic smell of a hospital, the frigid air and scratchy blankets. Fumbling at her face, she dragged the mask down and let her hand fall limply back onto the sheets.

     

                “What happened?” Lena asked, her voice barely a sigh as her head rolled to the side and her fingers ran over the coarse sheets. “What are you doing here?”

     

                “You were shot, honey.”

     

                Lena choked on a quiet laugh that made her stomach ache and her brow creased with a small furrow. “Shot? I’m in hospital?”

     

                “Mhm. They did a laparoscopy to get the bullet out; it didn’t take long. You’re lucky it didn’t hit anything.”

     

                Blinking slowly now, Lena stared up at the white panels of the ceiling, numb but strangely cold as some nagging thought troubled her, just out of reach as she tried to piece together the dim memories of what had happened. Yes, there had been a gun, that much she was aware of from Eliza’s explanation, but beyond L-Corp, she didn’t have the ability to parse through the ensuing events yet. 

     

                Her eyes drifted over to Eliza, who was lowering herself back down onto the vinyl covered chair situated near the bed, the metal creaking as she settled back down, just out of reach of the beeping monitors and snaking wires. Raising a leaden hand, Lena took in the needles and wires that connected to her and let out a faint sigh before she blinked and looked back at Eliza. The older woman looked tired, her face drawn and pale with bags beneath her eyes.

     

                “You look tired,” Lena rasped.

     

                Eliza quietly chuckled, propping her face in her hand as she studied Lena’s face for a moment before sighing. “I’m fine. You just had me worried, that's all.”

     

                “Sorry,” Lena mumbled, a sheepish smile twitching her lips as her eyes slid closed again, the lights overhead too bright to bear. She was silent for a moment, staving off sleep, when a thought struck her. “How did you get here?”

     

                “The EMT’s found you in an alley but they had no clue who you were. They brought you in and one of the interns found your medical ID on your phone, so they tried calling Kara. She didn’t answer, so they tried Alex next, and then she called me. We didn’t want you to wake up alone.”

     

                Exhaling fully, Lena deflated and nodded, swallowing dryly as she listened to the steady beeps. “Kara doesn’t know yet?”

     

                “Not yet. I thought- well, she’s at work and she shouldn’t be distracted.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena gratefully murmured.

     

                “I called your mom as well,” Eliza hedged, “I wasn’t sure if I should , but for medical reasons … she’s your next of kin.”

     

                Lena quietly groaned, “what’d she say?”

     

                “She’s on her way here.”

     

                Lena’s mouth thinned and her cheeks dimpled slightly at the expression, but she was too tired to protest. Eliza murmured something that she couldn’t bring herself to concentrate on as the ache in her stomach sharpened, and Lena blinked sluggishly, looking at the seat she occupied and then in between one moment and the next, was empty.

     

                She returned only minutes later, although Lena had no concept of time, a doctor in tow, who closed the door behind himself and gave her a warm smile. “Miss Luthor, I’m glad to see you’re awake. I’m Doctor Gilcrist. How’re you feeling?”

     

                “Tired,” Lena said with a wispy sigh.

     

                “That’ll be the morphine. Do you mind if I take a look at you?”

     

                Mumbling her consent, Lena let her eyelids droop as the doctor pulled his stethoscope from around his neck and stepped up beside her bed. He loomed over her as he listened to her breath sounds, the head of the stethoscope cold against her skin. Goosebumps rippled down her arms and she lay there, vulnerable and small, as the doctor pulled the blankets down to her legs and peeled back the surgical dressing covering the site of the gunshot wound. He inspected the stitches and the nurse that arrived a few minutes later took over to clean and apply a new one while he made notes on her chart and conversed quietly with Eliza.

     

                Lena was oblivious to most of it, her cheeks pale and eyes ringed with dark bruises from her ordeal as the drugs continued to wear thin in her bloodstream. The blossoming pain in her abdomen made her face taut and Eliza held her hand, shifting the creaking chair closer as the nurse worked quickly and pulled the blankets back up over her, tucking her in.

     

                “Any pain or discomfort?” Doctor Gilcrist asked, glancing up from the chart.

     

                “No,” Lena lied, her drawn face belying her words.

     

                “We’ll give you another round of painkillers.”

     

                She shook her head slightly, cracking her eyes open to look at him. “No. No more drugs.”

     

                Eliza gently squeezed her hand, a grave look on her face. “Sweetie, they’ll help you recover faster. You need your rest; you can’t do that if you’re in pain.”

     

                Shaking her head again, more insistent this time, Lena shifted herself up onto her elbows, gritting her teeth as she leaned more to one side and lay her palm over the right, aching side of her abdomen. 

     

                “I need to go home,” Lena protested, “I have work. I have a meeting and Athena- oh, God, she didn’t get fed last night. I didn’t take her for a walk.”

     

                “Hey,” Eliza murmured, rising from her seat and gripping Lena’s shoulders gently as she pushed her back down. Her face was creased with worry and she held her in place until she felt the tension bleed out of Lena’s body, sagging against the mattress of the hospital bed. “You’re not going anywhere. And don’t worry about Athena; I’ll go and check on her, okay? You just focus on getting better.”

     

                Relenting with a terse nod, Lena felt the cool trickle of morphine in her veins as the doctor injected it into the canula on her hand. Immediately, she was swept away on a euphoric tide, blissfully drifting away from the conversation. She slept then, unable to stop herself from succumbing to the drowsy heaviness in her body. 

     

                It wasn’t a peaceful kind of sleep, but a cold, glitching kind, where bad dreams started over and over again, interrupting themselves before they could reveal themselves fully, but leaving Lena with an unnerving restlesses that the painkillers couldn’t stifle. She woke long enough to register how cold and uncomfortable she was on the narrow hospital bed, her mind fuzzy and a nauseous feeling in her stomach. She didn’t even manage to get her eyes open before she was out cold again.

     

                It had been dark outside when she’d first fallen asleep, although Lena couldn’t have said what time of day it was - had it still been early morning, or had she been out for most of the day after surgery? - and the next time she woke, the sky lingered in the violet inbetween of day and night, although, again, she wasn’t sure whether it was dusk or dawn. The room was still and quiet, save for the whir of machinery, and Lena could hear the overlapping tenors of familiar voices, but distant and dim.

     

                Turning her head to the side, she sought out the source of them, staring at the half-open door through slitted eyes. She could see the tall and striking form of her mother, dressed elegantly and looking as polished as ever, as if she’d taken the time to visit the salon before coming to see her hospitalised child. Eliza was beside her, shorter and flagging from exhaustion as they conversed with Lena’s doctor.

     

                Slipping in and out of unconsciousness as she tried to fight off the drugs, Lena opened her eyes at the sound of heels clicking on the linoleum flooring of the hospital room, watching as Lillian quietly eased the door open and then pushed it wider as she noticed Lena was awake. Barging inside, she quickly crossed over to the bed, looking pale and pinched with worry.

     

                “Thank God,” Lillian quietly exclaimed, lips thinning as her shoulders drooped, a sigh of relief expelled through her nose. “You had me worried sick.”

     

                “Mom,” Lena murmured, her eyelids sliding closed.

     

                “I came as fast as I could,” Lillian earnestly assured her, dropping down onto the nearby chair, while Eliza hovered back, arms folded over her chest and a look of wary curiosity on her tired face. “I missed Eliza’s call and then I couldn’t get the jet ready for another hour .”

     

                Her blue eyes were bright but dry as they appraised Lena’s body, seeking out the small wound with a perturbed look on her face. Eliza softly cleared her throat and took a step forward, looking at Lillian with a polite smile on her lips.

     

                “I’m going to get some coffee - can I get you anything, Lillian?”

     

                “Coffee would be lovely, thank you.”

     

                “Can I have some?” Lena hoarsely asked, hope welling up in her eyes as her eyebrows rose a fraction. 

     

                Her throat was dry from the surgery and the oxygen, and she didn’t like how sluggish she felt. It didn’t make Eliza more inclined to agree though; she just laughed softly and grimaced as she shook her head.

     

                “Drink some water. I’ll see if they’ll bring you something to eat as well; you’ll feel nauseous, but you need to eat.”

     

                Lena pursed her lips, disgruntled, and watched her leave, closing the door behind herself to give them some privacy. She almost wished she’d stay, the awkward tension of Lillian at her bedside making Lena feel uncomfortable. Or that might have just been the gunshot wound, she couldn’t rightfully say.

     

                “She seems nice,” Lillian noted.

     

                “She is nice,” Lena mumbled, wincing and then collapsing back down as she struggled to sit upright.

     

                “Hey,” Lillian sharply warned her, on her feet in an instant, hands outstretched and nervously fluttering around Lena’s shoulders, although she didn’t quite touch her. “You shouldn’t exert yourself. You just had surgery, you know? Lay back down.”

     

                Mouth turning down at the corners, Lena blinked slowly, her eyes rolling slightly beneath closed lids, and allowed Lillian to push the button to incline the top of the bed slightly before she fluffed the pillows behind Lena’s head. Her last dose of morphine was wearing off now, the dulled pain slightly uncomfortable and growing stronger as she leaned back against the pillows.

     

                “I want to go home,” Lena quietly said after a moment, a plea in her voice as she looked forlornly at her mother.

     

                Chuckling, Lillian sank back down onto the chair, crossing her legs as she leaned back, lounging as if she owned the hospital. Lena doubted she was at the children’s one though, or that might have actually been the case.

     

                “Of course you do,” Lillian said, clicking her tongue disapprovingly. “You never did like hospitals.”

     

                “Mm. They’re where you used to vanish for days. You used to leave me at home with him.”

     

                She laughed bitterly and then groaned as agony ripped through her stomach, placing a hand against it as she blanched, turning a shade whiter. Face twisting with the pain of it, Lena sagged against the pillows and struggled to catch her breath for a moment, the sour taste of bile at the back of her dry throat as a prickle of sweat dotted her brow.

     

                “Sh, it’s okay,” Lillian murmured, surprisingly tender as she reached out to smooth dark hair out of her face with slender fingers. “I know it hurts.”

     

                Pushing aside the uneasy thoughts of whether this was how her mother’s bedside manners were with her patients when she’d still been a practicing surgeon, Lena bared her teeth in a gritted grimace as she screwed her eyes shut and then relaxed as the flare of pain dimmed. Eyes snapping open, bright and piercing, she let out a breathless laugh and arched an eyebrow.

     

                “Yeah? How many times have you been shot?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lillian shot her an exasperated look, lips twisting sourly. “I’ve never been shot because I’ve never been stupid enough to walk through a city alone in the middle of the night. Honestly, Lena, what were you thinking?”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena swallowed thickly, silent for a long minute as she collected her thoughts. Things were less patchy now, her mind catching up with her body, despite the hours she’d spent asleep, and she was filled with sudden anger as tears smarted her eyes. Wiping at them angrily, she clenched her teeth.

     

                “Don’t lecture me. He- he said it was for his sister. I think … his sister was one of them.”

     

                The air was expelled from Lillian’s lungs as she drew back, caught off guard and left silent for a long moment. Lena fought to rein in her emotions as she stared up at the ceiling, thinking about which one was the woman her brother had killed in his moment of destructive madness. She would know her by face if she’d known the name, from the hours spent seeing them up there on the news coverage, in newspapers and trending on social media, and on two anniversaries since. Lena knew the name of all of them - not that it made a difference.

     

                “The perfect revenge, I guess,” Lena snorted after a moment, shaking her head as her lips twitched with a ghost of a smile. “It’s too bad I’m too stubborn to die from a little bullet. Maybe next time I’ll avoid the sarcasm though.”

     

                “Sarcasm? What did you do?”

     

                “Up to more trouble?” Eliza asked as she stepped back into the room, nudging the door shut behind her and looking at Lena expectantly.

     

                She handed off a cup of coffee to Lillian, who thanked her and grimaced as she took a sip. Hospital coffee was never good, yet she sipped it anyway, and Lena would’ve killed for a cup of cheap coffee if she’d been allowed it.

     

                Flushing slightly, Lena scowled as she bristled. “It wasn’t my fault. He pulled the gun on me and I asked if he was seriously going to shoot me. I didn’t think he actually would.”

     

                “Lena,” Lillian roughly exclaimed, pinching the bridge of her nose as her eyelids shuttered and she exhaled sharply. “Do you have any common sense? You’re not supposed to provoke someone holding you at gunpoint.”

     

                “You could’ve been seriously injured,” Eliza stressed, a disturbed look on her face as she perched on the edge of the mattress. “What if he’d had a better aim?”

                Clicking her tongue with irritation, Lillian scoffed and shook her head. “Maybe you’ll finally listen then.”

     

                Lena opened her mouth to reply but trailed off as her phone started vibrating on the unit beside the bed.                 “It’s Kara,” Eliza read off the screen, quickly glancing at Lena. “I’ll fill her in for you, so you can rest.”

     

                Nodding, Lena lay back down, her skin prickling with a cold sweat as she tracked Eliza’s movements to the door and strained to catch the sound of Kara’s voice as the video call connected.

     

                “Mom?”

     

                Swallowing thickly as a pang of longing knifed through her chest, Lena drew in a shallow, shuddering breath and shivered slightly. Lillian was quiet for a minute and then shifted forward, the chair creaking beneath her weight.

     

                “She cares about you.”

     

                “Who? Eliza? Yeah,” Lena mumbled in agreement.

     

                “That’s good,” Lillian replied, her voice firm and quiet as she clenched her jaw and nodded to herself. Her smile when she looked at Lena was thin. “This family … I’m glad they’ve taken you in. They seem like good people.”

     

                Humming, Lena’s lips twitched faintly with a rueful smile. “They are. But … thanks for coming. I know you’re busy; I don’t mean to be a burden.”

     

                Surprise flickered in Lillian’s blue eyes and she let out a soft huff of laughter. “Family causes pain and makes mistakes, but it’s never a burden . You’ve never been a burden, Lena.                 “You never said. You made me think it was me . You made me think you were disappointed in me.”

                “Someone wants to talk to you.”

The sight of Lena made her burst into another round of tears, covering her face with a hand as her shoulders shook. 

     

                “We’ll wait outside,” Eliza murmured, backing away to the door as Lillian hesitated and then followed after her, giving Lena some privacy.

     

                “Hi,” Lena murmured, her voice light and warm, even if she looked and felt rough.

     

                “Oh, God, Lena,” Kara breathlessly sobbed, wiping at her cheeks as she looked at her with gut-wrenching misery and regret. “What the hell happened? How could I not have been there? I should’ve been there, I- I should’ve known you were in the hospital, I-”

                

                A tender smile softened Lena’s face as she listlessly sighed, the knot of tension in her chest loosening at the sound of her voice, as panicked as it was. “Hey, I’m fine .                 “Minor?” Kara choked, a slightly hysterical laugh bubbling up, “are you out of your goddamn mind? People die from gunshot wounds. Loads of people die.”

                Lena’s face crumpled with discontentment and she smudged her thumb across the screen as if she could wipe away the fresh tears that spilled down Kara’s cheeks. “Hey, hey, come on. I’m fine, baby. Really. I don’t want you worrying about me, okay? That’s my job.”

     

                “Who would’ve thought that you’d be in more danger over there than I am here? Is this how it feels for you?”

     

                “No. I have it much worse; I have to worry every day.”

     

                Letting out a tearful laugh, Kara looked at her with yearning in her blue eyes, suntanned and exhausted and brimming with nervous energy as she rubbed at the back of her neck. “It’s fine, I’ve put in a request for some leave anyway, so I’ll be home as soon as possible.”

                Lena laughed, the sound frayed and hitching as she fought back the building tears behind her eyes, blinking rapidly as her body convulsed slightly with the force of the laughter that shook her. A twist of agony knifed through her stomach and she let out a hiss between her teeth before groaning softly.

     

                “Don’t make me laugh ; it hurts,” she complained, looking a little grey as her body went lax again and she sobered up. “But you know that I do. More than anything in the world.                 “Lena, they found you bleeding in an alleyway and they didn’t even know who you were. You could’ve died and I wouldn’t have even known,” Kara flatly replied, her mouth a grim line as her eyes shone with tears.

     

                “Of course you would’ve; someone would’ve told you.”

     

                “Yeah, eventually.”

     

                Frowning, Lena’s mouth thinned. “You just- you haven’t been gone for that long, and if- if you come home now … I don’t think I’ll be able to bear being away from you for another seven months, okay?”

     

                “I know, but … I should be there,” Kara replied, a resigned sigh falling from her lips as her shoulders dropped, the fight draining out of her. “I hate that I’m not there. I should be … feeding you jello and making sure your feet are warm, because I know hospitals can get really cold.”

     

                Lena weakly chuckled, her eyelids sliding closed as she smiled warmly and listened to the list that Kara rattled off before she replied. “I think most importantly, you should be here so I know you’re safe. Like permanently be here. But you have to finish your tour first; I can’t have you being court-martialed on me. That would ruin all of my plans.”

     

                “You have plans?” Kara asked, raising her eyebrows and nudging her glasses up her nose. “Would you mind sharing?”

     

                “Maybe in the future,” Lena murmured, her eyes cracking open as she grinned to herself. “But for now, you need to stay where you are and stay safe. I have my mom and your mom here with me, so I’m fine.” She paused for a moment, swallowing thickly. “Honestly, that’s two more people than I expected here so … I’m happy.”

     

                “Happy?” Kara repeated, a pained look on her face at the fact that Lena would’ve found joy in being shot, if only because it had made her realise she wasn’t quite as alone as she’d thought, even without Kara there. Shaking her head, Kara softly exhaled and then gave her a weak smile. “Alex and Kelly should be there soon, anyway.”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena made a sound of objection. “No, they’re still in Joshua Tree until tomorrow. I think tomorrow; is it day or night? I’m not sure.”

     

                “It’s day for you,” Kara murmured, “you weren’t out for long, apparently. But, Eliza said they’re coming back early. They’re probably already driving as we speak.”

     

                “No, no, no,” Lena groaned, squeezing her eyes shut as she clenched her teeth. “Why would they do that? It was supposed to be a nice trip.”

     

                Chuckling, Kara gave her a disbelieving look, “well, I think a midnight call about their friend being shot would’ve put a damper on the whole thing. They care about you. Way more than they care about a weekend getaway.”

     

                “I wanted to surprise them,” Lena grumbled.

     

                Choking on a laugh, Kara’s eyes creased at the corners and Lena’s annoyance receded as warmth spread through her chest. “Yeah, I think you managed that. It was one hell of a surprise.”

     

                Pulling a face, Lena laughed as well. “I’m sorry to surprise you too.”

     

                Sighing heavily, Kara looked at her with exasperated amusement. “What am I going to do about you? Nothing works without me.”

     

                “Just come home safe,” Lena murmured, “that’s all.”

     

                “I will. And I might have to ask everyone to keep a closer eye on you before you end up with more holes in you.”

     

                “Well, your mom has already given me an earful about resting, if that helps. And then my mom gave me another one about walking alone late at night. I feel like I’m a kid again. It’s a bit annoying, actually.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose slightly as she smiled, a crease formed between Kara’s eyebrows. “Our moms there together … that’s weird.”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena agreed, “I’m not sure how I feel about it; they’re two worlds that should never mesh. My mom’s on her best behaviour though - I think she might actually have been worried about me. Funny.”

     

                “Of course she would have been. And don’t worry about her behaviour; Eliza might seem all sweet and soft to you, but she doesn’t take shit either.”

     

                The door cracked open a moment later and Lena glanced up, watching as they both filed back into the room and giving them a thin smile. Truthfully, she was starting to feel the dull ache in her stomach a little more keenly, the morphine slipping away and leaving her feeling groggy and restless at the throbbing pain. She knew the moment she was given more though, she’d slip away into that euphoric sleep again and have to say goodbye to Kara. A little more pain was worth the extra time.

     

                Lillian was perceptive though, gripping the back of the chair as she looked at the tautness of Lena’s face and let out a quiet laugh, shaking her head as she gave her a wry smile. “It hurts, doesn’t it?”

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena muttered, glancing back at the screen.

     

                “I’ll let the nurse know you’re ready for more painkillers,” Lillian said.

     

                “No,” Lena loudly exclaimed, shifting up in bed and gasping as she pressed a hand to her side, her hand with the phone dipping.

     

                “Lena,” Kara murmured, “take the painkillers. You need to rest.”

     

                Grimacing disapprovingly, Eliza moved to lay her back against the pillows and pushed the button to lower the bed back down as well. Not all the way, but Lena was almost flat, holding the phone up as she scowled at the screen.

     

                “Listen to her,” Eliza quietly cautioned her, “you can talk more tomorrow.”

     

                Snorting, Lena closed her eyes and smiled, cheeks dimpling slightly. “Well, if there’s one thing worse than one doctor parent, it’s two.”

     

                “I’ll talk to you tomorrow,” Kara quietly promised. “Please, get some sleep, okay? It’ll make me feel better too.”

     

                “You get some sleep,” Lena retorted, “that’ll make me feel better.”

     

                “Liar,” Kara weakly laughed, a pang of longing on her face as her amusement faded away and she was left looking tired and worried. “I love you, okay? Don’t exert yourself.”

     

                A small smile graced Lena’s face and she swallowed thickly, shifting onto her side as she felt the prickling heat of embarrassment in her cheeks with their mothers watching. Quietly clearing her throat, Lena shifted and looked at Kara’s face for a moment longer.

     

                “You too,” she murmured, “I love you too.”

     

                Feeling vulnerable and resentful as the call ended, Lena lay with her back to them as she stared at the brightening light seeping around the blinds. A few minutes later, the nurse was there, deep in conversation with Lillian before she quickly administered more painkillers and left again. 

     

                The effects were immediate, the tension bleeding out of Lena as she was buoyed by the elation the drugs brought, wrapping her in its warm embrace as her body went limp and her eyelids grew heavy. She was out cold by the time Eliza left, fulfilling her promises to Lena to walk and feed the dog, while Lillian kept a bedside vigil that would’ve surprised Lena if she’d been awake to witness it. 

     

                The day spun past in brief bouts of wakefulness that she didn’t remember, the hot and cold flushes that swept through her carefully monitored under her mother’s stern gaze. Lena opened her eyes to the yellowy-gold light of the early morning light seeping in through the window, and when she blinked, it had changed to a deep periwinkle as sunset crept up on her without her knowledge. The wasted day would have been regretful if she’d had the capacity to form the thought, even if it was a Saturday, but Lena slumbered until she roused with the night.

     

                The room was dim when she shifted, sheets rustling and the pressure behind her eyes heavy and blurry as she parted her eyelids. A soft orange glow from the lamp cut through the darkness and she could see the silhouettes of two sleeping figures in chairs at her bedside. She needed to use the bathroom and lay there for a minute, unwilling to ask for help, before she slowly eased the covers back and swung her legs over the side of the bed.

     

                Her feet touched the cold linoleum for a moment as she pushed herself up and slid off the side of the bed, but as soon as her body weight was fully supported by her own legs, they gave way beneath her. She fell down heavily to her knees, quietly cursing as she curled in on herself, her vision dimming as pain made the already dim room darken for a brief moment. She still had the vitals machine hooked up to her and the grogginess of lingering anesthesia made her clumsy as she dragged it with her downwards motion, the wheeled machine skittering across the floor.

     

                Swearing fell on her ringing ears, muffled and distant as she stayed hunched over on her knees, the back of her gown parting as cold air hit her spine. Cold hands gripped her arms and hauled her to her feet, her sagging weight an imposition until another set of hands, warmer and gentler, helped guide her back onto the bed. Head throbbing, Lena squeezed her eyes shut and listened to the rushing sound of blood pulsating in her head as she was tucked back into bed, the sounds slowly becoming sharper as her blood pressure steadied.

     

                “What’s the matter with you?” Lillian sharply asked. “You don’t get out of bed by yourself after surgery .”

     

                “I need to use the bathroom,” Lena listlessly sighed, unable to open her eyes.

     

                “There’s spotting on the dressing,” Eliza murmured, and Lena was too tired to care that Kara’s mother had her hospital gown rucked up around her waist to bare her pale stomach and the dressing that was slowly blotting with crimson.

     

                “She probably ripped a stitch,” Lillian quietly seethed.

     

                Lena clenched her teeth as her face crumpled and her lips parted as she drew in a shaky breath. “I’m sorry,” she whispered.

     

                “It’s okay, sweetheart. Don’t move, okay?” Eliza gently reassured her.

     

                As sleep wore off and she lingered in that hazy place of weaning morphine and groggy anesthesia, Lena became more aware of her pain and her wakefulness, blinking slowly as she let her eyes adjust to the blue hue from outside and the soft glow of the lamp.

     

                An intern returned with her mother five minutes later, and as worn out as she was, Lillian still managed to look regally pissed as the lights were switched on and she stood at the foot of the bed, watching as the dressing was removed and the two inch sutured wound put on display for them. A nurse wheeled in a trolley with medical equipment laid out and the bed was fully reclined, leaving Lena staring up at the ceiling as the doctor donned latex gloves and disinfected the site, sitting on a boosted stool as the bed was lowered for her to work. She seemed terrified at the prospect as Lillian and Eliza hovered.

     

                “What sutures did they use in surgery?” Lillian asked.

                

                “Oh, um, Polydioxanone,” the intern replied.

     

                “It’s deep; did the surgeon do a double layer?” Eliza chipped in, raising her eyebrows slightly.

     

                “Yes. He did a double layer of mattress stitches in the dermis and interrupted stitches in the epidermis for better closure at the wound edges. She’s only ripped the epidermis - I think.”

     

                Bristling slightly, Lillian arched an eyebrow, “you think?”

     

                “I’ll, uh … check?”

     

                Nodding, Lillian quickly backed down, placated for the time being, and watched the intern like a hawk as the torn stitch was snipped and removed and another was carefully put into place. Lena didn’t feel a thing with the local anesthetic injected around the edges of the wound to numb the area, and as she slowly managed to focus, the fog in her mind somewhat clearing, she watched with morbid fascination. A new surgical dressing was applied and the intern wearily told her to take it easy, looking slightly vexed at the nuisance after a long shift doing the grunt work.

     

                Afterwards, Lena was helped to the bathroom by Eliza, infinitely gentler than her mother, who was prickly and annoyed at Lena’s stupidity, and lingered in there for a few minutes afterwards, standing alone before the mirror as she stared at her sallow reflection. It hadn’t even been a full day yet, but her eyes and cheeks looked hollow, exhaustion and pain weighing heavily on her and writing themselves into her face as she clung to the edge of the sink and squinted against the harsh whiteness of the bathroom. A knock on the door and a quietly concerned voice brought her back out of her brooding thoughts and she allowed herself to be helped back into bed.

     

                Food was waiting for her on a tray. Bland chicken and frozen vegetables and a cup of jello, and it was only under the watchful gaze of two doctors that she propped herself up and peeled back the lid on the jello, spooning in a mouthful and forcing it down. It was pulpy and too sweet and she grimaced as she forced down a second mouthful before setting it back down.

     

                “You need to eat more than that,” Eliza encouraged her.

     

                “I’m not hungry.”

     

                Sighing, Lillian’s lips thinned, “well, of course you’re not - look at it. Is there anything you feel like? A favourite takeout place? I’ll go and pick up something for you; whatever you want.”

     

                Lena shrugged indifferently, a nauseous edge to the dwindling morphine lingering as her stomach roiled and her dry mouth struggled to swallow, the sickly sweet taste of jello clinging to her tongue.

     

                “How about sushi? You like sushi.”

     

                “Sure,” Lena said with a wan smile, mostly to placate her mother.

     

                Perking up slightly, looking pleased with herself for knowing that facet of information, and that Lena had readily agreed, Lillian nodded to herself and donned her coat and fetched her bag. Eliza looked up at her from her seat, gripping the arms of it as she made to climb to her feet.

     

                “Would you like me to go so you can stay with Lena?” she offered.

     

                With a polite smile, Lillian shook her head, “thank you, but I’ll go.” She glanced over her shoulder at Lena, her expression softening minutely. “I’ll be back soon.”

     

                Nodding, Eliza settled back down and Lillian slipped out on a mission. The room was quiet after that and it wasn’t long before the nurse came in with another dose of painkillers, checking the dressing and her vitals and asking Lena to rate her pain. She lowballed it, her voice hoarse as she asked when she’d be discharged. Tomorrow was optimistic, and she resigned herself to a night spent in the bland room and uncomfortable bed, the smell instilling uneasiness in her, so stagnant and sterile.

     

                “How’re you really feeling?” Eliza asked as the nurse left.

     

                “I don’t like the morphine,” Lena quietly admitted, her voice a sigh.

     

                “I know,” Eliza murmured, climbing to her feet and pulling the blankets up a little higher before she smoothed Lena’s hair back and sank down onto her seat. “It’s better for you if you’re not in any pain though; you should sleep while you wait for your mom to get back.”

     

                “I don’t like sleeping.”

     

                Quietly chuckling, Eliza looked at her with fond amusement, looking even more exhausted than when she’d landed. Lena wondered how many hours she’d slept recently, if any, and felt a prickle of guilt at keeping her away from Midvale, away from her home. 

     

                “I figured that out for myself; you’re always staying up so late. Yes, I know. Kara used to tell me, and Alex tells me too. I’m a mom, I know everything. But you need your rest.”

     

                “You need yours too,” Lena said with a thin smile.

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Eliza chuckled, “oh, don’t worry about me. I’ve worked shifts longer than I’ve been awake so far. I’ll be fine. I’ll stay at Alex’s tonight though; your mom will still be here.”

     

                Snorting, Lena screwed her eyes shut as her brow creased. “I didn’t expect her to come.”

     

                “She was worried.”

     

                “I know. It scares me.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                Chewing on her words for a moment, Lena finally admitted the truth. “If she cares … it means I have more to lose.”

     

                “And so much to gain,” Eliza fiercely whispered, giving her hand a squeeze.

     

                Lena smiled as she hummed in agreement, her eyelids sliding shut of their own accord as her mind grew fuzzy. It no longer whisked her away to blissful unawareness, but she dozed lightly, slipping in and out. She came to at one point, which could’ve only been minutes later, as Eliza was still there alone, sitting in the lamplight as she typed on her phone. 

     

                “Is Alex back yet?” she mumbled.

     

                Eliza looked up quickly, her surprised expression softening as she smiled. “They got back around lunchtime. I told them to come in tomorrow.”

     

                “Mm. Okay.”

     

                “Your mom should be back soon.”

     

                The door cracked open almost immediately after Eliza finished speaking and Lena watched Lillian step inside through narrowed eyes, a laugh welling up in her chest and slurring together as it fell from her lips.

     

                “Speak of the devil.”

     

                “I thought I was starting to grow on you,” Lillian drawled, shutting the door and setting down a paper bag on the tray. “Here. Eat.”

     

                Lillian pressed a paper bowl into Lena’s hands and she popped the lid off to a waft of steam hitting her face, the tangy smell hitting her first.

     

                “Eat the soup first,” Lillian quietly ordered, slipping a spoon into her hand. “If you can keep it down, there’s sashimi and sushi too. Careful - it’s hot.”

     

                Resisting the urge to roll her eyes, Lena gently blew on the miso soup as she watched her mother unpack the bag and hand a box to Eliza. “I got you some too; I assumed the food here would be terrible.”

     

                Chuckling, Eliza took the box. “Thanks, that was kind of you.”

     

                The three of them ate in silence and Lena found the soup gentle on her stomach, a warmth spreading through her as she sipped it slowly, her hunger gradually reigniting. She still couldn’t manage more than a few pieces of salmon and sushi and lay slumped against the pillows as she watched the two older women eat, quietly conversing about their work. It was a bizarre sight to Lena as she watched with apprehension, her mind slowly giving into sleep, even as she fought it off.

     

                It was dark outside by the time Eliza climbed to her feet and announced that she was leaving. She gave Lena’s hand a quick pat as she stood beside her. “I’ll be back in the morning. Get some rest and listen to the doctor’s orders, okay?”

     

                Promising that she would as she gave her a tired smile, Lena watched her leave and closed her eyes as she listened to the hum of the hospital room, which was never quiet but passed for white noise as the silence stretched between her and her mother. Lillian knew she wasn’t asleep though and spoke after a couple of minutes.

     

                “I like her.”

     

                “Mm, she’s nice. She’s been kind to me.”

     

                “I’m glad.”

     

                They lapsed into a moment of silence before Lena sighed. “Did they say if I can go home yet?”

     

                “You know they haven’t.”

     

                “But I don’t like being here.”

     

                “No one likes being in hospital,” Lillian scoffed, rolling her eyes. “You’re here so they can keep an eye on you. They know what they’re doing, so just let them do their job.”

     

                Leaning back against the pillows as disgruntlement washed over her, Lena folded her arms over her chest and pursed her lips. “You’re a doctor; you can look after me.”

     

                “Don’t sulk ,” Lillian said with a quiet tsk. “And I would, but you and I both know I wouldn’t be as soft on you as these doctors here, and neither of us wants that. It’ll only be a few days; I’ll bring you a book tomorrow.”

     

                “Wow, a book,” Lena dully replied, “thanks.”

     

                “Well, you’ll hardly be doing work while you rest. I’ve already called your assistant - Tess, is it?”

     

                “Jess.”

     

                “Right, Jess. I told her you’d be out of office for a couple of weeks.”

     

                Struggling against the soft pillows, Lena scowled as she propped herself up on her elbow. “Weeks? Maybe a week, at the most. But I can’t afford that much time off work.”

     

                Lillian chuckled, her smile thin as she arched an eyebrow, “if ever there was someone who could afford a week off work, it was someone with the surname Luthor. But , to ease your concerns, I’ll be staying until you’re back on your feet again, so I’ll manage the company.”

     

                “Staying?” Lena warily echoed, an apprehensive look on her face, “where are you staying?”

     

                “At a hotel. I’ll call my assistant to book me at my usual one before I leave for the night.”

     

                “Oh.” A frown creased her forehead as she thought for a second, reluctance brewing inside her but quickly quelled as she decided to give her mother the benefit of the doubt. “Well … you could just stay at my place. I have enough spare rooms.”

     

                Blinking in surprise at the forthcoming offer, Lillian opened and closed her mouth for a moment, caught off guard and left stammering. “Oh, well, that’s- thank you, that would be nice.”

     

                “Just don’t go snooping,” Lena snarkily warned her. “And how long are you going to stay for?”

     

                “Until you’re better. Don’t worry, I won’t be interfering in the business; someone just needs to keep a close eye on you to make sure you’re actually resting.”

     

                “Don’t you have your own work to do?”

     

                “I do,” Lillian said with an easy smile, “but all things considered … well, it’s not important.”

     

                Expression clouding, Lena was silent for a few minutes, the quiet noises of the hospital growing louder as the time stretched between them. It could’ve been an hour before she spoke again, her body heavy and the darkness from outside giving no impression of what time it was.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena eventually muttered, “I know how busy you are. I appreciate you coming.”

     

                “You don’t have to thank me for it, Lena,” Lillian said as her mouth turned down at the corners and regret welled up in her eyes. “I know I haven’t always shown up for you in the past, but that’s done now. I like to think if you’d ended up in hospital before now, I would’ve come then too, though.”

     

                A quiet huff of laughter was roughly expelled from Lena’s lungs as her lips twisted into a bitter smile. “I was in the hospital before; I had viral pneumonia a few months after I turned nineteen. I was still working on my own stuff and the flu spread through the office. I guess … I’d been spending more time working than not so my immune system was shot to pieces. Took me out for a week. ”

                

                “You didn’t tell me,” Lillian murmured, her shoulders stiff and an affronted look on her face as she frowned. “I didn’t know.”

     

                “Of course you didn’t,” Lena softly replied, no accusations in her voice. She’d purposely kept it to herself, so wrapped up in her resentment that her mother’s scornful remarks would have been the last thing she’d wanted. Especially so soon after escaping the house, of setting out to do it all on her own with her trust-fund and her ideas. “I didn’t want you to. But … I do now. I believe you, too, when you say you’re trying.”

     

                And she did. Things had shifted with Lillian, and she knew that even if Lillian had shown up at her bedside five years ago, it wouldn’t have been like this. Lex’s death had changed so much between them, and while she was hesitant to trust her, she did believe that Lillian had every intention of trying to patch things up. The rest would come with time and effort, for both of them, and Lena knew it would be painful. 

     

                Lillian stayed until visiting hours ended an hour later, and a nurse came to give her another dose of painkillers for the night as she watched her mother gather her things through hooded eyes. Her fingers were clumsy and cold as Lillian squeezed her hand gently, a clouded expression on her face as she stood over her before she reached out to cup the side of Lena’s face.

     

                “Never scare me like that again,” Lillian firmly muttered.

     

                “I’ll try my best,” Lena said with a wan smile, already inching towards sleep.

     

                Nodding, satisfied, Lillian shifted the blankets up a little higher and smoothed out the scratchy cotton before snatching her hand back. Slinging her handbag over one shoulder, she turned and made for the door, pausing on the threshold and looking back over her shoulder as buttery light made a silhouette of her. Lena couldn’t see her expression but her stomach clenched slightly when she spoke.

     

                “I love you, Lena.”

     

                She didn’t reply, wasn’t even sure if it was something she was supposed to have heard, as genuine and soft as she’d ever heard her mother be, and Lillian slipped out, leaving her to sleep. The night passed by in a drug-fuelled haze with periodic bouts of consciousness as doctors and nurses woke her with their rounds, and once morning had arrived, she found her mother sitting at her bedside, reading through the morning newspaper as sunlight slanted in through the windows.

     

                Consciousness didn’t last long though, and the next time she woke the sunlight was brighter and Lillian was talking quietly on the phone. Blinking back the fog of sleep, Lena yawned and covered her mouth, attracting her mother’s attention, and Lillian quickly hung up after a few muttered words.

     

                “Who was that?”

     

                “Lawyers,” Lillian said after a moment of hesitation.

     

                Eyebrows rising, Lena let out a snort of laughter, “malpractice suit? Malfunctioning products?”

     

                “Family lawyers,” Lillian retorted. “They caught the man who shot you. Otis Graves. They’re already working on the case.”

     

                A faint sigh worked past Lena’s chapped lips as her eyelids closed. Mercy Graves. The name appeared in her mind with the face of the woman her brother had killed. Dark hair, dark eyes. Anger made her tense as she clenched her teeth, feeling her face warm as she drew in a shallow breath.

     

                “Just … leave it.”

     

                “Lena,” Lillian sharply replied, “you could’ve died . He had a gun. I will make sure he’s put away for the maximum sentence.”

     

                Groaning, Lena rubbed at her eyes and pinched the bridge of her nose. “Lex killed his sister, mom. Where’s his sentence? Huh?”

     

                “That’s not a good argument,” Lillian snapped, sinking down onto the chair and sitting ramrod straight as she seethed. “You can’t just let a dangerous man walk free because of guilt.”

     

                “I’m not saying that,” Lena bitingly replied, “but let them sort it out themselves, okay?”

     

                “Lena-”

     

                The door opened then and Lillian trailed off as she glanced over her shoulder and then deflated in her seat. Lena smiled weakly as Alex filed in first with a bouquet of flowers in hand, followed by Kelly with another and then Eliza bringing up the rear. The small room felt crowded with all of them in there and Lillian cleared her throat, still tense and angry as she climbed to her feet.

     

                “I’ll go and get you a proper breakfast,” she told Lena, snatching up her bag and nodding to the three women as she squeezed past and out into the hallway.

     

                Alex arched an eyebrow and Lena shook her head, swallowing the lump in her throat as she pushed herself up more. Her stomach twinged but she pushed through it, sitting upright as a genuine smile stretched across her face.

     

                “You ruined my surprise,” Lena grumbled, narrowing her eyes accusingly. “I really wanted you to have a good weekend.”

     

                “We did. Well, for the first night. That phone call? Not so much,” Alex wryly said, setting the flowers down on the end table. “These ones are off Kara. Those are off us.”

     

                She jerked her thumb at the bouquet that Kelly held and Lena’s heart swelled with fondness for them as she quietly thanked them. Eliza sank down onto a chair while Alex perched on the end of the bed and Kelly stood, arms folded over her chest as she looked at Lena with concern.

     

                “I didn’t think you could get any paler,” Kelly said with a relieved smile.

     

                “Yeah,” Lena roughly sighed, running a hand over her face.

     

                “How’re you feeling?” Alex asked, eyebrows rising as she inspected her.

     

                Grunting, annoyed and exhausted despite getting more sleep in the last twenty-four hours than she had over the last two weeks, Lena shrugged nonchalantly. “I’ve been better.”

     

                Snorting, Alex shook her head as a slow smile spread across her face. “Oh, I bet you’re hating this. Being laid up in bed, everyone fussing over you.”

     

                Making a sound of indignation at the back of her throat, Lena scowled. “Hopefully they’ll let me out tonight.”

     

                “Have you walked today?” Eliza gently asked.

     

                “Not yet. Although, I really could use a shower. I smell … sick. Hospitals smell awful.”

     

                The three of them laughed and Lena flushed but was helped from the bed by strong hands that kept her on her feet as she blinked back the black spots across her field of vision and let her body get used to holding her weight. Eliza went to inform the nurse while Alex hefted a leather overnight bag.

     

                “Is this your stuff?”

     

                “Oh, yeah, I guess my mom brought it in.”

     

                Kelly helped her into the bathroom and a sheen of sweat covered Lena’s brow by the time she made it into the frigid room, harsh light leaving it stark white. She was deposited onto the toilet, clutching her stomach as Kelly ran the water and Alex rummaged through the bag, pulling out new pyjamas with the tags still on that Lena definitely hadn’t bought. They were embroidered silk and she knew without glancing that the labels would be designers frequented by the sort of circles her mother ran in.

     

                “Don’t take the dressing off,” Eliza warned her as she stepped into the open doorway, “you can’t get it wet.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                “Have you been telling them how to do their job again?” Alex snorted, flashing her mother a smile.

     

                Clicking her tongue, Eliza gave her an exasperated look and beckoned her out of the bathroom as she slipped past her and checked the temperature of the water, adjusting it slightly and then stepped up beside Lena and gently tied her hair up out of her face.

     

                “Leave your hair until tomorrow; I know it’s annoying, but you should make it a quick shower this time. Someone will need to stay with you, just in case. Would you prefer if it was ...”

     

                “It’s fine.”

     

                “Alright, sweetie,” Eliza murmured, moving to close the door and then helping Lena to her feet.

     

                It pulled at her stitches and she grit her teeth but allowed herself to be helped towards the cordoned off shower, the plastic curtain drummed with water as steam caressed her clammy face through the gap. Eliza was quick and efficient as she undid the ties at the back of the gown, Lena haughty and unabashed and in too much pain to care - she was a doctor; what hadn’t she seen before? - and as she stepped around the curtain, she listened to Eliza’s stern warning to hold onto the rail.

     

                It was icy to the touch and she hunched over, letting water course down her pale back as it warmed her slightly. It wasn’t hot, and it didn’t scald her skin and strip it of the sickly, antiseptic odour of the hospital, but she worked quickly with the fresh bar of soap Lillian had bought, the smell of cypress and geranium slapping her with the stinging memory of her childhood, the scent so wholly her mother’s that Lena almost dropped it. She gently washed herself clean, resenting the smell but welcoming it in contrast to the stale odour of sweat and the chemical operating room, and when she was done, she shut off the water.

     

                Shivers immediately wracked her shoulders as she clung to the rail and slowly moved towards the curtain. Eliza’s hand shoved a towel through and Lena thanked her through chattering teeth, her body seizing as it tried to quell the tremors, and she wrapped it around herself, wiping her face dry as the curtain was ripped aside.

     

                It was only slightly mortifying to be standing in a towel, dry and shivering, as her girlfriend’s mother helped her dress, mindful of the towel and the dressing on the wound, and Lena studied the ceiling as a muscle twitched in her jaw. She was too proud to need someone to help her like this, but she swallowed it, knowing she couldn’t bend over to pull on the silk pants, that she couldn’t balance on one leg as she pulled warm socks onto her feet. The only way it could’ve been worse was if it had been her mother.

     

                Warm and dressed in soft pyjamas, Lena brushed her teeth mechanically in the mirror with the new toothbrush, rinsing away the foul taste and running her tongue along her clean teeth with palpable relief. The clean smell of deodorant and perfume made her feel more like herself, no longer the dishevelled patient in the hospital bed, and after letting Eliza brush her hair for her, Lena looked more like herself too as she stared at her reflection. Face bare of makeup, she looked young - even younger than she was - and there was a fragile quality to her, eyes wide and sad with bags beneath, and a softness to the sharp edges of her usually taut face.

     

                “You’ll need a new dressing,” Eliza said, resting her hands on Lena’s shoulders and smiling grimly at her reflection.

     

                Turning beneath her touch, Lena felt uncomfortably grateful as she smiled slightly, crooked and rueful. “Thanks, Eliza.”

     

                Briefly touching her face as she gave her a grim smile, her blue eyes radiating warmth, Eliza nodded and then helped her towards the door. When a nurse wheeled in a trolley with medical paraphernalia on it, the trio made space for the young woman as she exposed Lena’s stomach and peeled back the dressing. It had been weeping slightly but wasn’t infected and was still dry, and everyone was silent as it was dabbed with bacitracin and then a fresh dressing was placed over it.

     

                Lillian returned just as the nurse was peeling off the gloves and checking her vitals and pain levels, and Lena met her eyes briefly before avoiding them again as she looked at the nurse and nodded along with her words. Once the nurse left, Lillian moved forwards, setting the bag down on the wheeled tray table and unpacking it quickly.

     

                “You look better,” she murmured.

     

                “Thanks for bringing everything,” Lena earnestly replied.

     

                Slowing, Lillian gave her a fleeting smile and nodded before pulling a tray of coffees out of the bottom and setting it down. She worked one free and smiled wryly. “Here. You’ll be fine to have coffee now.”

     

                Gratitude swept through Lena and she let out a short laugh as she raised the paper cup to her lips and took a sip. It was bitter and hot and she hummed in satisfaction, watching as Lillian handed out the rest and then unloaded the food.

     

                “Bagels and breakfast burritos for everyone,” Lillian announced, handing them to Alex to hand out before she pulled out two containers and set them firmly before Lena. “Granola and fruit salad for you.”

     

                Lena muttered her thanks and slowly ate a few pieces of melon and strawberries under her mother’s watchful eyes, but mostly sipped her coffee, content with the invigorating warmth of the caffeine sliding through her veins.

     

                Alex and Kelly only stayed for an hour, and Eliza left after lunch, Lena already out cold, missing Kara’s call to check in on her, although she wouldn’t know that for hours yet, and Lillian lingered at her bedside long into the night. She’d been hoping to get discharged that evening, but groggy and restless, she found herself succumbing to more painkillers and out cold before she could even voice the idea.

     

                They let her out the next morning though, Lillian calling Eliza to inform her as Lena was given a quick exam and the discharge papers signed with a flourish. A prescription for painkillers was written out for her and she was wheeled out to her parked Porsche, trying not to be too churlish about her mother driving her car, and sat uncomfortably in the passenger seat as they moved through the slow Monday morning traffic, commuters clogging the streets.

     

                Once they reached her house, Lena had to rely heavily on Lillian to get her up the front steps of the brownstone, surprisingly grateful for her mother’s stature as she leaned against her and staggered up them in her pyjamas. Lena nudged Athena away as the dog excitedly bounded over to her upon entry and Lillian towed her through to the living room, easing her down onto the sofa before she went outside to fetch the bags and flowers. 

     

                After fussing around, making tea and watching Lena take her pills, lamenting over the bare state of Lena’s fridge and the mess Athena had made with her water bowl, Lillian busied herself with fetching a blanket and some pillows and ordering groceries for delivery. After that, Lena asked her to help her into the bathroom and endured the bickering argument of whether she needed to be monitored while showering, before Lillian relented and went to fetch clean pyjamas for her to change into.

     

                Washing her hair made Lena feel more herself and she even let her mother change the dressing after she’d dressed, stretching out on the sofa while Lillian perched on the edge of the coffee table and leaned across, doing what Lena could have done for herself but looking particularly pleased with herself as she did it. Then, Lena was left to doze, her tangled hair air drying as Lillian went to shower herself.

     

                The sound of the door opening caught Lena’s attention a few minutes later though, the pipes already hissing with the sound of running water upstairs, and she pushed herself up onto her elbows, craning her neck to see over the arm of the chair.
