She heard the scratching of Athena’s claws on the wooden floorboards, scrambling for traction, and heard Alex’s voice soften as she cooed over the German Shepherd.

     

                “I’m in here,” Lena called out.

     

                Alex stepped into the open archway and raised her eyebrows, hands in her back pockets. “Glad to be home?”

     

                “She’s driving me insane,” Lena hissed as Kelly appeared behind her.

     

                “Your mom?” Kelly asked, looking around. “Where is she?”

     

                “She’s in the shower. It’s the only time she’s left me alone; I don’t know how long she’s staying for but I’m not sure I can handle it for much longer.”

     

                Alex laughed, walking into the living room and flopping down onto the sofa across from Lena, lounging with ease as she raised her eyebrows. “Do you want me to shoot you again so you can go back to the hospital?”

     

                “That’s the sweetest thing you’ve ever said to me,” Lena crooned, pressing a hand to her heart as she smiled wryly and then started to push herself up, pulling the blanket aside and attempting to swing her legs around.

     

                “Where do you think you’re going?” Alex sternly asked her, straightening up just as Kelly quickly crossed the threshold of the room and bore down on her, a hand clamping down on her shoulder.

     

                Lena let out a hiss of pain and frustration, pressing her hand to her side as her heartbeat picked up and her breathing bottomed out. “I was … going to make us some coffee,” she spat through clenched teeth, putting her head in her hands as she waited for the pain to recede. “I can walk, you know.”

     

                “Well, I told Kara that I’d look after you, so how about you sit your ass down and stop trying to do things.”

     

                “Excellent advice,” Lillian called out, materialising in the doorway, nettled as she fixed Lena with a piercing stare. “Good morning.”

     

                “Morning,” Alex cordially greeted her, raking a hand through her hair, “coffee?”

     

                “That would be lovely. Thank you.”

     

                Alex nodded and disappeared through to the kitchen, while Kelly covered Lena with the blanket and then took a seat at the foot of the sofa, fixing her with a stern look. Lena wrinkled her nose at her until they both smiled and then she glanced up at her mother as Lillian’s shadow fell across her.

     

                “You need to take more painkillers.”

     

                Groaning, Lena’s lips thinned with a grimace. “I’m fine . They just make me sleep.”

     

                “I don’t care. You’re taking them,” Kelly said.

     

                “Why is it that you always make such a fuss whenever I ask you to do something, but when it’s Eliza, you give in without argument?” Lillian snippily replied, picking up the bottle of rattling pills and thrusting them out. “Actually, don’t answer that. Just take them before I have to call her and get her over here to force them down your throat.”

     

                “What, are you guys best friends now,” Lena snorted, taking the bottle and shaking two out into her palm.

     

                Ignoring her, Lillian looked down at her. “You should take them with food; what do you want?”

     

                Shrugging, Lena twisted her torso and reached towards the coffee table for the half-full glass of water, wincing as pain lanced through her stomach, pulling taut. Slender fingers wrapping around her wrist, Lillian stopped her, stooped over as she fixed Lena with a hard stare.

     

                “Don’t. You’re going to rip your stitches again.”

     

                A rough sigh was exhaled forcefully as she snatched her hand back and watched as Lillian picked the cup up for her. “Can’t I do anything?” she muttered.

     

                “Don’t sigh. And no, you can’t. Not until the stitches are out.”

     

                “That’ll be another two weeks. You know I live by myself, right? Like, I am capable of looking after myself.”

     

                “That’s yet to be proven,” Lillian sniffed derisively, watching as Lena swallowed the pills and washed them down with a mouthful of water. “Bacon and eggs, then?”

     

                Raising her eyebrows, Lena snorted with laughter, “you know how to make bacon and eggs?”

     

                “Really, Lena,” Lillian tutted, “how hard can it be? It’s bacon and eggs.”

     

                “You’d be surprised.”

     

                Kelly covered her mouth with a hand, stifling her laughter as her cheeks dimpled with a smile. “So, that’s where you get your cooking skills from?”

     

                With a grim look, Lena slyly flipped her off as Lillian stalked out to the kitchen. Alex returned with four mugs of coffee gingerly grasped in her hands and she set them down on the coffee table before sinking back down onto the sofa and reaching for the remote. She flipped through the channels while Kelly showed Lena photos of their sole day in Joshua Tree, looking like they’d made the most of their short time there while they’d had the chance. 

     

                The banging and cursing from the kitchen didn’t escape their notice as they chatted away and shared knowing grins over coffee, and it was ten minutes later when Lillian reappeared, looking haughtily flustered as she set a plate down in Lena’s lap. She was pleasantly surprised at the relatively normal looking bacon and eggs, even if the eggs weren’t soft and the smell of burnt toast lingered in the air, begging the question of how many slices she’d gone through to present her daughter with the ones on her plate, just a little too heavily toasted, but still edible.

     

                She thanked her and dutifully ate it all, the nauseous edge of the pills vanishing by the time she was done, right on time for the drowsy side effects to kick in. Lightly dozing, Lena made mumbled conversation as she drifted in and out, but couldn’t recall what they all talked about as her mind aimlessly wandered in and out of sleep.

     

                Alex and Kelly left around lunchtime, and Lena slept through the afternoon, until she was shaken awake by Lillian. Blinking in surprise, Lena rubbed at her eyes and frowned, trying to get her bearings as the blue of dusk stretched the shadows and shapes of the room, the muted TV flashing as commercials played, and she shifted up slightly with confusion on her face.

     

                “It’s Kara,” Lillian softly told her, holding out the phone that had escaped Lena’s notice.

     

                It would’ve been early hours in the morning in Afghanistan, and Lena was suddenly wide awake, clearing her throat as she took the phone. Her heart lurched in her chest and a sleepy smile crossed her face as she looked at Kara’s face on the screen.

     

                “Hi,” Kara murmured, her expression sheepish. “Sorry, I didn’t realise you were asleep. Your mom insisted on waking you up.”

     

                “She’d kill me if I let her miss another call,” Lillian scoffed as Kara laughed, her eyes crinkling at the corners on the screen. Lillian softly cleared her throat and arched her eyebrows, pointedly. “I have some calls to make; let me know if you need anything and don’t get up.”

     

                Nodding, Lena settled back down on the sofa, raking a hand through her hair as she blinked owlishly as Lillian switched the lights on as she left. Her voice was thick with sleep when she spoke. “Hi. I missed you.”

     

                “I missed you too,” Kara lovingly smiled, looking marginally less stressed than the last time Lena had spoken to her. “How’re you feeling?”

     

                “Well … Alex offered to shoot me again to put me back in the hospital, so … there’s that.”

     

                Shaking her head, Kara softly laughed, “Listen to your mom, okay? Just this once. And my mom. They both know what they’re talking about.”

     

                “I know, I know,” she sighed defeatedly. “You know I don’t like being told what to do though. And my mom. God. I almost preferred it when she ignored me.”

     

                “You don’t mean that.”

     

                Pursing her lips, Lena’s eyelids shuttered as she inhaled. A sigh - caught and held. “No, I don’t,” she admitted, rubbing her eyes. “I just … I want to do something. I haven’t looked at any paperwork in three days. The business-”

     

                “I, for one, am glad you’re being forced to take a break. It’s well overdue. You work too much - it’s not good for you. You need to take care of yourself, okay? And promise me you’ll work from home if you’re ever going to be doing work that late.”

     

                “I promise,” Lena ruefully swore, a glimmer in her green eyes as she smiled. Studying Kara’s face for a long moment, Lena cocked her head to the side, her eyelids closing as she smiled wryly, the wariness and sadness so plainly written there that it couldn’t have been about her gunshot wound. “Now, are you going to tell me what’s wrong?”

     

                “Wrong?” Kara laughed, the sound strained, “it’s nothing.”

     

                With an exasperated groan, Lena fixed her with a stern look that would’ve rivaled Lillian’s. “Don’t try that with me, baby. I might not be there with you, but I can see you, and I can see that none of your smiles have reached your eyes. And don’t lie - I can tell when you do.”

     

                “You need to rest. We’ll talk about it when you’re better.”

     

                Roughly sighing, Lena’s tone was brittle as she replied, “I’m fine . Don’t deflect; tell me what’s wrong. Otherwise … I’ll just think it’s worse than what it actually is.”

     

                They were both quiet for a minute, and she would’ve thought the call had frozen with a bad connection if it wasn’t for Kara’s rapid blinking and restless shifting. She silently debated whether or not she should tell her, that much was abundantly clear, and Lena’s patience was wearing thin as her chest ached sharply.

     

                “Kara-”

     

                “It’s just … you know I enlisted so I could go to college. Well, they were talking and they said- well, if I signed another contract I could do my masters, you know? They’d cover my tuition for it too.”

     

                Lena’s mouth opened and closed as she was struck speechless, the breath caught in her throat as if the air had been stolen from her. Her voice was hoarse when she replied, dread spreading through her as her body stiffened.

     

                “You- you mean … you want to stay longer? You want to- to reenlist?”

     

                “Lena-”

     

                “No,” Lena snapped, her eyes bright with panic and wounded confusion as she struggled to her feet, kicking off blankets and feeling the white-hot pain in her stomach as she stood and started anxiously pacing.

     

                “Wha- sit back down. Now.”

     

                “What the hell is wrong with you? Why would you do that? Why would you even think- you said that this was it, that you’d be home for good afterwards.”

     

                “I know what I said,” Kara passively replied, rubbing at the back of her neck as she gave Lena a pleading look. “But, it’s just- what am I going to do when I get back? Work at a fashion magazine? Run a column? No one is going to hire me for anything worthwhile when all I have is just … this. This is the only thing I know how to do, okay? And it’s not real journalism, and I don’t have billions to throw at a masters course or a doctorate. I wasn’t raised like you; when Jeremiah died, we were lucky that Eliza has a good job, but even then, a small town doctor isn’t exactly making a lot of money. And Alex will be paying off her debt for a long time, so what else am I supposed to do, huh?”

     

                “I’ll pay for it,” Lena adamantly replied, “if it’s money you want then I’ll give it to you.”

     

                Kara scoffed, her face flushing as she turned her head aside, a muscle twitching in her jaw. “Don’t be ridiculous; I don’t want your money. ”

     

                “Don’t be so proud,” Lena snapped, coming to an abrupt stop. 

     

                “I’m not being proud,” Kara defensively replied. “I’m just not looking for a handout. That’s not what I was asking for. Now, sit down.”

     

                “I didn’t say you were,” Lena heatedly replied, bristling now as she sank back down to the sofa, spine stiff and shoulders tense, even as her body gratefully sank onto the pillows. “But why do you think you don’t deserve anything good without having to kill yourself for it? Huh? If you want to go back to college, I have money - take the money.”

     

                “No,” Kara exploded, brimming with frustration. She ran a hand over her face as they both sat there in silence for a second, and she wilted as she exhaled slowly, her voice softening when she continued. “I just- I want you to tell me what to do.”

     

                “You already know what I want you to do.”

     

                “No, but … I need you to tell me. I need to know that if- if I don’t come home, you’ll still be there. Because if you won’t, then … well, then it’s easy.”

     

                Lena made a scathing sound at the back of her throat, a bitter taste in her mouth as she squeezed her eyes shut and shook her head. “You need to make that decision for yourself; I won’t be the one who decides what you do with your life. I’ll still be here but … you know how I feel, so if you do it, then do it for yourself, but don’t put it on me to ease the guilt by choosing for you, okay? Because I won’t do that.”

     

                Tears stung her eyes and she could see Kara’s throat bob as she swallowed thickly, “I’m sorry. I-”

     

                “You should go,” Lena told her, her head aching as she rubbed at her forehead, unable to meet Kara’s eyes, even through a camera. “I, uh, I need to have dinner so I can take more painkillers so …”

     

                “Okay,” Kara miserably murmured, surreptitiously wiping at her eyes as she cleared her throat. “Well … I love you.”

     

                “Yeah, I love you too.”

     

                “Try and get some rest, okay?”

     

                Lena snorted with laughter and murmured a vague assurance before the line went dead and she tossed the phone onto the coffee table. Stretching out on the sofa, she dug the heels of her palms into her eyes and breathed slowly, trying to unwind the tension in her body as a shakiness in her stomach made her feel sick.

     

                Lillian found her like that five minutes later, murmuring a sound of surprise as she walked in and found her already done talking to Kara. She inhaled deeply and exhaled roughly, her body going limp as she blinked up at the ceiling.

     

                “Mom? Can you help, please,” she asked in a halting, pitifully small voice.

     

                “What’s wrong?”

     

                Her cheeks burned with shame and she covered her face with a hand, swallowing past the constricted feeling in her throat. “My stitches. I- I think I … pulled them.”

     

                Lillian murmured something about the first aid kit and vanished, the sound of running water and then her footsteps nearing falling on Lena’s ears as she waited. The smell of the hand soap Lena preferred clung to Lillian’s hands as she squeezed onto the edge of the sofa beside Lena, unzipping the first aid kit and setting it on top of the rumpled blankets.

     

                “Let’s take a look,” Lillian gently murmured.

     

                The patient understanding caught Lena off guard and tears stung her eyes as she blinked rapidly, swallowing audibly. She could feel her mother’s eyes on her face, but Lillian was silent for a few moments as she eased Lena’s shirt up out of the way and inched the waistband down. Peeling back the dressing, Lillian took in the sight of the stitches, a neat row along the short incision where they’d extracted the bullet. It was beaded with red, and as Lillian felt around the angry red edges of it, she hummed disconcertingly at the heat in the inflamed wound.

     

                She’d expected anger and scorn, but Lillian was unusually kind, which only made the building urge to cry in Lena’s chest that much more unbearable as she watched her mother assess the injury, gently pressing around the edges of it with her cool hands. Lena winced when she dabbed an antiseptic topical solution on it, cleaning it out to stave off infection, and at the sharp intake of breath, Lillian murmured softly without looking up.

     

                “It’ll be okay.”

     

                Lena made a vague sound of acknowledgement, struggling to draw in shallow breaths as anger simmered below the surface. 

     

                “Do you want to tell me what happened?”

     

                “Nothing,” Lena said with a jaded sigh. “I just … got up too fast.”

     

                “Well,” Lillian murmured, choosing to ignore the obvious omission, “you don’t need me to tell you that was stupid.”

     

                Letting out a weak chuckle, Lena hummed in agreement and watched as Lillian opened a new dressing and carefully stretched it over the wound. She smoothed out the edges and Lena brooded until she was done.

     

                “There. All done. Don’t irritate it again; you’ll only end up with an infection and an ugly scar if you do.”

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                “Pain levels?”

     

                Lips twisting sourly, Lena hesitated. “Three.”

     

                “So, a six,” Lillian coolly replied, gathering up the used supplies and climbing to her feet. “Don’t worry, I’ll leave the painkillers until you’re ready for bed. Can I make you some tea?”

     

                A timid smile reluctantly curled Lena’s lips and she nodded. “Please.”

     

                She wallowed in her other thoughts as she listened to the sound of the kettle and her mother’s movements in the kitchen. It struck her as odd - Lena had never grown up in anywhere that had felt and sounded like a home, but hearing Lillian moving around, caring for her while she was injured, it felt like how she imagined her childhood had been if they’d been normal.

     

                When Lillian walked back in and set a cup down on the coffee table, she noticed the thoughtful look on Lena’s face and cocked her head to the side. “What is it?”

     

                She leaned down to press the back of her hand against Lena’s brow, checking her temperature and then arching an eyebrow expectedly. Lena gave her a thin smile, her eyelids closing for a brief moment as she conjured the images to her mind.

     

                “I was just thinking about something I’d almost forgotten.”

     

                “Oh?”

     

                “The last time I can remember you looking after me when I was unwell. I must’ve been … twelve?”

     

                “Thirteen. You were thirteen. You had chickenpox. It was the first week of the school holidays; we’d just gotten back from Switzerland. We were only there for two days and then your father brought us all home and went on one of his ‘business trips’ . You managed to hide it from me until it showed up on your face. You wouldn’t let me put the lotion on for you and I told you you couldn’t do everything yourself, which only made you fight harder. I think we drove each other mad the entire time you had it.”

     

                Lillian chuckled fondly, shaking her head as she dwelled in the memory. Lena stared at her for a long moment, a slack look on her face as surprise washed over her that Lillian could so easily recall the details.

     

                “I think I’m driving you mad now,” Lillian chuckled, amusement softening her gaze as she pressed her lips into a flat line and stared at her. 

                

                “I think the feeling is mutual.”

     

                “You should eat. Anything in particular for dinner?”

     

                “I don’t know. Just have a look at some good takeouts.”

     

                “Takeaway isn’t nutritious,” she lectured her, taking a sip of tea. “You need something with nutrients. Something home cooked.”

     

                Snorting, Lena’s eyebrows flew up in a sceptical look. “And are you going to be cooking? Because, no offence, mom, but I think bacon and eggs was your limit.”

     

                Lips thinning, Lillian thought for a moment and then nodded, an anxious edge to the motion. “A valid point. Takeaway it is.”

     

                The two of them ate ramen and watched a movie, the night spent in companionable quietness, and Lena didn’t strain herself further. Lillian insisted she have an early night, and it was a long, bickering process to get Lena upstairs. For the first time, living in a house with so many stories seemed like a hindrance, and she cursed the old steps as each one made her side ache and Lillian berated her for going too fast.

     

                Getting into her bedroom, Lena sank down onto her bed with relief, breathing heavily and covered in a cold sweat as she shakily wiped her brow on her sleeve. Lillian turned the sheets down for her and made sure she had a glass of water and some painkillers for the middle of the night before she quietly bid her goodnight and left her in the comfort of her own bed.

     

                She couldn’t remember sleeping so well, waking later than usual and fully rested. If not for the pall that her conversation with Kara had cast over her mood, she would’ve felt fine. After showering in her ensuite and dressing in clean loungewear, she made her way out into the hallway and to the staircase, easing herself down a single step, which creaked, when her mother’s voice called out from above her.

     

                “You’d better not be on the stairs by yourself.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, slightly peeved that Lillian had, potentially, commandeered her office, Lena sighed. “Should I teleport then?”

     

                Lillian’s footsteps grew louder and she appeared around the end of the switchback, giving Lena an exasperated look before she helped her downstairs, one hobbling step at a time, her manner brisk and her grip tight, as if she was afraid Lena would trip and fall down two flights. Situating her back on the sofa, Lena brought her another breakfast of bacon and eggs, pleased to be able to cook something, and Lena ate quickly, chasing it down with pills as her mother picked at her own.

     

                It was a quiet day and Lena spent most of it flicking through various books and versing Lillian at chess after they ate lunch together, her side pulling taut whenever she moved a piece, but the stitches staying firmly closed. She thrashed her three times in succession before Lillian told her to lay back down and rest, although there was a note of pride in her voice, pleased that her daughter had retained her skills at the game Lillian had helped teach her. 

     

                At mid-afternoon, there was a knock on the door while Lillian was upstairs working on something or another in Lena’s office, and Lena was stretched out on the sofa, Athena’s head in her lap as she sat dutifully beside her to have the scruff of her neck scratched. At the sound, Lena hauled herself up with mild discomfort and opened the door to reveal Alex, Kelly and Eliza, smiling widely as she ushered them into the hallway.

     

                “Hi. Hi, Eliza.”

     

                “Hi, sweetie, how’re you feeling today?” she asked, cupping Lena’s face in her hands as she studied her.

     

                “Better,” Lena said with an uneven smile, hesitating before she continued, her expression darkening. “I, uh, did you- did you speak to Kara yesterday?”

     

                Eliza rubbed her back and Alex made a scathing sound as she hung her coat up and moved through to the kitchen, while Kelly gave her a grim look. “We did. I was hoping she’d choose differently now that she has you.”

     

                “I was hoping she’d choose differently for herself,” Lena murmured, her brow creasing with worry.

     

                “It’s selfless that you’d let her make her own decision,” Eliza said, squeezing Lena’s arm and then looping her arm through the crook of her elbow to give her some support as she led her through to the living room. “I, on the other hand, am too selfish; it’s hard to be a mother without your kids at home, but it’s even harder when one of them goes off to a warzone.”

     

                A prickle of guilt made Lena duck her head as she chewed her bottom lip and quietly admitted, “I’m not as selfless as you think; I don’t want her to reenlist.”

     

                “I’d be a bit concerned if you weren’t,” Eliza chuckled, the sound warm but laced with sadness. “Now, you need to sit.”

     

                “You know, I used to think that having one mom was bad,” Lena said, her face puckering with bewildered amusement as she sank back down onto the couch cushions, paling slightly at the twinge. “But having both of you here has made me realise that having two is much worse.”

     

                Eliza laughed as she tucked the blanket in around her and then stroked her hair, her face creasing with warmth as she looked lovingly down at Lena. “I, on the other hand, thought that having three daughters was wonderful , but then you came along and I realised that four is much better. Now, speaking of your mother, where is she?”

     

                “The office.”

     

                Nodding, Eliza left her to rest until Alex and Kelly descended on her and walked upstairs, her footsteps growing fainter as she disappeared up through the old bones of the house.

     

                “Hey, can I open some wine?” Kelly’s voice carried through to her.

     

                “Help yourself,” Lena called back, “just pour me a glass too!”

     

                Alex barked a laugh and shouted back, “don’t even think about it, kid.”

     

                “It’s medicinal!”

                

                “That’s bullshit! No alcohol with strong painkillers; you already know that. And as a pharmacist, I certainly know it.”

     

                She materialised at Lena’s side with a mineral water a moment later, and Lena was feeling sorry for herself as she twisted the cap off and scowled as Alex patted the top of her head. Taking a sip, she watched as Kelly brought Alex’s glass in for her and they cozied up together on the sofa. It made Lena’s mood sour, missing Kara and feeling equally angry at her too.

     

                The three of them bickered about dinner options as Alex scrolled through their options on her phone, and Lena and Kelly shot them down, and they’d narrowed it down to pizzas or kebabs by the time Lillian and Eliza came downstairs. They were at odds with each other as they stood in the doorway, Lillian standing inches taller and coolly regal, every inch the businesswoman, while Eliza was softer in her jeans and cardigans, radiating warmth, yet Lena knew a unified attack when she saw one.

     

                She was already softly groaning when Lillian stepped into the room, arms folded over her chest and cleared her throat. “Word leaked that you were shot and that an arrest has been made. The prosecution will be quick but there’ll be a lot of buzz around it, so I was thinking it might be good for you to take a break until it’s all over.”

     

                “You’re more than welcome to come and stay with me,” Eliza took over, picking up the thread of the conversation and revealing the purpose of their coordinated attack. “The fresh air in Midvale will do you some good - without reporters hovering around the office.”

     

                “I spoke to your CFO; she seems capable of keeping things under control. And, of course, you’ll be working from home,” Lillian continued.

     

                Lena hated to readily agree with them, and thought they were being too overly-cautious, and hated to be away from the office for longer than strictly necessary, but she knew they were right. Reporters and a high-profile trial with her name attached to it would only make it harder for her to go about her usual routine, and she bit the inside of her cheek as she was quiet for a minute.

     

                “Alright. Fine.”

     

                “I’ll be heading back tomorrow,” Eliza said with a small smile, “you can come whenever you’re up to the flight.”

     

                Nodding, Lena grimaced faintly and brooded as the conversation turned back towards dinner. They decided on pizza and she picked at her two slices as they cooled, the cheese hardening and the fact that Kara hadn’t called yet weighing heavily on her, while the other four women drank wine and chatted away amicably. 

     

                When they left, it was late and Lena was tired, but she still saw them to the door, rubbing Kelly’s arm as she passed by before she gave Eliza a hug, mindful of her stitches, and felt the swell of gratitude in her chest.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena whispered. “Thank you for being there when I woke up, for looking after me.”

     

                Pulling back, Eliza cupped her cheek and smiled. “I’ll see you soon, okay?”

     

                Nodding, Lena gave her a quick smile and Eliza kissed her cheek before she left. Once the three of them were gone, Lena locked the door and rubbed at her burning eyes, the painkillers she’d taken earlier wearing off and leaving a dull ache spreading throughout her heavy body. Her wince as she walked didn’t go unnoticed by Lillian, who had been hovering in the foyer.

     

                “Pain level?”

     

                “A four,” Lena shrugged.

     

                “So, a seven,” Lillian surmised with faint amusement. “Come on. Time for bed.”

     

                Lena didn’t argue as Lena fetched painkillers and a glass of water, holding them in one hand as she wrapped her other around Lena’s waist and helped guide her upstairs. Athena followed them up and curled up on the bed set up in Lena’s room, while Lena gingerly sat down on the bed and got beneath the covers. 

     

                Knocking back the pills without protest, she lay down and her face crumpled with amusement as Lillian tucked her in, only offering a small sigh and eye roll as she let her do it. Secretly, she was grateful that Lillian was there to look after her - it almost made Lena feel like a child again, or rather, the way she should’ve felt growing up. Telling the lights to dim, Lena felt her eyelids grow heavy and stared at Lillian through slits as her mother lingered on the edge of the bed, smoothing out the quilt.

     

                “Goodnight,” Lena whispered.

     

                Softly sighing, looking weary and regretful, Lillian reached out to brush the hair out of Lena’s face, her touch light and gentle. “You’re so beautiful; you deserved more.”

                

                “More?”

     

                “Mm. You were always the best of us all; I should’ve given up more for you.”

     

                Lena noticed the sheen in her eyes, caught by the dim lights, and the slight tremor in Lillian’s voice. It frightened her a little and her voice was thick when she replied.

     

                “It’s okay, you- you did the best you could. I forgive you.”

     

                She’d never imagined being able to say those words to her, never while actually meaning them, and she wasn’t sure if it was the drugs blurring the edges of her mind that made her tongue looser, or whether the honesty came from days of Lillian caring for her. All Lena knew was that it surprised her how much she meant it, and how easy it was to let go of old resentments for the sake of herself. She felt lighter for the admission.

     

                Lillian’s smile turned bitter, but her eyes were tender as she stroked the curve of Lena’s cheekbone. “I still remember the first time I met you.”

     

                “Me too.”

     

                “No,” Lillian whispered, her eyelids closing. “That wasn’t it. I never told you, but we met before; you were still a baby.”

     

                The jolt of surprise banished the haze of sleep that had been creeping up on her, and Lena’s eyelashes fluttered as she tried to keep her eyes open. “Can you tell me now?”

     

                Sighing, Lillian got to her feet and then rounded the bed, climbing on and stretching out parallel to her daughter. Lena let her head loll to the side as she looked at her, watching the tautness of Lillian’s face as she picked her words carefully.

     

                “You were … six months old. Your mother was paid off to get rid of you, but she never did. She never asked for anything either, but … when I found out, I secretly went to see her. You look so much like her.” There was a note of pain in Lillian’s voice as she spoke slowly, quietly, reopening an old wound as she spoke. “She had red hair though; I’m not sure if you remember. And that accent , dear lord, I could barely understand a word. I went there with every intention of taking you home with me, writing her a cheque for as much money as she wanted, just so I could look at your father and say ‘ see? She’s mine too. I won’t let you ruin our family.’ But, of course, I didn’t. I- I couldn’t . I couldn’t bring myself to do that, because … I saw how much she loved you, and I knew that I could’ve given you the world, but never that. I couldn’t have loved you like that. I left instead, and then four years later, she died and I- … I argued to let them give you to someone else, but he brought you home without telling me. Opposing him was never a good idea, so you stayed, but I knew even then that it would ruin you. I’m sorry.”

     

                Lillian sighed, the sound soft and regretful as she blinked up at the ceiling and stewed in her bitterness. “I’m sorry. Do you hear me?”

     

                But Lena didn’t, already fast asleep from the pills, her breaths deep and slow as her lips parted and her eyelashes fluttered. Smiling bittersweetly as she looked at her, Lillian studied Lena’s profile and reached out to lovingly stroke her cheek, sadness filling her cold, blue eyes as she clenched her teeth. 

     

                She eased herself up, careful not to jostle the mattress too much, although she doubted Lena would notice, as far gone as she was. Moving around the bed, she pulled the blankets up under her daughter’s chin and looked down at her with a clouded look on her face before she leaned down and softly kissed her forehead, something she would never have attempted if Lena was awake, as angry and resentful as she was.

                “I love you, my stubborn girl,” Lillian sighed, smoothing her hair back and then switching off the lamp before she left.

    Chapter 33

                Friday evening, Lena found herself on her jet again, heading to Midvale for her sabbatical with Alex and Kelly. They were just staying for the weekend, keeping her company as she settled in, and Lena would’ve been lying if she said there wasn’t some lingering anxiety about living with Eliza for the next week or so while she waited for things to blow over. A part of her was relieved though; Lillian had left that morning, back to Metropolis and her research, and Lena wasn’t quite ready to be left alone in her empty house again.

     

                Her bullet wound was healing well, scabbed over and not quite as sore, leaving her able to walk without relying on someone else - for the most part - and dress herself with only some pain as the stitches pulled. She would’ve been fine to go back to work, if it wasn’t for the arraignment, but she doubted anyone would have let her even without it, Alex and Kelly almost as bad as her mother for fretting over her. 

     

                Brooding as she lay stretched out on the leather bench, where she’d been pretending to sleep as her painkillers left her drowsy, Lena listened to the quiet murmur of Alex and Kelly’s conversation from where they sat at the other end of the plane, on opposite sides of the table. Kara’s absence was keenly felt by Lena, and she felt wallowed in dejected annoyance as she listened to the sounds of the jet, feeling cold and restless as she thought of her girlfriend. 

     

                She’d spoken to Kara every day since the day she hadn’t called, Lena’s nettling remark about her not calling making Kara realise that avoidance wasn’t the best option, but they still never broached the topic of what choice Kara was going to make. Lena wanted to yell at her, to curse her out for even considering it, but most of all she just wanted to cry at the thought of Kara going again. She wasn’t even back and she was already considering being okay with going again. Lena was committed to her earlier words though, that it was Kara’s decision to make alone, and she wouldn’t tell her what to do. Kara knew what she wanted her to do, but Lena wouldn’t pick for her and carry the burden of that choice around with her. There could be a day where Kara would resent her for it.

     

                Still brooding when the captain let them know they were going to be landing soon, Lena pushed thoughts of Kara aside and sat up, her stomach flaring up with a dull ache as she raked a hand through her hair and murmured softly to Athena as she scratched her beneath the chin. Buckling herself in, Lena opened the shades covering the window and looked out at the sprawling pines and the sliver of the coastline, the ocean grey and the sky overcast.

     

                A car was waiting for them when they touched down on the private airstrip and Lena shivered as she donned a coat and stepped out of the jet. Oregon was already well into autumn and rain lightly dotted the tarmac as they all rushed towards the car, bundling into the back as Athena tried to squeeze in with them, before Lena nudged her through the partition and into the passenger seat. 

     

                Still groggy, she somewhat dozed as they made their way through the forest of coniferous trees, crowding in close on either side of the twisting roads, short cliffs or lichen covered rock and mossy logs making the place feel so green , an alien contrast to National City’s dusty browns and greys. Lena already felt that strange sensation of peace spreading through her chest at the prospect of Midvale and all its quiet, small town charm. A break didn’t seem like such a bad idea.

     

                She was doubly glad for it when they pulled up outside the house, the car parked on the steep driveway behind Eliza’s SUV, watching as Eliza opened the front door and stepped outside, wearing a puffer vest over a plaid shirt and jeans and holding her arms open. Alex hugged her mom as Lena took her time getting out of the car, Kelly hovering nearby as she resisted the urge to help her. Slightly out of breath, Lena emerged and squeezed Kelly’s arm as they moved towards the front door, the driver fetching their things and Athena already roaming the front yard.

     

                “My girls!” Eliza beamed, wrapping Lena and Kelly in a double hug, kissing their cheeks and then putting her arms around their shoulders as she ushered them towards the door.

     

                “Thanks again for having me,” Lena said as she wiped her feet on the bristly door mat.

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Eliza brought up the rear, holding open the screen door for Athena to slip past her, while the driver left their bags just inside the door. Kicking off her heeled boots inside the door, Lena sighed contentedly at the faint smell of salt air and petrichor as rain clouds rolled in. 

     

                “Let me get a good look at you then,” Eliza said as she slipped into the kitchen and looked over her shoulder, taking in Lena’s drawn face and tutting. “You haven’t been resting.”

     

                “All I do is sleep,” Lena said with a strained laugh.

     

                “But you’re not resting . You carry so much stress with you; it’s not good for you, honey. How’re your stitches healing?”

     

                Lena shrugged half-heartedly as she smiled softly, “my mom says they’re fine.”

     

                “Good, good. Are you having tea or coffee?”

     

                “Whatever you’re having. I’ll be back down in a minute.”

     

                She moved back out into the hallway and took in the pile of bags and dog supplies left in the hallway, the driver slamming the trunk closed outside. Lena pushed open the screen door and raised a hand in thanks as he glanced over before ducking into the car with a terse nod. Grabbing her bag, she lifted it with a grunt and looked up at the bark of objection.

     

                “Hey! Leave it,” Alex called down to her from the top of the stairs, hands braced on either side of the wall at the top before she came thundering down the steps. “I’ll get it.”

     

                Lena let her take it from her and murmured a quiet thank you before following Alex upstairs and into Kara’s bedroom. She paused in the doorway, a sad smile curling her lips as she looked around at it, taking in the unchanged decor from her last visit and deluding herself into thinking, for a brief moment, that Kara would come walking up behind her, safe and sound. Of course, she didn’t, and after Alex set her bags down for her, Lena sank down onto the bed.

     

                “You good?”

     

                She looked up and smiled tiredly, rubbing at her eyes, “yeah, fine. Thanks, Alex.”

     

                Nodding, Alex made her way downstairs and Lena smoothed her hands over the freshly washed sheets, breathing in the lavender detergent and sighing softly. Her attention snagged on the framed photo of Kara and her parents, her expression softening at the sight of Kara, so young and a completely different person to who she was now. Lena wondered how much would have been different if they’d been raised by completely different people, and she couldn’t bring herself to resent the way that things had turned out, for all the pain and hurt she’d felt because of it. Even now, as annoyed as she was with Kara, it was worth it.

     

                Sighing again, she pushed herself to her feet and made the slow, arduous process back downstairs to drink her coffee and relax. They bundled up on the sofas in the living room, Lena pulling a blanket into her lap as she stared out at the dark rain clouds sweeping in over the choppy ocean, a chill seeping in through the windows as the wind rattled them. It was peaceful and Lena sipped her coffee and mostly listened, preoccupied with her own thoughts as the painkillers left her vaguely muddled and reserved.

     

                They hadn’t left until Alex and Kelly had finished work, and the sunlight was already fading fast as they talked and relaxed after the flight, and as the shadows lengthened and they sat in the warm glow of the living room lights, Lena felt herself nodding off every few minutes, her eyelids growing heavy. Eliza was next to her and occasionally shifted the blanket further over her knees or adjusted the pillow as she carried on the conversation without interruption. Lena would’ve been content to fall asleep right then and there, a sense of peace spreading through her, washing away the culminating stress of a long week. 

     

                Eliza had made a chicken noodle soup and Lena roused herself from the sofa, disgruntled and heavy-lidded, long enough to slowly spoon some into her mouth at the kitchen table, her shoulders sloped and a permanent furrow to her heavy-set brows as she squinted through sleep. She insisted on helping tidy up afterwards, stacking bowls and drying cutlery, before Eliza tugged her away with a glass of water and her pills waiting for her.

     

                “Go to bed,” Eliza gently ordered her after that, cupping Lena’s shoulders as she opened her mouth to argue. “You came here to rest.”

     

                Smiling tiredly, Lena reluctantly agreed and ended up turning in for an early night, murmuring goodnight before slipping away upstairs. Changing into Kara’s pyjamas that she’d packed, she crawled in between the sheets and felt her body go slack, her mind quick to follow as everything darkened.

     

                The next day, she woke before the sunrise, her phone vibrating on the nightstand as the pre-dawn dimness lightened the sky to deep grey through the open curtains and the window beyond. The faint orange glow of a streetlight cut through the dark and Lena blinked back sleep as she raked a hand through her hair, reaching for her phone. 

     

                It was Kara, and answered it as she reached for the bedside lamp, snapping it on to offer some light. From the clock on the nightstand, she could see that it was just past five in the morning, which meant it was almost six at night for Kara. Rubbing at her tired eyes, she watched the video connect on the screen and her face creased with a tender smile.

     

                “Hi,” she thickly greeted her.

     

                “Morning,” Kara softly murmured in reply, looking antsy and tired as a sad smile twitched on her lips. “Sorry, I didn’t want to wake you, but I- well, I miss you.”

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena lightly replied, opening her eyes wide as she tried to make herself wake up properly. “You look tired. Long day?”

     

                Kara hummed distractedly, running a hand over her face as she looked away from the camera. “I, uh, there was a skirmish last night, on one of the missions. A few casualties. We had to go and report on it. I’m sure it’ll be all over the news soon.”

     

                Lena stilled, a quiet rigidness to her shoulders as she hunched in bed, the blankets pulled around her as she huddled. “I- you- were you there? I mean … you’re okay, right?”

     

                Sighing heavily, Kara nodded, “I’m fine. We got there for the aftermath. It just- it was … it’s not … pretty.”

     

                Choking on a breath, Lena’s mouth thinned and she swallowed around the lump in her throat. Bitterness welled up and she clenched her teeth as she breathed slowly for a second, her stomach twisting itself into uncomfortable knots. 

     

                “Hey, it’s okay. I’m fine.”

     

                “No, it’s not okay, Kara,” Lena quietly snapped, trying her hardest to keep her voice down as everyone else slept. “It’s not- none of this is okay. I don’t want to hear about how- how dangerous it is, about … people dying.”

     

                “What, do you want me to lie to you instead?”

     

                “I want you to come home,” Lena exclaimed, her voice sounding too loud in the stillness of the early morning, hanging heavily in the air as suffocating silence punctuated it.

     

                Her breaths were coming faster, shallow and uneven, and she could feel the pressure of a headache behind her eyes as she closed them, rubbing at her forehead. Licking her lips, she swallowed and hesitated, the sound of a creaking floorboard reaching her ears. 

     

                “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to snap, I just-”

     

                “No, it’s fine,” Kara replied with a strangled laugh, her thin smile strained.

     

                “It’s not fine,” Lena whispered. “I promised you I wouldn’t come between you or your work, or let it come between us, but I- I don’t like having to hear about it. It makes me … I feel so helpless. All the time.”

     

                Gently shushing her, Kara gave her a pained look. “I know. I- I wish it was different but-”

     

                “Do you?” Lena sceptically asked, arching an eyebrow, “because unless you’ve made up your mind …”

     

                Wincing slightly, Kara chewed on the inside of her mouth and then exhaled heavily, wilting in her seat. “Lena, look … can we just not talk about this right now? It’s been a really shit day, so …”

     

                “Fine,” Lena muttered.

     

                “How’s my mom’s?”

                Nodding as her lips twitched faintly, Lena sank back down onto the pillows and turned onto her side, holding the phone at arm’s length.                 The lights were already on downstairs and she made her way down, blinking at the brightness as she stepped into the kitchen.                 “Morning.”

     

                Mumbling a greeting, Lena made straight for the coffee pot and filled a clean cup as she wedged in alongside Alex, hiding a yawn behind her hand as she blinked and moved over to the table.                 “Was that Kara you were talking to?” Alex asked after a moment.

                “Was it- was it about enlisting?” Kelly asked, cautious curiosity in her brown eyes as Lena looked up at her.

                Simmering in her anger for a minute as the uncomfortable tension encompassed the room, the silence so deafening that she could hear her heart pounding in her ears, Lena abruptly jerked her chair back, legs scraping against the floor and shot to her feet.                 A gust of wind made her shiver and she felt tears prick her eyes as she let out a shuddering breath, bare feet hitting the sandy deck as the deafening roar of waves crashing on the shore drowned out everything else.                 It was still dark, the morning shrouded in grey shadows as the sun started rising behind her, to the west, and Lena stared out at the roiling darkness of the ocean, a faint glimmer of silver cresting the waves as she wallowed.                 A ghost of a smile thinned Kelly’s lips as she murmured, “yes, aside from that.”

                “My dad was in the army too, you know,” Kelly suddenly blurted out, a sharp smile curling her lips as she looked at Lena, taking in the look of shock on her face. "He died over there. I grew up thinking her was ... this big hero. Same with Alex and Kara with Jeremiah."

     

                “That’s why you joined?” Lena started, her expression crumpling.

     

                “Yeah,” Kelly whispered. “I didn’t meet her until after I was discharged. Had been for a couple of years. But … while I was over there, I met someone. Being there and losing someone.”

     

                Her eyes were filled with tears and Lena’s were likewise, reaching up to angrily wipe them away as she drew in a shuddering breath, a sob bubbling up in her chest and forced back down. “Kara- Kara knows this?” she asked, her voice cracking.

     

                “Mm. She didn’t know her, but … she knows what happened.”

     

                Lena nodded, tears spilling down her cheeks as she hunched over, dread and anger and pity overwhelming her. She wasn’t good at managing how she felt, save for locking it all away to never be confronted or understood and then dealing with the fallout when it became too much to handle at once and consumed her. It was too much for her right then, breathless sobs catching in her throat as she wiped at her cheeks and tried to force it all down.

     

                Kelly rested her forehead on Lena’s shoulder, shaking with her own quiet sobs and Lena felt her heart break, just a little. “I’m sorry,” she gasped, turning her head and murmuring into Kelly’s hair. “I’m sorry.”

     

                Setting her trembling cup of coffee down, Lena wrapped her arms around Kelly and felt a sort of kindred pain there.                 “I don’t tell you to scare you,” Kelly said, wiping at her own eyes as she pulled back, “only so you- you know that … if you can make her stay, do it. I love Alex, but … losing her broke me.”

     

                “Kelly-”

     

                Squeezing her arm, Kelly gave her a tight smile. “Lena, do yourself a favour,” she whispered, “and be honest. You don’t want to go through that kind of pain. Trust me.”

                Alex still lingered there, against the counters, looking irked but apologetic as she glanced at Lena, a muscle jumping in her jaw. “Sorry,” she muttered.

     

                Ducking her head in a nod, Lena’s mouth thinned and a shiver wracked her before she quietly replied. “I’ll talk to her.”

                “Thank you,” Alex whispered, her voice a soft sigh.

                They walked into Midvale along the beach, watching the few surfers brave enough to face the cold as they straddled their boards, waiting for waves, fishermen down the coast with their lines cast out and a few elderly people taking walks. Lena looked out onto the horizon. The ocean was steel grey, the sun watery to the east as it hid behind clouds, and seagulls chirped sharply as they dove and rose over the sea. They walked in companionable silence for the most part, Eliza dutifully stooping down to fetch the branch Athena kept coming back with before she tossed it ahead of them once more, while Lena watched the tiny crabs digging deeper into the sand and the myriad of shells and smooth glass deposited by the sea as they gouged footprints in the damp sand in their wake.

     

                She bought everything on her list, as well as a few things that weren’t, and boxed it all up at the post office before buying them both chai lattes to nurse as they browsed the trestle tables of wares set up outside stores and bought food for dinner. Eliza was going to show her how to make bolognese and they slowly walked home afterwards, Lena looking a little pale and drawn as her side twinged.

     

                It was a slow week spent in Midvale, long stretches of it by herself as Eliza pulled long shifts at the quiet hospital with stern warnings for Lena to take it easy. She spent most of her time working from the kitchen table or the sofa, spending long hours talking on the phone with Sam and Jess, and less time than she would have liked on the phone with Kara. 

     

                The arraignment came and went during that time, with no option for bail and a date set for trial early next year, and after days spent holed up in the small coastal town, going for walks along the beach as September’s temperature plummeted, Lena was finally set to go home. It had been peaceful and she was almost reluctant to leave, enjoying quiet evenings watching Jeopardy with Eliza and sharing glasses of wine as she was weaned off the painkillers. But still, the night before she left, she let Eliza remove the stitches, holding her shirt up as she watched her snip them and pull the threads out with interest, the scabbed over pinkish line of the wound held together as it healed. When she said goodbye the next day, Lena found herself already wishing she could come back soon.

    Chapter 34

    Dear Kara,

     

    It’s been three and a half months since you left, and yet it feels like a lifetime. But hey, at least we’re over a third of the way through it (look at that optimism) and we’re still standing strong. It’s been a close call more times than I like to think about, but you’ve put this stupid thing people like to call hope inside me and now I’m clinging to the day you eventually come home, because it’s a day I know will come. It’s the only thing that’s getting me through this - the thought of seeing you again, holding you again, is the only thing I can think of these days.

     

    I think of you all the time, and all the things you’ve told me. I know we get to talk almost every day, and that nothing in these letters will be surprising to you, only that I have so much worry that comes out in word vomit whenever I sit down to write to you. It keeps me sane, being able to say what neither of us are willing to say on the phone. I love those light-hearted (for the most part) talks where we pretend you’re okay and you tell me about work as if you were as safe as you could possibly be. I like getting to tell you that my stomach doesn’t hurt, even though I pulled the stitches twice and haven’t felt like myself in weeks, because it makes it easier to make the most of what precious few minutes we have.

     

    I wonder - how much do you really hide from me, in calls and letters? It’s enough to keep me up at night. Of all the awful things you’ve told me, I think that’s just the surface. It frightens me that there are things that you can’t talk about - you, who have always spoken your mind, of all people. It makes my heart ache and it’s why I can’t help but put it here in writing because I don’t have it in me to ask you when we speak: don’t go back. Don’t reenlist. I think it’ll break my heart if you do, even if you were wrapped up in bubble wrap the entire time and never had to go back overseas. Even working from base is more than I can bear when the possibility is there. It might be selfish and you might hate me for it one day, but you asked me to tell you what to do, so I’ll ask you now. Don’t do it. I don’t know what to do without you anymore.

     

    It’s strange that now, after so many years of loneliness, and being surrounded by more people than I ever have before, I feel lonelier than ever. I miss your loud laugh, I miss your warmth and I miss your blue eyes. I could list everything about you, from your freckles to your scars and the way you trip over your words and the optimistic drive that never wavers, but I think it would be too long to fit in a letter. Truthfully, I love everything about you. I’ve always thought it was childishly naive to have that view of someone, that romance films were just some sham but you’ve turned me into a believer. I’m annoyed at you for that; I vowed to always be bitter and alone and look what you’ve turned me into. Love letters? I can hardly recognise myself through all the sappiness.

     

    I think maybe I’m just missing you a little bit extra today. Mostly it’s because I’m thinking of your birthday, which is coming up in a couple of weeks, and how you won’t be here for it. It’s the first one to celebrate since we met each other and it makes me sad to think about how we’re missing out on so much with you being over there. Our first Halloween and Thanksgiving and Christmas and New Year. Valentine’s Day too, if you’re not home before then too. It’s silly to focus on things that don’t really matter, but I think about what I’ve missed out on before and how I’m actually looking forward to them now, and I wish you could be there too to make them perfect. 

     

    I’ve never had to put so much effort into buying someone a gift before, but I don’t think something flashy is going to impress you much. You deserve thoughtfulness and care and something picked out specially for you. I hope you like it when you get to open it; I hope you get to put it to good use one day. You have to come home for that though, so just focus on that. Make sure you get enough rest and eat enough. You look more exhausted and tanned every time we talk - I’ll hardly recognise you when you’re back at this rate. I’m sure I’ll love my Kara the same no matter what, so just look after yourself. Please.

     

    I miss you. I love you.

     

    Lena x

    Chapter 35

                “Happy birthday!” Lena brightly exclaimed as the video connected with Kara’s tanned face filling the screen.

     

                She smiled at the wide grin on Kara’s face as her eyes creased at the corners, propping her chin up in her hand as she hunched forward on her desk. 

     

                “Hi! Thanks,” Kara laughed, rubbing at her forehead as she sank down onto the edge of her cot, sunlight seeping in through the open mouth of the tent as the sun still lingered in the sky. “I just finished up for the day so I haven’t opened my cards and presents yet. Which is first?”

     

                “Do the card first.”

     

                Nodding, Kara fished it out of the box that Lena had sent, filled with essentials and a few wrapped luxuries, and slipped her finger beneath the flap to tear it open. Her eyes skimmed the words Lena had written inside in her blunt, scrawling script and her expression softened as she finished, hugging it to her chest with a look of adoration in her blue eyes.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Go on then,” Lena said with a knowing look, “open the presents.”

     

                With childlike eagerness, Kara sifted through the contents of the box, unwrapping two new books, some expensive moisturiser and perfume, a few photos of Lena that made her flush bright red as she quickly hid them, glancing around sheepishly, and then reached for the small box with a ribbon tying it closed. Popping off the lid, she fished out a small key and frowned as she held it up.

     

                “Is this another key to your apartment?”

     

                “Obviously not,” Lena rolled her eyes with exasperated amusement, “that’s your present you’re going to have to come home to get. The key’s for show, so it’s not actually useful , but I wanted you to have something to open. I mean, you can lock it, but I doubt you’d want to- well, anyway, it’s the key to a room at the house that I had converted into a photography room for you. You know, space for your cameras and it doubles as a darkroom so you can try your hand at developing them yourself too, if you’re interested. I even got you a vintage camera that looked really cool - I’m no expert on photography, but it came highly recommended.”

     

                “You researched all of that?” Kara asked, a yearning look of love blossoming on her face as her brow furrowed together and her shoulders dropped. 

     

                Her eyes were bright, as if she was about to cry, and it made Lena smile slightly as she nodded, her nose wrinkling. “I did. I wanted it to be something you’d actually like, because … well, you deserve good things. You deserve the world , so … I’ll try and give it to you it, if I can.”

     

                “Lena, this … thank you,” Kara said, her voice low and slightly hoarse with emotion, “really, I mean it. I don’t even know what to say, I just- I love you.”

     

                “I love you too. Now, get your cake out.”

     

                Perking up, Kara’s eyebrows raised as she nestled the key back into the box and pulled out the white box. Opening it, her face creased with a wide smile at the sight of the brownie, decorated with a message for her on top, and Lena lurched into an off-key rendition of ‘happy birthday’ as Kara covered her mouth with a hand, shaking with silent laughter. Rolling her eyes, Lena came to an end and let out an embarrassed laugh.

     

                “Sorry, a brownie cake was the best I could do without it getting too stale before it reached you,” she said, grimacing slightly, “but … make a wish.”

     

                Humming as she pressed her lips together, eyes sparkling with warm mirth, Kara squeezed her eyes shut and then nodded, and Lena wondered if they’d chosen the same wish as she met Kara’s eyes a moment later. Lips twitching with grim resignation, Kara’s cheek dimpled faintly.

     

                “Thank you, it’s perfect.”

     

                “It’d be even more perfect if you were here, with a real cake and presents,” Lena said with a half-hearted laugh. “But maybe next year, right?”

     

                “Mhm,” Kara said with a strained smile, “yeah, definitely, I just- well, I’m sorry that I won’t be there for yours either. I know it’s coming up in a few weeks and I wish we could’ve spent it together, but-”

     

                Lips twitching ruefully, Lena shrugged, “don’t worry about it. You just focus on looking after yourself, okay? And enjoying your birthday right now. Come on, tell me about your day - do you get any special treatment because it’s your birthday?”

     

                Kara snorted and launched into a vague explanation of her day, digging into the squares of brownies neatly lined up in the box. They talked for longer than they had since Lena had come back from Midvale, staying on the line longer than they should have as night descended in Afghanistan and Kara’s birthday came to a close. Lena told her about an upcoming business trip to London, just for a few days, which would put them in a closer time zone to each other, and showed her the healing scar on her stomach, a pink line against her pale skin before conversation turned to her plans for the rest of the day.

     

                Despite wanting to wallow, Lena had volunteered to help Alex move some of her things into Kelly’s apartment that afternoon as they finally made the jump into moving in together. They’d spent a few weeks tying up loose ends with the apartment, and Kara had told her to sell her furniture on Craigslist to free up the burden of trying to figure out what to do with it until Kara could come back and sort it out herself, and Lena had repurposed an L-Corp delivery truck for the purpose of moving Alex’s boxes. She couldn’t help but wonder if it was a deliberate conspiracy on behalf of the couple, coordinating the official move-in date to coincide with Kara’s birthday as a distraction from her brooding, and Lena wouldn’t have been surprised if it wasn’t Kara who’d plotted it herself, but she was glad for the company. They’d made plans to get Chinese takeout from her favourite restaurant and watch Working Girl in her honour and Lena looked forward to the distraction.

     

                Eventually, Kara had to go, soldiers bedding down for the night in the spacious tent, and it was with a final murmured ‘happy birthday’ that Lena hung up, a heaviness in her chest as she longed for Kara to be there. They should’ve been having a party, inviting all of Kara’s local friends and going out for drinks and surprising her with breakfast in bed and a mountain of silly gifts that she would love anyway because it was Kara. It struck a pang of longing in Lena’s chest but she pushed it aside with a weary sigh and climbed to her feet to get ready.

     

                “Hey,” Lena said as Alex picked up her phone, “I’m about to leave; I just got off the phone with Kara.”

     

                “Did she like the surprise?”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena said, glowing with pride, “hopefully she’ll be back soon to actually use it, but … well …”

     

                “Did you talk to her?”

     

                She could hear the pointed accusation in the undercurrent of Alex’s words and winced slightly, rubbing at the back of her neck as she perused the rack of shoes and deliberated between a boot with a heel or something flat and practical. Snagging a pair of boots that had a slight heel, she compromised and sank down onto an ottoman to wrestle one onto her foot, phone trapped between her ear and shoulder as she tried to skirt around the question.

     

                “I mean- well … not yet. I will though,” she quickly assured Alex. “It’s just that she hasn't really brought it up again since, and then her birthday was coming up so I didn’t want to spoil it and then-”

     

                “You’re stalling,” Alex pointed out.

     

                Spluttering as her cheeks coloured, Lena reached for the phone and sat there with one shoe on as her stomach clenched uneasily. “I’m not stalling. I’m just … waiting for the right time. It’s … this whole issue with her wanting to do her masters and the money and … I’m trying to figure out a way to make her let me pay for it without wounding her pride. I didn’t even know she was that proud.”

     

                Alex chuckled ruefully, “oh, yeah. She’s a sweetheart, but God damn, if you even try to insinuate that she can’t do something or offer to help her when she doesn’t want it …”

     

                She let out a low whistle and Lena exhaled fully, “yeah, well, your stubborn sister is a pain in my ass right now with this stupid thing. I mean, she’s going to be living with me and she can’t accept free tuition? Maybe I’ll talk to my mom; I’m sure she knows someone at some college that could offer a scholarship if I give them the funds.”

     

                “Don’t do that,” Alex cautioned her, “she likes to do things on her own merit and I can guarantee you, tricking her into taking your money won’t go down well when she finds out the truth. It’s a nice gesture, but … yeah, you’re just going to have to be honest, kid. No way around it.”

     

                Making a scathing sound of contempt at the back of her throat, Lena pulled a disgruntled face in the full-length mirror across from her. “And you’re sure you won’t tell her how it is?”

     

                “Me? No. I’ve tried it before; not even close to convincing her not to do it.”

     

                “You’re her sister; what hope do I have if she won’t even listen to you?”

     

                “A fair amount, I’d say. She knows she would never lose me over a choice like that.”

     

                Lena made a squawking sound of protest, scowling as she roughly tugged on her other boot. “And neither would I,” she bristled at the insinuation.

     

                “Easy, kid, I didn’t say you would, and she knows that too, but there’s always that doubt, isn’t there? Now, how long are you going to be? It’s already ten-thirty and I’ve got a shit load of boxes to move and some asshole is apparently on his way to buy my kitchen table so I can’t go anywhere until he gets here.”

     

                “I’m coming, I’m coming,” Lena sighed, hanging up and dragging on a jacket.

     

                She drove the Porsche to an upscale coffee shop first though, ordering two coffees of varying types and half a dozen donuts before making her way to Alex’s place. The removal truck was already outside, one of Lena’s employees loitering about, smoking as he scrolled through his phone, and she breezed by and into the lobby. Taking the elevator upstairs, she let herself into Alex’s apartment, looking like a bomb site at the mess of boxes and disassembled belongings that had yet to be taken downstairs or gotten rid of.

     

                Kelly was at work all day but Lena had left Sam to lead a project meeting as she took the day to help her friends, a tiny bit of payback for all the help they’d shown her over the past four months. Inside Alex’s apartment, she tracked her down in her mostly empty bedroom and handed over the coffee.

     

                “What’re we doing?”

     

                “Moving,” Alex stated, grinning at Lena’s jaded look thrown at her. “Boxes first.”

     

                “Okay, I’ll stack them in the living room.”

     

                “Alright. Hey, there’s a box of random crap that’s Kara’s if you want to take that home with you too. Put it with the rest of her shit.”

     

                Nodding, Lena moved back out into the small open space, weaving around stacks of boxes and bags labelled for charity or trash, and set the donuts down on the counter before sipping her coffee. She indulged in plain glazed one as she dawdled, nodding to her employee, who eventually made his way upstairs, smelling of tobacco and silently started removing boxes, and then washed the icy from her fingers before moving into Kara’s room to fetch the box that Alex had left labelled with her things.

     

                Curiosity got the better of her and Lena opened it, rifling through worn, borrowed books, a rumpled shirt and loose polaroids scattered amidst beauty products and trinkets she’d overlooked when packing up her room. Lena plucked a few photos from the box and smiled as she looked down at them, taking in the dates scrawled beneath. They were some of the ones she’d sent to Alex over the years - and some recent too - and Lena squinted at the face of a guy in one of them.

     

                “Can you give me a hand with a heavy one?”

     

                Lena looked up, eyebrows rising, as Alex poked her head inside. A smile crossed her face as she stepped further inside, hands in her back pockets. 

     

                “Oh, some of her photos?”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena murmured, holding one up. “Who’s this with her?”

     

                Crossing over, Alex peered down over Lena’s shoulder and then let out a loud laugh. “That’s Mike. Grade-A asshole with a huge crush on Kara, as you can see.”

     

                Annoyance threaded through Lena and she flicked the photo back into the box, clearing her throat. “She’s never mentioned him.”

     

                “Yeah, well, he was in her squadron last time, before you met. She wasn’t too keen on him, but he was … persistent.”

     

                “What do you mean by that?”

     

                “Well, she went on a pity date with him just to get him to leave her alone, but then he got transferred and moved to Metropolis, so she was pretty relieved all up, but they’re over there together again. He’s a photojournalist. Why? You jealous?”

     

                Scoffing, Lena bristled as she wiped her hands on her thighs and climbed to her feet, easily lifting the light box as she scowled at Alex, haughty and defensive. “Why would I be jealous? I’m the one that’s dating her.”

     

                Chuckling, Alex prodded her ribs and Lena flushed, which only made her laugh harder, before she pushed past her and out into the hallway. Depositing the box with the rest to be loaded into the van, Lena went to give Alex a hand with the other one and they quickly fell into the slow and steady rhythm of work. Lena spent most of the time labelling boxes properly and sorting them into piles for efficient unloading, by order of priority, while Alex did some last minute packing.

     

                “Hey, you know how it’s Kara’s birthday?” Alex said at one point, walking past with a trash bag full of clothes for the charity pile. “Well, she mentioned yours wasn’t far off.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena murmured, rubbing the back of her neck. “Yeah, I mean, it’s a month away yet, but … yeah. October twenty-fourth.”

     

                “Any idea what you want to do?” Alex asked, eyebrows raised expectantly.

     

                Lena’s face crumpled and she bit her bottom lip as she contemplated for a second. “I don’t really do anything, so … I don’t know, maybe we can get dinner.”

     

                “Okay, we get dinner like three times a week. It needs to be something more than that.”

     

                Shrugging self-consciously, Lena pressed her lips together, her stomach twisting uncomfortably. “I just … don’t really do birthdays. It’s fine.”

     

                “Well, hey, how about just a quiet few days up in Midvale. My mom would love to see us again. We could just relax and … I don’t know, grill some stuff and enjoy the beach.”

     

                A small smile curved Lena’s lips as she ducked her head, “yeah, sure. If Eliza wouldn’t mind.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Alex rolled her eyes, “please, she’s barely ever home anyway.”

     

                “Yeah, but I did just spend a week parked up on her sofa.”

     

                “It’s fine. She likes it when we visit. I’ll sort it out.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena agreed with more conviction as her smile grew. “Thanks, Alex.”

     

                A wry smile twisted her lips as she waved away Lena’s gratitude, brown eyes softening as she glanced at her. “Yeah, yeah. Also, by some miracle, is there something you don’t have yet that Kelly and I can get you as a gift? A Rolex might be out of our price range but …”

     

                “Oh, no, you don’t have to get me anything,” Lena said as surprise flashed across her face. “Your company will be more than enough.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Alex groaned softly as her shoulders dropped. “I’m going to pretend you didn’t say something lame like that. I’ll pick something out myself.”

     

                Chuckling, Lena relented and grabbed one side of an end table to help carry it out to the living room. 

     

                It was mid-afternoon by the time they were done, the apartment bare, save for a few things that needed to be thrown out, and the L-Corp driver had finished delivering the heavier items to people Alex had sold the furniture to and gone home when they locked up the apartment and left. Lena’s Porsche held bags and boxes of clothes and old books and kitchenware that they took to the nearest thrift store and helped the employees unload.

     

                Afterwards, they made their way to Kelly’s apartment, spacious and modern and perfect for two, and started the arduous task of unboxing things. The sun started sinking lower outside the wide windows as they worked, Lena neatly hanging Alex’s clothes in the empty space Kelly had made for them, in the drawers that had been emptied to make room, and felt the warmth of excitement in her chest. Kara’s things were still boxed up in her house, but this would be them when she got home, entwining their lives and making space for each other. It was a nice thought, and when Kelly arrived home, Lena felt a pang of envy and longing, wishing for the future when she’d do the same with Kara.

     

                The three of them worked efficiently, emptying boxes of Alex’s CD’s and framed photos and shoes while they listened to music and shouted back and forth, finding places for things. She caught fleeting moments of the couple, loving glances and lingering touches and whispered words, and found herself smiling at their happiness.

     

                Eventually, she excused herself and drove to the Chinese restaurant to pick up their pre-placed order. Stopping at a liquor store on the way back, Lena grabbed a few bottles of wine - the good stuff to celebrate their moving in together - and made her way back to the apartment. Riding the elevator up to Kelly’s floor, she let herself in and they decided to go up to the roof to eat.

     

                Holding the bottles of wine close to her chest, three glasses in hand and a wine key in her pocket, she followed the duo up to the top floor and then up the emergency exit, before pushing out onto the roof. The sky was like the paintings, orange clouds rimmed with purple and violet descending in on it as the light faded. 

     

                The windows in each high-rise were lit up like the buildings were burning down and they sprawled down onto the cool concrete, close to the edge but far enough away to be safe as the wind clawed at them. Lena popped the cork from a bottle of wine as Alex spread out the cartons, and the three of them toasted twice - to Kara’s birthday and their move-in date.

     

                They stayed outside until the blue of dusk made it hard to see, despite a thousand squares of light from the scattered windows of the skyline, and the air made them shiver where they sat. Inside, they watched Working Girl and finished off the wine, and when Lena caught a cab home that night with the box of Kara’s things held safely on her lap, she was filled with the tiny victory that she was another day closer to getting her back.

    Chapter 36
