                Lena ordered them both whiskey and carried the glasses back to the table, talking about their weekend plans as they sipped and tried to make themselves heard over the thumping music. Alex and Kelly joined them shortly afterwards and Lena reintroduced everyone before swallowing the last mouthful of whiskey and ordering a round of beers.

     

                The more she had to drink, the more relaxed she became, a warmth in her stomach as her eyes became heavy-lidded and her inhibitions lowered. Laughing more than she had all week, pink-cheeked and glassy-eyed, Lena was animated as she spoke, regaling the table with funny stories, bickering with Alex as they wound each other up, and she found herself glad that she’d made the spur of the moment decision to go out. 

     

                The bar filled quickly, Friday night bringing out a rowdy crowd, and it was starting to get late, everyone in the place more than a few drinks in, when Lena went to order the next round of drinks. Flushed and serene as she moved through the packed bodies, passing by a group of guys playing pool beneath naked bulbs as she made for the bar, waiting her turn and ordering another round of beers for them all.

     

                Clutching the necks of the four bottles in her hands, she turned and almost walked into a tall man standing behind her. Blinking in surprise, Lena gave him an apologetic smile, twisting to the side. “Sorry.”

     

                As she brushed past, he snagged her arm in a vice-like grip, pulling her to a stop as she sloshed beer all over her feet. “I know you, you’re that Luthor. The rich girl with the brother.”

     

                Stiffening, Lena swallowed, her heart fluttering in her throat as her stomach jolted with dread. Her breaths were sharp and quick as she tried to pull herself free. “Excuse me,” she murmured, head ducked down.

     

                “They were my family ,” he slurred, leaning in close, close enough that his nose was almost touching her cheek, his sour beer breath making her feel sick. “You have a lot of nerve showing your face around here; I bet you have blood on your hands too, you smug little bitch. You should’ve died when you got shot.”

     

                He spat on her and she stiffened with revulsion, skin prickling with fear as she looked up at him, gorge rising at the feeling of his saliva sickeningly warm on her cheek. Trying to pull her arm back, she sloshed more beer over her feet, panic settling in until Alex was at her side a moment later, having caught sight of the odd altercation from where she sat shelling peanuts.

     

                “Are we good here?” she asked, looking up at the man, a challenge in the curtness of her words, the arched eyebrow and unimpressed expression.

     

                “Let’s go,” Lena murmured, cheeks flaming.

     

                “Hey! I’m talking to you,” he shouted, dragging her closer, pitching Lena off balance as she lost her grip on the sweating bottles.

     

                They slipped through her fingers and shattered on the grimy floor, splattering the three of them with beer, and she opened her mouth to reply but couldn’t even get a word out before a heavy fist slammed into her face. The pain was blinding, the entire left side of her face going numb as her vision blurred. She went limp in his grasp, dropping hard to her knees on the floor as he still held her up, his other hand coming down to wrap around her throat.

     

                Ears ringing and eyes closing, Lena couldn’t focus, the world pitching as vertigo overwhelmed her. She could taste something coppery filling her mouth, something hot and fluid over her lips and chin, and she made a mewling sound of protest before a shuddering laugh squeezed past her lips. 

     

                Then Alex was there, in his face, prying at his hands and pushing him back as she cursed him out, hitting whatever she could reach. Lena was oblivious to it all, slumped on the floor amidst the broken glass and puddle of beer, but she winced at the white-hot pain lancing through her wrist as the man stumbled back beneath Alex’s tirade and stepped on her arm.

     

                “Get your fucking hands off her,” Alex snarled, continuing her defence as he drunkenly slurred at her, swinging and missing.

     

                And then warm hands were on her shoulders, her arms, her face, panicked voices falling on deaf ears as she was pulled to her feet, unresponsive and shivering from the shock, her shaking knees unable to bear her own weight. Kelly hauled her a few feet back and slowly lowered her back down to the dirty floor, Sam on the phone nearby as she called the cops, while Alex was held at bay by a few men at the bar who had stepped in, one of them laying into the guy while his friends shepherded the brawl to the back alley.

     

                The noise dimmed as a bigger guy tossed him outside into a dirty puddle of water, shouting and jeering before the door closed and the sound was cut off. The bass in a song was deafeningly loud inside and Lena felt hot and drunk, pain making it hard to concentrate as she struggled to draw in a shallow breath.

     

                “Lena? Lena?”

     

                A crowd had gathered around her and she took in the shadowed shapes through one slitted eye, a small groan slipping from numb lips as her right hand fluttered around her tingling face. 

     

                “Here’s some ice.”

     

                “Ice? What’s that going to do?”

     

                “Shit, there’s so much blood.”

     

                “Hey, hey. Back off.”

     

                Humming disconcertingly, Lena swallowed painfully, her eyes closing as she swayed where she sat. “Alex.”

     

                The voices continued to clamour over her as a feverish flush made her skin prickle with sweat and Lena blindly reached out for whoever had her propped up. “Alex, I feel sick. I’m going to throw-”

     

                She didn’t even manage to finish rasping her sentence before she heaved and vomited right onto the bar floor, sounds of disgust and surprise rippling around her, cut through with curses and a loud voice.

     

                “Oh man, seriously?”

     

                “Cut her some slack, Al,” Alex snapped, “Jesus.”

     

                Blinking, Lena was dimly aware of someone gently wiping at her mouth and chin, the sour taste of bile caught at the back of her throat as she struggled to swallow. After a moment, she was dragged to her feet, hands under her arms, a person on each side, and carried out into the street.

     

                It was cold, a light rain pattering on the sidewalk as they huddled under the overhang, smokers leaning against the wall and people waiting for cabs. Lena could barely keep her good eye open, the rest of her face feeling oddly absent, and she hummed to herself as she was kept upright by Alex and Sam.

     

                “Do you think she needs to go to the hospital?”

     

                “No, she’ll be fine.”

     

                “Are you sure?”

     

                “I’ll take her home.”

     

                At some point there was a cab, the four of them piling in and Lena unresponsive as she lay against the door, someone else buckling her in, and then there was the front stoop of her brownstone, the steps so much of a struggle with the four drunk women that they had to deposit her on the sofa. The stairs up to Lena’s room were unmanageable and Alex rifled around in Lena’s purse for cash to give to Sam for the cab home as Kelly pulled her heels and coat off. The latter roused a hissing response from Lena as the dull throbbing in her wrist flared up.

     

                She woke the next morning, stiff and cold on the sofa, pale morning sunlight streaming in through the tall, uncovered windows, and blinding pain consuming her as she tried to push herself up. Her whole body felt battered and bruised, her mouth filled with the clinging taste of blood and vomit, and she could smell the bar on her, the hems of her grey pants reeking of beer. Forcing herself to sit up as the room pitched around her, her left hand almost gave out beneath her as pain shot up her arm, tingling in her fingertips like her nerves were on fire.

     

                Letting out a soft gasp as her breath hitched in her throat, Lena pushed herself up and staggered out of the living room. Feeling drunk, she stumbled down the hall to the downstairs bathroom and paused at the sight of her face as she looked across the room to the bloody reflection staring back at her. A small cry escaped her and she lurched over to the sink, reaching up with a shaking hand to press her fingers to the swollen shut eye, dark bruises ringing it. Her lips were no better, split and puffy and numb, her cheekbone mottled purple and finger marks from being choked striping her throat.

     

                Sucking in a shallow breath, Lena wanted to cry, staring at the overwhelming amount of blood dried and flaking on her face, her neck, her hands. Tiny pieces of glass were embedded in the palms of her shaking hands and she stared at the dark bruise of her swollen wrist with frustrated anger.

     

                Trying to undress herself and finding the pain too unbearable, the nauseous hangover stripping what little ability she would have had from her, Lena abandoned the idea in favour of going to the hospital. She’d broken bones before while still riding horses as a young girl and the pain was distantly familiar enough for her to know that one or more of the small bones in her wrist had been injured last night.

     

                Dragging her coat and shoes on from the night before, Lena grabbed her purse and ordered an Uber from her phone. It was still relatively early and she stood on the stoop, shivering in the grey morning as the wind whistled down the street, stirring up fallen leaves as she waited patiently. Upstairs, Alex and Kelly presumably slept, and she brooded, her head throbbing with pent up pain as she left them to sleep off their hangovers.

     

                The Uber pulled up and as she walked down the steps and slid into the back of the car, reeking of alcohol and sour vomit, and buckled herself in, she caught sight of the driver eyeing her with panic in the rearview mirror as she mumbled a greeting. It was a tense and silent drive, hot air pumping out of the vents and making Lena’s skin prickle with sweat as she sat covered in her own blood and vomit, trying not to dwell on how mortifying the whole ordeal was. Only once, after five minutes, did the driver as if she was okay, silently accepting her affirmation without further questioning before he deposited her outside the emergency room entrance of the hospital.

                

                Despite it being a private hospital, it was still a long wait in the queue with other soon-to-be patients, nursing her arm as she closed her eyes to the harsh fluorescents and breathed in the sickly antiseptic smell through her nose. After an hour, she was taken through and an intern gently probed at her face with cold gloves fingers until Lena wearily insisted it was just her arm and she was taken for an x-ray.

     

                It was a distal radius and scaphoid fracture and Lena waited patiently in the private consultation room for the intern to return and put her hand in a cast. It was the last thing she wanted, but she resigned herself to walking around in plaster for six weeks, grateful that she’d at least be able to hide it with sweaters. Her face was another matter entirely.

     

                Her phone started ringing as she was sitting there, wet plaster being wrapped around her wrist, and she glanced down at Alex’s name and answered with a soft sigh, her voice a rough rasp. “Hi.”

     

                “Hi, where are you?”

     

                “At the hospital?”

     

                “Which hospital? Your one?”

     

                Snorting, Lena’s eyebrows rose with amusement, pulling at her bruised and swollen face and making a groan work its way up her throat before she swallowed it back down and gritted her teeth. “Why would I be at the children’s hospital? I’m at St. Rao’s - the private one. My hand is broken.”

     

                “That bastard. Why didn’t you wake us up?”

     

                “No one was in a state to drive this morning,” Lena chuckled.

     

                “Alright, well, sorry to make your morning even worse but the cops just showed up.”

     

                Biting back a curse, Lena exhaled a long sigh as she deflated in her seat, mouth thinning and the cut on her lip pulling.

     

                “Want me to come and pick you up?”

     

                “I’m almost done; I’ll get a cab.”

     

                It was another twenty minutes before she was finally free, after awkwardly navigating the clipboard and pen to sign her paperwork, and the cab ride home was no less uncomfortable, given the state of her face. When she pulled up outside her house, she handed the driver a few bills, eyeing the police cruiser with wary grimness, and walked up the steps to let herself in.

     

                Stopping in the open doorway to the kitchen, Lena took in the sight of the two officers sitting at the table with coffee before them, Alex across from them and Kelly nowhere to be found. Chairs scraped as they moved at the sight of her, surprise flashing across their faces, while Alex winced.

     

                “Miss Luthor,” the young woman greeted her, “we’d just like a quick word, if you have the time.”

     

                “I- do you mind if I …”

     

                Lena gestured at her face and there was an uncomfortable round of assurances, she slipped down the hallway and paused at the steps. Hauling herself up each step, she made her way into her ensuite and started running the bath. Steam billowed up and fogged up the glass and Lena winced as she undressed, arm held awkwardly out, before climbing into the tub.

     

                Her knees were blackened with fresh bruises and her right palm stung as she put her hand into the water, tiny cuts screaming at the temperature. Trying to be quick, she scrubbed the beer from her ankles and the vomit and blood from her neck, staining the water pink as she washed it away to reveal more bruises beneath.

     

                In the mirror, she eyed her pale face, taking in the angry marks, the mottling that even concealer wouldn’t fully hide, and painfully brushed her teeth, spitting out pink, before fetching soft cashmere loungewear. There was a knock on the door as she awkwardly pulled on her pants, and she turned to watch Kelly step inside as she picked up the shirt.

     

                “How’re you feeling?”

     

                Sighing heavily, Lena pulled it on over her head and grimaced lopsidedly, her vision skewed by the one eye that refused to open. “Could be worse.”

     

                “Here.”

     

                Kelly gestured her onto the bench at the foot of the bed and fetched her hairbrush from the bathroom, gently pulling it through Lena’s damp hair as they sat quietly.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lena mumbled, thick lips feeling clumsy as her eyes stung.

     

                “Why are you apologising?”

     

                “It was supposed to be a nice night.”

     

                “It was - well, until … but that’s not your fault.”

     

                Shrugging, Lena laughed softly, the sound sad and sharp, “somehow, it always feels like it is.”

     

                “Come on, go and speak to those cops so they can leave and we can have breakfast.”

     

                Making her way downstairs, Lena walked through to the kitchen and fetched a clean glass from the cupboards, filling it with water and then fishing out two Tylenol, the foil tearing as she popped them out in the quiet room.

     

                “So, what’s this about?” she politely asked, popping a pill in her mouth and swallowing with a gulp of water, her voice hoarse as she tried to clear it.

     

                “Ma’am, we made an arrest last night. At Al’s bar, just past eleven o’clock. Witnesses gave your name, so we’re just following up on a statement, if that’s alright with you.”

     

                Lena was quiet as she popped the other pill in her mouth, the powdery taste coating her tongue as she rolled it around and then washed it down with water. Setting the glass down, she softly cleared her throat.

     

                “What was his name?”

     

                “Benjamin Lockwood.”

     

                Peter Lockwood. Lydia Lockwood. The names came to her easily as she tapped a nail against the side of the glass, a dulcet tone ringing out. “I’m not looking to press charges.”

     

                “Ma’am, with all due respect, you really should consider-”

     

                “No, thank you,” she interrupted with a tight smile.

     

                “Lena,” Alex sharply whispered, a confused look on her face. “He broke your arm. Just tell them what happened; don’t be dumb.”

     

                Kelly was behind her in the kitchen, leaning against the counters and eyeing the scene warily, and stepped across the space, reaching out to nudge Lena encouragingly. With a sigh, Lena closed her eyes and rubbed at her forehead.

     

                “We were at the bar, drinking, and then I ordered us another round and … he hit me because his father and wife were killed by my brother, so … and that’s it.”

     

                “What did you talk about?”

     

                “Nothing. That’s it.”

     

                One of the officers nodded, a pen scratching across a small notepad, and the other one shifted in her seat. “He’ll be charged with assault and battery. We have statements from several eyewitnesses but if you have any further information you think may be useful, I’ll leave my name and number for you.”

     

                Swallowing painfully, Lena nodded, running her fingertips over the worktop as she stared down at it. “Thank you for your time.”

     

                “You have a good day now,” the man said, rising from his seat and draining the dregs of his coffee.

     

                They left and Alex sighed sharply, hands on her hips as she shook her head at Lena, who could see from the corner of her good eye. “Don’t lecture me; please don’t fucking lecture me.”

     

                “Here,” Kelly murmured, pushing a cup of tea into Lena’s right hand.

     

                She took it and shouldered open the wide doors leading outside, sitting on the slightly damp furniture as she cradled her cup and listened to the quiet bickering inside, cut through by the clattering of breakfast being made. Alex came out five minutes later with a bowl of oatmeal for Lena, setting it down before her before she flopped onto a chair and took a bite of her bagel.

     

                “How come you get a bagel and I get oats?”

     

                “Because I didn’t get the shit beaten out of me last night; I’m surprised you’re talking. Did they x-ray your jaw?”

     

                “No,” Lena muttered, spooning oats between her swollen lips, wincing as she swallowed the hot mouthful.

     

                Kelly walked out with her own breakfast and joined them, sipping her coffee as she looked at Lena with concern. “Can we all agree now that you aren’t going to work on Monday.”

     

                Pulling a face, Lena let out a scathing sigh, touching her cold fingertips to her cheek. “I can hardly show up to the conference meeting looking like this. Which is annoying.”

     

                They snorted with laughter, Lena more put out about having to reschedule than the fact that half of her face was swollen and blue. Finishing her oats, Lena rose from her seat, chair scraping along the deck and she let out a wispy sigh.

     

                “Well, I should go and call Kara.”

     

                “Take some water up with you; you look like you’re going to throw up again.”

     

                “I look better than you,” Lena shot back at Alex, a loud laugh following her inside as she smiled thinly to herself.

     

                Refilling her glass of water, she awkwardly cradled the glass in the crook of her elbow, wedged against her chest by the plaster cast, and tugged her phone from her purse before slipping it into her pocket. Walking upstairs to her room, Lena set her glass down and drew the curtains before sinking down onto the edge of her wide bed, sheets smooth and unslept in, and called Kara. She didn’t video her, just called, and put the phone to her ear as she waited for it to connect.

     

                The line was tinny as it connected. “Hello?”

     

                “Hi.”

     

                “Where are you?”

     

                “I’m … home. Listen, there’s- I don’t want you to freak out when you see me, okay?”

     

                Kara’s laugh was garbled as the line distorted it. “Why would I freak out?”

     

                “We went out last night and …” Lena trailed off and sighed softly, “there was this guy and things got out of hand. Anyway, I don’t look so great.”

     

                There was silence on the other end for a moment. “Turn your camera on.”

     

                Obliging, Lena nervously ran a hand over her thigh as the pixelated screen slowly came into focus. She watched as Kara’s face went from wary confusion to unabashed shock, her blue eyes quickly filling with tears as they widened and she seemed to pale.

     

                “What the hell happened to you, baby?”

     

                Tears stung Lena’s eyes at the tender concern in Kara’s voice, and she sniffed as her throat closed up. “I’m alright.”

     

                “That is not alright. What- I-”

                

                Reaching up to wipe away her tears with her fingers, Lena watched as Kara’s face turned from surprise to outrage at the sight of the cast. “Some guy,” she explained with a withering sigh. “His family were victims of my brother’s, so …”

     

                “Lena-”

     

                “It’s fine,” she dismissively replied, clearing her throat and then letting out a strangled laugh as it bubbled hysterically, pulling at her lips and cheeks as she winced. “I mean, it hurt a hell of a lot more than my dad’s, but I’ll live.”

     

                Kara swallowed a sob, her face flushing dark with anger as she looked away, letting out a shuddering breath through gritted teeth. “I swear to God- you shouldn’t be making jokes about it.”

     

                “It’s better than the alternative,” Lena whispered as her smile slipped. 

     

                “I wish I was there,” Kara said, swiping a thumb across her eye as her voice broke.

     

                “I wish you were too. A week ago we were getting engaged and you were still here and everything was fine, and now … you’re gone and I look like this and I’m not speaking to my mom. How did it all go to shit so fast without you?”

     

                “You haven’t told her?”

     

                Gesturing off-handedly and wiping at her nose, Lena grimaced. “If she can’t be happy for me about the good, why should I let her worry about the bad?”

     

                “She’d want to know.”

     

                “Yeah, I just- I’m tired. I think I need to sleep some more.”

     

                “You should go,” Kara murmured, her face crumpling with agony and yearning. “I love you. I hate seeing you like this, I- I should’ve been there.”

     

                Letting out a soft laugh, Lena’s good eye creased at the corner with a smile, “Alex sorted him out for me, it’s alright.”

     

                Chuckling, Kara nodded, wiping at her cheeks, “good. Just … try not to hurt yourself anymore before I get home, okay? Or there’ll be nothing left for me to come home to.”

     

                “I’ll try. Just be safe for me; that’s all I need.”

     

                “Mm. I love you.”

     

                “I love you too.”

     

                They lingered a minute longer, Lena drinking in the sight of Kara’s tanned and worried face while Kara took in her bruises and swelling with a dark flicker in her blue eyes, and then Lena hung up. Setting her phone down, she pulled the blankets back and switched off the lamp, plunging the room into darkness, an outline of sunlight seeping in through the curtains, and she turned her back to it, holding her arm carefully against her chest as she let herself slip into a merciful sleep.

     

                She slept fitfully, waking often with a frown on her face before she drifted off again, and it was early evening by the time she finally woke. Making her way downstairs, groggy and uncomfortable with the aching pain, she walked into the kitchen and grumbled an indecipherable greeting, making for more Tylenol as she passed by Alex, who was washing dishes in the sink.

     

                Soft music drifted through from the living room and Lena found comfort in how homely it all felt, having the other two women there, filling the routine she’d found herself in with Kara. It was both agonising and comforting. She ate the dinner set aside for her and made quiet conversation before they all went to bed.

     

                Her Sunday was spent much the same, moping around the house as she nursed her injuries while Alex and Kelly kept her company, but they left after lunch, grocery shopping and laundry calling them before work on Monday. They left with strict orders for her to rest, and Lena rolled her eyes and grumbled but was secretly pleased by how much they cared and heeded their instructions, laying up in bed with copious amounts of green tea as she spent the night checking spreadsheets and then reading through her old copy of Pride & Prejudice in an effort to feel closer to Kara.

     

                On Monday, holed up in her bed as she stretched out and worked as Eve unloaded groceries and laundry and vacuumed downstairs, Lena declined several calls from her mother, assuming they were about the cancelled conference meeting Lillian had intended on flying into National City for. Her assumptions were proven wrong as she spooned the chicken soup that Kelly had stopped off to bring her into her mouth, split lip stinging from the salt, and chatted to Sam on loudspeaker as they finetuned a document.

     

                Voices sounded downstairs and Lena frowned faintly, listening to loud footsteps on the stairs grow louder, and it was with very little surprise that Lillian opened the door a moment later after knocking. Her haughty bearing quickly melted into sagging shock, her stoicism replaced with fleeting panic before cool anger hardened her face.

     

                “Wha- Jesus . Who did this to you?” Lillian demanded, striding inside as she made a bee-line for the bed.

     

                “What’re you doing here?” Lena gravelly asked.

     

                Lillian reached out for her, fingertips falling short of Lena’s good side before she pulled her hand back, the tendons in her neck taut with outrage as she silently drank in every shadow of a bruise on her daughter’s face.

     

                “What happened?” she tightly demanded.

     

                Lena let out a broken laugh, good hand reaching up to touch her purple throat, soup bowl balanced in her lap as she steadied it with her cast. The sudden realistion that she was still on loudspeaker with Sam made Lena hurriedly hang up on her before she fully faced her mother, letting Lillian see the full damage done to her.

     

                “It’s nothing.”

     

                “Lena,” Lillian whispered, a spasm of pain crossing her face before she drew herself up and sank onto the edge of the mattress. “Why didn’t you call me? I mean … I’m your mom ; you should’ve told me.”

     

                “Last time I told you something personal, it didn’t go over so well, so …”

     

                Softly sighing, Lillian’s mouth thinned and she slid her handbag off her shoulder and set it on top of the sheets. “I’m sorry. I know I was … a little harsh. The truth is, I’m happy for you - if she’s what makes you happy, the of course I am!”

     

                “You didn’t approve,” Lena snapped, “you didn’t-”

     

                “I’m scared. I’m allowed to be scared for you! There are a lot of people out there who would use you-”

     

                “Do not insinuate what I think you are. Don’t you dare; she didn’t even know who I was when we met.”

     

                “Look, I’m not saying she’s after you for your money, I’m just asking you to be cautious. I’ve always been the person in your life who’s caused you pain; I didn’t want someone else to do it too, and there are a lot of ways to get hurt. Especially when you’re young. But … if it means anything to you …”

     

                Lillian dug into her bag and pulled out a black velvet ring box, snapping it open to reveal a large oval sapphire ringed with diamonds in a sunburst. Lena’s brow creased with confusion. “Grandma’s ring?”

     

                “It was always meant for the oldest son, but … given the circumstances, I think you should have it. For when Kara comes back. I thought she might like a ring too.”

     

                Opening a closing her mouth, Lena’s vision blurred slightly with tears as she reached out to take the box, staring down at the ring for a moment before snapping the box shut. She set it down beside her on the bedspread and swallowed thickly.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Nevermind that, what happened to you?”

     

                Brushing her hair out of her face as she gestured dismissively, Lena laughed hollowly. “What always happens? This family. ”

     

                Understanding and guilt softened Lillian’s face as she reached out to cup Lena’s chin, tutting as she stared at the left side of her face. Her mouth thinned with regret and she dropped her hand back to her lap as Lena ducked her head and fiddled with the spoon in her soup.

     

                “The blame isn’t yours to shoulder; don’t make yourself a martyr, Lena.”

     

                “I’m not making myself a martyr,” Lena rolled her eyes, sinking back into the pillows as she spooned chicken soup into her mouth. “I just … how can I blame them?”

     

                “You keep getting hurt by them,” Lillian tightly replied.

     

                “It’ll heal.”

     

                They lapsed into silence for a moment, Lena eating her soup as Lillian looked around the room and then reached out to lay a hand on Lena’s leg beneath the blankets. “I-I really am sorry- I … don’t know … how-”

     

                “Neither do I.”

     

                “But I want you to be happy, I want to be at your wedding. You might have yourself a new family, but you’re all I have left and … I’d hate to lose you again, Lena. I’m trying for you, it’s just- it’s hard. ”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena set the bowl aside and laced her fingers behind her head as she slowly shook her head, staring up at the ceiling and exhaling slowly. For some inexplicable reason, her eyes stung with tears and she couldn’t bring herself to look at Lillian. 

     

                “Are you okay?”

     

                Like a child, she pressed her face into the blankets as she hunched forward, hands fisted in the sheets, and shook her head, fighting back the urge to cry. “I’m just so …”

     

                Lena didn’t even have the words to articulate how she felt, how everything inside was all so knotted up. Roughly letting out a breath, she turned her head to the side, cheek pressed against the linen as she looked at the curtained window, feeling her mother’s patient stare on her.

     

                “You’re angry. Because I’m your mother, and I’m always supposed to be here for you, and I haven’t done a very good job of it.”

     

                “What if you’re right?”

     

                Sighing softly as she reached out and laid a hand on Lena’s back, feeling the ridge of her shoulder blade as her chest rose and fell with shallow breaths, Lillian’s mouth curled into a half-smile.

     

                “I won’t be right. If there’s one thing we both know, it’s that you have existed out of pure spite to prove me wrong at every turn. Prove me wrong once more.”

    Chapter 45

    Dear Lena,

     

    I’ve been in Afghanistan for sixteen hours now and all I’ve thought about is the overwhelming loss of you beside me. Two weeks seems like such a short time to have changed so much but it was long enough for me to get used to waking up beside you, to kissing you when I feel like it and hearing you laugh. And now it feels like a different life, already so long ago that the thought of another four months without you feels like a personal hell designed just for me. The only consolation for me now is that, hopefully, it wasn’t as bad for you this time. They tell me it doesn’t get any easier, but I think someone who’s so used to their own company might find it easier to adjust back. I just hope you don’t feel lonely.

     

    There’s still so much we didn’t get to talk about when I was home, firstly, being my future in the army. Honestly, I think you only cared about how I’m not going back, and I don’t blame you, but I like my job, I really do. All I wish now is that it was already over so that we could start our future together. I didn’t tell you when I was home, but I think that future might still be in journalism for me. I think I was a bit too harsh when I said I didn’t have it in me to write puff pieces about fashion trends, but that was me trivialising what goes on in America because I was angry at what goes on over here. There are injustices everywhere; why should I give up on writing about them just because I’ll be doing it out of uniform. Who knows, maybe I’ll have more liberty to speak about what I want to. I think I’m sick of writing the stories I have to, boring facts about places and people and numbers - maybe I’d like to write about ‘who wore it best at this year’s Met Gala’ for a change.

     

    My point is, we didn’t get to talk about our future much, but I want you to know I’ve given it a lot of thought, even if you haven’t. And don’t worry, none of it is concrete and I’m not going to be uncompromising. I just think I’m not as scared at the prospect of this chapter of my life coming to an end as I’d thought I would be. I’ve had a few months since that first fight about it to come to terms with the fact that I’m too young to have it all figured out anyway. Maybe Lillian is right in that regard, but I am sure about you, even if nothing else. The thought of us, together, in our own house with our dog and a couple of kids, enjoying life, seems almost too good to be true. I sometimes have to pinch myself to check if you’re real and not some dream, especially out here in the middle of nowhere. It’s late right now, the same stars overhead and it makes me think of you and what you’re doing. 

     

    It’s cold here. The desert is surprisingly cold. I feel like that’s something one should know, but the first time I wasn’t prepared for it, and even now it’s cold enough for me to think of you, wrapped up together in bed, and the thought warms me a little. Not as much as you would, but you’re there and I’m here and we’ll have to wait for that. It doesn’t seem fair that we’ll miss out on so much together over the next few weeks, that our first Thanksgiving and Christmas and New Year will be spent apart, and how I bet you’ve never even really celebrated them properly. But I’m glad you have Alex and Kelly and Eliza, because I know they’ll look after you while I’m away, and it’s a nice thought to know that while you can’t have me, you still have a family. I know it’s always been a difficult point for you, but you’ll never have to be alone again, with or without me there, but I hope it’ll never be without me again. Keep my heart safe - I left it with you. 

     

    Love always, 

     

    Kara xxx

    Chapter 46

                The first month passed by shockingly fast, Lena’s injuries fading to nothing - except for the cast she still had to wear - and Thanksgiving coming and going with a quiet dinner at Alex and Kelly’s with a few of their friends. Lena invited Sam and Ruby, and Nia and Querl brought Kara’s favourite chocolate pecan pie which invited a pang of longing as she wished her fiancée was there with her to enjoy the dinner and company.

     

                The fact that they were a quarter of the way through Kara’s deployment was a cause for quiet celebration, or at the very least a small consolation for not being able to see her every day. It never got easier for Lena to adjust to not kissing her good morning or good night, to not hold hands as they walked down the street or hear her singing drift through their house. Perhaps it should’ve felt weird that she’d grown so accustomed to Kara taking up so much space in her life, where previously there had been a giant hole of nothing and no one, but it never felt that way; it only ever felt wrong to her. Lena had been good at being alone, but now it was completely intolerable, and she often found herself eyeing Alex and Kelly and their easy comfort and availability to each other with envy.

     

                Looking forward, the three months stretching out before her felt like an eternity, and it was only in hindsight that she was able to find comfort in how fast time actually passed. Before she knew it, it was L-Corp’s annual Christmas party, weeks of Jess’s frantic planning coming to fruition with the employees of the National City office and all the local subsidiaries, benefactors and investors finally gathering in the open gallery of the National City Museum.

     

                She’d had her hair and makeup professionally done and had been driven to the venue early, wearing a deep green wrap dress beneath her camel overcoat, lips a neutral shade and hair elegantly waved. Security waved her in and she found Jess talking into her earpiece as she directed waitstaff and ticked things off her clipboard.

     

                “I do hope you’re planning on clocking off tonight,” Lena laughed as she approached her, slipping her phone into her purse and snapping it closed. “You’re also an employee, in case you’ve forgotten.”

     

                “Miss Luthor,” Jess greeted her. “You look nice.”

     

                Smiling slightly as she tried to lower the cuff of her sleeve further over the offending cast, Lena murmured her thanks. Jerking her head towards the almost empty room, ancient artefacts behind cordoned off ropes and the blue twilight seeping in through the skylight giving the place an old feeling, Lena wrinkled her nose.

     

                “Come and get a drink.”

     

                “I-“

     

                “They’ll figure out the rest of it.”

     

                She swept through to the next room, giving everything an appraising look before she made for the bar. Ordering two vodka cranberries, she handed one off to Jess and took a sip of her own, watching as a few early-comers trickled in. Sam was one of them and Alex and Kelly arrived shortly afterwards, a little in awe at the grandeur of hosting a Christmas party inside a museum a sort of novelty for them.

     

                “I’m glad you guys came,” Lena said with a small smile, eyes flitting around the room as more people started to arrive. “Now, it’ll be tolerable.”

     

                Alex nudged her, “it’s a party , you should have fun. It’s kind of a requirement for these sorts of things, you know.”

     

                Sam came up behind them after fetching herself a glass of wine and clapped a hand down on Lena’s shoulder as she sighed morosely. “Ah, but that’s just the thing; Lena prefers to watch from the sidelines and scowl at the staff. It’s a bit off-putting having your boss stare at you like that while you’re trying to wolf down a dozen hors d'oeuvres on the sly.”

     

                “I don’t scowl.”

     

                “Yes, you do.”

     

                “Also, remember what happened last time I had fun,” she objected, raising her cast and waving it in their faces.

     

                They laughed and Lena rolled her eyes, sipping her drink and smiling and nodding at employees that passed her. She always felt out of place at business events - whether it galas, fundraisers or conferences - and trying to make small-talk with employees she barely knew, hadn’t even been in National City long enough to know, was at the bottom of her list. Still, she made it a point to do so, greeting interns and benefactors and making chit-chat with strangers as they oggled her.

     

                The wealthier attendees started showing up later, as the place filled and the alcohol flowed, white-gloved waitstaff doing the rounds, and she caught sight of Andrea Rojas on the arm of her fiancé and drew herself up as she plastered a smile on her face, walking over to her.

     

                “Andrea, it’s lovely to see you,” she greeted her, exchanging kisses on their cheeks, before she greeted Russell similarly. “I had no idea you’d be coming.”

     

                “Oh, well, you know, it’s not every day I’m lucky enough to receive and invitation from an old friend.”

     

                “Well, it’s hard to know where you are, most of the time.”

     

                Raising an eyebrow, Andrea cocked her head to the side as she smiled thinly. “Is that the reason why? And here I thought you were still angry at me.”

     

                Lips twitching, Lena took a sip of her drink. “About forcing me out of that business deal in Costa Rica? I can’t imagine why you would think that.”

     

                “Just think, if I hadn’t , you probably wouldn’t have taken over the family business. Believe me, when I heard that news I was sure they’d gotten it wrong.”

     

                “I’ve never done what was expected of me, though, have I?”

     

                Andrea hummed in distracted agreement, her eyes scanning the room, “and where’s blondie tonight? Are you two still a thing or have you upgraded to a socialite? I hear Jack’s still soft on you. Shame, he was nice.”

     

                “Kara’s actually away on deployment, at the moment,” Lena curtly replied before off-handedly continuing, “we actually got engaged not too long ago, so...”

     

                “Really?” Andrea exclaimed.

     

                Russell shot her a bewildered look before he smiled at Lena, charming and polite, “congratulations to you both, that’s wonderful news.”

     

                “I never would’ve picked you as the type to settle down,” Andrea said, eyeing her dubiously. “You’ve changed a lot.”

     

                “I have,” Lena nodded, smiling softly as her eyes creased at the corners. “Well … you both have a lovely night. I need to do the rounds.”

     

                She stopped to greet a few more people, briefly caught up with Alex and Kelly to quietly grumble about a few select people she didn’t like, and then helped herself to a spinach puff before she forgot to remind herself to eat. Fetching a glass of red wine for herself, she turned and caught sight of her mother walking in, wearing a black dress and casting her cool eyes around the place.

     

                Lena froze for a second. She hadn’t spoken to Lillian much since her mother had visited her at home, and there was a vague feeling of awkwardness twisting her stomach as she stood there waiting to be spotted. What was confusing about the whole thing was that Lena wanted Lillian to spot her, didn’t want to run away from the discomfort of their argument like she previously would have, and yet she was still hesitant to speak to her. Lillian had apologised but the doubts had taken root within Lena, even though she knew that it wasn’t true.

     

                In the end, she took a sip of her wine, head tipped back and neck elegantly arching and then moved through the room towards her mother, standing at the bar, intent on proving that she was a different person now, as Andrea had said. To avoid Lillian would have only served to make her like childishly stubborn, given her mother’s apology.

     

                She approached her mother on her left and gently cleared her throat. “Mom.”

     

                Lillian glanced down, blinking in surprise before giving her a warm smile, reaching out to touch her arm. “Oh. Hi. I didn’t- I mean … you look nice.”

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                Silent for a moment, Lillian’s face clouded. “How are you? I know we haven’t really spoken since …”

     

                “I- yeah. I’m okay.”

     

                “Well, you look better. How’s the hand?”

     

                Raising the cast and turning her hand, Lena grimaced. “It’ll be off next week.”

     

                “Good.”

     

                Lena nodded and took a sip of her wine as Lillian’s whisky was set down on the bar before them. “Look, can we … talk?” Lena asked, shifting restleslly and flexing the fingers of her broken hand as she frowned off into the distance, staring at an Ancient Greek installation.

     

                “I’d like that.”

     

                Turning, Lena led them through the room, catching Kelly’s eye and encouraging nod, before leading her mother through to another gallery. It was dark, security patrolling and giving them a once-over before continuing to pace, and Lena sank down onto a stone bench, setting her wine glass down beside her. Legs stretched out, she stared at a marble bust as her mother sank down beside her.

     

                “I was going to call,” Lena insisted, lips twitching wryly. “At some point.”

     

                “No, I understand. You’re still upset.”

     

                Shrugging, Lena looked down at the smooth stone as she trailed her fingers over it and then reached for her glass, raising it to her lips as she sipped and rolled the taste around her mouth. 

     

                “I think … I was still being stubborn. I’m not really good at forgiving you - just you, apparently.”

     

                “With fair cause.”

     

                Swallowing, Lena shook her head, shoulders high and tense. “No. Sometimes … I think - I know - that … I’ve blamed you more than I ever blamed dad or Lex. You didn’t hurt me as much, but … it hurt that you didn’t protect me. That hurt more.”

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lillian apologised, “I understand I hurt you. You were just a kid and I … I shouldn’t have- but I need to hold myself accountable for that.”

     

                Head jerking up, Lena gave her a suspicious look. “Who have you been talking to.”

     

                Straightening up as she raised her chin, Lillian’s eyes shone with a faint challenge as her lips twitched slightly at the corners. “I’ll have you know, I’ve started seeing a therapist.”

     

                “You? In therapy?” Lena exclaimed.

     

                Humming pensively as her face pinched with consideration, Lillian crossed her legs and touched her chin. “I wanted a second opinion on how to repair our relationship. Apparently … I’ve not been very good with boundaries. And did you know that a lack of affection during childhood can make it harder for adults to form relationships? I think I should be grateful that you’ve turned out so well, then. And maybe that’s why I didn’t.”

     

                “I- okay, that’s … a lot to process. What else did your therapist say?”

     

                “Never you mind,” Lillian said, giving her a coy smile as she raised her glass and then hesitated, arching an eyebrow as she glanced sideways at her. “You might benefit from it, you know.”

     

                “Therapy?” Lena scoffed, shaking her head. “I tried it. Not even close.”

     

                “You did?”

     

                Pressing her lips together, Lena nodded, rocking slightly as she hesitated, feeling Lillian’s surprised eyes watching her closely. “I went for six weeks after Lex died.”

     

                “You never told me that.”

     

                There was the sting of sadness in Lillian’s quiet reply. Giving her a rueful smile, Lena arched an eyebrow. “We weren’t exactly speaking, were we? When should I have told you - at the funeral?”

     

                “You didn’t go.”

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena gave her a sheepish look. “Well, I didn’t go for very long, anyway. I realised that I’m not the kind of person that likes to talk about these things, so, shockingly, spilling my guts out to a stranger in therapy didn’t help much.”

     

                “And are you doing better now?”

     

                Her smile was sweet, almost shy as she ducked her head in a nod. “Much.”

     

                They lapsed into a comfortable silence for a moment, Lena’s pent up frustration and confusion loosening in her chest as things eased between them. Finishing off her glass of wine, she set it down beside her and cleared her throat.

     

                “You know, Christmas is coming up,” she slowly started, an uncertainly hopeful look in her green eyes as she looked up at Lillian, whose expression was patient and serene. “Alex and Kelly will be going to Midvale, and Eliza invited me to go too. She also invited you but … well, I didn’t know- but you should come if you’re not busy.”

     

                Lillian let out a soft laugh, face crinkling with amusement as Lena eyed her, sceptically. “What?”

     

                “Eliza already invited me.”

     

                “I- she did? Why? I mean … you have her number,” Lena concluded with a resigned sigh.

     

                “I wanted to make sure you were okay.”

     

                Letting out a loud laugh in the silence of the spacious gallery, Lena shook her head and pushed herself to her feet, stooping down to pick up her glass. The alcohol had warmed her considerably, a gentle flush to her cheeks and a spark to her eyes, and she gave Lillian a grudging smile as she straightened up, amused by her gall and this new version of her that cared. Although, Lena was still getting used to the idea that perhaps she always had, in her own distant way.

     

                “Come on. Let’s go and enjoy the party.”

    Chapter 47

    To Kara,

     

    I wish you’d been here last night. It was the Christmas Party, and by the time you read this you’ll have already heard about everything that happened, but it felt strange. My mother swallowed her pride and apologised weeks ago - with the ring and everything (I can send it to you if you want, but I’d like to put it on you myself) - but I guess I was still nursing my own hurt feelings, even though I’d already forgiven her. But I swallowed my pride this time and went over to her and we talked and it didn’t feel the way it used to. It wasn’t infuriating and snarky and sarcastic; I think we’ve both grown a lot since my brother died. 

     

    It was actually nice, and if you said that to me a year ago, it would’ve been the worst thing in the world to think I’d ever make myself so small and meek that I could enjoy my mom’s company, but now I know that I didn’t have to compromise myself to get here. If anything, she’s the one who’s compromised, and maybe she’s always been this person and wasn’t able to be it around my dad, but I think she’s a mom that I would’ve liked to have had growing up. 

     

    For now, we’re both trying to move past it all, and Lillian’s even going to therapy, which is something I would never have imagined her doing. I can’t help but laugh at how contradictive I feel now though, because I told you that you should go to therapy when you get home to work through it all, but when my mom suggested that I start going too, I knew I wouldn’t. I don’t know if I ever told you, but I’ve gone before and I didn’t find it helpful because I couldn’t bring myself to admit everything to a stranger. I’ve always been too vulnerable to let myself be vulnerable with someone else, if that makes sense. I think I have things I need to work on with myself though, and it’s not going to work if I don’t try and work on them in some way, but I’ve come a long way from where I was and looking back, I’m happy. Happier than I can ever remember being - broken hand and all.

     

    I’ve been thinking a lot about my relationships with other people lately. You told me that I need people - people that were mine and not just ones that have come from our relationship - and I think you were right. Obviously things with my mom will always be a little bumpy, but I’ve also decided to make more of an effort making friends. Really, it’s just Sam, and maybe it doesn’t really count because she’s a work colleague, but I’ve known her for a few years now and she’s followed me across the country and been as close to a friend as I’ve had in a long while - your annoying sister and her wonderful girlfriend aside - and it’s been nice to do things outside of work. Look at me, making some sort of life for myself for you. 

     

    But that’s a whole other tangent, because what I’ve actually been thinking about is how different things would’ve been if I hadn’t met you. What if I’d decided to stay in my office that day instead of taking a rare break? What if you’d come in for coffee half an hour earlier and been able to find an empty table? We never would have met. I like to think that we would’ve in some way - maybe not that day, but a different one, on the street or in another coffee shop where we would’ve bumped into each other and just known. I think this because I don’t want to imagine a world where we didn’t meet; all I can think of is that if I’d missed you that day, missed that smile you gave me, I would have missed the rest of my life.

     

    You know, sometimes I forget how much I’ve changed since I met you. They say you can’t change someone by loving them, but that’s not true. I guess what they mean to say is that you can’t force someone to change if they don’t want to, but you can definitely change someone with love. I’m grateful for it. I don’t really know what kind of person I was before - I don’t think I was much of one - but I know I prefer the one I am now. You make me a better person, and that’s a fact. I was so alone for the longest time that, for a while, I used to think I was undeserving of love and I got good at being alone, and I would tell myself it was because I wasn’t built to be around someone else. That wasn’t true though, because the moment I met you, your smile changed everything, and the moment your hand first slipped into mine, it was like my hands knew they were made to only hold your hands, and the first time we kissed it was like my lips were only made to kiss only yours. Anyway, I keep thinking about all these things and I realise that I was wrong, although I hate to admit it. It’s not that I was ever undeserving of love, it was the exact opposite; I just had to find the people who wanted to love me. I truly feel like I found those people with you. I think you can understand that more than anyone, how much it means to have someone want you when you have no one left.

     

    This letter got depressing very fast. I’m sorry. Anyway, the whole point is I underestimated you and your fortune cookies of love, and since that moment, I have learnt to never underestimate anything ever again. Which is probably why, with everything going on in my life at the moment, I’ve been thinking about the past a lot. I guess I underestimated a lot of things that have happened – well, how much these things have affected me. I think most of all, I underestimated my mom. I know she never meant to hurt me – it doesn’t change the fact that she did, but I underestimated how much she loved me because I made it so hard for her to show it. Thank you for pushing me to try and fix things with her. We haven’t really solved anything, and we’ve taken a few steps backwards, but I feel like I’ve changed enough to want to work through this, which is something I’ve never wanted to do. Even over the past few months, I have a sneaking suspicion that I was just waiting for the chance to self-sabotage this whole thing, because if I’m being honest, I’m still scared about having a normal relationship with her. You’d think it’d be easy, after all, I get along great with your mom, but I guess what frightens me the most is that this is my mom. 

     

    I just wish you were here to talk about all of this with me. Being able to see your face on a screen and hear your voice is the best part of my day, but it’s just not the same. I miss you more and more every day, but it only brings me closer to seeing you again. I love you.

     

    Lena x

    Chapter 48

                Mid-December came around fast, and Lena spent every moment at the office, pulling sixteen-hour days and, once or twice, falling asleep on the sofa mid-document and waking to the grey dawn breaking over the city. The weather grew frigid, a disgruntling prospect for Lena, considering that she’d left Metropolis and its sleet and snow behind, only to find herself in a windy city that, while mercifully didn’t snow, was still rather wet and cold. It had been just over a year since she’d initially made the move, and the searing heat of summer had all but eclipsed her memories of the early cold months of the year, and she found that she’d acclimated. 

     

                She saw less of Alex and Kelly, only catching their calls half of the time, and on the nights that she came home to them sitting in her living room, they’d already made dinner and eaten, leaving a bowl of leftovers for her before they left shortly afterwards, having work the next morning. It was taking its toll on Lena, wearing her down, and she was plagued with persistent headaches and a fleeting bout of coughing that made her chest ache as she ran her immune system down. The only person she regularly made time for was Kara, dropping everything for their ten-minute video calls where everything was pixelated and lagging, clinging to them for some sense of reprieve from her job. But at the same time, she threw herself into her work as a way to pass the time without Kara too, and took her work lunches with Sam as a way to insist she was taking time to branch out and make friends.

     

                Never one for the holidays, Lena was almost oblivious to the decorations that went up, the frantic stress of people gift shopping and picking out trees and the other stuff that didn’t affect her, and she had to listen to Alex pester her for two weeks about her lack of decorations at home before she impatiently handed her a credit card and told her to buy it herself. That in itself was a mistake, and Lena spent one of her rare evenings at home hanging baubles off the branches of a modest-sized douglas fir that had taken up residence in the corner of her living room.

     

                Perhaps she would have enjoyed it more if Kara was there with her ever-present cheeriness, knowing she would have loved decorating the tree, the new Christmas drinks at Starbucks and the ice skating rink they set up, the gingerbread cookies that Lena sent Jess off to buy for the office. Lena was somewhat brooding about her first good Christmas being overshadowed by the absence of the one thing that would have made it perfect. Still, she was happy to be going to Midvale for a couple of days, knowing she’d enjoy herself anyway and eager to give everyone the gifts she’d picked out for them. 

     

                That was one of the few things she’d taken the time out of her busy day’s to do, poring over her laptop as she browsed sites and brainstormed. She’d chosen gifts for Kara too and had already sent a care package on ahead to make sure it would get to her in time, packing in sealed packets of gingerbread cookies, sachets of peppermint hot chocolate and a Christmas card and a multitude of little knick-knacks for her to open on the day. She imagined it wouldn’t feel much like Christmas over there, but was intent on trying her best to make it feel like it as much as she could.

     

                Still, her moods were contrary and she found herself troubled more often than not. Even the removal of her cast, just a phantom twinge now and again reminding her of her broken wrist, wasn’t enough to dispel the brewing sense of unease within Lena. She watched the news religiously, keeping it on in her office as background noise, scouring news sites and various papers every day as she read up on the conflict and politics and saw the worsening state of things. It only served to make her quietly panic, but she couldn’t help herself.

     

                Things only got worse when she didn’t hear from Kara for two days. It wasn’t unusual for a day here or there to go without a video or phone call, but two days were rare, and her worry was only exacerbated by what she saw on the news. Late one night, pacing back and forth in her office, Lena called Alex, voice haggard and fraught with worry as she anxiously bit her nails.

     

                “Hello?” Alex grumbled.

     

                “Hi, it’s me. I just- something’s wrong, isn’t it? I mean … it’s been two days.”

     

                Letting out a listless sigh, Alex was gentle as she replied. “Lena, go to bed.”

     

                “But you haven’t heard from her?”

     

                There was a momentary pause before Alex reluctantly replied, “no. But it’s not the first time it’s happened; it’s usually nothing.”

     

                “But what if-”

     

                “Do you want me to come over?”

     

                She chewed on her lip, brimming with nervous tension as she rubbed at her forehead and then exhaled heavily. “No. No, you- you sleep. I’m sorry for calling; I don’t mean to be a nuisance.”

     

                “You’re not-”

     

                “Night.”

     

                She hung up and swallowed thickly, dropping her phone onto the nearest armchair and then scrubbed her hands over her face, digging the heels of her palms into her eyes. Pale moonlight seeped in through the tall windows and she sighed before picking her phone back up and wandering downstairs.

     

                In the light of the fridge, she made a cup of tea and passed by Athena’s bed, the dog raising her head slightly off her paws to watch her go, and Lena moved into the living room. In the dark, she sank down onto the sofa and stared at the chess set before her. After a long few minutes of sitting silently in the dark, the old house shifting and creaking around her as the windowpanes shuddered in their frames at the battering wind outside, Lena shifted forward.

     

                Eyeing the blurred shapes of black and white pieces, she reached out and picked up the white knight before setting it back in its spot and slowly reaching for her phone. Her thumb hesitated over her mother’s name before she, ultimately, called her.

     

                “You’re calling late,” Lillian greeted her.

     

                Humming, the sound slightly hoarse and distracted, Lena raked a hand through her hair. “Mm. You still answered.”

     

                “I just finished a meeting with business associates in Shanghai.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “What’s wrong?”

     

                Lena swallowed and took a sip of her scalding tea. “Nothing,” she murmured. “I was just thinking … what Sicilian Defence variation did you use to play against me when I was younger?”

     

                “You’re thinking about chess plays at eleven o’clock in the night?”

     

                She didn’t reply, was just quiet and thoughtful as she stared at the chessboard in the dark, thinking about the way she used to thrash her brother at the game, even at four years old. The only time she could ever remember spending much time with Lillian as a child was on the opposite side of the checkered tiles to her, sitting silently for the most part as her mother dutifully taught her the proper openings, the proper theory and tactics behind the game. Lena was better than her, instinctive and clever, but it was her ability to learn the theory behind it that garnered some grudging, silent respect from Lillian.

     

                “Sveshnikov,” Lillian answered after a moment, her voice tender.

     

                “Sveshnikov,” Lena echoed, “that was it. Of course you preferred the most aggressive variation.”

     

                “It’s aggressive, yes, but it’s very sharp, very theoretical. I personally think it’s the most unforgiving Sicilian to play with the D5 hall, but some people argue that the Dragon has more theory or the Yugoslav attack is sharper and more dangerous against the black king.”

     

                “Of course Sveshnikov is trickier,” Lena agreed, reaching forward and playing E4, C5 with the black and white pawns, reaching across the board to move the pieces. “It has more positional factors.”

     

                “Exactly. Although, the Dragon can be strong against the right opponent. I see why you preferred it.”

     

                “Run me through the Sveshnikov again,” Lena murmured.

     

                “E4, C5.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “Nf3, Nc6. Do you remember it?”

     

                They played through the sequence, Lillian calling the moves for white while Lena silently counteracted them with black’s next move, her eyes closing as she ran through her vague memories of the sequence. It was calming and familiar and they played through most of the game, Lena quietly giving Lillian her moves as it moved away from the opening and into the middlegame. Their replies came later as they were left to envision the strategy and theory behind each other’s move and after Lena checkmated Lillian, they lapsed into silence.

     

                “I wish you would tell me what’s wrong,” Lillian eventually murmured.

     

                “It’s nothing. It’s … silly.”

     

                “I’d still like to hear it; if you’re upset … well, it clearly matters to you.”

     

                Pressing her lips into a flat line and her eyebrows pinched together in a troubled look, Lena sank back against the sofa cushions. “I haven’t heard from Kara in a couple of days.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “I know it’s probably nothing, but … with everything in the news, I mean-”

     

                “That’s not silly,” Lillian slowly replied, “and … I won’t dismiss your concerns by telling you that you’re worrying over nothing, but I do hope that it is nothing.”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena wearily sighed. “Thanks.”

     

                Neither of them spoke for a moment and then Lillian cleared her throat, as if discomforted by the vulnerability of their conversation. “Would you like to play another game?”

     

                “Shouldn’t you sleep?”

     

                “Shouldn’t you?”

     

                “I don’t want to.”

     

                “Then let me keep you company for a bit.”

                

                It was well past midnight by the time Lillian declared it was time for her to go to bed, and Lena felt slightly guilty at how late she’d kept her mother up but was genuinely touched by the effort. She even told her as such before wishing her goodnight, and was left mulling it over as she reset the chessboard, wondering how she’d gone from an estranged mother who had been oblivious to the inner workings of Lena’s life, from her short stint in therapy to what the inside of her house looked like, to be one who stayed up half of the night playing chess to keep her company and caring for her while she was in the hospital.

     

                Pottering around the house in the wan light above the stove, Lena rinsed out her teacup and stepped outside into the bitter night to water her herbs, plucking errant weeds and wilting leaves, before she hesitated. Shoving her feet into a pair of heeled boots beside the door, Lena pulled on her discarded coat and grabbed Athena’s leash, whistling softly to get the dog’s attention. Sinking to a crouch, she clipped the leash on and ruffled her fur before snagging her keys and stepping outside.

     

                It was dark and late and she was alone as she walked down the wide, affluent street, staring at dark windows as they passed them by. The row of brownstones, the parked Audi’s and Lexus’ familiar as she eyed stoops with wreaths on the doors and lights trimming the railings. It was cold enough that her cheeks ached a little as they turned rosy, but it was peaceful to walk, grey clouds obscuring most of the stars and moon as she went around the block, and then again and again.

     

                Eventually, she went off on a tangent, following the end of the street to another, then another, and wound up at a nearby 7/11. Buying a cup of cheap coffee, she lingered outside in the neon glow, Athena sitting beside her, a non-threatening guard dog watching a few drunks, a homeless man and a delivery guy. The coffee was bad but it was hot and Lena bought one for the homeless man, setting it down in front of him and pulling a few hundreds from her purse before tucking them into the hat with a handful of coins.

     

                Afterwards, she walked home, shoulders slumped, eyes burning and worry making her head pound. She needed to sleep but she was reluctant to, and she cursed that it was the early hours of Saturday morning, wishing that she’d be able to sit in a five-hour business proposal, quietly countering the points of her staff as they finetuned a project. She’d just have to work from home, but it wasn’t quite the same, and she knew her mind would get stuck on Kara instead of focusing.

     

                She got home just before four and shed her coat and boots inside, shivering in Kara’s sweatpants and the thin sweater as she unclipped Athena and then wearily trudged upstairs. Falling onto the mattress, she curled up under the covers, warming herself in the cold and empty bed and waited for sleep to drag her under. It was quick to come but wasn’t the reprieve she’d hoped for, and it was almost noon when she was woken by the sound of the front door being shut a little too loud.

     

                Groggy and exhausted, Lena rubbed at her eyes and dragged herself out of bed, yanking open the bedroom door and quickly making her way downstairs. Alex was unwinding a scarf from around her neck in the hallway, a bulging tote bag on the floor beside her, and they stared at each other for a long moment, Lena willing her to not break her heart.

     

                “I just- now it’s been three days so … now we start to panic.”

     

                Swallowing thickly as she nodded, Lena descended the rest of the steps and cracked her knuckles in an agitated manner, watching as Alex shed her coat and picked up the tote bag. “Where’s Kelly?”

     

                “She got pulled into an emergency session, but it’s fine. I bought eggnog and gingerbread houses.”

     

                The breath was forced from Lena’s lungs as she closed her eyes and rubbed at her forehead. “No offence, Alex, but I really couldn’t give a shit about gingerbread houses right now.”

     

                “It’s not about the gingerbread houses.”

     

                “I’m exhausted, okay? I was up all night playing chess with my mom and-”

     

                Alex snorted and gave her an amused look as she dumped the bag on the counter and started unpacking it. “Chess? Really?”

     

                Flushing slightly, Lena rolled her eyes. “Coffee?”

     

                “Sure. I’ll save the eggnog for later.”

     

                “Is- is your mom coming?”

     

                “After work.”

     

                “Can I get her a ticket or-”

     

                Alex laid a hand on her arm and smiled slightly, “it’s fine.”

     

                Nodding, she moved over to the machine and started making two cups, pensive and resentful as she felt the knot inside her constrict. Company would take her mind off things but it was the last thing she wanted, and still, Alex unloaded the gingerbread houses, the flat sides ready to be glued together with icing and colourful candy decorations, indifferent to what Lena wanted. In a way, Lena had to grudgingly appreciate her for it, and even more so as she set a coffee cup down in front of Alex and she jerked her head to the open doorway.

     

                “Come on then, teach me how to play.”

     

                “Play what?”

     

                “Chess.”

     

                “You want me to … teach you how to play chess? Why?”

     

                “Well, you don’t want to build gingerbread houses, so we’ll play chess instead.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena shook her head, eyes rolling, and walked off towards the hallway. “Fine. Come on then.”

     

                Sitting on the rug on opposite sides of the coffee table while Home Alone played on the TV, Lena slowly taught Alex how to play, teaching her the basics of each piece and how they moved and laying off the theory as she distractedly played against her. It was child’s play to someone who had been a chess champion since early childhood and she found herself growing increasingly amused by Alex’s frustration as Lena trounced her within a dozen moves over and over again.

     

                “You’re not very good at teaching, you know,” Alex brittly replied. “You keep doing all these fancy moves.”

     

                “Do you want me to let you win one?” Lena grinned, moving her rook.

     

                “Yes. Thank you.”

     

                She snorted, “too bad; I hate losing.”

     

                “You’re annoying.”

     

                Giving her a sweet smile, Lena gestured to the board. “It’s your move.”

     

                They played for the next hour, Lena going easy on Alex and correcting her moves, explaining the errors as she painted out the subsequent dozen moves that would lead to her eventual victory if Alex took her knight instead of her bishop, or if she moved her rook there and left an opening. By the time Home Alone finished, Lena was feeling marginally less anxious, although there was still a heaviness in her chest, and she found herself glad for Alex’s company as they made grilled cheese in the kitchen and then prepped the groceries in the fridge for a roast chicken dinner. 

     

                Kelly arrived mid-afternoon to find Lena quartering onions while Alex basted the chicken, eyeing the rain spattering the windows with a gloomy look on her face. “Shit weather we’re having; I may as well be in Midvale in the snow.”

     

                “You’ll be complaining about that when we’re there,” Kelly called out, shedding a raincoat and smiling before she crossed the room and kissed her girlfriend. “You two doing okay?”

     

                “Mm, I have a newfound interest in chess,” Alex snippily replied, glaring sideways at Lena, “I’m making it my New Year’s resolution to learn as much theory as possible and wipe the smile off Miss Chess Champion’s face.”

     

                “Did you let her win?” Kelly whispered.

     

                Grinning, Lena wrinkled her nose as she leaned in, whispering back, “once or twice.”

     

                Squeezing her shoulder, Kelly fetched herself a seltzer from the fridge and vaguely described her day to them as she sat on one of the counters, grimly skirting around the details of one of her more difficult cases while the other two finished up prepping the food and Alex shoved it all into the oven.

     

                Alex broke out the gingerbread houses then and they crowded around the kitchen table while listening to an old vinyl from the other room. Sitting cross legged on her chair, Lena carefully assembled the front and left side, her icing neat and precise in comparison to the other two women’s icing monstrosities.

     

                “You’re supposed to make it look Christmassy,” Alex complained.

     

                “It’s fine like this.”

     

                “That’s not very into the Christmas spirit, is it?” Kelly said with a grin.

     

                “Ah, yes, something I’m most definitely known for being.”

     

                “Add some candy.”

     

                She relented and added neat rows of gumdrops and crushed candy canes, artfully drizzling icing to look like snow, and was quite pleased with the finished result. It was already growing dark outside and the house smelled of roasting chicken and it wasn’t long before a cab pulled up outside with Eliza. She had a worn overnight bag with her and looked exhausted yet warm, wrapping Lena in a gentle hug as she swayed her from side to side for a moment, squeezing softly.

     

                They ate dinner and sipped wine in the bright kitchen light, Lena toying with her food until Alex nudged her and she made more of an effort to eat. After they’d finished, she insisted on cleaning up, shooing everyone into the living room for another Christmas movie, but Eliza insisted on staying and giving her a hand. They were silent for a long while, Eliza up to her elbows in hot soapy water while Lena waited for the next plate or fork, a damp dish towel in hand and a brooding aura about her.

     

                “How’re you holding up?” Eliza eventually asked, giving her an expectant look.

     

                Lena took the wineglass and carefully wiped suds out in the bowl, shrugging nonchalantly as she hunched her shoulders slightly. “I’m alright.”

     

                “I know how you’re feeling. I felt it for years; I’m glad she won’t put you through that.”

     

                Eliza’s laugh was strained as she scrubbed at a plate, a grim set to her mouth. Lena wondered what it must have been like for her, to have her husband spend so much time away, leaving her alone to worry and raise their daughters in between long shifts at the hospital. Mouth turning down at the corners, Lena hesitated, taking the plate and slowly wiping the dish towel over it as she chewed on her words.

     

                “Did you ever- did you ever feel angry?”

     

                “All the time,” Eliza softly admitted. “I was so angry at him - at her - for making me worry. I think that’s normal.”

     

                Nodding, Lena’s mouth thinned and she put the plate on the others stacked on the counter. She could feel Eliza watching her and briefly met her eyes before looking back down, hand out for the next dish.

     

                “You look tired.”

     

                “Work’s been busy,” Lena said with a wan smile, the lie easily rolling off her tongue. “Christmas, you know. It’s been a bit hectic planning the annual business plans and budgets for the new projects in the new year. Lots of phone calls and that sort of stuff.”
