                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes, “is it actually a month, though, or are you lying and coming home early again? Because I loved the surprise last time, but if you make me wait even a second longer than I have to to see you again …”

     

                “Two weeks. I promise. I don’t think I’d even be able to wait the cab ride from the base before seeing you again.”

     

                “I’ll be there the moment you walk off that damn bus, ready to tackle you to the ground to make sure you don’t run off again.”

     

                “I’m counting down every moment.”

    Chapter 57

    To Kara,

     

    Happy Valentine’s Day! It feels strange to think we’ve known each other for a year now, and this year we get to celebrate this day together. Did we really meet so close to Valentine’s Day and not spend it together? If only we’d known. Of course, this will be the first time for me, and as always, I’m glad it’s with you. That day you sat at my table, I never would’ve thought that in a year’s time I’d be sending a cheesy card with a heart on it and feeling so giddy at the thought of you, but here I am. We’re so close now, I can feel it. It makes me nervous and excited and I feel like I’m going to explode whenever I think about it too much. For so long, this is the thing I’ve been holding onto to keep me going and I don’t know what I’m going to do with myself when you’re back. Probably never let you go again.

     

    Thinking about how this could possibly be the last letter that I send you over there is a funny feeling. It’s about two weeks away now (I’m assuming this got to you in time to open today) and I think it’ll be strange to be able to say all of my thoughts to you as I have them. This won’t be the last letter that I ever write to you though, because why shouldn’t I write to you when you’re home too? They’re not really love letters, and I’m sorry I can’t write all that sappy shit for you because of the way I am, but I’d write you a letter every day if it meant I could see the look on your face when I give it to you.

     

    Do you remember that night you took me to the carnival? You dragged me onto the Ferris wheel and I didn’t tell you I was afraid of heights because you were so excited about it. How it feels right now, waiting for you to come home, is the same feeling. Those butterflies right at the very top, that feeling when your stomach lurches and you feel a little breathless because you’re nervous about what happens next but the thrill is exciting. Although, now that I think about it, those butterflies probably had less to do with how frightened I was hanging thirty feet above the ground and more to do with how much I liked you, and how I felt like I was a nervous wreck because I’d never liked anyone before. And you made us do that silly love test machine and it lit up all the way to the top and then I ruined it with the science behind how it works. I wanted to kick myself but I was so scared of reading into things that I didn’t want to think you were flirting with me.

     

    Well, look at us now. You were right and we really are meant to be, because everything has miraculously worked out better than I could’ve planned it myself. You’ll come home safely and we’ll be back together and we’re going to be happy. God, we’re going to be so happy, Kara, I just know it. This is the end of all the struggling and the worrying; the minute you get back we’re going to start the rest of forever.

     

    Not to get too ahead of myself though, because like I said, we probably still have two weeks by the time this reaches you, but I’m so excited - in case you couldn’t tell. That’s not like me, I know, and I know I’ve been stressed and worried sick the entire time you’ve been gone, but I almost feel like I don’t have to worry anymore because you’ll be home in no time. What’s two weeks compared to how long you’ve been gone? It’ll be the most agonising wait of my life but I’ve waited longer. I’ll still be worried sick, of course - you know me - but it all feels so soon that it’s starting to feel real. Finally, everything we’ve talked about will be here.

     

    You better not ruin my plans for us, Kara Danvers. You better keep your head down and make it back to me like you promised. I love you more than I can explain in a letter, but trust me that I love you so much. Possibly more than you will ever know, but I’ll try my best to show you. I’ll prove it every day.

     

    Love always,

     

    Lena xxx

    Chapter 58

                The next week dragged by, and then suddenly all that separated them was ten short days and a few thousand miles. It didn’t feel real that Kara would be home, but there was palpable excitement in the air between the trio as they made plans. Chinese the first night she was home, drinks the next weekend with Nia and Querl and Sam and whoever else they could get their hands on. They’d have a game night at Lena’s and visit Lillian and Eliza in turn, a week or two in the Napa Valley as Lena had promised, and even more. 

     

                Soon enough there would be nothing standing between them, not even an inch, and Lena was counting down every second, even as time dragged on. She couldn’t help but feel a little bit bitter about the fact that time had flown by when Kara had been there - especially during her two weeks off - and dragged while she’d been gone, but it was hard to stay resentful when there were only a handful of days left. Never had a week felt so agonisingly far away though.

     

                Still, Lena had work to distract her, although at eight-thirty in the morning, as she enjoyed her second coffee for the day in the pale sunlight of late February, she was only thinking of Kara. Watching the clock as she made a half-hearted attempt to do the crossword, she was waiting for Kara to call. The schematics and proposal for a new project were sitting on her desk, untouched, and she faced the wide windows, waiting patiently as she idling swayed the chair from side to side. Any minute now.

     

                It was another five minutes of waiting, answering seven down and ten across and checking her schedule for the day, before her phone finally rang. A wide smile split her face, eager excitement perking her up as she answered the video call and leaned back in her seat, taking a swig of her oat milk latte as her eyes shone.

     

                “Hey, you.”

     

                “Good morning, Miss Luthor. How are we today?”

     

                “Missing you. Nothing new.”

     

                “Oh, God, I really do miss you,” Kara sighed, a rosy-cheeked glow of delight on her face as if the prospect of home had filled her with new light. “I know it’s soon, but … well, don’t lose hope now.”

     

                “Never,” Lena murmured, “if there’s one thing I’m sure of, it’s you. I can feel it though; it feels … strange . Everything’s just waiting - even the weather is weird. I’m getting impatient now. It’s hard to concentrate.”

     

                “Well, you’d better get as much work in as you can because I’m going to be an even bigger distraction when I’m home.”

     

                Lena chuckled, straightening up in her seat and reaching for her pen and the journal on her desk, smoothing the open page down as she raised her eyebrows slightly. “That reminds me, I was going to go shopping and get some things for you. You know, a new toothbrush, new pyjamas, things like that. Is there anything in particular you want me to pick up?”

     

                “All I need is you,” Kara murmured, pausing momentarily as she deliberated and then impishly continued, “and possibly two packs of cookie dough and some Chinese takeout.”

     

                Grinning, Lena rolled her eyes, “we’re already all over the takeout, don’t worry about that. Alex has it penned in for our first stop on the way home. Cookie dough, I can do too.”

     

                “I could marry you right now.”

     

                “No need to rush,” Lena lightly teased her, “we’ll have all the time in the world soon enough.”

     

                “You know, knowing that should make me more patient, but if anything it just makes me want to marry you the second I’m back. I mean, obviously I want to do it properly with the whole thing - we can talk about it, anyway, but I just- I love you. I love you and I can’t believe I get to marry you. How did my life change so much in a year?”

     

                “Your life? I’m practically unrecognisable now, thanks to you and your family. All because of that baseball game.”

     

                “That was what did it, huh?”

     

                Rolling her eyes as Kara grinned smugly, Lena pursed her lips together as she tried to fight back a smile. “I still think about that kiss, you know. Not the kiss cam one, the other one, under that streetlight. I’d never been kissed like that in my entire life; it felt like I’d never been properly kissed until that night.”

     

                Kara laughed softly, a rosiness to her cheeks as she propped her chin up in her hand, raising her eyebrows as her glasses slipped down her nose a little. “Yeah?”

     

                “I surprised myself that night,” Lena admitted. “I’d kept all of my confusing feelings for you locked inside, and that was the first time I realized that I didn’t have to, because you said you liked me. That kiss, oh God, I could’ve stayed wrapped up in that moment for the rest of my life.”

     

                “I’m just glad I didn’t mess things up like I thought I had, ” Kara said, giving Lena a wry smile. “I thought for sure you were going to take off running. I had you pegged wrong, and you surprised me too.”

     

                Lena’s tone was light and soft as her solemn green eyes creased faintly at the corners, “I’m not running anywhere.”

     

                “I know, and I’m sorry ever doubted how stubborn you could be.”

     

                “A rookie mistake, but you wouldn’t be the first.”

     

                They talked for another hour until Kara started flagging, masking yawns and humming in reply as she started talking less. Eventually, Lena told her to go to bed, as reluctant as she was to hang up. But they’d be able to stay up all night talking when she was back, if they wanted to. It was a strange luxury and she’d be able to go another week without it if she had to.

     

                “I don’t want to say goodbye,” Kara murmured. “I miss you.”

     

                “I miss you too. Go on, sleep. I’ll talk to you tomorrow.”

     

                “I love you. I can’t wait to see you again.”

     

                “I love you too. Stay safe for me, okay? It’s less than two weeks now.”

     

                “Eleven days,” Kara heavily sighed, giving Lena a tired smile. 

     

                Tracing her face on the screen, Lena softly smiled back, “I’ll see you soon.”

     

                “Wait for me a little longer.”

     

                “Always. I love you.”

     

                She was late for her first meeting with Sam and the head of finance, brusquely apologising as she swept into the boardroom and set down her tablet and journal, quickly slipping into the middle of their conversation as they ran through numbers and Sam gave her a quick recap, setting annotated documents before Lena. It was tedious and long and Lena was itching for another coffee by the time they wrapped up, lunchtime not too far off.

     

                Inviting Sam along to her office, Lena had Jess order lunch for them and made herself a quick coffee on the machine in the communal kitchenette before they took a seat on the sofa and rehashed the same conversation from the meeting, jotting down notes and finetuning things until their lunch came. The office was cool and the sky had lightened to grey as clouds swept in and Sam asked about Kara as Lena picked at her salad, distractedly. She was all Lena could think about, even in the midst of profit margins and expenses. 

     

                Work seemed to drag by, as busy as she was, and Lena drove home with the bone-deep, weary satisfaction of another day coming to a close. She was almost one day closer to picking Kara up from Fort Rozz, from never letting her go again, and she basked in the warmth of that thought as she cooked dinner for herself. She had been slowly perfecting a fried rice dish to cook for Kara when she came home, the recipe improving in fits and starts as she made it semi-regularly, measuring out soy sauce, learning the right length of time to fry the egg in it and when to add the peas. The motions were comforting at this point, a loving act of cooking as she listened to Billie Holliday and nursed a rum and coke.

     

                After eating dinner alone, curled up on the sofa as she watched an old movie off the long list she’d been given by Kara - tonight she was finishing off the second half of Ghost - Lena donned her coat and shoes and took Athena for a walk in the cool dusk, watching as the sky purpled and then deepened. 

     

                It was dark when she returned home, shrugging off her coat as Athena made straight for her water bowl, and Lena rubbed at her eyes and sighed softly as she walked into the kitchen and made a cup of green tea for herself. She was trying to cut down on caffeine as well, drinking it only for work purposes - which sometimes meant she was still drinking it at midnight for a particularly busy night - but overall, she felt well rested now. The Valium was still a sore point but she took it regularly, the nights she found herself restless or too alert tempered with the effects of the drugs, and she’d made a point of sending her mother a photo of Alex refilling her prescription at her pharmacy.

     

                Taking her tea upstairs to her room, Athena following on her heels, Lena climbed beneath the blankets after changing into pyjamas, nestled in one of Kara’s tattier sweatshirts that still smelled like her, and reached for the letter that had been waiting on the console in the hallways for her. Even now, after so many months, the sight of her name in Kara’s looping hand still sent a thrill through her. Perhaps it was even more so now with it being one of the last ones she’d receive of Kara - possibly even the last one. 

     

                Sliding a finger under the edge of the envelope’s flap, she tore it along the top and slid out the folded pieces of paper pulled from a legal pad and leaned against the pillows to read it. She couldn’t help but smile as she savoured the words, sipping tea in between paragraphs, and eventually slid it back into the envelope with a warm glow in her chest. Draining the rest of her tea, she picked a book up off her nightstand at random and settled in to read for a bit, until it was late enough to shake two pills out of the orange bottle on the bedside table and swallow them dry. 

     

                In the glow of the lamp, Lena lay stretched out in bed, prising open the locket around her neck and staring at the photo of Kara that she’d put inside. Thumbing her face, which was now partially rubbed away from Lena’s frequent touch, she let out a soft sigh, a tender look of yearning on her face. As the effects of the sleeping pills started to set in, she snapped the locket shut and turned off the lamp, before rolling onto her side and clutching the delicate silver pendant in her fist as she slowly sank into sleep.

     

                It was Wednesday the next day, seemingly ordinary and a little muggy as Lena woke. Her head felt foggy from the sleeping pills and there was a languid air about her movements as she sat up, rubbing a hand over her face and checking the time. Five o’clock. With a faint sigh, she climbed out of bed and walked into the bathroom, the slate floor cold beneath her bare feet, and showered before fishing out a dress from her closet and getting started on her makeup. 

     

                Breakfast was overnight oats and a cup of green tea, taken in her little garden as Lena stared up at the sky. There was a certain weight to the day that she couldn’t place - perhaps the nostalgia of so many similar days without Kara that were finally coming to an end now, or perhaps something else entirely. But as she sat in the shade of the tall tree, sipping her tea, Lena felt like there was a peculiar quality to the day, the shadow of leaves on the wooden decking and motes of pollen swirling through a shaft of early morning sunlight seeming tranquil and unusual, as if the whole world was holding its breath, the city seeming another world away from the stillness of the garden.

     

                Everything felt eerily calm and Lena couldn’t shake the feeling that it was a day for something big. She had that new deal they were hoping to close and felt a flicker of eagerness, anticipating a long phone call with good news when she went into the office later. Or perhaps Kara’s service would end a few days earlier. Sitting in her garden with the white sky overhead, the air soupy with the approaching spring, she couldn’t help but smile, thinking about how things were on the up for her.

     

                Leaving for work at seven-thirty, she stopped off for coffee and took a photo of the first blooming flowers, texting it to Kara with a quick message and a heart before making her way into the office a little early. Jess wasn’t in yet, so Lena got settled in, checking her emails and confirming her attendance at a meeting for the afternoon as she checked her schedule. 

     

                It was a busy day, and Lena gleefully did close the deal with a new local distributor - something that would boost local employment in the surrounding suburbs - and splurged on donuts for the office to celebrate. Feeling bolstered by a productive day, she was in a good mood through the afternoon meetings, listening to the HR Department talk about position description revisions with earnest interest as they altered the internal structure of the company ever so slightly, streamlining the flow of different departments. 

     

                By the time it was five o’clock, she was content with a day’s work and decided to leave early, heading off within the hour and making it home just past six. Parking in the empty spot before her house, she frowned at Alex’s car in front of hers as she cut the engine and climbed out of the Porsche, wondering what she was doing there as Lena wracked her brain to try and figure out if they’d made plans for dinner tonight. She knew they’d made plans for Teppanyaki tomorrow night, and as she locked the car and walked up the steps she wondered why Alex was at her house so early.

     

                The front door was unlocked and Lena shut it behind her, dropping her handbag onto the narrow bench along one side, dropping her keys into the dish on the console and kicked off her heels. She was pulling off her coat and trying to wave an exuberant German Shepherd down as she frowned.

     

                “Hey, you’re here early.”

     

                She got no response and frowned, the silence of the old house confusing her. The TV was off and so was her record player, and the kitchen was absent of anyone moving about, pouring themselves a drink or making coffee.

     

                “Alex?” she brusquely called out, poking her head into the front living room and finding it neat and empty, before walking through the open archway to the kitchen and dining room. “What are you-”

     

                Alex was sitting at the kitchen table, the house dim in the early twilight, and Lena’s stomach jolted at the sight of her. Pale and red-eyed and silent, her face blank and stiff, Alex turned to face her, the movement slow and jerky. It was all the explanation that Lena needed, the breath clawing its way up her throat as a pitiful, cracking exclamation fell from her numb lips.

     

                “No,” she hoarsely whispered, bone white and trembling as she went cold all over, the numbing sensation of dread leaving her light-headed as a faint ringing sounded in her ears. “No, no, no.”

     

                She staggered back, the door frame painfully slamming into her shoulder blade before she slid down, her legs giving out beneath the weight of her. Alex’s silence reinforced her assumption, the thing she’d thought about, dreamed about and dreaded every sindle day since Kara had gone back. It didn’t seem real, it felt like some sort of sick joke, but she knew that this was something that none of them would have ever joked about. A mewling sound of pure anguish tore from Lena as her vision blurred, hot tears overflowing as the breath hitched in her chest and she clutched at her chest. 

     

                “No, no, no. You’re lying,” she sobbed, anger making her voice rough as she squeezed her eyes shut. “She’s- no, … I spoke to her yesterday.”

     

                Her voice cracked and hitched with rough sobs that wracked her whole body, and Lena clutched the front of her dress and the hard lump of the locket beneath it as if trying to hold her heart together. 

     

                “I’m sorry,” Alex listlessly whispered, her lips barely moving as she stared blankly at Lena, as if she wasn’t even seeing her fall apart.

     

                Lips parting as she stared at Alex accusingly, in disbelief as she frowned, tears stained with cheeks, Lena realised it wasn’t a joke. A gut-wrenching sob escaped her, almost a scream, as she screwed her eyes shut and wrapped her arms around herself, rocking as the pain split her open. She sobbed so hard it felt like her ribs were breaking. Gone. She was gone . As easy as that, with no goodbye and no warning.

     

                And then Lena was screaming, loud, wordless screams of pain and grief, so loud that it shook Alex out of her own quiet grief, stirring her to robotically climb to her feet and walk over to Lena, before she sagged heavily to the wooden floor before her. Reaching out, Alex grabbed her shoulders and shook her, an emptiness to her brown eyes as if she wasn’t truly inside of herself, before she pulled Lena into her arms, her face pressed into the shoulder of her shirt, and muffled her keening cries and screams. 

     

                Lena couldn’t even feel how much Alex was shaking as she cried in her arms, feeling the world ripped out from right under her feet as she clutched at her. They wept there on the cold floor, the river of Lena’s sorrow washing through Alex, until, at last, she fell straight into black emptiness, an infinite space of nothingness, as the deafening grief of Kara’s loss overwhelmed her and her body took pity on her. There was nothing else after that.

    Chapter 59

    Lena,

     

    I’m not sure at what point in time this letter is reaching you, but I’m guessing it’s roughly one week until I see you again! I’m not going to stop counting down until the final second that I see you again. Not even when I’m running off the bus, pushing everyone else out of the way if I have to. Until I have my arms around you, I won’t feel like I’m home again.

     

    Perhaps it’s bad luck to say it and I’m hoping it won’t jinx us, but there’s nothing in this world that can keep me away from you now. You’re stuck with me now! Of course, a week is a long time when I’m stuck over here, and I’d hate for everything to go wrong right at the very end, but one way or another I’ll be home on time. I promise.

     

    I think I must be driving everyone up here insane with how much I keep talking about going home, about how excited I am to have you to come home too. I think they're secretly jealous but I couldn’t care less right now. I’ve been holding onto the thought of being on the plane for so long that I feel like I might burst with excitement at how soon it is. It’s still two weeks away while I’m writing this, but I’m on the home stretch now as you’re reading it. And now I can’t help but feel guilty at how much the job has cost me in time, about how much we’ve missed together. But please don’t think I haven’t appreciated those firsts we’ve had any less though, because you’ve made thousands of miles seem small with how much love you’ve showered me with while we’ve been apart.

     

    So thank you, Lena, for showing me what it’s like to really be loved. Thank you for your patience, thank you for your selflessness, your kindness, your stubborn determination to not give up. It means more to me than you could ever know and has truly shown me what kind of person I’m marrying. I can honestly say with every bit of me that there’s no one else in the world that could ever make me feel this way. I think I made that clear when I proposed, but you’ve reinforced my decision to spend my life with you every day. I promise I’ll spend the rest of my life making it up to you because I know how hard it’s been for you over these past few months, and I know you’d never ask me to do that, but I’ll do my best to make sure everything else is easy. Because loving you is so easy, Lena - as easy as breathing - and I know you don’t think so but it really is. We’re going to have an easy life, full of love and happiness and kids and me and you and I can’t wait to come home and give that to you. It’s what you deserve.

     

    This is probably the last letter I’ll write to you from over here, because I’ll be home before the next one reaches you. Honestly, I’m filled with relief at the thought of our first last. It’s a good one to start with. I love you more than you can possibly imagine, or maybe you can because over the past few months you’ve shown me just how much you love me, and I think it’s pretty close. Thank you. I love you.

     

    See you soon,

     

    Kara xxx

    Chapter 60

                Somewhere in the infinite stretch of time between when Lena’s world had fallen apart and when she gained awareness of her surroundings again, she had stopped crying, exhaustion making her body incapable of another heaving sob, another tear or hiccuping breath. Sitting on the floor at the base of the wall, she stared dead-eyed ahead, seeing nothing and feeling empty.

     

                Alex was similarly spent and her voice was hollow as she explained in fits and starts, her voice cracking and words stuttering in between audible swallows, the story that Eliza had told her over the phone. Her Commander at Fort Rozz, Hank Henshaw, was the one who’d shown up at Eliza’s house in Midvale, just around lunchtime, with a public affairs representative too - knowledge of her engagement to Lena requiring certain precautions - to break the news to her mother. It had been an airstrike, they said, killing her in action in the Sangin Province while reporting on a recent skirmish with British troops. The airstrike killed eleven soldiers - two rifle squads, Kara and her photojournalist friend, Mike, and the squad leader. 

     

                Lena couldn’t even bring herself to remotely care about the other ten; she only cared about the one. The one that had shattered her heart to pieces and torn her world apart. She’d been dead for hours before Lena had even known, and she craved that ignorance bliss again, she wanted to bask in that happy glow of knowing her fiancée would be home in a few short days. Only, now she wouldn’t be coming home at all. Just an empty box in an empty grave, based on Alex’s next words to fall on Lena’s deaf ears.

     

                “They- they found them … the- the bodies. Or … what was left of them, at least. Not all- some weren’t … identifiable. Too- too close to the blast, so … they were- hers was … there’s nothing. Nothing left. They found her … her tags. They can’t- that’s all- all that was … left of her.”

     

                Stomach twisting with nausea, Lena curled in on herself as she let out a sharp breath, snatched from her lungs as her chest ached painfully. She couldn’t make a noise, could barely breathe. Lena didn’t even know what time it was, what day it was, the house dark and cold as she sat on the floor, only that her throat was dry and her eyes were sore and her stomach hurt. And all of that paled in comparison to the way her heart felt like it was going to give out, the vivid image of Alex’s halting explanation painted in her mind as clear as day, like one of the bad dreams she’d been plagued by for months. Only there was no waking up this time.

     

                It was all she could think about, her mind feeling, the world shrinking and widening in a nauseating, turbulent manner that left Lena feeling like she was on a boat, pitching from side to side. Her mind was blurry at the edges and she could feel the sharp pain in her chest as her throat constricted, but couldn’t make sense of much else. It was almost like she was catatonic, her body frozen while her mind played a film reel of horrors.

     

                Even the sound of a phone ringing wasn’t enough to break her out of her numb state of shock, Alex’s broken, sobbing words incomprehensible to her as she broke the news to Kelly in the briefest terms before dissolving into tears and hanging up. Lena just turned her head aside, resting her temple against the wall as she stared ahead with a vacant look on her face, her throat painfully tight as she blocked out Alex. She was too numb to cry again, too tired and broken to even make another sound.

     

                She wasn’t sure how long she sat there, blinking occasionally, breathing slowly, shallowly, before the front door opened and slammed shut, frantic footsteps squeaking on the herringbone floors before Kelly was falling to her knees beside Alex. Lena was dimly aware that she was crying, her voice thick and hoarse as she held Alex, the two women quietly talking in between sobs while Lena tuned it out, stubborn and immovable. Even when Kelly coaxed Alex to her feet and then reached down for Lena, grabbing her biceps and attempting to haul her up, Lena couldn’t bring herself to move. Try as Kelly might, Lena couldn’t make her limbs work, couldn’t make her body respond to anything other than its base need for oxygen.

     

                “Hey, hey, come on, you need to get up now, Lena,” Kelly sweetly coaxed her, her voice raspy and thick as she gave her a tenous smile, dark eyes brimming with fresh tears. “You need to get up. Alex, please, help me. I don’t- I can’t- fuck . Just stand up, Lena. Please.”

     

                Rough hands pulled her to her feet and Lena blinked, in a daze as she swayed, staring into Alex’s brown, bloodshot eyes. Kelly propped her up on one side and opened and closed her mouth, speechless as she found herself lacking any sort of excuse, comfort, explanation.

     

                “I- we need to- to go. Let me get … your coat. You need your coat, yes.”

     

                Alex was covering her face with a hand, head ducked down as her shoulders shook, and Lena watched her, expressionless, finding herself being jerked around a moment later as Kelly returned with her coat and started shoving her into it. Uncooperative, Lena blinked and then swallowed before forcing her body to move. 

     

                Kelly was left standing with the coat in her hands as she watched with parted lips as Lena walked through the hallway and through the opposite archway, jerky and unbalanced as she walked over to the sofa and took a seat. All of the fight seemed to drain out of Kelly because she let the coat pool to the floor, took Alex’s hand and led her over to the sofa as well, both of them sitting down heavily beside her as the three of them sat with the oppressive weight of their silent grief.

     

                She thought she slept then, or was at least unaware of things for a period of time, slumped against the pillows, dead-eyed and senseless, and it wasn’t until the sound of the door opening and closing again that Lena blinked herself back to her surroundings. Even as removed from it all as she was, she would’ve known the sound of those heels anywhere, the way they seemed to dominate whichever room they were in, purposeful and sounding a warning. But this time they were frantic and worried and Lena blinked as she watched her mother sink to a crouch before her.

     

                “Lena,” she breathlessly murmured, reaching out to cup her face in her cold hands. “Hey, look at me. It’s okay. It’s-”

     

                Slowly pulling her face out of her mother’s hands, Lena’s dry eyes stung with fresh tears and she made a rough squawk of protest at the back of her throat, searing anger bubbling forth with such frightening speed that she let out a quiet gasp as she clutched at her chest. Shaking her head, Lena rocked slightly, a sob building in her chest.

     

                “Don’t,” she rasped, “don’t say anything.”

     

                Lillian reached out and took her daughter’s hands in her own, clutching them tightly as she looked at Lena with such devastation that Lena couldn’t bear to look at her. Clenching her teeth together, a muscle twitching in her jaw, Lena squeezed her eyes shut and swallowed a sob.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lillian whispered, reaching up to touch the back of her hand to Lena’s cheek.

     

                Jerking away from her touch, Lena rocked backwards and dug the heels of her palms into her eyes, quietly overcome by fresh sobs as she felt Kelly pull Alex against her. 

     

                “She’s not coming back,” Lena said in a strangled whisper, her hands sliding down to clap over her mouth as she stifled another sob.

     

                “Sweetheart,” Lillian pleaded, a pained expression on her face as she looked at Lena.

     

                Breaths turning ragged as she let out a shuddering, hollow laugh, Lena wiped away hot tears and staggered to her feet. Rising from her crouched position, Lillian reached out for Lena and found her hand batted aside as her daughter resisted. The scorn on Lena’s face was brutal and Lillian’s quiet sound of surprise died in her throat.

     

                “Why are you even here? You didn’t care about her. Go . I don’t want you here.”

     

                Her voice cracked and her chest heaved and Lena looked at her mother with such heartbreak that Lillian’s shoulders drooped as she sharply exhaled. She reached for Lena again, pulling her against her in a crushing hug, holding her even as she fought, until she slowly dissolved into loud, ragged sobs in her mother’s arms.

     

                “Oh, my little girl,” Lillian whispered, stroking her hair as she gently lowered Lena back down onto the sofa, twisting her body so she could sit beside her.

     

                Kelly climbed to her feet and vanished, a hand pressed to her mouth, while Alex watched Lena let her mom cradle her for the first time in more than a decade. There were sounds coming from the kitchen, but Lena just cried, her mother rubbing her back and murmuring soothing nonsense into her hair until she wore herself out again, too tired to keep crying. Even then, Lillian still held her close, her own heart hurting at the sight of her daughter grieving for her lost love. 

     

                Returning with tea, Kelly pushed a burning hot cup into Lena’s hands, and Lena held it until it cooled, the quiet conversation between the other three women going over her head as she drew in shuddering breaths and stared at the fireplace with vacant green eyes.

     

                Eventually, the cup was gently taken from her stiff fingers and she was pulled to her feet and led to the stairs, where she numbly walked up, relying on familiarity to guide her up each step as her mother gripped her elbow. She was still in her work clothes, the dress rumpled and too thin for work, and Lillian pulled her out of it in the bedroom and pulled on clean pyjamas before leading her over to the bed. Turning down the sheets, Lillian put her to bed, tucking her in and smoothing dark hair off her brow as a tear slid down Lena’s temple as she stared at the ceiling. 

     

                Even then, it still felt surreal. There was a part of her that was convinced it was a mistake, that it was a bad dream she’d wake up from any second now, finding it a side effect of the Valium she’d taken before bed. But the pain was like a sharp-edged knife, too keen to be anything but real, even in her insensate state. Staring up at the dark ceiling, she heard her mother speaking softly to Kelly.

     

                “You should get some rest too.”

     

                “I’ll sit with Alex. Will she-”

     

                “I’ll stay. Eliza will be here soon.”

     

                Things were dark for a little while after that but Lena was once again unsure if she slept of just blocked everything out and let the grief conume her. She didn’t feel rested, didn’t feel much of anything, she just came to thinking she’d woken up from a horrifying nightmare, only to discover it hadn’t been a nightmare at all.

     

                Still, somehow, Lena found it within herself to climb out of bed, the effort so taxing that she had to stand for a moment, curling and uncurling her fingers until she felt the engagement ring on her left hand and felt her knees go weak beneath her. Sinking down to the carpet, Lena struggled to catch her breath, and it was an age before she managed to drag herself back to her feet and stumble to the door.

     

                The wooden floorboards of the hallway were cold beneath her feet and Lena’s skin rippled with goosebumps as she made her way downstairs, quiet voices audible in the kitchen. Hand gliding against the wall to steady herself, Lena felt the horrible coldness inside her, pale and haunted as she stepped off the stairs and stopped in the open doorway. Eliza was there, sitting at her kitchen table, looking haggard and hollow-eyed as she looked up, tragic blue eyes finding hers. Lillian’s hand was on her arm, in the middle of offering what empty consolations she could, and she half-rose from her seat at the sight of her daughter, looking similarly ashen with the agony of her grief.

     

                The air was expelled from Lena’s lungs at the sight of Eliza, who rose from her chair, legs scraping against the floor, and opened her arms to her. Almost tripping over her feet, Lena went willingly into Eliza’s embrace, hugging her tightly as she clutched at the back of her cotton shirt, a hiccuping sob catching in her throat as she fell to pieces. They stood in the open kitchen for a few minutes, Lena reluctant to let go as she cried against Eliza’s shoulder, and Lillian busied herself with making tea for the three of them, setting the cups down on the table and reclaiming her seat.

     

                Rubbing Lena’s back, Eliza extracted herself from Lena’s embrace and shepherded her over to the table, pulling her chair out further and guiding her down onto it. Sitting heavily as her knees almost gave out, Lena swallowed and stared down at the mug set before her. Reaching out with shaking hands, she held it, feeling the heat seep into her, but couldn’t bring it to her lips.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lena whispered, her bottom lip wobbling as tears slid down her cheeks and splashed onto the table. “I’m so … sorry, Eliza.”

     

                Eliza softly hushed her, the sound thick and uneven as she gripped Lena’s arm and squeezed tightly. Swallowing, Lena closed her eyes and shook her head as if she could clear the events of the last twelve hours away as easily as she could shake off the lingering fuzziness of sleep. Raking a hand through her hair, she hunched forward and suppressed another sob.

     

                “I just … don’t understand . How … I spoke to her- she was fine. We were laughing.”

     

                “Don’t,” Eliza hushed her, rubbing her back as Lena bowed forward, tears falling onto the table as she fought to muffle her sobs as best as she could.

     

                “I should’ve known. I would’ve felt it.”

     

                She took a deep breath and blew it out, wiping at her face with the cuff of her sleeve, and stared down at the dark grain of the table as her mind reeled, still incapable of processing the harsh truth.

     

                “You should eat something,” Lillian said after a long minute.

     

                The thought of food was nauseating, sour bile at the back of Lena’s throat as she vehemently shook her head, clutching her tea a little tighter as a muscle twitched in her jaw. “I’m not- i’m not hungry,” she haltingly rasped, the effort seeming to drain her further.

     

                “You mom’s right,” Eliza managed to choke out, rubbing at her eyes before she gave Lena a wan smile, full of agony and pity.

     

                Shaking her head again, Lena swallowed the sour taste at the back of her throat and managed a small sip of tea. It pooled in her stomach and warmed her slightly, and so she kept drinking it, until she was down to the dregs and her body grew heavy, the slight fogginess in her mind giving her the nagging suspicion that perhaps her mom had spiked her tea with a dose of sleeping pills. 

     

                Sitting at the kitchen table, sagging as her eyelids grew heavy, Lena’s last thought before she became unaware of anything else was of Kara’s face. That crinkling blue-eyed smile behind her glasses, the curve of her lips, the wrinkling of her freckled nose. The agony split her anew and it was with merciful relief that Lena surrendered to sleep, if only to escape her grief for a little while.

    Chapter 61

                The press got ahold of the story the following day, and one William Dey was the only one with the inside scoop on the fact that Kara had been engaged to Lena, dropping that bombshell in an article detailing their tragic love story instead of focusing on the other ten people that had died too. She didn’t read it, of course, didn’t turn on the TV and see the running stories or the search results on her laptop; Lena stayed in bed, oblivious to everything else. Even if she’d been aware of it, she doubted she would’ve even had a shred of energy within her to care. 

     

                As it was, Lena couldn’t even lift her head off the pillow, slipping in and out of sleep and bouts of wakefulness where she stared at the wall and waited for sleep to come again. Periodically, someone would open the door - her mother, she assumed; the only one who wasn’t a wreck right now - and check on her before leaving her alone again. Lena stayed curled into a ball, her body heavy and her mind muddled as she nursed the gaping wound inside her

     

                It was the sound of a raised voice that stirred her, more so out of aloof curiosity than anything else, and Lena dragged herself from her bed and wearily plodded downstairs as the conversation grew louder. The raised voice was unmistakably Alex’s but it wasn’t until Lena reached the bottom of the stairs that Lena could pinpoint who her anger was directed at and why.

     

                “It hasn’t even been two days. How are you even talking about this right now?” Alex snapped, standing with her shoulders taut and her hands balled into fists.

     

                Eliza looked up at her with resigned exhaustion, “she doesn’t … have a- a body. We have to assume …”

     

                “It’s too soon.”

     

                “We need to … make arrangements. We need closure.”

     

                “Putting an empty box in the ground isn’t going to fix anything.”

     

                The breath rushed from Lena’s lungs at the devastating realisation that they were discussing her funeral. It didn’t even seem possible that they could be having a conversation like that. Not about Kara. Feeling faint as she paled, Lena hugged her arms to herself and swallowed, her chapped lips trembling slightly as she watched, hollow-eyed.

     

                Alex noticed her presence and gave her a pleading look, “Lena, tell her.”

     

                “You’re the executor,” Eliza hoarsely told her, clutching an envelope tightly in her hands, “she wanted you to do this. I- please, Alex, we have to do this. Do this for her.”

     

                She held it out to her daughter and Alex scoffed, batting it aside. Eliza’s hand lowered back to her lap as she looked down at it and Lena swallowed thickly, rubbing at her stinging eyes as she willed everyone to just leave. They’d all stayed at her house, craving the comfort of being together, but she just wanted to curl up in a ball in bed and let the rest of her life quietly pass her by.

     

                “She didn’t deserve this,” Alex cried, gesturing widely as she let out a huff of defeat. “She should be coming home next week. Not- not being remembered because we don’t even have a fucking … body. I won’t be a part of this. I can’t.”

     

                Kelly reached out for her to soothe her, to calm her down, but Alex shrugged off her touch and stalked towards Lena, towards the door. Looking at her and seeing the same hollowness of grief inside her, Lena stepped aside and let her slip past, her footsteps loud and angry on the stairs until a door shut up on the second floor.

     

                Lillian hovered in the kitchen, looking uncomfortable as she held a small espresso cup and stayed out of it. Kelly ran a hand over her face but didn’t chase after Alex, giving her space as she took a seat at the table. Staring at Eliza, Lena took in the silent grief, the weight of it curving her shoulders, and felt the all-too familiar urge to cry building in her chest as she watched her hold the envelope with a lost look on her face. It was then that Lena realised that she couldn’t open the envelope and read her daughter’s will, the plans she’d etched out with Lena’s lawyers before going back the first time. She couldn’t make these plans alone and it was with stomach-lurching sickness that Lena stepped forward.

     

                Numb to it all, she crossed the room and slipped the envelope from Eliza’s limp hands, her mother-in-law looking up at her with mild surprise. With shaking fingers and a lump in her throat, painfully contracting, she opened the envelope and let the paper slide out, reading over it as she tried to detach herself from the moment.

     

                “She wants to be buried in Midvale,” Lena hollowly whispered.

     

                “Midvale?”

     

                “Next to Jeremiah. She’s a Danvers. But … she’d like her name on- on her parents grave.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena looked at Eliza. “She’ll have military honours, I presume?”

     

                “Yes. They said- when they came they …

                “Good,” Lena whispered. “When?”

     

                “I- next Saturday. She was supposed to- to be home then so …”

     

                Lena choked on her next breath, swallowing painfully as she absorbed the news and nodded in silent acceptance. It did feel too soon. She knew it was normal to do it that soon, but it felt too fast. How was she supposed to bury her fiancee when she hadn’t even accepted the fact that she was dead? 

     

                Wiping at her cheeks as she realised she was crying, a tear soaking into the paper, Lena roughly cleared her throat and tried to keep the tremor out of her voice as her hands shook. “Her finances … for you and Alex. It’s not in here but I- I bought some shares for the company in her name. So … that’s yours too.”

     

                “You keep them.”

     

                Lena shook her head but didn’t press it. It had been for Kara’s financial stability, for Lena’s peace of mind to know she’d be taken care of, and she knew it would bring Kara some peace to know her family was looked after. She didn’t want it back.

     

                “Her polaroid camera is left to- left to me. And the … photos,” her voice broke and she had to pause for a moment, drawing in a shuddering breath, “they go to whoever- whoever is in them or whoever they hold meaning to. Her books … to Kelly, except-” Lena choked on a frayed laugh, wiping at her cheeks, “except for the copy of Pride and Prejudice I never gave back.”

     

                Eliza let out a quiet sob of laughter, shaking her head as a wan smile crossed her face. On and on the list went, growing difficult with each new thing split up amongst themselves, and by the time she reached the end of it, Lena was barely coherent in between breathless sobs. Kelly had reached for her hand at some point, squeezing it tightly, and as Lena finished reading, she found herself unable to stand anymore, swaying on her feet before she reached out for the back of Kelly’s chair to steady herself and was soon being helped down onto it as Kelly vacated it.

     

                Holding the will in her hands, Lena stared down at it for a long minute before setting it down on the table and sliding it across to Eliza. Picking it up, Eliza tugged the envelope from Lena’s stiff fingers and slipped it back inside.

     

                “We- I’ll need to get a- a certificate. Get it … officiated.”

     

                Lena squeezed her eyes shut, holding another sob at bay as she nodded weakly, feeling the cracks in her heart widen slightly. She didn’ trust herself to speak. It was inevitable that they’d have to do it, have her officially declared dead so they could manage her affairs, so they could hold a funeral for her. That was their main priority now; sorting through Kara’s personal belongings was something that could wait. Lena couldn’t even consider going into that spare room upstairs and going through each box, choosing what to keep for herself, giving pieces of her away to her family and deciding what to donate. How was she even supposed to do that?

     

                “I’ll go and tell Alex,” Lena rasped after a long period of silence.

     

                She was still slow to move, forcing her body to move as she climbed from the chair and walked out of the room. Her whole body sagged as she forced herself upstairs, the aching emptiness inside her making her feel sick as she walked up to the spare room Alex and Kelly claimed for themselves.

     

                Stopping outside the door, Lena hesitated and then lightly rapped on the door with her knuckles. “It’s me.”

     

                No reply was forthcoming and she closed her eyes, swallowing as she leaned her forehead against the door and inhaled deeply. After a moment, she opened the door and took in the huddled form on the edge of the bed, Alex’s taut back facing her, pausing before she spoke.

     

                “Can we talk?”

     

                Turning her head to the side, not quite turning to look at Lena, Alex swallowed as her mouth thinned. “What?”

     

                Her voice was dull and lifeless, a mirror to Lena’s, and Lena felt exhaustion wash over her as she slipped inside and shut the door. Crossing over to the bed, she sat perpendicular to Alex so they didn’t have to look at each other, didn’t have to see the other falling apart - or struggle to pretend that they weren’t. Blinking rapidly as she tried to dispel the heavy pressure building behind her eyes, Lena ran a hand through her lank hair.

     

                “It’ll be next Saturday,” Lena eventually informed her. “She’ll get military honours. Her things … she left some stuff to you.”

     

                “Fine.”

     

                Lena nodded and that was the end of the conversation, neither of them having the energy to speak or even comfort each other. They sat there for five minutes and then Lena pushed herself to her feet and left, heading upstairs to her room where she stood in the middle of the open space for a moment and then let out a breathless sob and sank down to the carpet. She didn’t know how long it was before gentle hands ushered her to her feet and guided her to the bed, pills pushed into her hand with a glass of water, taken without complaint because she knew they’d knock her out for a few hours, and that was all she really wanted. If she couldn’t have Kara, Lena wanted the relief of oblivion.

    Chapter 62

                The next day, she woke around noon, her tongue thick in her dry mouth, her eyes gritty and her mind foggy with sleep. She’d slept through most of it in a drugged haze, despising the moment she woke and craving sleep again, but she couldn’t sleep forever. Still, even when she woke, she couldn’t bring herself to move, to eat, to drink or shower. Laying in bed, she just cried until she exhausted herself all over again and then slept some more, but even that stopped being a relief as dreams tortured her.

     

                The entire time Kara had been in Afghanistan, Lena had been plagued by nightmares of gruesome deaths, but now that her worst fear had come to pass, her mind tortured her in new ways. Every time she slept, she was greeted with dreams of Kara in bed beside her, echoes of her laughter weaving through her sleep and her voice as she whispered how much she loved Lena, memories playing on loop. She woke from each one forgetting for a brief moment, clinging to the blissful haze of those warm dreams before she was doused in cold reality. Every time, the weight of losing Kara came crashing down on her anew and the cycle repeated itself.

     

                The past few days had been a void. Anything had to be better than this life without Kara, and Lena felt the ache of her absence in her very bones. Every waking second she was suffocated with the loss of her, and yet, there was a sense of something loosening inside her. For so many months now, the anticipation of disaster had left her carrying a knot of unease within her, and now that it had come to pass, that dread had left her. What was left behind was infinitely worse, but it just left her limp and empty.

     

                Even though they were all grieving, Lena couldn’t bring herself to sit with them downstairs, couldn’t bring herself to join them for dinner or help with the funeral plans. That was left up to Eliza to plan with Kelly’s help, while Lillian silently pulled strings in the background to get things sorted with as little fuss as possible. The most she managed was to occasionally use the bathroom, and on one occasion, pace around the room for a bit while she stared unseeingling, trapped in her own spinning thoughts, until she ended up in her closet, sobbing into one of Kara’s worn sweaters.

     

                Her mother had enough eventually though, her compassion and patience only tolerating so much before she grew brusque with her daughter, although still mindful of her grief. Sitting on the edge of her bed on the fourth morning, Lillian forced soup down her throat, pressing the spoon to her lips until Lena parted them and forced herself to swallow. She only ate a few spoonfuls but it was more than she’d eaten in days and Lillian seemed relieved.

     

                Setting the bowl down, Lillian forced her out of bed then, running the hot water in the shower and pulling the covers off Lena, firmly urging her to get up and shower. Her hair was greasy and she was still in the same pyjamas she’d been dressed in the night her mom had shown up, looking far from the rich CEO with her hollowed out cheeks and sunken eyes, but Lena couldn’t bring herself to care. Still, she didn’t have the energy to fight her mother and drifted towards the shower like she was sleep walking, stripping off her clothes and stepping beneath the water, the stinging heat of it making her skin prickle as she stood motionlessly beneath the waterfall.

     

                Lillian fetched clean clothes for her, more soft loungewear she’d be able to comfortably languish in for a few more days, and clicked her tongue at the rigid sight of her daughter through the fogged shower door. It took some gentle coaxing but when the shower gel was pressed into her hand, Lena looked down at it in surprise and slowly squeezed some out, going through the motions as her body took over and left her mind to detach itself.

     

                She stood beneath the shower until Lillian shut off the hot water, bundling her in a fluffy towel as she started to shiver and then dissolved into ragged, gasping sobs again as she was plunged back into reality. Dressing robotically, Lena cried quietly as she brushed her teeth with the toothbrush put in her hand and then let her mother brush her damp hair, before she walked back into her bedroom to find the bed bare of its sheets. The curtains were open and fresh air cut through the closeness of the room, airing it out as Eliza shoved the pillows into clean pillow cases.

     

                Lena watched as her mother helped, the two of them remaking her bed for her, and then she turned around and walked out of the room. Making her way downstairs, she made for the front door, grabbing her discarded coat and slowly pulling it on before she fumbled with a pair of sneakers that weren’t hers. Footsteps sounded behind her but she was oblivious as she steadied herself against the console.

     

                “Where are you going?” Alex hoarsely demanded.

     

                “I have- I have to work,” Lena mumbled, her eyes glazed and red as she looked at Alex.

     

                She looked lost, dressed in her pyjamas and her coat, her hair damp and sticking to her pale cheeks as she struggled to lace on someone else’s sneakers. It shoul’ve been comical to see Lena show up at L-Corp in such a state, but instead it was just sad.

     

                “Work? What the hell-”

     

                Kelly materialised, laying a hand on Alex’s arm, as she murmured, “she’s in shock.”

     

                Brushing past Alex, Kelly gave her a kind smile, reaching out to take Lena’s shoulders in her hands and help her down to the narrow bench against one wall. Kneeling before her, Kelly helped slip the shoe on and lace them up for her, glancing up at Lena once she was done.

     

                “All done. But, it’s Sunday today.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “How about we go and sit out the back instead? You can go to work tomorrow.”

     

                Jerkily nodding, Lena climbed to her feet and let Kelly take her hand, towing her through the ground floor of the house and out into the small garden. It was a strange day, the air feeling oppressively warm despite the overcast skies and the feeling of rain on the horizon. Lena breathed in the smell of exhaust fumes and the desert, cicadas humming in the plants, and she sank heavily onto a chair as memories of summer days spent reading out the back with Kara, of late night dinners and pitchers of sangria and little herbs bought together lashed at her.

     

                “Lena?”

     

                She blinked as she looked at Kelly as if surprised to find her sitting there at the little garden table. A faint frown puckered her brow and she swallowed thickly. “I don’t know how to exist in a world where she doesn’t,” she roughly whispered.

     

                “That never really changes.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena swallowed and sniffed, wiping at her face. They stayed outside for half an hour, Lena vaguely aware of her mother moving around in the kitchen, eyeing her through the doors or windows as she kept tabs on her. Eventually, Kelly coaxed her back inside and Lena sipped a cup of coffee in the living room. Afterwards, she rinsed the cup out in the sink and then walked back upstairs, climbing into her freshly made bed and staring at the ceiling.

     

                She hadn’t had any sleeping pills that morning and was left wide awake, although she wished to be anything but, and it wasn’t long before there was a light knock on the closed door and her mom let herself in. Walking over to the bed, Lillian sank down onto the edge and stared down at Lena’s pale, thin face, her mouth thinning with regret and sadness as she reached out to touch her daughter’s cheek.

     

                Lena let her, her eyes sliding closed as fresh tears welled up, spilling down her temples as her chin dimpled with the effort it took to sob quietly. Laying on her back, it left her shaking, her back arching off the mattress slightly, and she threw an arm across her face as she sniffed, feeling her mother move onto the bed. Lillian drew her against her side and Lena clutched at the front of her silk blouse as her tears soaked into the fabric, while Lillian softly shushed her and stroked her hair. She’d barely left Lena’s side since the moment she’d gotten to her house, and in a twisted way, Lena had never been closer to her mother. She despised it, hating the fact that Kara’s death had left her so helpless that she’d resorted to allowing her mother to take care of her. She hated that this was the thing that had finally torn down those last few walls between them, allowing Lillian to hold her daughter in her arms as she fell apart. But most of all, Lena hated that Kara wasn’t there, how she’d broken her promise and left her all alone.

     

                Once her breathing had levelled out into the occasional shuddering sob, Lillian softly exhaled, rubbing Lena’s back as she pressed her cheek to the top of her dark hair. Lena couldn’t close her eyes, plagued with the image of Kara painted inside her eyelids, so instead, she stared at the wall, her gaze unfocused.

     

                “When you were nine, you were learning to ride the bike you’d gotten for your birthday the week before. You fell off and broke your elbow and cried the entire car ride to the hospital. You wouldn’t let me hold your hand. You were twelve when we went out on the boat and your brother pushed you into the lake. I’d never seen you so scared before - you still didn’t know how to swim - but you wouldn’t let me pull you out of the water. You didn’t take my hand, you just- you fought your way to the ladder and climbed back in and your tore up all of his blueprints when we got home. When you were fifteen, your father died and you wouldn’t even let me come near you at the funeral, not so much as a hand on your shoulder. And then you refused to go to your brother’s funeral after everything that had happened. The point is, I know how much you’re hurting, I know your heart is breaking, because this is the first time that I- that you’ve ever needed me. Needed me to hold you and to help you and I just- I’m sorry , because I don’t know how to help you. I can’t help you and I can’t tell you it’ll be okay and I’m just … so sorry.”

     

                And then Lena was crying again, loud, broke sobs, and it was all her mom could do to gently rock her as she kept her company through the agonising pain. “It hurts,” Lena cried, her voice muffled as she pressed her face into Lillian’s shoulder. “How do I make it stop? I just- I need it to stop.”

     

                Her mom whispered an apology to her and somehow that was worse , because Lillian had an opinion on everything, and for her to admit that she didn’t know how to help only reinforced Lena’s heartbreak. There was nothing to do except dwell in misery and pray that one day her pain would be a little less, but in her heart she knew it was a prayer made in vain, because she would hurt every day for the rest of her life.

     

                When she woke later that evening, the blueness of dusk seeping in through the open curtains, she was confused as to what time it was and when, finding herself alone in her bedroom. Her appetite evaded her but Lena climbed out of bed and made her way downstairs anyway, taking a seat at the kitchen table as everyone else picked at the pizza that Lillian had ordered. A box was set in front of her but Lena couldn’t even take a bite, knowing it would taste like ashes in her mouth, a dry lump she’d have to force down.

     

                “We’re leaving tomorrow,” Kelly quietly informed her. “To Midvale.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                “I can help you pack,” Lillian offered.

     

                Lena nodded and stared at one of the textured paintings hanging on the wall, the old house creaking and groaning quietly in the background as everyone sat around the table and ate their dinner while Lena tuned it all out. If anyone spoke, it washed over her head as she bit her nails down to the quick, that hollowness in her chest expanding, a chill in her stiff body that wouldn’t go away. It still didn’t feel real that she could be gone with no warning, that one day she would just be gone somewhere even further than half a world away. 

     

                But Lena knew that was how life was - tragic and unexplainable. It had been Kara who had changed her cynical perspective of things, Kara who had wrapped her up in so much love and filled the empty parts of her that had missed out on so much, and all along it had been Lena who had been right. She should have known to be cautious; she was never wrong. Perhaps if she’d held onto Kara a little looser, she wouldn’t be in so much pain, but even her bitterness left a sour taste in her mouth. Lena knew that if the pain and memories were all she had left of her, she’d never regret it for even a moment. 

     

                That was just the cost of love - caring for someone so much you couldn’t imagine living without them, while knowing one day, somehow, you’d have to. You could plan for a lifetime, each tiny action and the expanse of consequences that unraveled from them, but you couldn’t know how it all played out. Not until knowing better was useless. And yet, all Lena was left with was anger . If she’d had the energy, perhaps it would’ve been loud anger, her sharp accusations and quick temper voicing itself, but she was so spent that she harboured it in silence, hardening her, chilling her to her empty core. Who could she even be angry at; Kara? 

     

                When it became obvious she wasn’t going to eat the pizza, Lillian fetched a yoghurt from the fridge and set it down before her, pulling Lena’s hand away from her mouth as she worried at a hangnail and quietly telling her to eat. She went through the motions robotically and when she was done she walked upstairs to pack her things. The only thing she knew she needed to pack was a black dress, but Lena couldn’t bring herself to choose. How could she care about her appearance at her fiancée’s funeral? The mere thought felt vain and selfish and she ended up sitting on the closet floor, staring at the vast array of designer clothes.

     

                Lillian picked for her, a modest black woollen Dior dress Lena had bought off the rack from the winter collection the year before, fetching black stockings and heels and a coat too, just in case. And then she fetched comfortable clothes for Lena to wear for the rest of the time, picking out a shirt Lena had worn the night she’d gone bowling with Kara, the pants she’d worn the first time Kara had surprised her at L-Corp with lunch, the coat Kara had poached a few times because it was slightly too long in the arms for Lena so it fit her well and Lena liked getting it back with the smell of her perfume lingering on the collar.

     

                It was unbearable to watch so Lena closed her eyes to it as her mother opened drawers and pulled things off hangers. It wasn’t even worth telling Lillian what not to pack because of the memories associated with it, because Kara was everywhere, in everything, and there would be nothing left if Lena got rid of everything that reminded her of her.

     

                Once Lillian was finished, she zipped up the leather overnight bag and called out to Lena, coaxing her to her feet and telling her to go to bed. Her mother shook two pills out handed them to her, and Lena swallowed them gratefully, knowing she’d need to be rested for their flight tomorrow and the days to come. It wasn’t long before things grew hazy and she was still conscious of her mother sitting on the edge of the bed when she let her heavy eyelids close and didn’t fight to open them again.

     

                Dawn broke with bright sunlight and a lavender sky and Lena stayed in bed as long as she was allowed to, before Lillian eventually roused her. More alert today, more autonomous, Lena showered and dressed in the folded clothes left out for her and brushed her teeth. Her reflection was far from her usual self and she made no effort to fix that beyond basic hygiene, pulling her tangled hair up and rubbing at her tired eyes before she walked downstairs.

     

                Managing a cup of coffee and a slice of buttered toast, she stood in the open doorway of the back door and watched Athena sniff around the pots while she breathed in the fresh air. Alex and Kelly had gone to their apartment to pack a few things and they were waiting on them to come back before leaving. Lillian had arranged things for the private jet she’d flown to National City on and Lena felt confused and grateful and resentful of the fact that her mother showed no signs of leaving her to suffer alone with the rest of Kara’s family. 

     

                Lillian at her funeral seemed so strange to her when she’d barely known Kara but no one suggested otherwise to her being there. In fact, they relied on her more than Lena suspected anyone had ever relied on her mother for anything, and Lillian was doing her best to take care of them all. The shocking twist of roles made Lena want to laugh, but there wasn’t a bone left in her body that would be able to do that now.

     

                By nine o’clock, the five of them were being chauffeured to the airstrip where Lillian’s jet was housed and they were in the air within the hour, Lena staring unseeingly out of the small window. She was so numb that even her fear of flying was secondary to everything else, and, eventually, Lena closed her eyes and let the motion of the plane lull her into a stupor, everything else fading as her world narrowed to the cutting pain of loss pervading her entire body, right down to her fingertips.

    Chapter 63

                The few days in Midvale before the funeral were a blur to Lena. She had no input in the planning and spent every day holed up in Kara’s bedroom like a ghost haunting the attic as she curled up in the old bed, staring at the knick-knacks left behind in her childhood bedroom, or paced back and forth, the old floorboards groaning beneath her zombie-like pacing. Strangers to her knocked on the door at regular intervals and someone would inevitably come upstairs with a small scoop of casserole or slice of pie that a kindly neighbour had brought over upon hearing the news. She didn’t even touch it, closing herself off from the world. Everything felt like a dream and she paced in a daze or slept through the fog of it all.

     

                Sometimes she’d wake in that bed, the wind howling in from the coast as the dampness of March left a rain pattering on the roof and windows, and she’d lay still in bed, pretending that Kara was downstairs in the kitchen, making coffee or sandwiches while she hummed along to the radio. If there was one place that she strongly associated with Kara, it was Eliza’s, even though she’d spent more time there without Kara than she had with her. Her memory was etched into the very walls of the place - in the framed family photos, in the growth measurements marked on the kitchen door frame, in the old CD’s and the plastic trophies and the beach where they walked and had a bonfire, the sofa she’d sprawl out on in her holey sweats - and it was unbearable for Lena. She couldn’t imagine what it was like for Eliza and Alex to be in that house where she grew up, knowing she would never come back to it.

     

                The numbness helped her cope to some extent, but beneath it was the cold anger cultivated by her heartbreak and grief. It wasn’t fair, perhaps, but Lena took that anger out on her mom, letting that anger that she still harboured deep down in the scarred parts of her yet to heal along with the rift rise to the surface and consume her. She wasn’t pleasant to be around, and she was aware of that in some regard but couldn’t bring herself to care or try and not let the twisted bitterness and churlish agony cloud her actions. And so much of it was because she felt like she couldn’t breathe. Maybe it was because her mom hadn’t spent so much time around her, even as a child, but it was almost suffocating, like Lillian was smothering her with too much attention when all she wanted was to be alone. 

     

                It was born from good intentions and concern for her daughter, but Lena couldn’t stop herself from snapping with cruel remarks, regretting it instantly but too tired to bring herself to feel remorse. So much of it felt like she was a teenager again, thrust right back into that past version of herself drowning in so much lonelines and anger and sadness. It wasn’t fair on either of them, but Lena was falling to pieces and she didn’t know how to make it stop, and in the midst of it all, she felt relief and some small gratitude for her mother’s efforts to be kinder and patient, never holding it against her, even though Lena knew some of her barbs struck home. 

     

                She didn’t truly move or function like a person until Saturday, the day of Kara’s funeral. The past few days she’d gone without her sleeping pills, which contributed to her bad mood without the haze of sluggishness to take the edge off it all, and she hadn’t slept all night, dreading the sunrise and the day it would bring with it. The dread of the funeral had haunted her, playing on her mind over and over again with thoughts of the empty casket and the gave that would mark the spot where nothing but her memory would lay. 

     

                Hoping to postpone it for as long as possible, Lena stayed in bed until six o’clock, waiting for her mom to get up while she pretended to sleep, before sitting up, swinging her legs out of bed and sitting on the edge of the mattress for a while longer as she fiddled with the chain in her hand. It was Kara’s ID tags, returned to Eliza a few days ago with the rest of her belongings shipped back from the base. The tags were the only thing left of Kara that they’d found in the wreckage of the explosion, and Lena clutched the little metal rectangles so tightly that they etched deep lines into her palms where they cut in. For almost two hours, she sat there gripping the tags and staring at the window, watching as the outline of light creeping in steadily grew lighter. She watched the time pass by with a glazed look in her eyes, not really seeing anything as her mind replayed moments with Kara over and over again.

     

                It wasn’t until there was a knock on the door that Lena stirred, blinking slowly as the door opened and Eliza poked her head inside. She looked ashen and aged, her face thin and the bags beneath her eyes heavy. Lena knew she worked long hours at the hospital but the grief of losing a daughter had exhausted her tenfold. Lena didn’t so much as look at her as she held the tags and stayed lost in her thoughts.

     

                “Good morning,” Eliza murmured after a moment, letting herself in.

     

                She walked over to the bed and took a seat beside Lena, reaching out to turn over her hand. Uncurling her fingers, Lena looked down at the tags as the air rushed from her lungs and she sagged as the reminder of the day caught her off-guard all over again.

     

                “She’s supposed to be home today,” Lena rasped, her eyes burning, even as she blinked drily, her tears already spent. “She’s supposed to be coming home. I promised I’d be waiting for her with a bouquet of flowers and instead … I’m putting flowers on her grave.”

     

                Her whispered words were said with disbelief and she felt the world pitch around her with that all-too-familiar sickening send of wrongness . Drawing in a ragged breath, Lena hunched over as Eliza pressed a hand to her back, feeling the ridges of her spine and ribs from where grief had carved pounds from her.

     

                “It’s okay. I know. I know it hurts.”

     

                “How do you even let go?”

     

                “The trick is you don’t let go; you always have a piece of them with you. The people we love … they all seem to leave us with something of theirs.”

     

                Lips trembling, Lena swallowed and nodded, turning the tags over between her fingers as her chest ached.

     

                “Did you sleep?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “You’ll need your strength today, sweetheart.”

     

                “I don’t think sleep is going to help.”

     

                She blinked, dry-eyed, burning with exhaustion as she turned to look at Eliza, her ears ringing faintly as her skin felt hot and her breaths came quick and shallow. Brushing dark hair out of her face, Eliza studied her for a long moment, her blue eyes travelling across Lena’s face while she kept whatever she was thinking to herself, before she gave her a thin smile and cupped her cheek in her hand.

     

                “You should shower; we need to be there at ten.”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena closed her eyes, a small sound of panic escaping her. “I can’t. I can’t do it, Eliza.”

     

                “I know it’s hard. Believe me, I know . But we have to - for her, for ourselves.”

     

                Letting out a shaky breath, Lena set the tags down onto the end table and swallowed a sob as she stared at them for a moment longer. She was slapped with the vivid memory of Kara’s glasses perched on the end table, a thumbprint smudge left on one lens as they magnified the grain of the wood. It knocked the breath out of her and she curled in on herself, the pain blinding for a moment, before the distant sound of her name being called brought her back to the moment.

     

                Abruptly lurching to her feet, Lena walked out of the room and locked herself in the bathroom, feeling clammy and faint as she leaned back against the wood. Closing her eyes, she breathed slowly until she was able to push herself off and strip off her clothes, the same pyjamas that belonged to Kara that she’d lived in for days now. Avoiding her reflection, not wanting to see the puffy-eyed, greasy image of the person she’d dissolved into within a matter of days , Lena climbed into the shower before turning on the water, the spray of cold a slapping shock that stole the breath from her lungs. It eventually warmed and she stayed in there until someone knocked on the door.

     

                Wrapped up in a towel, she made her way back into Kara’s room and pulled on underwear and the black stockings before faltering at the ironed black dress hanging up on the back of the door. She loathed the idea of putting it on and ended up sitting on the edge of the bed, half-dressed while her damp hair dripped onto the bed sheets and she rubbed at her forehead, a headache blooming already. 

     

                It was Alex who found her, stepping inside in a black suit, looking spent and miserable, and taking in her half-dressed appearance.
