She grabbed the dress off the back of the door and carried it over to Lena, holding it out until she eventually took it. Slipping it off the hanger, Lena stepped into it and Alex turned her around, zipping her up and then vanishing for a moment before she returned with a hairbrush and hair dryer. Pushing Lena down onto the bed, she set about untangling her hair and then drying it before she pinned it back neatly. Then she rifled through Lena’s bag until she found her makeup and knelt on the floor before her, turning her head this way and that as she blended foundation and concealer while Lena closed her eyes to it all, not having the energy to fight her off making her look presentable.

     

                Once Alex had finished dabbing on a nude lipstick and packed everything away, Lena opened her eyes. “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Alex’s lips twisted ruefully and she sat down beside Lena, taking her hands in her own and staring at her with desperation in her brown eyes. “Listen, I- today … it’s going to be hard. The hardest day of our lives, so …I- I need you to be strong, please , because … I can’t do this without you.”

     

                “Strong. Right.”

     

                “Just until after. There’s … something for you. From her. You might want to save it … until after.”

     

                She pulled an envelope out of her blazer pocket, slipping it into Lena’s hand, her name written on it in Kara’s handwriting. The breath rushed out of her and she felt like her chest was about to cave in, tracing a finger over the lines of her name as her vision blurred with tears. She’d known that Kara had written letters for everyone but it had never even seemed like a reality that they’d all one day have to read them. Lena knew this one would be the hardest letter of all, harder than any of the ones Kara had left when she’d gone, harder than anything Lena would ever read. She clutched it tightly, this last little piece of her, and felt her stomach tie itself into knots at the thought of making it through it.

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                Nodding, Alex hesitated and then walked out of the room, leaving her alone. Taking her advice, Lena decided to wait until after the service to read it, knowing she wouldn’t be able to make it there if she read it now. Tucking it into the pocket of her black overcoat, she lingered upstairs until Lillian opened the door a few minutes later, dressed in black and looking grim and resolute.

     

                Walking over to Lena, she sank down into a crouch before her and took her hands in her own, kissing her cold fingers and holding them tightly in her warm grasp. “How about some breakfast before we go?” she gently asked.

     

                Lena vehemently opposed the mere idea of breakfast, shaking her head as she pressed her lips into a thin, bloodless line. She wouldn’t be able to get it down, and even if she did, she felt so nauseous that it inevitably would’ve come back up again.

     

                “Okay,” Lillian murmured, quickly caving in as she gave her daughter a long, searching look. “I- you can do this, you know. I know you don’t want to, but you’re strong - so strong - and braver than you know, and … you’ll get through it because you love her. And I’m sorry - so sorry you have to go through this. I- I never wanted this for you; I wanted you to be happy.”

     

                “I was,” Lena choked out. “She … I wouldn’t change a thing.”

     

                “I know. I just wish you’d had more time to be happy.”

     

                Swallowing, she nodded as her mouth turned down at the corners, chin dimpling with the effort it took not to cry. Wiping at her eyes, she sniffed and looked down at her pale hands in her mom’s, thinking about how Lena really did love her, and how Lillian loved her too, even though they never seemed to be able to get along with each other, and maybe they never would but Lena was grateful all the same. Through Kara, she’d found herself surrounded by people who loved her and Lena knew she wouldn’t have made it past the last ten days without them. It didn’t make the pain or loneliness any less though.

     

                Kelly appeared in the doorway a minute later, apologetically intruding on the moment as she gave them a grim smile, “we should get going.”

     

                Nodding, Lena reached down for her heels and slipepd them on, pulling on her coat and reaching into the pocket for that letter, her fingers brushing it reassuringly, as if taking strength from Kara’s unread words. Lillian squeezed her arm and Lena nodded, moving towards the door as her stomach twinged with that feeling of dread that had eluded her for the past week but had been a constant companion over the past year.

     

                Downstairs, they all climbed into a black car, Lena sitting beside her mom on one bench while the other three sat across from them. Nobody spoke as they made their way through the town, early spring bringing a fresh green and smattering of colourful wildflowers to the damp forest as they wound through the narrow, tree-lined roads.

     

                Once they arrived, the row of damp, moss-covered headstones and bowed oaks shading them filling Lena with a sense of unease, she climbed out of the car and watched as Kelly held Alex’s hand tightly, guiding her up the path. Lena numbly reached out for Eliza’s, the other woman’s loneliness as vast as her own, and squeezed, clinging to her like a lifeline. Lillian followed up the rear, her hands hovering at Lena’s back as if to catch her if she fell or prod her forward if she faltered. 

     

                It was a drizzling day of misery, a chill permeating everything and the sunlight struggling from behind a blanket of clouds. The small church was clean but did nothing to keep the cold out, even with a noisy heater pushing out warm air. Sitting in the front row, wedged in between Kelly and her mother, Lena stared at the empty mahogany casket resting at the front with a flag draped over it and a flower arrangement. She had a hard time feeling anything as she looked at it, not feeling Kara’s presence at all as she looked at the empty box and knew that it was meaningless. Eliza was wrong; this wouldn’t bring closure for her.

     

                There were dozens of other people there too, packing into the narrow pews and standing at the back, everyone dressed in black and looking sombre as they waited for the service to start. Lena didn’t turn and look, didn’t care who was there and wouldn’t have recognised Eliza’s colleagues and half of the town and military personnel from Fort Rozz and other bases. She didn’t notice Nia and Querl, Winn, Lucy or James. She was oblivious to everything, to the droning words of the minister as it started, to the heartfelt speech given by Kara’s old Lieutenant at Fort Rozz, to the official military proceedings as pallbearers in uniform raised the empty coffin with ease and walked it outside to the freshly dug grave.

     

                Family followed it out first and Lena put one foot in front of the other without consciously choosing to, a lump in her throat as she stared blankly at the stripes of the flag. She couldn’t find it within herself to cry - she’d spent ten days crying over Kara’s absence, and an empty coffin was much the same. Still, as they all gathered around the rectangle dug beside Jeremiah’s grave, silent tears slid down her face as she stood stiffly, her mom gripping her arm to steady her while her heart felt like it was going to stop in her chest with the overwhelming pain of it.

     

                She didn’t move again until she tossed a red rose on top of the wood and let a handful of wet, black earth crumble on top of it. Everything else faded to nothing; the military rituals, the sound of the bugle as they played the taps, the shots fired from the gun, deafeningly loud but not eliciting so much as a flinch from her. Lena felt distant from it all, like she was watching from outside of her body, not really processing what was happening around her. All she knew was other people were crying and she wanted to laugh as anger knifed through her, keen and hot, because she’d lost so much and she couldn’t believe anyone else would dare mourn her as well when they didn’t even know her.

     

                Once the service ended, Kara’s Lieutenant brought the folded flag over to Eliza and thanked her for Kara’s service before offering them his condolences. That’s when the flood of empty words and hugs started and Lena gave them the cold shoulder, standing rigidly at the side of the open grave as she ignored everyone else. The smalltown folk might think she was rude, might gossip later about how aloof and cold she’d been, but she didn’t care. They couldn’t offer her anything; the only people she drew any comfort from were Kara’s family and friends, but even they weren’t the arms she wanted wrapped around her.

     

                People trickled away afterwards, the town hall repurposed for a wake with tea and coffee and sandwiches. Lena hadn’t even considered going and couldn’t even bring herself to leave the graveside as she stared down into the long hole and the empty coffin. Soon enough it was just the five of them, a light rain starting up as they lingered, and Lena was pale and tense as she tried to stop shaking. Eventually, Eliza hesitantly approached her, reaching out to take her freezing hand.

     

                “Sweetheart, it’s time to go home now.”

     

                “No,” Lena choked out, pulling her hand back slowly as she kept her eyes on the hole.

     

                “You can’t stay here all day.”

     

                “Just a little while longer.”

     

                She hesitated, looking at Lillian, before nodding, cupping her ashen cheek in her hand before stepping back. Lillian kissed the side of Lena’s head, closing her eyes as she sighed softly, before the four of them retreated, leaving Lena alone. Alone, she stood there for a few minutes in the fine mist of rain, strands of her dark hair whipped around her head and plastered to her bitten cheeks. The wind howled through the trees as they bowed beneath it, leaves rustling and the emptiness of the cemetery seeming vast as she stood alone, a small black figure at the side of an open grave with no one in it. Lena knew they were waiting for her to leave so they could fill the grave in, but she wasn’t ready to leave just yet. It might have been a farce of a funeral but it was all Kara would be given and she didn’t want to let go, to say goodbye.

     

                After a few minutes of silence, a sob burst from her chest, ragged and broken as she collapsed to her knees at the edge of the hole, grabbed at fistfuls of wet grass as she hunched over and cried. It was a breathless, quiet sobbing, the undoing after hours spent holding it together, and it was almost a relief to let it all out. 

     

                “Oh, God. I’m so sorry,” she whispered, hands digging into her eyes as she felt her heart break a little bit more. “I can’t do this. I can’t do this without you; I need you. Why did you go? You promised me. You promised- oh God , it hurts so much. Please.”

     

                The midday sun shone weakly overhead, hidden behind grey clouds as Lena sobbed over the empty grave, mumbling intelligible words. It was an age before she calmed down enough to pull the envelope out of her pocket with a shaking hand, staring down at her name written on the front of it as she smoothed her thumb over it. Clumsily wiping at her tearstained face as she drew in hitching, hiccuping breaths, Lena slid a finger beneath the flap and opened it.

     

                She drank in each word slowly and it was a miracle she made it through the whole thing, the sour taste of bile at the back of her throat as she read it silently, trying to stifle her crying as tears fell onto the paper. She cried for what felt like forever once she was finished, one hand crumpling up the letter while the other one clutched at her heart, the agonising loss of Kara aching so keenly that she felt like she’d never feel okay again, not even for a second. For a brief moment she wondered whether it was harder to die or harder to be the one who survived.

     

                Gut-wrenching sobs wracked her whole body as she knelt on the grass, amidst all the flowers that people had left behind, trying to catch her breath as the last shreds of her self-control fled her. Raw-eyed and freezing, she stayed even as the rain turned heavier, soaking her through as she shivered, unmoving, unfeeling. The only thought she had was to stuff the letter back into the envelope and into the pocket, not wanting to ruin the last gift Kara had left for her. 

     

                At some point, she stopped being aware of her surroundings, her mind seeming to drift elsewhere, protecting her from what it could, and she came to, curled up at the foot of the grave, with an older man in a grey raincoat shaking her awake with a look of concern on his face. Sitting up, feeling exhausted and empty, Lena ignored his distant words and pushed herself to her feet. Kicking off her heels, she lurched unsteadily to her feet, walking down the path to the carpark where they’d entered, feeling drunk and disoriented as she blinked rain out of her eyes and let it drip down her face and soak into her clothes.

     

                A car pulled her up short a moment later and Lena reeled backwards, finding herself staring at Eliza’s SUV. Of course someone would have come back to get her and she moved forward, reaching for the car door and opening it to the sight of her mother behind the wheel. It was jarring and she hesitated before climbing in, heedless of her wet clothes and torn stockings as she shivered in the hot air stuttering out of the vents.

     

                Looking at Lillian, Lena startled at the sight of her mother’s bloodshot eyes, her lips parting numbly as she gave her a mystified look. “Mom?”

     

                Shaking her head, Lillian sniffed and gripped the steering wheel tightly. “I just- that poor girl. I’m sorry.”

     

                Nodding, Lena swallowed thickly, pulling her seatbelt across her and sinking into the seat. A breathless sob built up in her chest and she closed her eyes, shivering even as the stale hot air made her feel nauseous, that sour taste burning at the back of her throat as she trembled and tried to get herself under control. 

     

                “Lena?”

     

                “I should’ve- I should’ve hugged her tighter. Last time, I should’ve- if I’d known …”

     

                “We’d be more careful if we knew which goodbyes were our last.”

     

                Lena hummed, the sound frayed and rough as she shook her head. Lillian put the car into drive again and peeled out of the wet carpark, puddles forming in the pitted asphalt, and started for Eliza’s home. 

     

                And somehow, that was the worst part. Driving back to that house after putting an empty casket into the ground was the worst part of the whole day, as if they were leaving her behind there, in the cold and wet, even thought Lena logically knew that she wasn’t there. It hurt so much that she rocked forward, arms wrapped tightly around her stomach as she closed her eyes, teeth bared in agony.

     

                “Are you alright?”

     

                Lena let out a whimpering sob, shaking her head as she squeezed her eyes shut tightly, feeling the panic set in as her breaths came short and fast. The acidic feeling in her stomach clawed its way up her throat as she wrenched the car door open without warning, Lillian slamming on the brakes, and promptly vomited what little was in her stomach all over the side of the road. 

     

                Gasping for air as she leaned out of the door, cold air caressing her flushed cheeks, she spat the bitter taste of bile out of her mouth and straightened back up, slamming the door shut as a sob escaped her. She shook as she sat slumped against the seat, crying her eyes out as she let all previous inhibitions go. Loud hitching sobs wracked her and her mother’s voice fell on deaf ears as she wrapped her arms around herself and rocked slightly.

     

                She didn’t even notice when they got home, didn’t feel the gust of cold air as Lillian opened her door, her hands unbuckling her seat belt or trying to urge her out of the car. Lena just cried, unashamedly as she curled in on herself and hid her face in her hands, her panicked breaths leaving her gasping as she choked and struggled. Oblivious to it all, Lena was unaware of Eliza’s presence at her side as she came out to help Lillian, both of them unable to drag her out of the car as some part of her resisted.

     

                “Do you have any lorazepam?” Lillian asked after a minute, looking worn and harried as she ran a hand over her face.

     

                “Lillian-”

     

                “She needs a sedative; look at her, she’s can barely breathe.”

     

                “I … all I have is haloperidol.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                The needle was a sharp prick of pain in her hand by her mother’s capable administration, Eliza’s voice gentle and soothing as she cupped Lena’s face in her warm hands, changed out of her black dress and into her usual comfortable clothes. Going limp as the drugs quickly took effect, Lena sagged against her and was easily pliable as she was maneuvered out of the car and her weight was shared between the two women.

     

                They somehow managed to get her upstairs and onto the bed, Lillian efficiently stripping her wet clothes off her and getting her beneath the covers. Lingering in that in between space of conscious and unconscious, Lena drifted, her body slack and weightless as her eyelids fluttered and opened and then closed again, her lips moving soundlessly as she murmured Kara’s name over and over.

    Chapter 64

    To my dearest Lena,

     

    If you’re reading then then the only thing I can say is I’m sorry. I promised you I’d come home and I didn’t intend for it to be in a box, but I broke that promise and I’m more sorry than you can ever imagine because I promised never to be the person in your life that causes you pain, and I don’t think it’s arrogant to say that you’re hurting right now. It’s something I’ll never be able to forgive myself for.

     

    As I’m writing this, you’re asleep in my bed at my mom’s house, curled up right next to me where you belong. You don’t know it yet but I’m going to propose in a couple of days and I hope that you say yes. If you said yes and you’re reading this then I’m sorry for breaking another promise to you. And, well, if you said no, I hope you know that I died so in love with you that you were the only person I wanted to spend my life with. Perhaps it’s selfish of me to ask you anyway when you might end up reading this, but I want you to know how much I love you while I can still tell you, and that I have a whole future planned for us. Right now, as I sit here, I want to do everything with you, so I’m sorry if there comes a point where you’re reading these words. 

     

    I know love isn’t supposed to hurt and it’s been painful enough as it is for us, but I can’t bring myself to regret even a second of our time together, even if it leads up to you reading this. How could I? And maybe that’ selfish of me to come into your life and shake everything up and leave in the cruelest way possible, after making you love me, but I want you to know that I loved you too, utterly and completely, with my entire heart. I hope you felt that and know that I’ll always feel that way about you. 

     

    I know it’s probably stupid to say this but I don’t want you to be sad forever, Lena. I wish I could be the person you’d live a long and happy life with, but I’m not, and I hope that one day you’ll be able to find it within yourself to open up to someone new. I know it’s asking a lot because I know how hard it was for you to trust me too, but please, for me. I don’t want you to give up on how far you’ve come and I don’t want to be the roadblock in your life for how far you still have to go. If there’s anything I’ve learnt from my parents dying it’s that it’s okay to be sad for a little while, but then you need to heal. So please, heal for me when you’re ready, and give all of that love inside you to someone who deserves it and who loves you as much as I do. 

     

    I know this will be the most challenging thing in your long life of challenges yet, but I know how strong you are and I know that with time the pain will get smaller and your life will grow around the hole I left behind. I’m glad we have all of those photographs together to remind you of our time together though, and I hope that one day you can look back on them - maybe with your kids and your new partner - and remember just how much we loved each other. Maybe it’ll still hurt a little, but I guess deep down I knew that I was taking them just in case something like this happened, and I hope that you’ll be able to find peace in them one day and think of me fondly. Just know that each time you think of me, I’ll be thinking of you too, and inside these pages our love will stay frozen exactly as it is now, where I’m right there with you, never letting go.

     

    Even now, maybe this isn’t the end of it all. You’re a scientific person but I know you don’t believe in soulmates and fate and all of that crap, but you believe in science. You know the quantum theory of entanglement, where particles become correlated with each other regardless of distance. I like to think that coincides with the first law of thermodynamics – that no energy is created and none is destroyed. At the beginning of the universe maybe the particles that made us up were separated, and over time, no matter what form our energy takes, they keep coming back to each other. Maybe that’s what soulmates really are. And if that's what they are, then I'll come back to you, over and over again, in every lifetime. 

     

    You think it was by some miracle that we met that day, but I never told you the truth. Every day that week I’d gone to that coffee shop and ordered the smallest, cheapest coffee I could get and sat in that shop. I’d just come home from overseas and gotten back from seeing Eliza and I was having a hard time adjusting. I was there again the day you came in and I saw you from across the room. I’d never seen someone so beautiful before, I knew I had to take your photo. and it was so busy in there that I gave up my table to someone else and asked if I could sit with you and you said yes and let me take your photo. So you see, I think I went there every day knowing you would turn up eventually, and even if we weren’t able to spend a lifetime together, we were meant to be together for as long as we’ve had.

     

    I’m not sure what the circumstances of my death might be - maybe it was a freak accident, or maybe it was something and violent - but I want you to know that you’ll be my last thought, and I won’t be afraid. Life isn’t about the final moments, it’s about the moments that lead up to them, and so many of those moments are full of you. Just know that loving you was the easiest thing I have ever done in my life, and if love was enough I’d still be there with you. 

     

    Now it’s time for me to wait for you to come home, because I believe that in some way (I’m not sure which) we’ll be together again some day. I’ll wait for you, for as long as it takes, because I’ll love you forever, Lena Luthor.

     

    Yours always,

     

    Kara xxx 

    Chapter 65

                She woke to a throbbing pain in her head, but it wasn’t all bad. There was a warm feeling in her stomach, a floaty feeling, something fuzzy and giddy and cozy as she lay beneath the heavy blankets, the consuming pain of her grief beating against the dam wall the sedative had erected, holding the flood at bay for the time being. Of course, Lena didn’t know she’d been sedated exactly, only that things had hurt and then it had stopped and now she was awake.

     

                All memory of arriving home was a blur to her, although she vaguely recalled her mother there, and she sat up in bed after a minute, hand pressed to her head, and stared down at her undressed figure. She didn’t remember taking off that black dress, remember walking upstairs or getting into bed, but she had and she’d slept and taken something - that much was clear. 

     

                Stiffly climbing out of bed, Lena pulled on a pair of Kara’s sweatpants, the waistband needing to be pulled in that little bit tighter now to stop them sagging around her hips, and she ran a hand over her face, tongue thick in her mouth. Despite the abundance of sleep she’d been getting lately, there was a bone-deep weariness to her that never seemed to go away, dark circles beneath her sunken eyes and a sallow pallor to her skin. She was sick with grief and there was no cure for it. The worst part was it hadn’t even been two weeks; she would have a lifetime of this.

     

                Perhaps worst of all was that Kara consumed her every waking thought in an endless film reel inside Lena’s mind; her face, her eyes, her lips, her mouth, her laugh, the smell of her perfume and the memory of how soft her hair was as Lena ran her fingers through it. Lena remembered it all. Every moment was a fresh memory come to torture her, and after dreams plagued with Kara’s homecoming, even sleep was no longer a comfort. 

     

                Her family might have been a comfort if they weren’t such a bitter reminder of Kara too. The hollow-eyed grief of a mother losing her daughter a slap in the face whenever she looked at Eliza, memories of bickering and laughter and inside jokes whenever she looked at Alex. It was too much and it was a relief that everyone had mostly left her alone, aside from her mother who seemed to relentlessly hover, worried sick over the frightening change in Lena. She’d always been a fighter - physically, verbally, emotionally - and even when she’d struggled to open up to people, she’d never been so closed off and quiet. The stubborn determination to fight for everything denied her was gone, and now Lena could barely get out of bed.

     

                When she woke, the sky the purplish blue of a bruise as rainclouds lingered and the weak sunlight slipped away, Lena found the stifling silence of the house suffocating though. It felt like the walls were closing in, her ears ringing as she looked around Kara’s room and the cotton wool feeling of the drugs left her feeling unbalanced. Gripped by the sudden urge to leave, she climbed to her feet and pulled on a sweater and shoes over her bare feet. Reaching for the damp coat hanging on the back of the door, Lena slipped out of the room and crept downstairs, the screen door squeaking faintly as she crept outside.

     

                No one stopped her as she hurried down the slick driveway, raindrops pattering against her shoulders as she hunched them, hands balled into her pockets and her breath a faint mist as what little warmth the day had held fled into night. The house was illuminated behind her against a bluish sky, warm yellow light spilling out, and she was quick, wondering how long it would take for someone to release she’d snuck out and not wanting them to stop her.

     

                Lena wasn’t too familiar with the outskirts of Midvale, but she walked north, heading up the road as she left the town behind. Her boots rubbed against her bare feet as she walked, the constant light patter or rain soaking her through as she shivered, eyes glazed and lips trembling as she put one foot in front of the other. A few cars heading out of town slowed as they approached her, headlights illuminating the shining roads as they wound down windows and called out to her. Lena didn’t even hear them, just kept walking, for over almost an hour as she tried to recall the place they’d gone to together that one day in Midvale.

     

                Eventually, she turned off the road near a rise of moss-covered rocks, sure that it was the right place, and spent another hour heading up the gentle inclines and over rotting logs and muddy trails made by local wildlife. She fell a few times, smearing mud all over herself as she fell onto the sodden, leaf-strewn ground, skinning her palms and soaking the knees of her sweatpants, but eventually she came out the other side, high above the sea.

     

                The air was bracing and freezing - even colder than it had been last time Kara had taken her out there - but it wasn’t the right place. It was close , one tree much like the other, the view the same along the rugged coastline, but she knew in her gut it was the wrong place. Winter had stripped most of the trees of their green foliage, now brown and rotting beneath her feet as she stood on the barren earth at the edge of the sheer cliffs, staring out at grey waves and dark clouds, the wind battering her back. It should have been devastating to not even know how to seek out that special place again, but it was actually a relief . There was no piece of her at that place, nothing alive and no haunting memories.

     

                And perhaps that made it worse in its own way, because Kara wasn’t going to tramp through the trees behind her, Athena on her heels and a hot thermos of coffee in hand. There would be no picnic and no drive home with the staticky radio and her singing along to fragments of old music. Only the barest hint of light illuminated the view, having taken her so long to get there, and she fell to her knees at the edge, breathing in the briny smell of the sea as the rain picked up a little.

     

                Clutching at handfuls of mud and leaves and grass, she let out a ragged shout, rocking forward as her hair was whipped around her face in a frenzy. It was cold and she was shaking as she fell apart again, the fractured pieces of her unable to hold their form any longer, no matter how many times she wore herself out and picked up the pieces. She always fell apart again the moment her body had the energy to. 

     

                Drawing in a hitching sob, she turned her face up to the sky, eyes creasing at the corners as she squeezed them shut, teeth bared as her lips trembled with the effort of her crying. “I’m so alone,” she whispered, her low voice rasping and cracking. “How could you leave me like this?”

     

                Gasping for air, her throat burning with the cold as her chest constricted painfully, she cried loudly, the sobs unhindered by anyone else’s presence, by her own reservations. She’d never been in so much pain before.

     

                The last hint of sunlight faded to black as the wind and the sea raged on, rain pelting down on her as she knelt, arms wrapped around herself, unable to move. Cold water snaked down the back of her neck and beneath her collar and her sobs slowly quietened to silence. Hollow-eyed and empty, she huddled on her knees, wracked by violent shivers, until she eventually became aware of the fact that she needed to leave. 

     

                Staggering to her feet, she turned towards the blackness of the trees, the pale moonlight unhelpful against the tightly packed trunks and treacherous paths, and plunged into the darkness. Tripping over tree roots and branches, slipping on slick mud and stepping into deceptively deep puddles, Lena spent the next hour in frustrating clumsiness, falling more times than she could count as she twisted her ankle and whacked her knee on a rock, scraped her cheek on a low-hanging branch and fell backwards on such a steep incline that she slid a few metres, banging her head against the ground as she was jolted and leaving her coated in mud as she came to a stop and lay there for a moment, staring up at the canopy overhead as rain dripped onto her face.

     

                By the time she made it back to Eliza’s street, that house shining warmly in the nearby distance, she was numb and stiff and aching with bruises and cuts and the toll it had taken on her body. And all of it had been futile because she didn’t feel any better for the solitude she’d been afforded for a handful of hours. Blinking slowly as she walked up the sloped driveway, her body uncooperative and jerky, she noted the missing car and walked right up to the door, where it was jerked open as she reached for the screen handle.

     

                That was pushed open too and Lena stepped inside, slack-faced and robotic as her mom grabbed her sodden shoulders in a tight grip and shook her, just a little too rough. “What the hell are you doing? Huh?”

     

                Lena couldn’t make her mouth work as it opened and closed, and Lillian’s fear-born anger guttered as concern lanced through her. “Jesus. Look at you. Let’s get you out of those clothes.”

     

                Hand in her pocket, curling around the damp letter still stowed there, Lena jerkily shook her head as her mom’s hands grabbed the collar and tried to drag it off her. Bottom lip wobbling as new tears filled her eyes, Lena shook her head, staring vacantly past Lillian as she dimly listened to Alex’s quiet voice on the phone, not hearing any of it.

     

                Another person materialised at her side then and Lena blinked as her eyes focused on Eliza. The tears in her eyes spilled over then as she let out a breathless sob, chest caving in, and crossed the space between them as she rested her forehead against Eliza’s shoulder, feeling her arms wrap around her, that comforting feeling of being held and understood by someone who had lost as much as she had.

     

                “Come on, sweetheart, you need to get changed. You’ll catch a cold if we don’t get you out of those wet clothes,” Eliza said, gently smoothing Lena’s hair and kissing her on the top of her head.

     

                “I’ll-”

     

                Her mother was cut off by Alex, who stepped forward and reached out for Lena. “You should rest, Lillian. I’ll take care of it.”

     

                Swallowing her words, Lillian nodded and rubbed at her forehead, the stress of worrying falling away to resigned exhaustion as she hesitated and then moved down the hallway. Eliza gently guided Lena towards the stairs, letting Alex take over propping her up while she went on ahead. The sound of water thundering into the bathtub sounded a moment later as Lena unevenly lurched upstairs, violently shivering as her teeth chattered and her leaden limbs struggled up each step.

     

                Eliza was putting clean towels in the bathroom when Alex led her inside, squeezing past, and Lena let the coat get dragged off her, a mewling sound escaping her as she reached for the dirty hem and dragged it back, fishing out the worn letter and holding it tightly in her trembling hands. Alex set the coat down on top of the toilet seat and reached for the letter with one hand while laying the other on Lena’s arm in a gently reassuring manner.

     

                “How about we put that somewhere safe so it doesn’t get wet?”

     

                Nodding, Lena let it slip from her fingers and Alex carefully set it beside the sink, out of harm's way, before Eliza slipped out and shut the door behind her. Alex was quick as she stripped off Lena’s clothes, leaving her shivering in the cold air of the tiled bathroom, pink skin rippling with goosebumps, and Lena moved towards the bath, climbing in and sitting as the hot water stung the myriad of cuts she’d accumulated.

     

                “Oh,” Alex murmured, turning around and finding her in the tub, her eyes widening a fraction as she hurriedly crossed over, leaning over as she reached for the taps. “How about some cold too.”

     

                Lena didn’t respond, didn’t even feel the burning heat of the hot water as it reddened her skin and surrounded her with wisps of steam. Sliding down until she was submerged completely, Lena let the scalding water burrow into her cold bones.

     

                A door sounded downstairs and Alex slipped out into the hallway, leaving Lena alone in the bath. She felt weightless in the water, her lungs burning as her back dug painfully into the porcelain tub and let the heat wrap her in its embrace. There were little pieces of snapped off twigs and rotting leaves tangled in her hair that came loose as she lay submerged, dark hair fanning out like spun silk around her in the water. 

     

                She was hauled up a moment later, a small sound of alarm escaping her as she opened her mouth and inhaled, water flooding in as she was rudely disturbed. Coughing and spluttering as she brushed her hair out of her face, Lena blanched at Alex’s angry voice.

     

                “What the fuck are you doing?” she growled, shaking her shoulder.

     

                “I- it’s warm.”

     

                “Don’t do that.”

     

                Blinking owlishly, Lena looked up at her and took in her pale face, brown eyes wide with panic. 

     

                Drawing her knees up to her chest and wrapping her arms around them, Lena propped her chin on top, wincing slightly at the pain of new bruises mottling her knees, and mumbled an apology. She was dimly aware of Kelly standing in the doorway, coat still on and a relieved slump to her shoulders at coming in to find Lena back safely. She mumbled another apology to her as well, rubbing at her stinging cheek where a shallow scratch marred it.

     

                Kelly shut the door after a moment, leaving Lena with Alex, and she stared down at the steaming water as Alex turned off the taps. “Here, let me wash your hair.”

     

                “I’m fine.”

     

                Nodding, Alex retreated to the pile of mud-stained clothes and dumped them in the laundry basket before taking a seat on the toilet, elbows on her knees as she pressed her fingertips against her forehead. It became apparent that she wasn’t going to afford Lena her privacy and leave her alone, and suppressing a sigh, Lena slowly reached for the shampoo, working it into her hair as she mechanically went through the motions. 

     

                “So, where did you go?” Alex asked after a silent few minutes.

     

                “For a walk.”

     

                “Not many good places for a walk on a rainy night.”

     

                Chewing on her lip as she studied one of her grazed palms, Lena shrugged nonchalantly. “She took me somewhere once. I thought- I don’t know … I might feel closer to her. Might hurt less. I couldn’t find it anyway.”

     

                Alex nodded as she glanced over at her, fingers laced together, a pained look of understanding on her face as if she wished for the same thing, the same kind of release from the longing for her sister and the suffocating grief that came with it. She looked awful, if Lena was being honest, and she knew if she looked in the mirror she’d find much worse there. Swallowing thickly as she averted her gaze, she washed the soap suds from her skin and climbed out of the bath, wrapping a towel around herself. 

     

                In Kara’s bedroom, she changed into clean pyjamas and went back to the bathroom to fetch her letter, leaving it out to dry, praying that the ink hadn’t bled too much. Her mom walked in as she was arranging it near a vent and watched for a long moment, taking in the sight of her lost daughter as pity welled up inside her.

     

                “I’ll make you some tea,” Lillian ventured, “and you should eat something. It’s been a long day.”

     

                Nodding, Lena pressed her lips together and hesitated before straightening up and looking at her. “Mom? Can you … not spike the tea? I don’t really feel like sleeping right now.”

     

                “Oh. Oh, no, I … I won’t do that.”

     

                Lena nodded again and raked a hand through her hair before she walked out into the hallway and made her way downstairs. In a way, the house was familiar to her with Kara’s absence, having spent time there with Alex and Kelly, or alone with Eliza, and so it felt natural in a way she was able to cling to for a brief bout of normalcy as she made her way downstairs to the kitchen for the first time in days.

     

                Sitting down heavily at the kitchen table, Lena’s shoulders slumped and she closed her eyes, listening to the sounds around her as a spoon clattered and a drawer opened, the fridge was gently closed. Her mom set a cup of tea in front of her a minute later and Lena made herself take a sip of it, Earl Grey no longer holding the comfort it used to as she forced herself to swallow and set the cup back down.

     

                She was aware of a quiet conversation held off to her left, her mom and Eliza whispering to each other before Lillian kissed the top of her head and vanished. Alone in the kitchen with Eliza, Lena swallowed the lump in her throat as she stared at the table, a bowl of soup appearing before her before Eliza dragged out a chair next to her and sat. Reaching for the spoon, she scooped up some of the pumpkin soup and held the spoon out to Lena, who met her sad eyes and then leaned in, lips parting, to dutifully swallow.

     

                Satisfied that she would eat, Eliza set the spoon in the bowl and nudged it towards her, keeping Lena company in silence as they sat together until she’d finished eating and drained her cup of tea. Even then, neither of them spoke as they sat and dwelled in their own thoughts for a while longer before Lena exhaled sharply, running a hand over her face.

     

                “Thank you, Eliza,” she gravelly spoke after a moment. “You’ve always been good to me. I know I haven’t always made it … easy, but thank you. I- even though- well … I’m glad we got to meet.”

     

                Giving her a wavering smile, Eliza reached out and stroked her dark hair. “It was always easy. From the moment she brought you home you were part of my family; I loved you before I even met you and, more importantly, you- you loved her. So thank you for- for giving her that before …”

     

                “I love her,” Lena whispered.

     

                “I know you do, honey,” Eliza miserably replied, pain flickering across her face as her old grief for her husband and the fresh loss of her daughter washed over her. “I know how this feels.”

     

                Wiping at her cheeks, Lena blew the air out of her lungs and swallowed, “I just- I want to see her. I want to … look at her, but if I … I won’t be able to stop myself from falling apart.”

     

                “You’re allowed to. For as long as it takes for it to hurt a little bit less. She’s everywhere; she’ll always be everywhere and … you can’t avoid that forever. When you lose someone, you don’t miss the big moments, you miss all the little everyday things and … it’s never really going to stop, so just- do what you have to. Okay?”

     

                “I just- I should’ve hugged her tighter last time I saw her. I wish I knew our last kiss was our last kiss. I just thought there would be so much … more . I thought we had so much more time together. There are so many things we said we were going to do that we never got to and I … I miss her. Everyday. I wish I could talk to her one last time and tell her that I- that I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have let her go. I should’ve made her stay. How am I supposed to- I mean … what do I do now?”

     

                She spread her hands helplessly, a lost look on her face as she looked up at Eliza with bloodshot eyes brimming with tears. Reaching across, Eliza took her hands in her own and squeezed tightly.

     

                “Now you grieve - and then you live.”

    Chapter 66

                Waking early the next morning, Lena blinked away the latest dream of Kara as she slowly came to, heavy-lidded eyes opening to narrow slits as she watched her mother fold the blankets neatly at the bottom of the mattress. She was dressed in her silk pyjamas with a robe over the top, bare-faced and grave as she quietly moved about the room. It was odd to see her doing such menial household tasks like making a bed and Lena watched her move around as she studied her. 

     

                Pretending to sleep until Lillian walked out, Lena lay on her back and stared at the ceiling after she’d left, her whole body limp as she sank into the mattress. She didn’t even have the energy to sit up, to move, a certain blankness to her mind as she tried to stifle the pain, the memories, the accusing thoughts. There was so much anger in her that she felt like she was drowning in it, cold and consuming and bitter. It was a familiar companion and with the absence of Kara’s light and warmth, she descended back into that pit with open arms.

     

                Lillian returned a while later, Athena nosing into the room after her and jumping up onto the bed, snuffling at Lena’s cheek before she obediently lay beside her, while her mother fetched clean clothes and informed her she was going to go to the store with Eliza in a bit. She didn’t invite Lena to go with her, knowing it was a futile question, a laughable prospect, and went to shower a moment later, leaving her alone again.

     

                Studiously ignoring Lillian’s presence as she got ready, Lena nodded distractedly at her mother’s goodbye as she lay propped up on the pillows, staring up at the faint cracks in the corner of the bedroom ceiling. It was a mild day, the sky somewhat blue and no sign of rain yet, although the nearby roar of the ocean would likely have drowned it out anyway, and Lena was content to stay in bed, warm beneath the blankets as she scratched Athena behind her ears and dwelled.

     

                Kelly knocked on the door a minute later, poking her head inside to see if she wanted breakfast, and when Lena blankly shook her head she vanished again, leaving her alone. It didn’t take long for Alex to barge in, her brusquness shocking Lena as she blinked and sat up a little straighter, hand curled in the bristly fur of the dog.

     

                “Come on,” Alex said, dragging the blankets back and gesturing. “Get up.”

     

                “No.”

     

                “You are not sitting here all day, again ,” Alex snapped, pale and angry and trembling with the effort it took not to fall apart as she grabbed Lena’s arm and pulled. “Get up, Lena. Get the fuck out of bed.”

     

                “No.”

     

                Making a sound of annoyance at the back of her throat, Alex grit her teeth as she let Lena’s arm fall limply back to her side, curling her hands into fists as she shot her a venomous glare. “She asked me to look after you, okay?” Alex said, her voice cracking painfully, “and she wouldn’t-”

     

                Faltering, Alex looked aside, a muscle twitching in her jaw, before she inhaled sharply. “She wouldn’t want you to do this to yourself.”

     

                “I don’t care.”

     

                “Lena,” Alex snapped, “fucking look at me.”

     

                Eyes drifting up to look at her, Lena blinked slowly, an emptiness to her gaze as she looked at Alex and felt only exhaustion and sadness. That bitter anger welled up inside her and her lips twisted ruefully as she swallowed.

     

                “I look at you and all I see is her,” Lena rasped, looking out the window as she turned over onto her side. “I don’t want to look at you.”

     

                “Well … you’re not staying here. Get up.”

     

                “Leave me alone.”

     

                “Get up.”

     

                “Alex,” Kelly murmured a warning from the doorway, stepping inside as Alex pulled the blanket off her again, startling Athena, who climbed to her feet and jostled the mattress. 

     

                Climbing out of bed in a surprisingly fast display of movement - considering she’d been sluggish and unresponsive for almost two weeks now - a glower on her face as she bristled with pent up emotion, Lena stood before her, hands balled into fists and the cold anger inside her hardening.

     

                “Stop it,” Lena firmly murmured, blinking back the stinging in her eyes.

     

                “I won’t let you do this to yourself,” Alex said, shaking her head as she looked at Lena with mournful brown eyes, full of pity and stubborn determination. 

     

                Lena felt her chest cave in as her shoulders slumped and a breathless laugh escaped her, caustic and tired and spiteful as her stomach twisted, the anger inside her spilling over as her tight grip on it slipped. Letting out another laugh, a hitching sob of cold humour, she wiped at her pallid cheeks.

     

                Brushing past Alex, Lena hauled her bag onto the bed and started snagging things that belonged to her from around the room; her cherished letter, her phone charger, the pile of folded laundry. Shoving it all into her bed, Lena was tense with pent up anger.

     

                “What are you doing?” Alex demanded.

     

                “Leaving,” Lena ground out, shoving in her hairbrush and a pair of slippers.

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Alex frowned at her, “no, you’re not.”

     

                “I can’t stay here. I can’t stay in this house, in this town. I can’t move a fucking inch without being reminded of her.”

     

                “Neither can I!” Alex exclaimed before she was cut off by a choked up sob.

     

                “Yeah, so … I’m going home.”

                A faint smile graced Lena’s face as she smiled serenely, unbothered. Letting out a soft huff of laughter, she shook her head, fitting in the crumpled black dress from the day before. “Call me whatever you want. I don’t give a shit.”

     

                “You’re a fucking coward.”

     

                “I’m a coward?” Lena echoed, straightening up and turning around to face her as she let out a strangled laugh, tears on her cheeks and a bitter smile twisting her lips. “You shouldn’t have let her fucking join.” 

     

                The words were harsher than if she’d shouted them at Alex as they struck her, face rippling with shock and pain as her brown eyes filled with tears.

     

                Another sob escaped Lena and she dug the heels of her palms into her eyes as she cried, her anger so awful that she couldn’t stop herself as it all bubbled forth.                 “Why the fuck did you let her join? How could you let her go there? How could you-”

     

                “Alright, alright,” Kelly gently murmured, her fingers encircling Lena’s wrist and firmly pulling her away.

     

                Her fingers were stiffly clutching Alex’s shirt and it took her a moment, holding Alex at arm’s length, to let go, stumbling back a step as Kelly stepped in front of her.                 “Stop it. Both of you.”

     

                Turning around, Lena rubbed at her forehead and flinched slightly as the door loudly slammed a moment later. Kelly let out a heavy sigh and Lena closed her eyes, willing her to leave.

     

                “Are you okay?” she tersely asked, clearly pissed off.

     

                “Fine,” Lena rasped.

     

                The door softly opened and closed a moment later and Lena let out a pent up breath, dropping her hand from her face as she reared her head. Athena fussed around her, nosing her thigh, tail thumping her shins as she got in the way, and Lena quickly packed up the rest of her things and called a cab. While she waited, she booked a ticket on the next flight to National City and then restlessly paced back and forth the room until she heard wheels outside. 

     

                Hauling her bag off the bed, she patted her thigh for Athena to follow her and walked downstairs, still wearing her pyjamas, and shoved her feet into the discarded boots on the shoe rack inside the door. The yellow cab was braking near the top of the sloped driveway and Lena stormed down the front steps and made for the trunk as the driver climbed out. Handing her bag off to him, she opened the car door and ushered Athena into the back as the screen door slammed open a moment later.

     

                Cheeks flushed with anger and a slightly stunned look of surprise in her brown eyes, Alex stalked towards her. “You think you’re the only person who lost her? Y-you think that running away is going to help? You’re smarter than that, Lena. You might’ve lost the love of your life, but I just lost my sister . Fourteen years! I’ve known her for- for fourteen years . I’ve got to come to terms with the fact that my sister is never coming back and I’m still fucking here.”

     

                Balling her hands into fists, Lena clenched her teeth as she looked at her. “Then go back inside!

     

                Alex opened her mouth to argue and Lena made a cutting motion back to the white clapboard house nestled beside the ocean as resentment spread through her. Feeling hot and lightheaded, a cold sweat covering her as she trembled and fought to rein in her anger, Lena gestured at the house and her voice broke as she spoke.

     

                “Go back inside with your mom and your fiancée and leave me alone.”

     

                Alex let out a scathing laugh of disbelief, her eyes harbouring wounded feelings and a little scorn as she gave Lena a crooked smile. “You know, she would hate the person you’ve become.”

     

                “Yeah, well, she’s fucking dead, Alex,” Lena said with a hollow laugh, spreading her hands out wide as she shrugged. “She’s not coming back.”

     

                The driver was back behind the wheel, awkwardly staring ahead as he patiently waited, but Lena didn’t wait for a response as she climbed into the back and pulled the door shut behind her. Tears blurred her vision and she drew in a shuddering breath, fingers fumbling with the buckle of the seatbelt before it clicked into place, and then she leaned her head back against the worn headrest and waited.

     

                They were hours from the nearest public airport and Lena’s phone rang non-strop in her pocket, until she turned it off, letting the motion of the cab lull her into a stupor. She had forty minutes to kill before her flight left so Lena bought a bitter coffee at a small kiosk and sat at a sticky table, Athena beside her chair, and sipped the caustic fluid without tasting it as she waited until they started boarding at her gate thirty minutes later.

     

                Handing over her ticket at the gate, she was given sceptical looks as they took in her attire and awful appearance and glanced back down at the First Class booking before slowly allowing her on the plane.                 Gathering her things, she blearily made her way off the plane and got her luggage from the carousel before walking Athena out into the muggy March air of National City.                 Fishing out a handful of bills from her bag, she handed them to the driver and then fetched her bag from the trunk. Walking over to the steps of the stoop, Lena stood at the bottom and stared up at the locked front door. At one point she’d set her bag down and crossed her arms over her chest, a cool breeze snagging at her pyjamas and unkempt hair. If any neighbours saw her, they didn’t approach or ask if she was alright, and eventually, Lena fished her car keys out of her bag and unlocked the Porsche, climbing into the passenger seat with her bag in the back and Athena beside it.

As the sky darkened around her, Lena’s eyelids grew heavier and her body relaxed into the seats, the quiet street beyond the confines of the car still and peaceful. 

     

                She startled away sometime in the early hours of the morning, dawn not too far off by the faint lightening of the sky, by a sharp rap on the passenger side window.                 “Are you coming inside?”

     

                Tears welled up in Lena’s eyes, a lump getting stuck in her throat as she shook her head and then inhaled, a long shuddering breath before exhaling fully, slumping in her seat. “No.”

     

                “Why not?”

     

                Bottom lip wobbling as a shaky hollowness in her stomach made her feel weak, Lena gestured vaguely. “I-”

     

                She faltered, sniffing as she rubbed at her eyes. “I can’t go back inside that house,” Lena tearfully confessed, “I can’t even walk through that front door.”

     

                Shutting the car door, Lillian rounded the bonnet and opened the passenger side, gently pushing Athena’s muzzle aside as she tried to lick her cheek, and shut the door behind her. Sitting beside her in silence, Lillian waited patiently while Lena balled her hands up in her lap, brimming with pent up tension.

     

                “Eating dinner without her? It doesn’t feel right. Laying in bed? We slept there every night. Taking a shower when all of her things are still there? I can’t even listen to music anymore because … all I think of is her. She was my life.”

     

                “Can I ask you something?” Lillian asked after a long bout of silence. Lena looked up at her, a gentle look of curiosity on her face. “Why her? I never understood- I mean … I never asked what it was …”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena wiped her cheeks on the cuff of her sweatshirt, a rueful smile curling her lips as her eyes softened with longing, love and pain. “She talked too much; it made me laugh. She just- she didn’t make me feel so alone. And now I …”

     

                “I know,” Lillian softly murmured, reaching out to take one of Lena’s cold hands in her own as she gave her a tender look of pity.

     

                “I just- I don’t know how to make it stop.”

     

                “The truth is, you never really stop loving someone. You just … you learn to live without them.”

    Chapter 67

                It took Lena until the sun was fully up to allow her mom to coax her from her car and into the dark house. The key shook in her hand as she fitted it into the lock and opened it, the yawning silence and emptiness feeling foreboding, and she had to stand on the threshold for another ten minutes, Lillian standing behind her, exercising her patience until Lena took that first step over the lip of the door. 

     

                Slowly setting her bag down on the bench in the foyer, Lena kicked off her shoes and moved through the house, switching on lights as Lillian trailed after her. Standing in the middle of the open kitchen and dining room, Lena was dimly aware of her mom using the coffee machine, the rattle of biscuits in the dog bowl and running water, the back door letting in a gust of fresh air to sweep away the staleness of the untouched house. It was pristine, Eve having been there in her absence, but it didn’t feel like home .

     

                Shooed upstairs to shower and changed into something clean, Lena came back down to a cup of black coffee and her mom staring into an empty fridge. Sipping her coffee as she cradled the cup and let the heat seep into her cold fingers, she felt the tiniest bit better, soft-skinned and pink-cheeked and clean. While she sipped her coffee, Lillian sat before her laptop and put in a grocery order to be delivered before she shepherded Lena into the front living room.

     

                “How about we play chess?” she suggested.

     

                Shrugging, Lena flopped down on the sofa, in front of the black pieces, and let her mom make the first move. It was the most engagement she’d shown in an activity in two weeks but she still lost the first game, and then the second and third. Under normal circumstances her mom would’ve chastised her for not putting in enough effort, for not running through sequences ahead of time or thinking a move through, but Lillian seemed pleased that she was at least making the effort to do something. They played for a couple of hours, until the groceries were delivered and Lillian went to put it all away. Lena helped, silently shoving lettuce and zucchinis and carrots into the correct spots, dimly wondering what her mom was going to do with them seeing as neither of them could cook.

     

                She heard her on the phone to Eliza a while after that as she watered the herbs in the garden, keeping her voice down while Lena made herself another cup of coffee and tried to eavesdrop. Guilt ate away at her, embarrassment flushing her pallid cheeks pink as she shifted from foot to foot, but she was too proud to even mention it to her mother and quickly vanished up to her office after that.

     

                Pacing the length of the brownstone as she nursed her coffee, Lena ran her fingertips along the spines of the books lining the shelves and came to a sudden stop as she hit the thick spine of a battered paperback. It was the first book that Kara had ever lent her, the pages fuzzy with Kara’s tears, quotes highlighted in neon yellow and the corners dog-eared. Lena had kept the movie tickets from their first date to see Pride and Prejudice inside it, tucked away somewhere safe and meaningful, a first within another first, and it gave her pause as she stared at it. The irrational side of her grief wanted to take the book and tear it in half but the rest of her wanted to cradle it in her trembling hands and let her own tears soak into the ink, blurring it some more with her own heartbreak.

     

                Scrubbing a hand over her face, Lena walked over to her desk and flopped down onto the seat, purposely avoiding looking at the framed photo of Kara on her desk as she reached out and set it face-down, knowing her resolve to keep it together for the rest of the day would fail abysmally if she looked. Opening the desk drawer, Lena stared impassively down at the collection of envelopes nestled in there, months worth, a relationship worth. There was one more to add to it - the last one - but that could wait for another day.

     

                Sitting there, staring at the pile of letters and knowing there wouldn’t be anymore, Lena wished for one more. Just one more letter. Maybe also one more breakfast, one more lunch and one more dinner. One more hug, one more kiss and the sound of her laughter just once more. Waking up beside her once more, and going to bed beside her at night. One more day. She wanted one more of everything, enough to make that moment suspend indefinitely so she would never have to get to the point where she said goodbye, where she had to let Kara go. Again, just more time. Just one more time.

     

                The days started to blur together after that, two weeks bleeding into three, but Lillian dragged Lena out of bed each morning to shower and change into clean pyjamas, plying her with food and sitting her down to play chess. She ignored phone calls from Kelly and Eliza, and on the fourth day after returning to National City, Lillian had a meeting with Sam to discuss the future management of the business, leaving Lena alone for a change. She hadn’t truly been alone in two and a half weeks and she seized the opportunity to drown her sorrows in the hopes it would take the edge off her pain. 

     

                She quickly descended into tipsiness, her lack of appetite, the pounds carved off her and her lack of drink over the past few weeks leaving her easily susceptible to the whisky as she drained glass after glass, wandering through her house like a ghost. And then came the drunken destructiveness as she broke down, awful hitching sobs that wouldn’t stop as she found herself confronted with memories of Kara. She tore the sheets from the bed and her clothes off their hangers, smashed photo frames with the photos still in them, unsteadily walking over shards of glass as she moved on like a whirlwind intent of bringing the house down. She avoided the attic where Athena was sprawled in a pale patch of sunlight, sleeping. The records came next, vinyls snapping in her hands as she broke each one that reminded her of Kara and nights spent listening to the music, a heavy marble bust shattering the fllatscreen TV where she’d shown her movies for the first time.

     

                And then the numbness settled in and the silent crying, and Lena put on the Florence + The Machine album bought for her by Alex and Kelly, turning it up as loud as possible, until it filled the house and she made for the pantry and the alcohol stored there. Opening a bottle of beer, she took a swig and then smashed it against the floor, a shout escaping her as her chest heaved with the exertion. Lukewarm beer splattered her feet and the hem of her pants and Lena reached for another one, repeating it as her mind grew fuzzy and her movements even clumsier.

     

                That was how Kelly found her fifteen minutes later, standing in a puddle of sour beer as she quietly cried and drank and destroyed. The must was so loud that she didn’t hear her come inside, not until the volume drastically dropped and she closed her eyes, exhaling sharply as a stab of irritation flashed through her. 

     

                “Hey,” Kelly softly called out as she stepped through the open doorway, pulling her handbag from her shoulder and slowly setting it on the floor as she warily eyed the scene before her. “What’re you doing?”

     

                Shrugging, Lena took a sip of the partially filled bottle of vodka she’d migrated onto and then dropped it. Letting out a squawk of surprise, Kelly took a step forward, reaching out her hands as if to keep her in check.

     

                “Hey, I think you’ve had enough.”

     

                “What are you doing here?”

     

                “Your mom said she had to go to L-Corp. She asked me to come around.”

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena bluntly replied. “I don’t need a babysitter.”

     

                Stepping over broken glass, her pants soaked through at the hem and no wince of pain marring her slack, pink-cheeked face as she moved towards the pantry, Lena fetched another bottle. With a soft sigh, Kelly shed her coat and picked her way across the kitchen and the spreading pool of alcohol, the smell stomach-turningly pungent.

     

                “Alright, well … I’ll help then.”

     

                She prised the half-empty bottle of tequila from Lena’s grasp and dropped it to the floor, vodka splashing over their feet. Lena looked down at it then up at Kelly and blinked for fetching another bottle from the cupboard. Twisting off the botte cap, she dropped it and took a long drink of beer before letting it fall from her fingers, while Kelly fetched another one and handed it off. After a few minutes of music in the background and Lena smashing bottles with Kelly, her friend handed her another bottle and glanced sideways.

     

                “You know, you kind of crossed the line the other day.”

     

                Drawing in a hitching sob, Lena’s shoulders slumped and her chin dimpled as she pouted, trying to stop the trembling in her lips. “I know, I just- I’m so … angry. And there’s no one to take it out on and she was just … there. ”

     

                “I know.”

     

                Wiping at her damp eyes, Lena sniffed. “I didn’t mean it; I’m sorry.” 

     

                “You don’t have to apologise to me.”

     

                “I don’t know how to call her.”

     

                Nodding, Kelly pressed her lips into a flat line. “Answering the phone might help.”

     

                Lena let out a strangled laugh as her breath hitched in her chest, and ducked her head in agreement. Pausing for a moment, Kelly cocked her head to the side, “shall we do the wine next?”

     

                Nodding, Lena watched her pull two unopened bottles from the rack. Holding out a bottle of Pinot Noir, Kelly gave her an expectant look while Lena looked down at the label pasted onto the green glass.

     

                “I paid four thousand dollars for that bottle,” Lena rasped, pushing Kelly’s hand aside. “You drink it.”

     

                Nodding, Kelly held out the other one - a Sauvignon Blanc - and raised an eyebrow. “This one?”

     

                “Forty dollars,” Lena sniffed, taking it and wrenching the cork free before she took a sip and handed it off to Kelly.

     

                Drinking from it, Kelly nodded in pleasant surprise. “This is a good one.”

     

                “Yeah.”

     

                “Seems like a waste.”

     

                Nodding, Lena took the bottle back and drank deeply before handing it back to Kelly again. A hitching sob built up in her chest and she struggled to catch her breath for a moment. Studying her as she silently drank from the bottle of wine, a look of sad understanding in her dark eyes, Kelly softly cleared her throat as she lowered the bottle.

     

                “Going to be a big mess to clean up,” Kelly commented. “And your feet too. Good thing your mom’s a doctor.”

     

                Lips twisting ruefully as she stood amidst the broken glass and the alcohol, the smell nauseating and her stomach churning uncomfortably, Lena suddenly turned and tripped towards the sink, vomiting up all of the alcohol she’d drunk. It was bitter and caustic as it burned its way back up and she let out a breathless sob, feeling gentle fingers gather her hair up a moment later.

     

                Dissolving into fresh sobs, Lena gripped the edge of the sink and let her tears drip into the basin as she hunched over, feeling like her knees would give out beneath her if she let go. Vision swimming and the dizzying sensation of being drunk and disoriented made her feel even worse, not better as she’d hoped, and Kelly was kinder than she deserved.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “It’s okay.”

     

                “It’s not okay,” Lena exclaimed, her voice scratchy and cracking as her shoulders shook. “What part of this is okay?”

     

                “Trust me, I know how you feel - I know this feeling better than anyone . You don’t have to tell me what this feels like.”

     

                A mewling cry fell from Lena’s trembling lips as she shook her head, “but you have Alex.”

     

                “And it took a long fucking time to get to that point, Lena,” Kelly whispered, hugging her from behind and resting her cheek against her shoulder as she held her while she cried over the sink. “A long, long time. It’s not going to be easy; it’s going to hurt like hell, and you’ll never get over it, you’ll just- you’ll grow around it.”

     

                “I can’t-” Lena exhaled sharply, “I just don’t know how I’ll ever be okay again without her. I wake up and I … just for a second , I forget. And then I remember. Oh , I remember, and it’s like … hearing it for the first time all over again. Every time. Except it never stops.”

     

                Pulling her away from the sink, Kelly led her around the large pool of liquid and over to one of the dining chairs. Wracked with tremors, Lena heavily sat on the chair and let Kelly pull the sodden pants off her, clucking her tongue with exasperation as she dropped them in a wet pile and then turned towards the kitchen.

     

                Fetching the broom and the bin, she crouched down and started picking up the bigger pieces of glass, bottles that hadn’t fully broken and shards that had remained intact. Climbing to her feet and wiping her face, Lena walked over to her and sank down to her knees beside her, picking up pieces with shaking fingers as she worked quickly, guilt creeping up on her.

     

                “I’ll do it,” she whispered.

     

                “I’ll help,” Kelly gently informed her. “That’s what family does.”

     

                It was no use arguing that they weren’t much of a family anymore without Kara, no matter how much she loved Kelly, and so Lena just nodded and kept on cleaning up. Once all the big shards of glass were in the trash, she pulled out the mop and bucket and started soaking up the alcohol under Kelly’s guidance, while the other woman swept up the smaller pieces. They didn’t mention the faint smears of blood Lena’s feet left behind as they cleaned, and soon enough the odour of alcohol had been obliterated by the acetic smell of bleach, sharp in the nose as Lena mopped up the last bit of alcohol. 

     

                With the back door open to let the floor dry fast, Lena showered in the downstairs bathroom and donned a fluffy robe afterwards before taking a seat in the kitchen. Kelly had made green tea and offered Lena some painkillers and a pint of water to try and stave off the effects of too much alcohol, although Lena supposed vomiting up most of it would have helped. Looking grey and spent, she sipped her tea and was kept company by Kelly, neither of them speaking, until Lillian came home.

     

                She paused in the hallway before stepping into the kitchen, her nose wrinkling slightly at the smell of bleach and lingering sourness of liquor, before her eyes landed on Lena, dressed in a robe with her dark hair damp around her shoulders. Lena looked at her mom as guilt and embarrassment flooded her grey face with colour, her cheeks blotchy and her eyes bloodshot.

     

                Lillian made for her but was cut off by Kelly, the two of them having a hushed conversation before her mother sighed and vanished for a moment. Returning with a heavy medical bag in tow, she knelt before Lena and grabbed one of her feet, furrowing her brows as she peered at the cut soles. Shaking her head, Lillian rummaged around in her bag and started removing certain items, until she had a neat row of supplies set on a pristine metal tray. 

     

                Lena didn’t so much as wince as her mother use tweezers to pry little shards of glass from where they’d been lodged deep into the gouges, the antiseptic sting nothing to the painful emptiness inside her. Her mother probably wouldn’t have even needed to numb the area with a small needle to stitch the deeper cuts closed - Lena wouldn’t have felt a thing anyway.

     

                Afterwards, on bandaged feet, she walked into the living room and surveyed the damage with a detached appraising stare before going to make tea for everyone and then returning with trash bags to shove fragments of vinyl into. As wasteful as it felt, as poignant as it made her feel to toss out the broken records she’d listened to with Kara, Lena couldn’t bring herself to regret it because she would never have been able to listen to them again and never would have been able to willingly get rid of them. She imagined there would be a lot of clutter in her house she couldn’t let go of but couldn’t stand to look at in the coming days.

     

                Lillian and Kelly left her to it, standing in the kitchen with their cups of tea as they spoke quietly, the conversation slowly growing audible to Lena’s ears as their exasperation and helplessness made them forget to stay quiet enough for her to remain clueless.

     

                “I think it would be for the best if I took her back to Metropolis with me.”

     

                “I know you think she needs to get away from here, but it won’t help, Lillian,” Kelly frustratedly dissuaded her. “I know how she feels about that house; she’ll regress even further back into the person she was when she lived there. Now isn’t a good time for that, on top of everything else.”

     

                “Look at her!”

     

                “I know. The healthiest thing for her now is to process her grief properly, though. She can’t just move to the other side of the country and hope it changes things.”

     

                “She moved here and it changed everything.”

     

                “And that was because of Kara . Sure, she put in the work, but she won’t do that if you take her back there. She’s not going to process it.”

     

                “I don’t know what else to do.”

     

                “I know that and I can see that you want what’s best for her, but please trust me. This is my job; I know what I’m talking about and taking her back to a place with so much trauma attached to it isn’t going to help her overcome this new trauma she’s experiencing. It’ll just add to it.”

     

                Swallowing as she closed her eyes, Lena held the trash bag in a white-knuckled grip and then slowly set it down. She was quiet as she picked up her tea and slipped out into the hall, bandaged feet silent on the wooden floorboards as she dodged the creaky steps and made her way up to her room. Slipping into her bedroom and easing the door shut, she climbed into bed and lay on a mound of pillows as she sipped her lukewarm tea and brooded over the conversation she’d overheard. The truth was that as much as she despised that estate in Metropolis, the empty rooms and sprawling warren of halls that had felt so lonely and bitter, it was preferable to the reminder of Kara and the future they were supposed to build in her brownstone bought as a fresh start.

     

                Eventually, she found herself curled up on her side, staring at the thin beam of sunlight slipping in through the crack in the curtains as they day dragged on around her. She expected someone to come and check on her at some point, so when the door opened and quietly closed and the mattress jostled beside her, she didn’t even stir. They’d leave after a few minutes of heavy silence and then she’d go back to the nothingness of her new life, nursing the slight hangover as her stomach roiled from the alcohol she hadn’t vomited up.

     

                “You asleep?”

     

                Lena’s eyes snapped open at the sound of Alex’s voice and she opened and closed her mouth soundlessly for a moment before swallowing and hoarsely replying. “No.”

     

                “You okay?”

     

                “No.”

     

                She was silent for a moment before she sighed listlessy and rolled onto her back, staring up at the ceiling. “I’m sorry.”

     

                “I know.”

     

                “Really, I am. I just-”

     

                “I know,” Alex interrupted, laying a hand on Lena’s arm.

     

                Looking down at it, Lena’s reply was cut off as a jolt ran through her. Picking up Alex’s left hand, she studied her bare fingers and gave her an accusing look. “Your ring …”

     

                “It didn’t seem fair.”

     

                “To who?”

     

                “You.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena couldn’t bring herself to speak as her expression crumpled into one of bewildered discontent. Alex gently tugged her hand back and covered it with her right one, her throat bobbing as she swallowed thickly, staring up at the ceiling.

     

                Her lips twisted wryly as she let out a bitter laugh, “don’t worry, we’re still getting married. I just … took the ring off.”

     

                “Oh. Good. I thought-”
