                “Yeah. I just- I didn’t want to … rub it in.”

     

                Lena let out a surprised laugh, a rare smile gracing her face as she turned her head towards Alex and reached out to pat the back of her hand. “Put your ring back on.”

     

                Nodding, Alex exhaled as she sank into the mattress. Looking up to the ceiling again, Lena didn’t speak for a few minutes as they lay in companionable silence. After a pause, Lena let out a soft sigh and rubbed at her eyes.

     

                “I’m sorry I’ve been so selfish. I know I’m not the only one who … it’s just hard and-”

     

                “It’s okay, I know you’re upset. We’re just worried about you. Whatever you said … it doesn’t matter.”

      

                Shaking her head as she vehemently rejected Alex’s excuse, Lena closed her eyes and let out a shaky breath as tears stung her eyes. “It does . You’re my family; I can’t lose anyone else.”

     

                “Then stop trying to leave,” Alex said with a weak chuckle. 

     

                “My mom’s trying to take me back to Metropolis.”

     

                “Are you going to go?”

     

                Shrugging indifferently, Lena wiped at her eyes. “Wouldn’t make a difference either way.”

     

                “You wouldn’t have us.”

     

                “I’m not much up for talking anyway.”

     

                “Well … how about we just look then? It’ll be painful for a bit, but all those photos … there’s a lot of good in them. Maybe … seeing her again and remembering is better than talking anyway.”

     

                After a moment of hesitation, Lena nodded, “the album …”

     

                Alex knew exactly what it meant and stood up, searching for it in one of the drawers where it had been safely stowed away with a few reminders of Kara. This one was the hardest to face though, photos of her stuck to each page, many of them alongside Lena, happy and smiling and so alive . It was a stark contrast to the current reality of things and Lena dreaded it. Still, Lena knew she had to look, even if the fresh wave of pain would break her heart all over again.

     

                Fishing it out of the drawer and climbing back on the bed, Alex sat shoulder to shoulder with Lena and placed the album in her lap. Unmoving for a long minute, Lena gripped the photo album tightly, staring down at the cover as a lump lodged itself in her throat. After a while, she took a deep breath and opened it to the first page.

     

                The first one was of her, one of the least painful ones she’d be confronted with but still a twist in her heart at the memories associated with it, of her clueless nature of the future in store for her. Lena had been ignorant of the fact that she’d fall in love with the girl behind the camera, so swiftly and completely. The first time they came to a picture of Kara, Lena let out a loud sob, clapping a shaking hand to her mouth as she stared down at the familiar face, tanned and smiling, blue eyes creasing behind glasses as her freckled nose wrinkled endearingly. Alex made choked up soothing noises as she rubbed her arm, and Lena couldn’t bring herself to look at her, knowing that she was crying too.

     

                They spent an hour flipping through the pages of the photo album, and after a while, Lena started telling Alex the memory behind each photo that she hadn’t been there for. She needed someone to know what each photo meant to her, she needed someone to know that they had loved each other with every fibre of their being, and that love was captured in every photo in the album. By the time that they reached the last one, an age later, Lena had worn herself out from crying, and it all got swept up into the empty blank of her shattered pieces. And Lena was left with nothing but memories that would fade, but for now she could hold them close in the photos before her.

    Chapter 68

                The next day she woke to a sunrise she didn’t deserve. Staying perfectly still she looked up at the ceiling, painted violet by the light spilling in from the quiet street beyond the window. She searched herself for signs of pain, for the inevitable headache of too much alcohol, the stinging in her feet that the drugs and numbing needle had banished yesterday. All seemed calm and somewhat subdued, a cotton wool effect overtaking her sluggish form as she blinked slowly, still half asleep and lingering in the mournful happines of a dream. 

     

                Taking a deeper breath, Lena prepared her body to sit up, the ceiling slowly transforming to a soft blush of pink. It looked like it was going to be a good day, the clear kind with a fresh wind off the bay and the foothills visible through the faint haze of smog shrouding the city. It was the kind of day she would have spent with Kara, hiking through the heat and coming home to dinner out the back and saccharine cocktails, the coconut smell of sunscreen clinging to their skin as cicadas hummed around them.

     

                Instead, she climbed out of bed and showered, dressing in thin loungewear, the oatmeal colour washing her pale skin out made her way downstairs. Making a cup of coffee, she stood at the open back door and watched Athena sniff around, the day already balmy as it strayed towards spring. It seemed peaceful, yet heavy, and she listened to the sound of cars pass by and a muffled vacuum cleaner as she sipped her coffee, Kelly making herself breakfast in the kitchen as she quietly moved around.

     

                The sound of footsteps thundering downstairs disturbed the peace a moment later and Lena frowned as she turned around in the doorway, meeting Kelly’s eyes as she raised her eyebrows sceptically, knife raised from where she was smearing avocado over a piece of toast. Alex was breathing heavily as she ran into the room, pale and wide-eyed, looking wild and caged as she walked towards them, mouth opening and closing speechlessly.

                

                “I- they found her.”

     

                Lena flinched and turned around, shoulders taut as she pressed her lips together. She felt slightly nauseous as the thought of what remains they’d found - how much of her had been left for them to find? How small were the pieces? The empty coffin seemed easier than burying scraps.

     

                “I … don’t want to know,” Lena softly replied, shaking her head as she raised her cup to her lips with a shaking hand and took a sip. “Don’t tell me how much-”

     

                Alex let out a choked laugh of elation, the sound breathless and light as she bore down on Lena and grabbed her shoulder, turning her around and cupping her face in her hands. Shaking her as she laughed, brown eyes filled with tears, Alex smiled widely.

     

                “She’s alive, Lena. They found her alive.”

     

                Pulling herself free and stumbling backwards, out onto the deck, Lena blanched as her stomach twisted and her eyes filled with tears. She was overcome with anger as she turned around, trembling all over as she squeezed her eyes shut and clenched her teeth.

     

                “No, stop it. It’s not fair. She’s gone, Alex.”

     

                “She’s not. They just called my mom; she tried calling you but you didn’t answer. They’re saying it’s her; we have to go and confirm it.”

     

                The coffee cup fell from her limp fingers and smashed on the decking, espresso splattering her pants as she turned to Alex, face slack with disbelief as a reluctant kernel of hope sparked in her chest. “It- it’s her?”

     

                “They’re saying it’s her.”

     

                The breath gusted out of Lena as she let out a breathless laugh that was half a sob, covering her face in her hands as she bowed over, elbows digging into her thighs. She was still so heartbroken that the brief chance that it was Kara and not someone else wasn’t enough to dull the edge of the pain, but an all-encompassing longing consumed her as she straightened up, wiping at her eyes as she shook her head. 

     

                “We have to- to go,” she stammered, suddenly filled with more purpose than she’d had in weeks. “Where are they taking her?”

     

                “Germany. They-they send injured soldiers to some place in Germany.”

     

                “Landstuhl Regional Medical Center,” Kelly cut in, her breakfast abandoned.

     

                “I- the jet. I need to get the jet …”

     

                She was frantic but helpless, not sure where to start or what to do. Alex went to find Lillian while Lena ended up shoving the first pair of shoes she found on, a coat going over her loungewear and Athena’s bowl filled to the brim with the knowledge that Eve would take care of her while they were gone.

     

                Lillian was coming downstairs with a stricken look on her face a minute later, already dressed and polished as ever in her understated designer brands, looking pale and disbelieving as she folded the cashmere cardigan at the front and crossed her arms over it.

     

                “But … how?”

     

                “My mom never said,” Alex said as she shook her head and gestured helplessly.

     

                A grave look on her face, Lillian’s mouth thinned. “I’ll get my jet to fetch her; Lena-”

     

                “I’ll get mine ready. I just- keys, keys.”

     

                Kelly dropped a pair of car keys into her hands and Lena nodded, distracted and unravelling at the seams as the shock got to her. Lillian took Lena’s phone from the console near the front door and called the airstrip for her, her words brisk and commanding as they quickly filed out of the brownstone and into Lena’s Porsche. Kelly took the keys from her and slid behind the wheel while Lena sat in the back beside her mother, her rapid conversation with the airstrip sharp and demanding as it grew increasingly frustrating for her to organise. They had to make a stop to pick up passports and Alex puzzled through visas in the front seat as they headed out of the city.

     

                They’d been to the private airstrip numerous times so Kelly needed no guidance as they sped down roads, cut off traffic and Lena suspected got more than one ticket - not that she cared either way - and they were soon pulling up at the spacious hangar. The jet wasn’t on the runway yet and her mother was out of the car, bristling with anger and snapping at the helpless man, half a head shorter than her and quaking where he stood as he caught the brunt of her barrage of angry words.

     

                “How much do you want? Twenty thousand? Fifty? Name your price,” Lillian said, rummaging through her purse for her cheque book. 

     

                “I’m sorry, ma’am, there’s nothing I can do until the jet is charged and the airspace is clear for takeoff,” the man said, looking slightly taken aback.

     

                “Then I suggest you get the jet charged, clear the airspace for takeoff and get us on our way to Germany right now before I buy this airstrip and fire you myself,” Lillian snapped.

     

                He floundered for a moment before swallowing audibly and giving her a stiff nod. Pulling a phone from his pocket, he started speaking hurriedly into it as he walked across the tarmac. They had no luggage and within fifteen agonisingly long minutes they were boarding the jet and buckling themselves in, waiting for a pilot to show up and the last minute preparations to be completed. 

     

                It still took the better part of an hour and Lena was restless and impatient as each minute ticked by. The knowledge that Kara could possibly be alive was tormenting them as they waited on the jet, and Lena could only imagine how much worse it would be for Eliza, alone for the same journey. Still, it was agonising as they waited for takeoff, as they buckled their belts and felt the ground drop away, that nauseating sensation of flying heightened by Lena’s bone-deep panic at what she’d find at the other end of that flight.

     

                As soon as they were able to, Lena unbuckled herself and climbed to her feet, anxiously packing back and forth as she brimmed with nervous tension. Hands balled into fists and her throat achingly dry, she couldn’t swallow and could scarcely breathe as she walked the length of the jet.

     

                “Stop pacing,” Lillian interrupted after five minutes of it, giving her a weary look. “Sit.”

     

                Dropping down beside her on the long leather bench, Lena ran a hand through her hair and leaned forward, elbows on knees. “What if- what if it’s not her?” she whispered.

     

                She couldn’t bear the thought of being let down, and she was trying her hardest not to get her hopes up, but she’d been wishing more than anything that it had all been a mistake and this was her chance for her wish to come true. Somehow it all seemed too good to be true and she didn’t know what she’d do if she was struck with a second loss.

     

                “If it’s not … nothing’s changed,” Alex softly called across the aisle.

     

                “Why don’t you rest?” Lillian suggested, reaching for the soft blanket draped over the arm of the nearby seat.

     

                She shook it out and motioned for Lena to lay down before draping it over her. Closing her eyes and focusing on her breathing, Lena tried to calm herself down but she was too tense to sleep, her body was coursing with adrenaline and thoughts of Kara swirling around her mind. Was she dead or wasn’t she dead? 

     

                Taking slow, even breaths, Lena ran over the facts in her head, trying to remain logical and not let her hopes get in the way of this. They had a body – an alive one – clearly a woman, and they believed it was Kara. Was it the woman who had told them her name? Or were they making assumptions based on where they’d found her? If that was the case, then it was possible that it wasn’t Kara. They couldn’t have identified her without her ID tags, still on Lena’s nightstand in National City, or the name tag on Kara’s uniform. Which led to the question – what state was she in? How badly was she hurt? 

     

                She’d been missing for almost three weeks, but perhaps she’d been found a few days after the explosion and had been unconscious or incapable of telling them her name. There were too many variables and Lena tried to stay calm as she spent the flight going over and over each scenario. The best case scenario that Lena could think of was that Kara had been found safe and sound, by some miracle, and had identified herself when found. She didn’t want to entertain thoughts of the worst.

     

                The flight dragged on and everyone was mostly silent, the tension hanging thickly in the air. Lillian was taking it the best out of everyone, naturally, with her main concern being for her daughter’s wellbeing – not that she wasn’t hoping it was Kara, but her daughter was her main priority and she was worried what it would do to Lena if it wasn’t Kara. 

     

                Finally, after eleven hours of non-stop flying, fitful napping and picking at the gourmet spread of snacks prepared for them, they started their descent into Germany. They landed at the airport in Zweibrücken, a forty minutes from the medical center, and it took a frustrating length of time to clear customs, Lillian’s brusque, shoddy German failing to speed things along as they were frisked and scanned and eventually had their passports stamped. 

     

                Eliza was still in the air on Lillian’s jet but she’d given them the go ahead to go straight to the hospital. Hailing a cab outside, Kelly gave them the name of the medical center and they all strapped in, Lena finding herself increasingly agitated as her stomach swooped and her heart fluttered, a cold sweat covering her as she anxiously bit her fingernails. The miles seemed endless as the radio spouted German and time slowed.

     

                They were stopped at the entrance to Wilson Barracks, the base housing the medical center amidst wings of buildings surrounded by green fields and thick clusters of trees. American soldiers at the gate questioned Alex, who produced her ID and was verified, before the rest of them had to show ID as well, handing over passports and their names being communicated via the small security hut at the entrance. Lillian paid the cab driver and they all piled out, waiting outside for them to be granted access.

     

                They had to wait a while before they were cleared and military personnel could be spared to drive down and pick them up in a Jeep. Their uniforms instilled a sense of foreboding in Lena, seeming rigid and serious in comparison to Kara’s unkempt and smiling appearance after a long day on base. It sent a shiver through her and she couldn’t even bring herself to talk as they were driven down a long road to the medical center.

     

                Once they came to a stop, Lena climbed out of the Jeep and followed the soldier, staggering into the hospital as desperation overcame her, cracking her elbow on the sliding door. Pain seethed towards her fingertips but it didn’t slow her down. She had to find Kara. They were met by a doctor, her name instantly forgotten by Lena’s one-track mind, and she felt the panic inside her growing, spreading throughout her in a tingling numbness. It had been downgraded to a trauma center but it still held the stale antiseptic smell that permeated all hospitals, the lights harsh and humming overhead as they walked down a long hallway. Lena made herself tune into the doctor’s words as she fidgeted with her fingers before her.

     

                “She’s given her statement and we’ve personally identified her, but due to her being missing in action, we understand the urgency to confirm it for yourselves.”

     

                “Is she … okay?” Alex hesitantly asked.

     

                “She’s recovering well. Of course, it’s been some time since the accident, but the severity of her injuries are good, considering that.”

     

                Lena’s stomach jolted at the mention of injuries, wondering what state she would find her in as she felt the sting of bile at the back of her throat. Running a hand over her face, Lena doggedly carried on, following the doctor and the soldier escorting them, the place relatively quiet as the occasional nurse or doctor passed by, various military personnel walking the halls, some bandaged and others purposeful.

     

                “She’s in this room,” the doctor said as she stopped outside a closed door. 

     

                The doctor stepped back and the soldier took up position at rest across from the door, feet spread apart and arms clasped behind his back, while Lena pressed a trembling hand to her mouth, shaking her head as tears blurred her eyes. She’d been trying to get to Kara as quickly as possible but now that she was here she was afraid to open the door.

     

                “What if … what if it’s not …”

     

                Drawing in a deep breath, shuddering and painful, Alex, reached out for Lena’s hand and squeezed it reassuringly. “It’s okay. We’ll go in together.”

     

                The window looking into the room was shuttered with blinds, the soft glow of lamplight visible beyond, and Lena wondered if Kara was there. Just a dozen feet away. Should she feel it? She hadn’t felt the loss of her the moment it had happened, but she wasn’t sure if she could feel her now. She felt like she would know if it was her beyond that door, and perhaps she did, because it had never quite felt real - not for the eighteen long days without her - that she was gone.

     

                Nodding, Lena’s bottom lip wobbled as she reached out with a shaking hand and gripped the door handle, turning it slowly as the breath caught in her lungs. Her whole body was taut with anticipation, desperation seizing her as her heart pounded, and as she pushed the door open, Alex squeezed her hand.

     

                At the sound of the door opening, a blonde head turned towards them, blue eyes in a peeling and suntanned thin face creasing at the corners as trembling cracked lips stretched into a smile. It was a face as familiar to Lena’s as her own, but hollowed out and haunted, and still no less the same. Kara. Her Kara.

     

                Lena let out a strangled sound of relief, hoarse as it tore from her throat, her stomach lurching as her knees felt like they were going to give out beneath her. She sagged slightly on her feet, tripping over herself as she hurried towards the bed, hitching sobs wracking her as Kara shook on the bed with her own silent sobs, even as she smiled. Despite everything, she was smiling and it hit Lena like she’d been winded.

     

                Reaching out with shaking hands as she stood over her, Lena cupped Kara’s thin face in her hands, a ragged sob escaping her as tears slid down her cheeks and she bowed her head. “Kara,” she whispered.

     

                She’d refused to say her name since she’d been gone, too painful to hear and too painful to bear it coming from her own lips, but she said it then and the sound of it was so sweet that she felt as if her heart was going to burst out of her chest. She hardly dared to believe her own eyes as she gently thumbed a prominent cheekbone, speechless as she stared down at her, conscious of Alex at her side, similarly in shock.

     

                “Lena,” Kara rasped, her voice a wispy sigh or relief as her eyelids closed and a thin smile crossed her face. “Alex.”

     

                Knees giving out, Lena sank down, the edge of the hospital bed catching her as she grabbed a fistful of the hospital gown and buried her face in Kara’s chest. A heavy hand came down clumsily on her back, cradling her as Lena sobbed with relief.

     

                She was dimly aware of words exchanged between the sisters over her head, but all Lena could do was cry. Her mind was reeling and she felt like she was about to pass out, but the overwhelming reality of Kara pressed against her was the only thing she could focus on. A shaking hand came up to touch her face, the rough and calloused pads of fingertips lightly pressing to her cheeks, so unlike Kara’s that Lena felt disturbed by the feeling, but leant into it as she peered up, green eyes swimming with tears.

     

                “I’m sorry I’m late,” Kara whispered, a pucker forming between her brows. 

     

                She was listless and thin, looking exhausted and haggard from just laying in the hospital bed. Lena didn’t even want to imagine what the past three weeks had looked like for her, what she’d gone through to end up missing for so long and wound up in an American military hospital in Germany. Covering her hand with her own, Lena let out a hitching sob and turned to press a kiss to the rough palm.

     

                “You’re okay?”

     

                It was a silly question - what person would be okay in these circumstances? Even Lena wasn’t okay and she’d only had to live through the grief. Still, Kara let out a frayed laugh, blue eyes brimming with tears as she swallowed audibly, and Lena thought it was the most beautiful sound she’d ever heard.

     

                “I’m okay.”

     

                Staring at her in amazement, in disbelief and confusion and adoration, Lena let out a laugh that was more of a sob, tears wetting her cheeks and her lips trembling as stared at Kara, drinking in the sight of her like it was the first time. 

     

                “I love you,” she fiercely whispered, bewilderment creasing her face at the fact that she was saying those words to her again. Drawing in a breathless, shuddering sob, Lena shook her head. “I didn’t think I’d get to- I love you. I love you, I love you.”

     

                She cut off after that, shaking her head again as she pressed a hand to her mouth. It was a conflicting moment for her, Kara’s tired smile as she quietly cried at Lena’s words making her heart swell in her chest with so much love and happiness and gratitude, while the odd sensation of grief still clung to her like a miasma of despair. A moment of blindsiding relief couldn’t shake that lingering overwhelming sadness, that part of her that was still mourning Kara, had buried her, but here she was, alive and real and solid beneath Lena’s touch as she buried her face in the front of her hospital gown.

     

                “I love you too,” Kara whispered, her voice rasping and low, somewhat shocked at the fact that she was saying it as well, thick with emotion as she raised a hand, swiping her thumb across her eyes.

     

                Lena forced herself to take a step back, not wanting to be too overbearing, to monopolise her too much, and she forced down a deep breath, not straying more than a foot from the bed as Alex filled her spot, perching on the side of the bed as she held Kara’s hand, Kelly stepping in closer while Lillian lingered silently inside the closed door.

     

                “What the hell happened to you?” Alex quietly exclaimed, a torn look of confusion on her face as she shook her head.

     

                Lena was too afraid to ask that question, twisting her fingers anxiously as her eyes roamed Kara’s face. She was home, she was safe, but what she’d been through was written all over her body, most of it hidden beneath the bed. Lena was frightened to see what was underneath, what had been done to her, and it was shocking how frail she looked in the bed. Kara had never seemed fragile, but Lena was afraid to touch her, wouldn’t be able to touch her without handling her like spun glass. 

     

                “It’s … a long story,” Kara haltingly replied.

     

                Her voice broke, sending a stab of pity and panic through Lena, who had to use all of her self-control not to bear down on her and smother her in a hug and kiss her temple and stroke her hair. Drawing in a shuddering breath, Kara shook her head, her chin wobbling with the effort it took to hold a sob at bay.

     

                “I can’t- I’m sorry, I can’t … talk about it.”

     

                “Hey, it’s okay,” Lena murmured, stepping forward to touch her cheek. “You don’t have to say anything.”

     

                “Just rest now,” Alex urged her, “mom will be here soon.”

     

                Kara closed her eyes for a moment, taking a deep breath, and Lena leaned down to press a gentle kiss to her peeling forehead, gently touching hers to it as she hunched over Kara. One of her arms was heavily bandaged and numerous wires snaked over her thin form, hooked up to an IV or beeping monitors, clipped to her finger and elsewhere. Lena couldn’t stop taking it all in, her mind reeling as she stood beside Kara, too anxious to ever leave her side again.

     

                “You’re safe now,” Lena reassured her.

     

                “I’m home,” Kara murmured, a faint smile twitching her lips. “I kept my promise. Just a bit late.”

     

                Tears pricked Lena’s eyes anew and she choked on a laugh. “You did. Thank you.”

     

                “I kept … I kept thinking about how we’re getting married. I had to come home; I would’ve actually had to be- be dead not to. I’m sorry.”

     

                Stifling a sob, Lena wiped at her cheeks and blew the air out of her lungs as she straightened up, giving Kara an agonised look. “I didn’t think I was going to see you ever again.”

     

                And then all of her bottled up emotions, the numb part of her that had suppressed everything and cried numbly through the emptiness of Kara’s presence, came pouring out of her. Kara was safe and she was going to be okay and all of Lena’s fears faded to the back of her mind as adrenaline made her shake as she buried her face in her hands. She couldn’t stop herself from crying, feeling weak and lightheaded and giddy as she laughed and choked on sobs and slowly tried to rein in her composure. 

     

                “Sorry,” Lena sniffed, wiping her face on the sleeve of her coat.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Kara croaked, “I- I didn’t mean to- I put you throught hell. I know. You were all that kept me … going. I knew I couldn’t let you think that I …”

     

                “It’s okay. It’s okay. I love you; you’re here . I can’t- God , I just- it’ll all be okay now. Alright? You just … you rest and we’ll get you home.”

     

                Nodding, Kara pressed her lips into a bloodless line, swallowing a sob as she wiped at her face. They slowly were able to calm down, tears kept at bay as they made halting conversation, still reeling and drowning in their emotions, while Kara wasn’t quite so chatty as she’d been before, drugged up on painkillers and wrapped up in her own thoughts and memories of things they couldn’t comprehend. Drawing a seat up next to the bed, Lena sat beside her, holding her good hand and staring at her face as she lapsed into silence for the most part.

     

                Lillian had vanished after a brief few words with Kara, a sort of serenity in her mother’s composure as if the world had righted itself and she was pleased. She gave Lena’s shoulder a squeeze before slipping out and returned an hour later with Eliza and coffee. Holding the paper cup of caustic coffee, Lena was brought to tears by the sight of Kara reuniting with her mother and she took a sip and forced down the mouthful, the lump in her throat going down painfully. 

     

                It was still relatively early in the morning in Germany but they were on National City time and Lena found herself flagging, strung out by the flight and the emotional turmoil of the day. But there was a bone-deep weary satisfaction as well, the nightmare coming to an end, seeming almost like a bad dream if it wasn’t for how drawn everyone was, how utterly spent from their grief and whatever horrors Kara had been through while missing.

     

                Eliza spoke to the doctors and one of the superior officers out in the hallway while Lena propped her cheek up in her hand and gazed at Kara, the soft limned golden light giving her a healthy glow, even as shadows pooled in what used to be full cheeks. The heart monitor was a steady reassuring beep in the background, a sound so sweet that Lena could have listened to it all day. Hunger eventually made itself known to Lena, her body sagging in the chair, but she was reluctant to move - not even to use the toilet.

     

                Eventually, Kelly went to go and get food for them all, falling into a reminiscent conversation with a soldier that escorted her. Alex was sitting on the foot of the bed while Kara dozed under the influence of strong painkillers. The silence was broken by the conversation between her and Alex.

     

                “It doesn’t feel real,” Lena murmured, wide-eyed and dazed as she stared at Kara’s face, unable to tear her eyes away, not even for a second. A part of her was afraid that if she turned away from her she’d disappear again.

                

                “I know. I never- we couldn’t have known.”

     

                “There were no signs … of course we would’ve thought- but we gave up on her. She dragged herself home and we didn’t even know she was alive.”

     

                “We can’t blame ourselves for that,” Alex firmly replied, “all the facts-”

     

                “Right.”

     

                The dog tags, the scattered remains of others, the absence of a body. It had all pointed towards Kara being completely obliterated by the air strike, turned into red mist, so of course they had assumed the worst. But it still hurt, still left a bitter taste in Lena’s mouth to think about what she’d endured while they were already burying her a week later. It broke her heart, and even more so to know that it was far from over just because she was safe and alive.

     

                They were silent for a moment as they watched her sleep and tears slid down Lena’s cheeks, quickly wiped away as she cleared her throat. Alex looked at her, expression softening with understanding.

     

                “You okay?”

     

                “Yeah, I just- I never thought I’d get to watch her sleep again.”

     

                The door opened a moment later, Kelly slipping in with bottles of water and packages sandwiches and snacks. Depositing it onto the wheeled tray over the end of Kara’s bed, she gave Alex a smile and touched her shoulder, Eliza sneaking in behind her and approaching the bed. Giving the machines and her daughter a once over to make sure she was okay, Eliza nodded in satisfaction and took one of the empty seats. 

     

                Kara came in and out of consciousness, groaning softly at one point as her eyes landed on Alex eating a sandwich - she was on a strict diet while they monitored her - which elicited a weak round of relieved laughter. The day dragged on and, eventually, Lillian left with talk of hotel rooms booked for everyone to use at their leisure, but it wasn’t until she was told that she had to leave that Lena reluctantly tore herself away from Kara. She would have fought them on it if it had been another hospital, not a military one, but she swallowed her objections, the hour already late enough, knowing that Kara needed her rest.     

     

                The last one out of the room, Lena hovered in the doorway for a moment longer, prolonging the last glimpse of Kara for the night, and she twisted her engagement ring around her finger as she took in the lamplit love of her life laid out in bed, fast asleep. It felt like a dream, one of the best kind, and Lena smiled softly, eyes shining with adoration even as her shoulders slumped with exhaustion. With a soft sigh, the tension bleeding out of her, she drank in the sight for a moment longer and then shut the door, content with the knowledge that she was finally safe, if not yet home.

    Chapter 69

                It was routine by that point. Another skirmish to report on, another drive through arid desert under a stretch of pale blue sky as they drove past husks of homes, through foothills and terrorised towns. The lull of the truck was almost enough to put her to sleep as she hugged her pack against her chest in the back, one of the soldiers driving them down a long and bumpy dirt road, bleached shrubs and yellowing grass scattered around them as a warm breeze blew in through the windows. Dust billowed behind them as the convoy roared past, out in the Sangin Province, the British staking their hold in the region with frequent skirmishes with rebels and civilians. 

     

                They’d been at it since dawn, the sky still purplish and a frigid edge to the morning breeze as they’d set out from the last base they’d been stationed at. The monotony of the drive was all too familiar to Kara and she closed her eyes to the brightness of the light, mind turning to thoughts of what this report will be about. They’d been briefed on the basics before leaving but Kara would have to parse through the information, coax more out of other soldiers as she liased, perhaps an eye witness or two and some offical, redacted documents to snatch a nugget of information from for the official piece. Mike was there with a sleek looking camera, far superior to the little film ones Kara used for her hobby, ready to take photos to document whatever they could find, while the other soldiers in the platoon were there for recon, for aid, for security or whatever else was required of them at the time.

     

                The drive took hours, until the heat inside the truck was suffocating with their layers and the burden of their equipment, sweat beading on Kara’s forehead beneath the brim of her helmet, and she pulled the worn photo of Lena out of the front pocket of her jacket, a tenderness to her face as she smoothed a gloved thumb over the image of her. 

     

                “Excited to be going home?”

     

                She glanced over at Mike and gave him a quick grin, “couldn’t come sooner.”

     

                “Well, I guess I’m the fool for signing up for more,” he said with a grudging smile, scratching at the prickle of overnight stubble shadowing his jaw. “You set a date yet? For the wedding, I mean.”

     

                “Not yet.”

     

                “You’d better get on that. Not very often a girl like that comes around, Danvers. You’ll be set for life.”

     

                Snorting, Kara elbowed him and shook her head as she pocketed the photo, “don’t be an ass.”

     

                He flashed her a smile and reached for the rubber drinking tube attached to his water bladder, taking a sip. Looking out the window, Kara watched the landscape pass by as her mind turned to thoughts of Lena, of marrying her, of just seeing her again. It wasn’t the same through the screen and there was a stomach-swooping sense of nervous excitement at the thought of seeing her again. And this time she’d never have to say goodbye again. Smiling softly to herself, Kara stared out at the bluish smudges of distant foothills as she rattled around in her seat.

     

                It was an eight hour car ride out, the Humvee’s roaring along the road as monotonous beige spread out, occasionally interspersed with pale green shrubs and trees. Kara was used to long car rides and managed to nap through some of it, the sun too warm on her and making her drowsy as they bumped along, clouds of white dust in their wake, and she was content to wait it out until it was time to do her job. That seemed to be most of being stationed overseas; waiting for something to do and trying to stay busy while you waited. Paperwork and cleaning seemed to be all she did most of the time, unless there was a story to be sought out, and then it was right back to the paperwork as she put it all into words for another press release, another junket, another headline for the news back home. 

     

                Eventually, they pulled up at a small town, armed soldiers climbing out of the massive trucks, locals shying away at the sight of them while the early afternoon heat beat down on them. It was searingly hot and Kara was sweating beneath her helmet as she shaded her eyes, a grave look on her face as she looked around. Everyone fell into their roles and she kicked up dust as she walked at Mike’s side while he fiddled with his camera, checking the settings while Kara pulled out a little notepad and a pen.

     

                They were quick and efficient, the other soldiers sweeping the area and sitting around eating lunch or trying to coax the locals near them in broken Pashto. One of them was particularly loud and confronting, kicking rocks towards a woman beating a rug outside, dust billowing from it in clouds as she nervously looked away.

     

                “O’Connor, quit it,” Tran, the Second Lieutenant, and platoon leader, softly called out, while Kara watched on with a pucker between her eyebrows as she wrote down something on her notepad about the sprawling town.

     

                Within the hour, she’d spoken to a couple of the British troops stationed in town, the slow drag of the Officer’s northern accent piecing the story together for her before she managed to find a local who spoke enough English to offer up a few words. She couldn’t help but wince, the sharp sting of guilt and pity inside her that she felt uncomfortable to feel, shifting awkwardly as she thanked the man and moved on.

     

                “Danvers, Matthews, let’s wrap it up. We’ve got a long drive back to base,” Tran called out, hefting his rifle with one arm as he waved them over. 

     

                Biting back a sigh, Kara pocketed her notepad, having enough factual information to cobble together the required report, and crossed the gritty road back to the Humvee’s. Mike followed at a slower pace, checking the small screen as he eyed his photos, while everyone else clambered into their seats, buckling in and resigning themselves to the long trip back. It almost seemed like a waste of everyone’s time, but they hadn’t run into any trouble and it saved most of them a day of manual labour at camp.

     

                In the back seat of the truck, as she was tossed from side to side, Kara scribbled down more notes, already stringing sentences together in illegible handwriting before she settled in for a late lunch and listened to Mike tell a story about this girl he’d gone on a date with before he’d been deployed. She tuned him out for the most part and it was a couple of hours later that they slowed to a stop. 

     

                “Why’re we stopping?” she asked, leaning forward to peer through the windscreen.

     

                They were at the rear of the convoy and it came over the comms a moment later. “We’re down an M6; DuBois has lost his rifle. Anyone got eyes on it in the truck?”

     

                Muttered curses ran through the soldiers packed in with them and Kara sat back with a sigh, fifteen minutes of idling resulting in them all soon finding themselves on the side of the road while each Humvee was checked, serial numbers matched to soldiers and subsequent orders to drive back to that middle of nowhere town in the foothills and find the misplaced rifle.

     

                It wasn’t the fire time it had happened, the base at Fort Rozz getting locked down because a Private had misplaced their weapon. Everyone on base made to stand outside in the boiling desert heat, under armed watch, while some Officer explained why a gun hadn’t been checked, why paperwork hadn’t been filed for it, ranks stripped away as they all sweltered in the heat or froze in the winter. This was one of many times and there was a general air of grumbling resentment at being forced to turn back, knowing their trip back to base would be delayed by four hours - at the very least.

     

                The drive back felt even longer and it took almost another hour to recover the rifle from the British, where a local had handed it in out of fear, before they were back on the road, delayed five hours. Tired and sweaty, uncomfortable in all of her layers as the sun sank lower on the horizon, Kara closed her eyes and tried to get some rest. 

     

                Ultimately, they came to a stop near one of the abandoned towns they’d come through on the way there. It was past midnight and everyone was cramped and exhausted, the drivers needing rest as much as any of them. The orders came from Lieutenant Tran and they all spilled out of their vehicles with relief, stretching out cramped muscles in the blackness of a moonless night, a cold wind coming in off the stretch of abandoned desert around them.

     

                “Someone get on comms with base and let them know our coordinates and situation. DuBois, O’Connor, get a fire started. Danvers, you’re in charge of shelter. I want this place scouted and secured in fifteen minutes. Lights out in an hour; we’ll be making an early start.”

     

                “Comms are down, sir. Must be the antenna - I’ll take a look at it but we’re probably still out of range.”

     

                It was a peaceful dusk, the burnt out hovel of a town offering a safe protection for them to eat dinner and bed down for the night away from prying eyes. A pile of dried out broken furniture and branches was used to start a fire outside one of the crumbling homes and they were a rowdy bunch as they laughed and joked, Kara laughing along as she ate her chicken curry, the packet still hot as she ravenously shovelled mouthfuls of food in. She was perched on a collapsed wall, the dilapidated roof of the building stretching above her as the abandoned house behind her lay piled with their packs.

     

                Finishing off her food, she went to have a drink from the water bladder in her pack, dusting off her palms on her knees as she took her trash with her. Perhaps it was fortunate that she’d gone into the next building, yards away from the bonfire, when the whistling sound of approaching missiles sounded over the raucous laughter and clamouring voices. It was too late to do anything by the time everyone else realised, the shout going up as rifles were readied and the others tried to run.

     

                If not for the ruins taking the brunt of the blast, Kara probably would have been obliterated along with them, but luck was on her side that night. As screams and shouts split the night, a dozen shoulders seeing their lives flash before their eyes, Kara watched with wide, horrified eyes, her face ashen with sickening resignation as she watched the first missile strike the ground in the middle of the street. She shut her eyes a moment before the inside of her eyelids was painted a fiery red, the blast of it physical as it tossed her back like a ragdoll, brick and first and rusted metal giving in. The sound of it was awful , a terrifying screeching that made her ears ring as she found herself dazed, facedown in the dirt, a heavy weight on her back and the coppery taste of blood in her mouth.

     

                Disoriented and slow, it took her minutes to move, her tongue feeling thick, her thoughts disconnected from her reality. It took great effort, tendons taut as she strained herself, to push up onto hands and knees, bricks and rubble and wooden beams shifting as she moved beneath the pile burying her, dust smearing her skin a ghastly white, pain blossoming all at once in white-hot patches. A pitiful whimper fell from Kara’s lips as her breath gusted in the small space between her face and the ground, dust motes breathed in as blood and sweat trickled over her face.

     

                Another blast a moment later flattened her again, more rubble shifting over her as her breaths game quick and panicked as she squeezed her eyes shut, trembling all over. After a few minutes, she managed to dig herself out, bare hands cut and bleeding and shaking terribly as she crawled over the pile of the collapsed building, finding herself alone in the flattened and ruined town, the acrid smell of smoke filling the air as she peered through the dark, blind and lost. The heavily armoured trucks had been demolished, blackened metal remains flickering dangerously with orange flames, and if she’d had the light to see by she would’ve seen the mangled remains of what few comrades hadn’t disintegrated to nothing. As it was she could smell the tang of blood in the air.

     

                “Hello?” she called out, coughing as she buried her nose in her ragged sleeve.

     

                “Danvers?” came the far off reply.

     

                “Who is it?”

     

                “It’s Matthews. I … I need help. Over here.”

     

                Blindly stumbling through the dark, tripping over the remains of a wall, she staggered towards the voice, heavy breathing becoming louder and the low murmur of a panicked voice making her feel weak with relief. She wasn’t alone; someone else would be there to get them through it. 

     

                The shadowed figure loomed out of the darkness so suddenly that Kara pulled up short before she could trip over the kneeling person. Dropping to her knees, she glanced sideways at the blurred face of the man beside her, low visibility making it hard to see.

     

                “Mike?”

     

                “It’s DuBois. He’s hurt. I don’t know …”

     

                He trailed off and Kara leaned forward, taking in the sight of the soldier who had caused them to spend the night away from base. One of his legs had been blown off, a ragged mess of flesh and blood at the knee, and that was about all she could make out in the suffocating darkness of night. A breathless sob built up in her throat and she blinked as she tried to clear the sluggishness of her mind.

     

                “I- um, okay. Okay, okay, we need to move.”

     

                “What.”

     

                “Mike, we need to move. Now. They- they could send another strike any second.”

     

                He climbed to his feet, unbalanced and shaking, his face a pale blur as Kara pushed herself up too. “Our packs … shit. We need to get them or we won’t last a day.”

     

                “We don’t have time-“

     

                She was already moving, her heart pounding with fear at the thought of another one of those bombs falling on them. Her breath caught in her throat and she struggled to speak as she hurried away.

     

                “We’ll be dead either way. Stay with DuBois. Try and … get him away. Get clear.”

     

                “Kara,” Mike hissed after her before she vanished, back then way she’d come.

     

                With shaking hands, she scrabbled through rock and debris in the collapsed building, hoping to find a back. Anyone’s pack. It didn’t matter whose, they just needed water, they needed that more than anything, and the first aid kit they were all issued. She couldn’t feel her body yet, but even she knew they were all in bad shape.

     

                She finally closed a hand over something soft, heaving it out from under a portion of cement and brick. Tossing it behind her she fished around for more, dragging out five packs in total and hurrying to find a flashlight. It illuminated a small circle of dirt, and she was wary of being spotted, quick to take what was in three of them and shove it into the other two with haste.

     

                The packs were heavy and her knees buckled slightly beneath the weight of two, her breaths shallow and quick and pure adrenaline of fear making her lug them after her with any sort of speed. Sweat trickled down her face, cutting through dust and wetting drying blood, and Kara used the small flashlight to follow the scuffed path Mike had made as he dragged DuBois with him.

     

                Kara found them quickly and shoved a pack at him before helping to support the lifeless figure between them, dragging an arm over her shoulder as her ribs dimly protested. They were barely at the outskirts of town when another airstrike hit, billowing dust and searing flames, bits of shrapnel and tiny stones stinging their cheeks as they were brought to their knees by the trembling aftershocks. Coughing at the acrid smoke, Kara rasped an encouragement, dragging DuBois with her as Mike struggled to his feet.

     

                It all became a sort of daze after that, fear of death forcing them to put one foot before the other, even as they found themselves stumbling and lagging. Dawn was still hours away and yet they couldn’t stop, didn’t want to be within reach of the town when people came looking, ready to take them hostage or put a bullet in them. Kara wouldn’t have had the words to try and explain to them that she was just a war correspondent, writing about the political strife and horrors, that she wasn’t the one who was killing then, ousting them in the name of justice or harassing and intimidating them as if they were wrong for living there. Even if they weren’t found by rebels, no one would look kindly upon anyone in uniform. Not unless it was another soldier.

     

                “Matthews,” Kara eventually rasped, her throat parched and gritty dust covering her tongue as her sloped shoulders sagged.

     

                There was no response and she turned around to find him lagging behind, DuBois still draped over him as he towed the unconscious man along. The air rushed out of Kara’s lungs and she blearily blinked, eyes dry and sore, and wiped sweat off her brow.

     

                “We have to stop,” she said as she waited for him to catch up. “We need to get out of sight.”

     

                Mike nodded, or she thought he did, the night being too dark for her to see much. She forced them to continue, sharing the weight of the unconscious man once more as they staggered onwards. Feeling sick and faint, Kara knew she wouldn’t last much longer. They needed rest, they needed water and to eat something and assess their wounds. Beyond that, she had no idea what to do.

     

                Eventually, by complete accident, they came upon a rocky outcrop jutting from the relatively flat surrounding land. Dry grass rustled as their dragged feet passed over it, the ground sloping up slightly, and Kara tripped over the first small boulder, jarring her injuries and banging her chin on the packed ground. Spitting out blood, she climbed to her feet and risked the flashlight, illuminating a few jagged rocks, a dozen meters across and offering a narrow cave-like mouth where they had fallen against each other over time, shifting as sand and dirt had been worn away.

     

                Dawn was already starting to lighten the night to a deep shade of navy and Kara was shivering as she tripped over her feet in her haste to find shelter. The day would be hot and they wouldn’t last long exposed to the stretch of sky, injured and dehydrated. Shelter from the sun while they slept would be hard to come by, especially after driving through the expanse of nothingness for hours on end only the day before.

     

                She dropped the bag and shoved it in ahead of her, collapsing to the packed earth, a dampness to it that only added to the chill of the desert night, but she was just glad to have stopped. Mike had followed the thin beam of light and lowered DuBois to the ground while Kara hauled him in under his shoulders, before Mike followed after. It was an uncomfortably tight squeeze for the three of them and their bulging packs, and Kara and Mike shifted around, trying to get comfortable in the cramped lean-to the rocks offered.

     

                “We need to check him,” Mike said. 

     

                He was pale and panicky as he fumbled for the clasp of his backpack, desperate to find a first aid kit. There was a glazed look behind Kara’s scratched glasses as she stared down at DuBois, unmoving.

     

                “Kara. Don’t just sit there-“

     

                “He’s dead,” Kara hollowly replied.

     

                Mike looked as if she’d slapped him, shock crossing his face as he stopped rummaging through the pack of sunscreen and food and spare clothes, leaning forward to touch dirty fingers to DuBois’s throat. Kara knew he wouldn’t be able to find a pulse, and perhaps she’d known that the entire time they’d dragged him through the shapeless landscape, his blown off leg dripping blood in their wake even as it was quickly covered with sand and dirt by the blowing wind. He’d lost too much of it, hadn’t so much as stirred since they’d made it a mile out of that town, but they couldn’t just leave him there so Kara hadn’t said a word.

     

                “He can’t- but … we got him out.”

     

                Unclasping her helmet, Kara let it fall to the ground as she stretched out, feeling sick and empty, her body parched and spent. Closing her eyes, she knew she couldn’t sleep yet, not without tending to her own injuries, which were starting to make themselves known now that they’d stopped.

     

                “Get the first aid kit,” she murmured through numb lips.

     

                Mike stared at the slack face of the dead man for a long minute before he obeyed, coming up with one and handing it to Kara. It hurt to move as she reached up to unclip and remove things, unbuttoning and unhooking, until she’d shed the blood-soaked and dusty camo jacket to expose the khaki T-shirt underneath. The front of it had a dark stain and she caught the dull brightness of metal catching the light, trembling fingers pulling the T-shirt up to reveal a piece of metal rammed through the left side of her abdomen. It must have missed any vital organs because her abdomen didn’t feel rigid as she pressed down on it, but it was still tender, eliciting a hiss from her.

     

                Panting in the confines of the cave, her vision blacked and swam and she blinked sweat out of her eyes as Mike loomed before her. He was pushing her shoulder down and she fell back against the ground, wondering if she’d ever be able to get up again.

     

                “What do I do? Kara, tell me what I have to do.”

     

                “Leave it in,” she choked out, face twisting with pain as she tried to sit up, her ribs protesting where they must have been broken. “It’s- it’s staunching the … the bleeding.”

     

                “It’ll get infected-“

     

                “I’ll bleed out-“

     

                “Fuck. ”

     

                Still, she let him pack antiseptic wipes over it with a wad of gauze and then bandage it around her waist. There was nothing to do about her cracked ribs, or the fractured wrist that was sending stabbing pains up her arm. Her bleeding palms were quickly cleaned out as best as possible and wrapped too, before she made him take his gear off too. His left shoulder sloped unnaturally and she thought he’d dislocated it, wondering how much muscle damage had already been done from lugging a back and a dead man across the desert with it out of place.

     

                Kara knew it had to be reset but didn’t have the knowledge to do it, cursing herself for choosing journalism instead of medicine like the rest of her family. Still, she knew she had to try and was breathlessly sobbing apologies as Mike screamed, filling the small pace with his sounds of agony as she clumsily jerked his arm around until she thought she’d managed to put it back in. He screamed loud enough, at any rate. 

     

                After tying his arm to his chest in an effort to keep it still, using one of the spare shirts in the packs, Kara bandaged his other wounds, not liking the colour of some of the bruising on his back, or the depth of some of the cuts, but there wasn’t much she could do for either of them. All they could do now was sleep and reassess in the morning.

     

                “We should sleep.”

     

                “What if someone comes?”

     

                “We’ll be dead either way; we have no guns.”

     

                “Right,” Mike murmured, hesitating as his eyes cast down to DuBois. It was light enough for Kara to see the unease on his face. “What about him?”

     

                Looking at the dead man’s face, Kara’s stomach twisted. It took her a moment to speak. “Leave him there; we’ll have to bury him tomorrow.”

     

                If the thought of sleeping beside a dead man disturbed Mike, he didn’t voice it and Kara had to stamp down the queasy feeling as she stretched out as best as she could and covered herself with her jacket. Sleep came surprisingly fast, despite it all. Her mind needed the reprieve from the trauma they’d endured, the terror of the bombs, the mindless walk for hours, the numbness hiding her injuries from her and the shock of losing their entire platoon - aside from her and Mike.

     

                When she woke, her eyes were gritty and her tongue stuck to the roof of her mouth. It was swelteringly hot but the cool floor of the cave was a sweet mercy, despite the dry heat of the air. Sitting up, the edges of her vision dimming as her head pounded and the world pitched, Kara brushed damp hair back off her brow and glanced over at Mike. Not for one second did she think it had been a nightmare, but she woke up to one, the stiff body of DuBois lying a foot from her while her own body protested with blinding pain.

     

                She was afraid to leave the small cave with the sun up and hardly dared to move in case she antagonised her injuries. Across from her, Mike was fast asleep, stubble coating his jaw and a ruddy look to his cheeks. Yet, he was alive, and it was a bizarre comfort to Kara that someone who’d been beside her for awhile now, annoying and persistent, could be a comfort in the midst of such awfulness.

     

                The day dragged by in a haze of nothingness or pain, hours moving by slowly as Kara swam in and out of consciousness. Her mind was slow when she woke, her headache growing worse, until it was a physical pressure behind her eyes, pounding . It wasn’t until dusk, hours after she’d first awoken, that she managed to force herself to move.

     

                Fishing through one of the packs, she found water and took a conservative sip, conscious of their limited supply. She scrounged up painkillers and swallowed them with another sip, whetting her throat and unsticking her tongue from the roof of her mouth as she felt slightly more refreshed. She reckoned they had enough rations to last them almost three days more - longer if they stretched it out - but water worried her. The lack of a plan worried her more and Kara wanted to cry but couldn’t spare the tears, instead, taking the photo of Lena from the front jacket pocket and staring down at her face in the waning light slipping in.

     

                It started getting dark swiftly after the purplish hour of dusk, the shadows lengthening and the day cooling, and Mike still hadn’t stirred, although he murmured to himself in a feverish state. Kara crawled out of the cave and stretched, her bandages spotted with blood and her body violently objecting to the movements, but she couldn’t stay in there with DuBois any longer. His body hadn’t started to smell yet, and she couldn’t bury him well without a shovel, but Kara couldn’t stay in that cave with him.

     

                It took all of her strength to drag him out a few minutes later, stripping everything of worth from him - and his tags too, to identify him; she hadn’t realised her own were missing up until that moment, yanked from her neck at some point in the air strikes - and dragging him around to a shaded cluster of rocks, where she set about building a cairn. Kara silently prayed that no wild animals would be drawn to the smell of his rotting body, it’s else they’d have more to worry about than rebels finding them.

     

                Still, she knew that exposure was their worst enemy then, and crawled back into the shallow cave to lay down again. Mike’s skin was hot to touch as she checked on him, but there wasn’t much she could do except wait out the fever and hope he woke up. She’d be able to force painkillers down his throat then, be able to concoct a plan with someone else and decide how to split the food and water, but for now she’d have to wait.

     

                Waiting seemed torturous to her at that moment, thoughts of Lena and Alex and Eliza swimming through her head. Did they think she was dead? Were they worried about her? Did anyone even know she was missing yet? Comms had been down when they’d stopped for the night, and she wasn’t sure if they’d ever made contact with base to give them and update on their coordinates. The thought that no one would be looking for them made her stomach lurch with sickening dread.

     

                She ended up sleeping a while longer, the pitch black of night greeting her when she woke, shivering from the cold and slightly feverish as she wiped sweat from her brow. Mike was still unconscious and she wasn’t sure if he’d woken at all while she’d been out cold. A throbbing pain in her ankle had made itself known to her and Kara was certain it was broken, adrenaline blocking it from her over the course of their long trek, but there wasn’t much she could do about it. Her boot kept it from swelling so she was hesitant to remove it and resorted to taking more painkillers, a dent already put into their supply, before she swallowed a mouthful of water and woke Mike up.

     

                He was groggy and listless, eyes roving wildly through narrowed slits, and it was all Kara could do to make him swallow painkillers and drink as much water as she dared to give him. He’d passed out before having any when they’d found the gave so she gave him a bit more to replenish what he’d sweated out, although it wasn’t nearly enough, and then went to stretch her cramped muscles. It was so cold that she paced to keep warm, her ankle troubling her as she limped, and when she eventually crawled back inside she helped herself to an MRE, choosing the crackers and cheese spread out of the pack of food, eyeing up the rest of their rations. They’d been sent with three each - enough for a day’s worth of meals - and most of them had put a dent into the third by the time the bombs had hit. Still, between the four packs she’d dragged out, they had three servings of dinner, a variety of snacks, from Skittles to Tootsie Rolls, and spreads and powders for drinks that hadn’t been used up. It hadn’t been an arduous day of physical work, which they should have been grateful for, but Kara worried over how little they had to sustain them.

     

                Falling asleep again, it was bright when she woke, and already she was starting to lose track of time. There wasn’t much else to do though, and as Mike slept on, she joined him, sleeping through her hunger and thirst and waking at night again, taking sparing sips and shaking Mike away to eat a slice of bread slathered with peanut butter, shared between them both with a few sips of water each. He was still burning up and his face had taken on a greyish pallor, not too different from Kara’s own beneath the layer of grime. Neither of them had the energy to continue so they slept again.

     

                On the fourth day, she was almost delirious, her body consumed by pain that seemed to be everywhere, her skin hot to the touch and unable to bring herself to hardly move. She’d grown weaker over the past few days, that much was clear as she lay in the cave, already thinner and hollowed out, bad dreams plaguing her as she slept. But that evening, right as the sun was sinking low on the horizon, Kara jolted awake from a dream about Lena, a cold sweat covering her skin, her mind clearer than it had been in days, and a sudden urgency gripping her as her heart hammered in her chest. If they didn’t move, they’d die out there, and Kara had made a promise.

     

                “Matthews! Wake up,” Kara hissed, shaking Mike awake with as much gentleness as she could muster. “We have to go. We need to find help.”

     

                He looked at her through slitted eyes, his cracked lips parting as he drew in a shallow breath, his voice a grating sound as he replied. “Help? Where?”

     

                “We have to walk. They knew we were in town to meet with the British; they’ll find us there. Or the British will. They … they have to. I’m … I’m getting married.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, she was overcome with the urge to cry and stamped it down as she pushed her scratched glasses up her nose. It was enough to rouse Mike though, her orders evoking some ingrained response from years of service, of being told what to do, and within minutes they were both outside, burdened with the weight of their packs and staring up at the deep blue sky of dusk.

     

                Staring at the stars for a long minute, Kara picked the right direction and set off, limping and bowed, while Mike followed after her, just as worse for wear. They ended up walking all through the night, ten hours of putting one foot in front of the other, sometimes at a snail’s pace as they flagged beneath the effort, but they didn’t stop once. If one of them fell or stumbled, the other one dragged them back to their feet and onwards they went. The whole time, they passed nothing but ruins of the occasional house, clusters of rocks or a skeletal tree. Kara prayed a patrol would stumble upon them and save them the walk, but they were utterly alone.

     

                They slept in the abandoned house of a goat herder, the roof collapsed in and the wooden door banging from the wind, sand blowing through the gaps as they stretched out on the dirt floor, barely enough room for them both. The overhead sun was harsh and they were sunburnt as they slept, but when they woke later that afternoon, just shy of dusk as they day started cooling off, Kara found stagnant water in a clay pot and the two of them drank their fill, knowing they wouldn’t be so lucky again and only had a few litres between them both.

     

                Splitting a the packet of Tootsie Rolls from one pack, they chewed the taffy and let the sugar invigorate them slightly , before they dumped the Gatorade powder in the remaining water in the pot and split that. It was a rare treat but it didn’t last long and they were back to walking, Kara stumbling along, covninced they were heading the right way as she looked to the stars, while they took the easiest path presented to them, one foot in front of the other. She reckoned they had enough food for a few more days, and perhaps not enough water for that, but they kept on and on, walking all night and stopping during the day, taking whatever shade was offered to them as they slept.

     

                The only thing keeping her going was her family. She’d promised Lena she’d be home, she’d proposed to her, promised her they’d get married, and the thought of Lena waiting for her, not knowing where she was, if she was dead, was too much for her to bear. Lena, Lena, Lena. She ran through every thought of Kara’s. Her and Alex, Eliza and Kelly. They were all expecting her home, in a couple of days, and then that day, and then she was late. She wasn’t sure if her day’s were correct, each sunrise and sunset melting into the next, but surely the day had come and gone. It had been so long, so much walking and so many miles, the distant foothills coming closer and closer until they were within sight.

     

                She’d brought them too far north by that point, but ten days after the airstrike, they made it to a town. A town with people, a town with a handful of buildings along a dusty road through the middle, chickens pecking about the dirt and wide, fearful eyes watching them as they struggled in just past sunrise. It was the wrong town, but Kara felt weak with relief, her knees giving out as she fell hard to the packed earth, head swimming and mouth gritty and dry with sand. Mike keeled over beside her, completely unconscious, and Kara let out a small whimper as her eyes closed, blackness rushing in on her too. They hadn’t had a bite to eat for two days, and the water had gone the night before when they’d stopped. 

     

                Tongue wetting her cracked lips, she let out a soft breath, shoulders sagging with resignation. “Help.”

     

                And with that rasping croak of a plea, she slumped forwards and passed out, face-first in the dust. Unaware of anything else, Kara didn’t hear the ripple of muttered unease, was oblivious to the kind hands that came and carried them inside, the water trickled down her parched throat with a rag as a goat lay beside the cot she’d been set down on and Pashto flew back and forth over her head.

     

                She awoke three days later, unable to move, her eyelids heavy and her body unresponsive, a fever burning through her. A gentle voice fell on her ears but she couldn’t even speak, a bowl pressed to her lips as a cold, oily broth was poured into her mouth. She had no choice but to drink it, as limp as she was while a hand held her head up, she slept awhile longer before rising.

     

                Next time, she was alone and staggered to her feet, feeling hot and foggy, her head pounding, her skin hot to touch, although a quick inspection of her wounds found a poultice spread onto the one in her stomach, the metal removed and inflamed stitches holding it together, while her palms had been spread with a paste. Hobbling to the open door, she squinted at the harsh sunlight and stepped outside.

     

                The quiet chatter of the town quietened as a ripple of fear ran through the women gathered around the well, washing clothes, while a man smoking in the shade, gripped the walking stick nearby a little tighter. Pressing a hand to her head, Kara couldn’t even make herself take another step, and a brusque voice fell on her ringing ears a moment later before hands shooed her back inside, words incomprehensible to her but the meaning clear. She wasn’t sure whether it was for Kara’s safety or the town’s protection that they made her go back inside onto that cot, but it had been a bad idea to move anyway.

     

                She slipped in and out of consciousness for the rest of that day but came to, groggy and confused, to the harsh light of a torch shone in her eyes as she clumsily tried to throw a hand across her eyes. Words were being spoken but she couldn’t comprehend any of it, her mind slow and the fever making her delirious as she slumped back against the hard cot.

     

                “Lena,” she listlessly spoke, the sudden memory of a dream coming back to her, of a warm summer’s night in their bed, the stillness of the evening and the sound of cicadas a comfort as she’d lain there, swimming in the pleasant embrace of unconsciousness.

     

                “Is that your name?” a distinctly English voice asked, demanding and impatient.

     

                A frown furrowed Kara’s brow as she restlessly moved, her body heavy and largely unresponsive. She didn’t understand what was going on, wasn’t truly aware of the fact that an English woman was leaning over her, other soldiers outside and idling trucks waiting, rifles in hand and the villager who’d gone to fetch them wringing his hands nervously.

     

                “Can you tell me who you are?”

     

                “Kara.”

     

                “Kara who?”

     

                “Danvers.”

     

                “She’s an American,” the woman said, turning to the soldiers behind her. “I thought so from the gear. We need to take her; assume she’s gone AWOL until we can let the Americans know we have two of their own. They’ll identify them themselves.”

     

                A listless sigh fell from Kara’s lips before they moved soundlessly, eyes moving rapidly back and forth beneath her eyelids as her brow beaded with sweat. “Lena.”

     

                “Get them ready to move. Her and the man.”

     

                She was out cold again after that, although over the course of the night, she woke at intervals to the bumpiness of a road, dark shapes inside the back of a truck with her and words in English lost to her in her feverish state. From there was a base, a bed and doctors, all unfamiliar, from their accents to the snatches of uniforms she saw. They treated her while she was out of it, giving her antibiotics and morphine and keeping her under while they relayed the information to the US Military. 

     

                From there, it was a long wait, most of it a blur to Kara, who only got snatches of too-bright lights and indecipherable noises, under guard until she was turned over to the custody of her own people. It took hours for them to reach the base, to clear security and all the two soldiers to be transferred over to their custody, the ID tags around Mike’s neck confirming his identity for them, while the lack of hers left them in the dark for the time being.

     

                It wasn’t for another few days that Kara finally woke, the fluorescents overhead seeming too bright, her body feeling strung out and weak as she listened to the beeping of monitors and groaned softly. Squeezing her eyes shut, she exhaled heavily through her nose and tried to feel her fingers and toes, her body so heavy and numb to her that she felt as if she was floating, so far above mortal pain that she felt nothing.

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                Forcing her eyes to open, Kara stared at the woman at her bedside. Blinking sluggishly, she looked around, taking in the apparent hospital room, the wires snaking all over her and the hospital gown she was wearing. The last thing she remembered was that town, and only that was vague, a snatch here and there of being awake. Fear made Kara’s skin prickle as her heart rate spiked on the monitor at the uneasiness of finding herself somewhere she had no recollection of getting to.

     

                “I’m Doctor Grace Parker. Trauma Surgeon with the US Military.”

     

                Kara suddenly went weak, the tension bleeding out of her as she went limp on the bed, tears stinging her eyes as a breath hitched in her throat, which was aching painfully. “I’m safe?”

     

                “Yes, ma’am. You gave us quite a fright though,” Doctor Parker said, giving her a thin smile as she scribbled something down on the clipboard.

     

                “How long have I been here?” Kara rasped, rubbing at her forehead, feeling out of it.

     

                “Four days.”

     

                “I … need to get- I’m supposed to be home. I’m- I’m late-”

     

                She was trying to rush but couldn’t make her body respond, fumbling with the wires, the cannula and the heart rate monitor, but didn’t get very far as Grace pushed her down by her shoulder, a grave look on her face.

     

                “I need you to stay where you are, okay? You were in a medically induced coma. You came around slowly - you might not remember it - but you’ve been under since you got here. Your throat must be hurting.”

     

                “No, you don’t understand- my fiancée … she thinks I’m dead.”

     

                “Your family is being notified as we speak. They’ll be here as soon as they can get on a plane.”

     

                Kara knew that wouldn’t be long, an abundance of private jets available to whisk Lena across the world at her whim. The only question was where was she, and how long would it be until she saw Lena and her family again?

     

                “Where are we?”

     

                “Germany. At the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “They’ll want to speak to you soon. Verify some things. I’ll have to clear you first; your injuries were numerous. You’re lucky to be alive.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Kara inhaled deeply, a shaky feeling inside her as her mind struggled to catch up with her body. It didn’t feel real and there was that feeling of dread that she’d carried with her for almost three weeks now that still lingered. Was she safe? It didn’t feel like a dream but it didn’t mean that she was in the clear now.

     

                “Perforated abdomen. Lacerations to the skin. Broken ankle, sprained wrist, multiple fractured ribs. Contusions on the skull. Second degree burns to ten percent of your body, as well as severe hydration and malnourishment. What the hell happened to you?”

     

                Tears made her eyes smart and she sniffed, turning her head aside as Doctor Parker leaned over her with her stethoscope, checking her breath sounds. 

     

                “I- it’s … a long story.”

     

                “Your Commanding Officer is here to speak with you.”

     

                Nodding, Kara’s lips thinned and her stomach coiled with unease. They would’ve thought she’d deserted, gone for as long as she was, or perhaps held hostage.
